title: Lemma 13.4.1
section: 13.4 Bounded factors and the first-degree product
text: Lemma 13.4.1 . 263D0F5AEE0A Let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(r,r)$, $r\geq 1$, on a coordinate domain $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$, and let $K,L$ be compact sets with $K\Subset \operatorname{Int}L\subset L\Subset U$. Let $V\leq 0$ be plurisubharmonic on $U$, and let $v$ be locally bounded and plurisubharmonic on $U$. Then \[  \int _ K(-V)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1} \leq C_{K,L}\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)} \int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ^ r,  \] where the right side may be infinite and the constant $C_{K,L}$ depends only on $K$, $L$ and the dimension, and not on $T$, $V$ or $v$. Proof. We treat $r\geq 2$ and smooth $V$ by an integration by parts on small balls, then general $V$ by monotone approximation, and reduce $r=1$ to $r=2$ by adding a variable. Step 1: $r\geq 2$ and $V$ smooth. Here $\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)}=\sup _ L|v|$, as in theorem 7.2.5 . If it vanishes, then $v=0$ on $L$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=0$ on $\operatorname{Int}L\supset K$, and the left side vanishes. Otherwise both sides are homogeneous of degree one in $v$, and the left side does not change when a constant is added to $v$; replacing $v$ by $v/(2\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)})-3/2$, it therefore suffices to prove that $\int _ K(-V)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}\leq C\int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ^ r$ for plurisubharmonic functions $v$ satisfying $-2\leq v\leq -1$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$. Cover $K$ by finitely many balls $B(a,R_1)$ such that $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset \operatorname{Int}L$ for some $R>R_1$; it suffices to bound the integral over one ball $B(a,R_1)$. Put $B=B(a,R)$, $\psi =|z-a|^2-R^2$ and $b=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta /\pi $. Fix $R_1<R_2<R$, and let $\widetilde v=\max \{ v,A\psi \} $, with $A=2/(R^2-R_2^2)$, be the collar modification ( 7.3.2 ) of $v$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$, with $N=2$ and with $R^2-R_2^2$ in place of $\delta $. Thus $\widetilde v$ is plurisubharmonic on $\operatorname{Int}L$ and takes values in $[-2,0)$ on $B$; it equals $v$ on $B(a,R_2)$, and $A\psi $ on the collar $\{ R^2-1/A<|z-a|^2<R^2\} $. Choose $0<\delta <1/A$ and put $B_\delta =\{ \psi <-\delta \} $, so that $\widetilde v=A\psi $ on $B\setminus B_\delta $ and $B(a,R_1)\subset B_\delta $. Choose a smooth function $\kappa $ with $0\leq \kappa \leq R^2$, with compact support in $B$ and equal to $-\psi $ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B_\delta }$; this is possible because $0<-\psi \leq R^2$ on $B$. Put $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge T$ and $Q=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\wedge T$; since $V$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, $Q$ is a closed positive current of bidimension $(r-1,r-1)$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa =-b$ near $\overline{B_\delta }$ and $S=Ab\wedge T$ on $B\setminus B_\delta $, \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _{B_\delta }(-V)S\wedge b^{r-1} & =\int _ B VS\wedge b^{r-2}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa -A\int _{B\setminus B_\delta } VT\wedge b^{r-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa \\ & =\int _ B\kappa \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge Q\wedge b^{r-2} -A\int _{B\setminus B_\delta } VT\wedge b^{r-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa . \end{aligned}  \] For the second line we integrate by parts against the smooth compactly supported function $\kappa $: since $V$ is smooth and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge T\wedge b^{r-2}$ is closed, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(V\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge T\wedge b^{r-2})=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge T\wedge b^{r-2}$, and the Bedford–Taylor product is symmetric with respect to the smooth factor. We bound the two terms on the right. Choose a compact set $L'$ with $\overline B\subset \operatorname{Int}L'$ and $L'\subset \operatorname{Int}L$. Since $0\leq \kappa \leq R^2$, the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality (theorem 7.2.5 ) applied to $Q$ bounds the first term by a constant times the trace mass of $Q$ on $\overline B$. To bound this mass, test $Q$ against a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ equal to one on $\overline B$ and supported in $L'$: \[  \int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}=\int V\, T\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1}\leq C\int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ^ r,  \] since $V\leq 0$ and the coefficients of $T\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ are bounded by a fixed multiple of the trace measure. The collar term has the same bound, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa $ is a fixed smooth form. Finally, $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$ on $B(a,R_1)$ and $-V\geq 0$, so the left side of the display bounds $\pi ^{1-r}\int _{B(a,R_1)}(-V)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}$. Summing over the finitely many balls proves the estimate, with a constant depending only on the chosen radii. Step 2: $r\geq 2$ and $V$ arbitrary. Choose a compact set $L_1$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L_1$ and $L_1\subset \operatorname{Int}L$, depending only on $K$ and $L$. The mollifications $V_ l=V*\rho _{\varepsilon _ l}$, with $\varepsilon _ l\downarrow 0$, are defined, smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $L_1$ for large $l$, and they decrease to $V$ (proposition 5.9.2 (2)); in particular $V\leq V_ l\leq 0$, so that $0\leq -V_ l\leq -V$. Step 1 only involves the weight on a neighborhood of the larger compact set, so it applies to $V_ l$ and the pair $(K,L_1)$ and gives \[  \int _ K(-V_ l)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}\leq C_{K,L_1}\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)}\int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ^ r .  \] As $l\to \infty $, $-V_ l$ increases to $-V$, and monotone convergence against the positive measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ proves the estimate. Step 3: $r=1$. Let $t$ be the coordinate of $\mathbb C$, put $\beta _ t=\frac{\mathrm i}{2}\mathrm dt\wedge \mathrm d\bar t$, let $D'\Subset D''\Subset D$ be the discs about $0$ of radii $1,2,3$, and let $P\colon U\times D\to U$ be the projection. By proposition 5.6.2 , $P^*T$ is a closed positive current of bidimension $(2,2)$ on $U\times D$. Moreover, by corollary 5.6.4 (1), the pullback of a current $R=\sum R_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ of order zero on $U$ is $P^*R=\sum (R_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ D)\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$, where $\lambda _ D$ is Lebesgue measure on $D$. Since $v$ is a locally bounded Borel function, $P^*(vT)=(v\circ P)P^*T$ by corollary 5.6.4 (2), and since $P^*$ commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ P)\wedge P^*T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (P^*(vT)\bigr )=P^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T).  \] The functions $V\circ P\leq 0$ and $v\circ P$ are plurisubharmonic (proposition 5.9.3 ), and $\| v\circ P\| _{L^\infty (L\times \overline{D''})}=\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)}$. We apply Step 2 with $r=2$ to these data, to the Euclidean form $\beta +\beta _ t$ and to the compact sets $K\times \overline{D'}\subset \operatorname{Int}L\times D''=\operatorname{Int}(L\times \overline{D''})$. Since $T\wedge \beta ^2=0$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta =0$ for bidegree reasons, the trace measures in Step 2 are \[  P^*T\wedge (\beta +\beta _ t)^2=2P^*(T\wedge \beta )\wedge \beta _ t, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ P)\wedge P^*T\wedge (\beta +\beta _ t)=P^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T)\wedge \beta _ t,  \] that is, the products of the measures $2T\wedge \beta $ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$ with Lebesgue measure on $D$. By Fubini's theorem (proposition 2.2.7 ), the inequality of Step 2 therefore reads \[  \pi \int _ K(-V)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\leq C\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)}\cdot 8\pi \int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ,  \] where $C$ is the constant of Step 2 for $K\times \overline{D'}$ and $L\times \overline{D''}$ in dimension $n+1$, which depends only on $K$, $L$ and $n$. This is the case $r=1$, with $C_{K,L}=8C$. $\square$

title: Lemma 13.4.2
section: 13.4 Bounded factors and the first-degree product
text: Lemma 13.4.2 . 5D93FCFBA57F Let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(r,r)$, $r\geq 1$, on a coordinate domain, whose trace measure gives zero mass to every pluripolar set. Then for every locally bounded plurisubharmonic $v$, the trace measure of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$ also gives zero mass to every pluripolar set. Consequently the same holds for every Bedford–Taylor product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge T$, $1\leq q\leq r$, of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions with base $T$. Proof. Let $E$ be a pluripolar subset of the coordinate domain $U$ on which $T$ lives. By definition 5.47.2 and since $U$ has a countable basis, $E$ is covered by countably many compact sets $K$, each having a compact neighborhood $L$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$, together with an open neighborhood $W$ of $L$ and a function $V\in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$ such that $E\cap K\subset \{ V=-\infty \} $; shrinking $W$ and subtracting a constant, we may assume $V\leq 0$. The set $\{ V=-\infty \} $ is a pluripolar Borel set, so it suffices to show that $K\cap \{ V=-\infty \} $ has measure zero for the trace measure of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$. Put $\mu =\mathbf1_ LT\wedge \beta ^ r$. This is a finite measure that does not charge $\{ V=-\infty \} $, so $V$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. Hence $\min \{ -V/R,1\} \to 0$ $\mu $-almost everywhere as $R\to \infty $, and by dominated convergence we may choose numbers $R_ j\geq 2^ j$ such that \[  \int \min \{ -V/R_ j,1\} \, \mathrm d\mu \leq 2^{-j}\qquad (j\geq 1).  \] Put $\widetilde V=\sum _{j\geq 1}\max \{ V/R_ j,-1\} $. The partial sums are plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 , and they decrease, because every term is nonpositive. Their limit satisfies $\widetilde V\geq \sum _ jV/R_ j\geq V$, since $V\leq 0$ and $\sum _ j1/R_ j\leq 1$; hence it is not identically $-\infty $ on any component of $W$, and it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.10.1 . Moreover $\widetilde V\leq 0$, $\widetilde V=-\infty $ on $\{ V=-\infty \} $, where every term equals $-1$, and by monotone convergence \[  \int _ L(-\widetilde V)\, T\wedge \beta ^ r=\sum _{j\geq 1}\int \min \{ -V/R_ j,1\} \, \mathrm d\mu \leq 1.  \] By lemma 13.4.1 , applied on $W$, the function $-\widetilde V$ is integrable on $K$ for the trace measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$. Hence this measure gives zero mass to $K\cap \{ \widetilde V=-\infty \} \supset K\cap \{ V=-\infty \} $, which proves the first assertion. The second follows by induction on $q$, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge T)$, where the base current in parentheses is closed and positive of bidimension $(r-q+1,r-q+1)$. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.4.3
section: 13.4 Bounded factors and the first-degree product
text: Proposition 13.4.3 . 90E0E28D9A95 Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ p$ be plurisubharmonic on a coordinate domain, $1\leq p\leq n$, and suppose that $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ are locally bounded for some $0\leq q\leq p$. If $S=\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle $ is locally finite, then the non-pluripolar product of $u_1,\ldots ,u_ p$ is locally finite and \[  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge S,  \] where the right side is the Bedford–Taylor product of definition 7.2.1 with base $S$. Proof. For $q=0$ there is nothing to prove. Inserting the bounded factors $u_ q,u_{q-1},\ldots ,u_1$ one at a time, we reduce to the case $q=1$. So let $v=u_1$ be locally bounded and $S=\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle $ locally finite. By theorem 13.3.1 , $S$ is a closed positive current, so $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge S$ is defined; it is closed and positive, and by lemma 13.4.2 it gives zero mass to pluripolar sets, because $S$ does. If $p=1$, then $S=1$ and the assertion is that of bounded Bedford–Taylor theory. Let $p\geq 2$. The assertion is local, so we may assume $u_ j\leq 0$ for $j\geq 2$ and put \[  \begin{gathered} O_ k=\bigcap _{j\geq 2}\{ u_ j>-k\} ,\qquad \Theta _ k=\bigwedge _{j\geq 2}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u_ j,-k\} ,\\ w_ k=\max \Bigl \{ 1+\frac1k\sum _{j\geq 2}u_ j,\, 0\Bigr \} . \end{gathered}  \] The functions $w_ k$ are plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 , and they take values in $[0,1]$ because all $u_ j\leq 0$. They vanish outside $O_ k$: if $u_ i\leq -k$ for some $i\geq 2$, then $\sum _{j\geq 2}u_ j\leq u_ i\leq -k$. The sets $\{ w_ k>0\} =\{ \sum _{j\geq 2}u_ j>-k\} $ increase to the set where all $u_ j$, $j\geq 2$, are finite. Take smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ decreasing to $v$ near a given compact set. By lemma 13.2.2 , $S$ and $\Theta _ k$ have the same restriction to $O_ k$; since $w_ k$ vanishes outside $O_ k$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l$ is smooth, \[  w_ k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l\wedge S=w_ k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l\wedge \Theta _ k.  \] The weighted form of theorem 7.3.7 , applied with the constant sequence of weights $w_ k$ and the fixed base currents $S$ on the left and $\Theta _ k$ on the right, gives $w_ kR=w_ k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ k$ in the limit $l\to \infty $. Multiplying by the bounded Borel functions $\mathbf1_{\{ w_ k>\varepsilon \} }/w_ k$ and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we see that $R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ k$ have the same restriction to $\{ w_ k>0\} $. Now fix an integer $m\geq 1$. For $k\geq m$, the bounded functions $\max \{ u_ i,-k\} $ and $\max \{ u_ i,-m\} $ coincide on $O_ m$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ m$ on $O_ m$ by theorem 5.47.22 . Since the sets $\{ w_ k>0\} \cap O_ m$, $k\geq m$, exhaust $O_ m$, we conclude that $\mathbf1_{O_ m}R=\mathbf1_{O_ m}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ m$. Consider finally the full tuple $v,u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ on a relatively compact open set on which $|v|<m_0$. For $m\geq m_0$, its level-$m$ set is $O_ m$ and $v$ needs no truncation, so its truncated product at level $m$ is $\mathbf1_{O_ m}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ m=\mathbf1_{O_ m}R$. These restrictions are bounded by $R$, hence have locally bounded mass, and they increase to $R$ because $R$ gives the pole sets of $u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ zero mass. Therefore the non-pluripolar product of $v,u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ is locally finite and equals $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge S$. $\square$

title: Lemma 13.4.4
section: 13.4 Bounded factors and the first-degree product
text: Lemma 13.4.4 . CA3A887474EE Let $Q\subset \mathbb C^ r$ and $D\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be open sets, $r,m\geq 1$, let $G\subset D$ be a Borel set, and for each $z\in G$ let $\mu _ z$ be a positive Radon measure on $Q$. Assume that $z\mapsto \int a\, \mathrm d\mu _ z$ is Borel on $G$ for every continuous function $a$ with compact support in $Q$. Then $z\mapsto \mu _ z(E_ z)$ is Borel on $G$ for every Borel set $E\subset Q\times D$, where $E_ z=\{ x:(x,z)\in E\} $. Moreover, for every nonnegative Borel function $f$ on $D$, \[  \lambda (E)=\int _ G\mu _ z(E_ z)f(z)\, \mathrm dV(z)  \] is a measure on the Borel sets of $Q\times D$, and \[  \int h\, \mathrm d\lambda =\int _ G\Bigl (\int _ Qh(x,z)\, \mathrm d\mu _ z(x)\Bigr )f(z)\, \mathrm dV(z)  \] for every nonnegative Borel function $h$ on $Q\times D$, the inner integral being a Borel function of $z\in G$. Proof. Fix open sets $Q''\Subset Q$ and $D''\Subset D$, so that $\mu _ z(Q'')<\infty $ for every $z$. If $A\subset Q''$ is open, the continuous functions $a_ l(x)=\min \{ 1,\max \{ l\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb C^ r\setminus A)-1,0\} \} $ have compact support in $A$ and increase to $\mathbf1_ A$, so $z\mapsto \mu _ z(A)$ is Borel by monotone convergence. Let $\mathcal D$ be the family of Borel sets $A\subset Q''$ for which $z\mapsto \mu _ z(A)$ is Borel on $G$. It contains the open subsets of $Q''$, which are closed under finite intersections and generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $Q''$. It is closed under complements in $Q''$, because $\mu _ z(Q''\setminus A)=\mu _ z(Q'')-\mu _ z(A)$ with finite values, and under countable disjoint unions. By Dynkin's theorem (lemma 2.2.6 ), $\mathcal D$ contains every Borel subset of $Q''$. Next, let $\mathcal D'$ be the family of Borel sets $E\subset Q''\times D''$ for which $z\mapsto \mu _ z(E_ z)$ is Borel on $G$. It contains the products $A\times A'$ of Borel sets $A\subset Q''$ and $A'\subset D''$, since $\mu _ z((A\times A')_ z)=\mu _ z(A)\mathbf1_{A'}(z)$; these products are closed under finite intersections and generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $Q''\times D''$, because every open subset of $Q''\times D''$ is a countable union of products of open balls. As before, $\mathcal D'$ is closed under complements and countable disjoint unions, so it contains every Borel subset of $Q''\times D''$. Exhausting $Q$ and $D$ by increasing sequences of such sets $Q''$ and $D''$, and using monotone convergence, we obtain the first assertion. By the first assertion, $\lambda (E)$ is defined, and $\lambda $ is countably additive by monotone convergence, applied first to the measures $\mu _ z$ and then to the integral over $G$. The formula for $\int h\, \mathrm d\lambda $ holds for indicator functions of Borel sets by definition, hence for nonnegative simple functions by linearity, and for nonnegative Borel functions by monotone convergence, applied in the same order; the inner integrals are Borel in $z$ as increasing limits of Borel functions. $\square$

title: Lemma 13.4.5
section: 13.4 Bounded factors and the first-degree product
text: Lemma 13.4.5 . 4AD0BFC1BFCD Let $r,m\geq 0$ be integers, let $Q\subset \mathbb C^ r$ and $D\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be open sets with coordinates $x$ and $z$, and let $p_ D\colon Q\times D\to D$ be the projection. Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ r$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $Q\times D$, and put \[  M=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ r,\qquad M_ z=\bigwedge _{j=1}^ r\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x u_ j(\, \cdot \, ,z),  \] the Bedford–Taylor products on $Q\times D$ and on the fibers $Q\times \{ z\} $; here $u_ j(\, \cdot \, ,z)$ is locally bounded and plurisubharmonic on $Q$ by proposition 5.9.3 . For every smooth real $(m,m)$-form $\eta $ on $D$ and every bounded Borel function $h$ on $Q\times D$ with compact support, the fiber integral $z\mapsto \int _ Q h(x,z)\, M_ z(x)$ is Borel measurable and 7F078C7DCBDD 13.4.6 \begin{equation}  \int _{Q\times D}h\, p_ D^*\eta \wedge M =\int _ D\left(\int _ Q h(x,z)\, M_ z(x)\right)\eta (z). \end{equation} If $\eta \geq 0$, the identity holds for every nonnegative Borel function $h$, with possibly infinite values. Proof. If $r=0$ or $m=0$, one factor of $Q\times D$ is a point, carrying counting measure, and the corresponding product is the empty product $1$; then the two sides of ( 13.4.6 ) are the same integral. Let $r,m\geq 1$. For smooth potentials the formula is Fubini's theorem; we pass to the limit for continuous weights $h$, and then extend the formula to Borel weights by the uniqueness of measures. Approximation. Let $Q'\Subset Q$ and $D'\Subset D$ be open. For $\varepsilon _ l\downarrow 0$, the mollifications $u_{j,l}=u_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _ l}$ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{Q'\times D'}$ for large $l$, they decrease to $u_ j$ (proposition 5.9.2 (2)), and they are bounded there by a constant $B$, since $u_ j\leq u_{j,l}\leq u_{j,l_0}$. Let $M^{(l)}$ and $M_ z^{(l)}$ be the corresponding products. By theorem 7.3.7 , $M^{(l)}\to M$ weakly on $Q'\times D'$, and for every $z\in D'$, $M_ z^{(l)}\to M_ z$ weakly on $Q'$, since $u_{j,l}(\, \cdot \, ,z)$ decreases to $u_ j(\, \cdot \, ,z)$. By theorem 7.2.5 , for every compact set $A\subset Q'$ the masses $M_ z^{(l)}(A)$ and $M_ z(A)$ are bounded by a constant depending only on $A$, $Q'$ and $B$, uniformly in $l$ and $z\in D'$; similarly for $M^{(l)}$ and $M$ on compact subsets of $Q'\times D'$. For positive measures with locally uniformly bounded masses, weak convergence implies convergence of the integrals of continuous functions with compact support, because such functions are uniform limits of test functions supported in a fixed compact set (lemma 2.5.1 ). Continuous weights. Let $\eta =f\, \mathrm dV_ z\geq 0$, where $\mathrm dV_ z$ is the Euclidean volume form of $\mathbb C^ m$ and $f\geq 0$ is smooth, and let $h$ be continuous with compact support in $Q'\times D'$. In the smooth exterior product $M^{(l)}$, wedging with the form $p_ D^*\eta $ of top degree in $z$ kills every term containing a differential $\mathrm dz_ i$ or $\mathrm d\bar z_ i$, so that $p_ D^*\eta \wedge M^{(l)}=f(z)\, M_ z^{(l)}(x)\wedge \mathrm dV_ z$, and Fubini's theorem (proposition 2.2.7 ) gives ( 13.4.6 ) for the smooth approximations. As $l\to \infty $, the left side converges to $\int h\, p_ D^*\eta \wedge M$, by the approximation step applied to the positive measures $p_ D^*\eta \wedge M^{(l)}$. On the right, the inner integrals are continuous functions of $z$, they converge to $\int _ Qh(x,z)\, M_ z(x)$ for every $z$, and they are bounded by $\sup |h|$ times a constant, uniformly in $l$ and $z$; hence the limit is a Borel function of $z$, and dominated convergence proves ( 13.4.6 ). A finite smooth partition of unity (lemma 2.5.2 ), subordinate to a cover of $\operatorname{Supp}h$ by such products $Q'\times D'$, treats arbitrary continuous $h$ with compact support. Measurability. For a continuous function $a$ with compact support in $Q$, the function $z\mapsto \int a\, M_ z$ is Borel on $D$: if the support of $a$ lies in $Q'$, then on $D'$ it is the pointwise limit of the continuous functions $z\mapsto \int a\, M_ z^{(l)}$, and $D$ is covered by countably many such sets $D'$. Hence lemma 13.4.4 , applied with $G=D$ and $\mu _ z=M_ z$, shows that $z\mapsto \int _ Qh(x,z)\, M_ z(x)$ is Borel for every nonnegative Borel function $h$, and hence for every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support. Borel weights. Let $\eta =f\, \mathrm dV_ z\geq 0$ as before, and let $\lambda $ be the measure of lemma 13.4.4 for $\mu _ z=M_ z$ and this function $f$, so that \[  \lambda (E)=\int _ D M_ z(E_ z)\, \eta (z)  \] for Borel sets $E\subset Q\times D$. The uniform local bound for the fiber masses makes $\lambda $ finite on compact sets, so it is a Radon measure by proposition 2.2.2 . By lemma 13.4.4 , $\int h\, \mathrm d\lambda =\int _ D(\int _ Qh(x,z)\, M_ z(x))\, \eta (z)$ for every nonnegative Borel function $h$, hence for every continuous $h$ with compact support. By the step on continuous weights, $\lambda $ and $p_ D^*\eta \wedge M$ therefore have the same integral against every test function, so they are equal by the uniqueness in theorem 2.5.6 . This proves the formula for nonnegative Borel $h$, and then for bounded real Borel $h$ with compact support, by splitting $h$ into its positive and negative parts. Finally, let $\eta =f\, \mathrm dV_ z$ be a smooth real form and $h$ a bounded Borel function supported in $K\times K_ D$, with $K\subset Q$ and $K_ D\subset D$ compact. Choose $\kappa \in C_ c^\infty (D)$ with $0\leq \kappa \leq 1$ and $\kappa =1$ on $K_ D$, and put $c=\sup _{\operatorname{Supp}\kappa }|f|$. Replacing $\eta $ by $\kappa \eta $ changes neither side of ( 13.4.6 ), and $\kappa \eta =\kappa (f+c)\, \mathrm dV_ z-c\kappa \, \mathrm dV_ z$ is the difference of two smooth nonnegative forms. This proves the formula for signed $\eta $. $\square$

title: Equation 13.4.6
section: 13.4 Bounded factors and the first-degree product

title: Proposition 13.4.7

Then its non-pluripolar product of degree one is locally finite and 6DEB3D875595 13.4.8  egin{equation}  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}uangle =\mathbf1_{\{ u>-\infty \} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u, \end{equation} where $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ on the right is the distributional complex Hessian. In particular the current $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-\infty \} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is closed. Proof. Upper bound. The assertion is local, so we may assume $u\leq 0$. The truncations $u_ l=\max \{ u,-l\} $ decrease to $u$ and converge to it in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ (theorem 5.10.1 ), so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l	o \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ weakly. For fixed $k$ and every $l\geq k$, plurifine locality (theorem 5.47.22 ) and lemma 13.2.1 give $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k=\mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l\leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l$, and letting $l	o \infty $ yields $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k\leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. The assertion is local, so we may work on a polydisc $P$ such that $u\leq 0$ is plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline P$. Fix one of the coordinates, denote it by $x$, and write $z\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$ for the others, so that $P=\Delta 	imes Z$ with a disc $\Delta \subset \mathbb C$ and a polydisc $Z\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$. Let $\mathrm dV_ z$ be the Euclidean volume form of the $z$-coordinates, viewed as an $(n-1,n-1)$-form, and $\mathrm dA$ the area measure on $\Delta $. We disintegrate $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm dV_ z$ along the fibers $\Delta 	imes \{ z\} $ and apply the one-variable case on each fiber. Since $u$ is integrable on $\Delta 	imes Z$, Fubini's theorem (proposition 2.2.7 ) shows that $G=\{ z\in Z:\int _\Delta |u(x,z)|\, \mathrm dA(x)<\infty \} $ is a Borel set of full measure in $Z$. For $z\in G$ the function $u_ z=u(\, \cdot \, ,z)$ is integrable, hence not identically $-\infty $, so it is subharmonic on $\Delta $ by proposition 5.9.3 ; let $\mu _ z=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ xu_ z$ be its Hessian measure. For a test function $a$ on $\Delta $, we have $\int a\, \mathrm d\mu _ z=\int _\Delta u_ z\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ xa$, and Fubini's theorem, applied to the positive and negative parts of the integrand, shows that this is a Borel function of $z\in G$. Uniform approximation by test functions supported in a fixed compact set extends this to continuous functions $a$ with compact support, since each $\mu _ z$ is finite on compact sets. Hence lemma 13.4.4 , with $f=1$, gives a measure $\lambda $ on $\Delta 	imes Z$ with $\int h\, \mathrm d\lambda =\int _ G(\int h(\, \cdot \, ,z)\, \mathrm d\mu _ z)\, \mathrm dV(z)$ for nonnegative Borel $h$. If $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Delta )$ satisfies $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ and equals one on a disc $\Delta '\Subset \Delta $, then $\mu _ z(\Delta ')\leq \int u_ z\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x\chi \leq C_\chi \int _\Delta |u_ z|\, \mathrm dA$, which is integrable over $G$; so $\lambda $ is finite on compact sets. For a test function $\varphi $ on $\Delta 	imes Z$, only the derivative $\partial _ x\partial _{ ar x}\varphi $ survives in $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \mathrm dV_ z$, and Fubini's theorem gives \[  \int \varphi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm dV_ z=\int u\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \mathrm dV_ z=\int _ G\Bigl (\int _\Delta u_ z\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x\varphi (\, \cdot \, ,z)\Bigr )\mathrm dV(z)=\int \varphi \, \mathrm d\lambda .  \] By the uniqueness in theorem 2.5.6 , the positive measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm dV_ z$ equals $\lambda $, that is, 71D090723F15 13.4.9  egin{equation}  \int g\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm dV_ z=\int _ G\Bigl (\int g(\, \cdot \, ,z)\, \mathrm d\mu _ z\Bigr )\mathrm dV(z) \end{equation} for every nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $\Delta 	imes Z$. Now let $g\geq 0$ be a bounded Borel function with compact support in $\Delta 	imes Z$, and apply lemma 13.4.5 , with $r=1$, $Q=\Delta $, $D=Z$ and $\eta =\mathrm dV_ z$, to the bounded function $u_ k=\max \{ u,-k\} $ and the weight $g\mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }$: \[  \int g\mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k\wedge \mathrm dV_ z =\int \Bigl (\int g\mathbf1_{\{ u_ z>-k\} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x\max \{ u_ z,-k\} \Bigr )\mathrm dV_ z.  \] As $k	o \infty $, the left side increases to $\int gS\wedge \mathrm dV_ z$ by lemma 13.2.2 , since $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k$ is the truncated product $S_ k$ of $u$. For $z\in G$, the inner integral on the right is the integral of $g(\, \cdot \, ,z)$ against the truncated product of $u_ z$ at level $k$; by lemma 13.2.2 and the one-variable case, it increases to $\int g\, \mathrm d\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ xu_ zangle =\int g\mathbf1_{\{ u_ z>-\infty \} }\, \mathrm d\mu _ z$. Since $Z\setminus G$ is a null set, monotone convergence in $z$ and ( 13.4.9 ), applied to $g\mathbf1_{\{ u>-\infty \} }$, give $\int gS\wedge \mathrm dV_ z=\int g\mathbf1_{\{ u>-\infty \} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm dV_ z$, so that $S\wedge \mathrm dV_ z=\mathbf1_{\{ u>-\infty \} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm dV_ z$. Since $ eta ^{n-1}=(n-1)!\sum _{j=1}^ n\mathrm dV_{(j)}$, where $\mathrm dV_{(j)}$ is the volume form of the coordinates other than the $j$th, summing over the $n$ coordinate directions shows that the trace measures of $S$ and of $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-\infty \} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ coincide. Thus $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-\infty \} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-S$ is a positive current with zero trace measure, and it vanishes by theorem 5.3.7 . This proves ( 13.4.8 ); closedness follows from theorem 13.3.1 . $\square$

title: Proposition 13.4.10
section: 13.4 Bounded factors and the first-degree product
text: Proposition 13.4.10 . FB5ACFB46DB8 Let $\mu $ be a probability measure supported on a compact set $K\subset \mathbb C\subset \mathbb P^1$, and let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form of example 10.6.7 , which has total mass one on $\mathbb P^1$. Then \[  q(z)=\int _ K\log \frac{|z-a|^2}{(1+|z|^2)(1+|a|^2)}\, \mathrm d\mu (a)  \] defines a nonpositive $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^1$ with $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=\mu $. Its Lelong number at every point $x\in \mathbb P^1$ is $\mu (\{ x\} )$, where $\mu $ is regarded as a measure on $\mathbb P^1$. Proof. In the affine chart put $\rho (z)=\log (1+|z|^2)$, so that $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $. The integrand is nonpositive, since $|z-a|^2\leq (|z|+|a|)^2\leq (1+|z|^2)(1+|a|^2)$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. On the affine chart, \[  q+\rho =p_\mu -c,\qquad p_\mu (z)=\int _ K\log |z-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a),\qquad c=\int _ K\log (1+|a|^2)\, \mathrm d\mu (a).  \] Since $\log |z-a|^2=4\pi E_2(z-a)$ with the fundamental solution $E_2$ of ( 3.1.14 ), the function $p_\mu =4\pi E_2*\mu $ is subharmonic and locally integrable with $\Delta p_\mu =4\pi \mu $, by proposition 3.4.11 . Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\Delta /(4\pi )$ on functions of one complex variable, as planar measures, this gives $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_\mu =\mu $ on the affine chart, and $q=p_\mu -c-\rho $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic there. Near infinity use the coordinate $w=1/z$, in which the integrand becomes \[  \log |1-aw|^2-\log (1+|w|^2)-\log (1+|a|^2).  \] Let $R_ K=\max _{a\in K}|a|$. For $|w|<1/(2R_ K+2)$ we have $|1-aw|\geq 1/2$, so this expression is a smooth function of $(a,w)$ on $K\times \{ |w|<1/(2R_ K+2)\} $ whose derivatives in $w$ of every order are bounded uniformly in $a\in K$; at $w=0$ it takes the value $-\log (1+|a|^2)$. Differentiating under the integral sign, we see that $q$ extends to a smooth function near infinity, and that $q+\log (1+|w|^2)=\int _ K\log |1-aw|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)-c$ is harmonic there, because each $\log |1-aw|^2$ is harmonic in $w$. Since $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|w|^2)$ in this chart and $\mu $ vanishes near infinity, $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=0=\mu $ there. Hence $q$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb P^1$, $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=\mu \geq 0$ globally, and $q$ is a nonpositive $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function. At infinity both the Lelong number and the point mass vanish, because $q$ is smooth there and $K\subset \mathbb C$. At an affine point $x$, the Lelong number of $q$ is that of the local subharmonic function $q+\rho $ (corollary 6.9.3 ), and by ( 6.7.8 ) and ( 6.7.5 ) it equals $\lim _{r\downarrow 0}\mu (B(x,r))=\mu (\{ x\} )$. $\square$

title: Example 13.4.11

text: Example 13.4.11 . E9D7DF5798B0 Let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^1$, as in proposition 13.4.10 . There is a nonpositive $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function $q$ on $\mathbb P^1$ such that \[  \nu (q,x)=0\quad \text{for every }x,\qquad \mathcal I(tq)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}\quad (t>0),\qquad \langle \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\rangle =0.  \] Let $\mu $ be the atom-free probability measure on the compact polar set $K$ of proposition 4.1.12 , and let $q$ be its potential from proposition 13.4.10 . Since $\mu $ has no atoms, all Lelong numbers of $q$ vanish, and corollary 6.9.3 gives the assertion on multiplier ideals. On the affine chart, $q$ differs from the function $p(z)=\int _ K\log |z-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)$ of proposition 4.1.12 by the smooth function $-\log (1+|z|^2)$ and a constant, and $p=-\infty $ on $K$; hence $q=-\infty $ on $K$. Applying proposition 13.4.7 to local potentials of $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$, we obtain \[  \langle \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\rangle =\mathbf1_{\{ q>-\infty \} }\mu =0,  \] because $\mu $ is carried by $K$. By contrast, the potential $0$ has the same multiplier ideals and non-pluripolar mass one. Thus exponential integrability at every scale does not determine the non-pluripolar mass.

title: 13.5 Global finiteness and bounded cohomological mass

section: 13.5 Global finiteness and bounded cohomological mass
text: From now on, $X$ is a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a fixed Kähler form $\omega $, and $\theta $ and $\theta _ j$ always denote smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$. (We exclude dimension zero, where the only product is the empty one.) If $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ (definition 6.14.3 ) is locally bounded, then near each point $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h+\varphi )$, where $h$ is a smooth local potential of $\theta $ and $h+\varphi $ is bounded and plurisubharmonic. By proposition 13.2.6 , the Bedford–Taylor products of such local potentials do not depend on the choice of $h$; hence they glue to closed positive currents $\bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)$ on $X$, which can be multiplied by smooth forms. We first prove Stokes' formula for these products and then show that non-pluripolar products on $X$ are always finite. Proposition 13.5.1 . 06A36B9354A5 Let $1\leq p\leq n$, let $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ be locally bounded for $1\leq j\leq p$, and let $\eta $ be a smooth closed $(n-p,n-p)$-form on $X$. Then \[  \int _ X\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\wedge \eta =\int _ X\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p\wedge \eta .  \] Proof. Fix $j$, let $R$ be the closed positive current $\bigwedge _{i>j}(\theta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i)$, and let $\eta '$ be a smooth closed form of pure complementary bidegree. Locally $\theta _ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ j$ with $h_ j$ smooth, and since $R$ is closed, the recursion gives \[  (\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\wedge R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((h_ j+\varphi _ j)R)=\theta _ j\wedge R+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi _ jR).  \] Here $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_ jR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ j\wedge R$ because $h_ j$ is smooth and $R$ is closed of pure bidegree, so that $\partial R=\bar\partial R=0$. Both sides are globally defined, because $\varphi _ j$ is a global bounded function. Moreover $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi _ jR)\wedge \eta '=\int _ X\varphi _ jR\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta '=0$, since $\eta '$ is closed of pure bidegree, so that $\partial \eta '=\bar\partial \eta '=0$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta '=0$. Hence $\int _ X(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\wedge R\wedge \eta '=\int _ X\theta _ j\wedge R\wedge \eta '$. Apply this successively for $j=1,2,\ldots ,p$, with $\eta '=\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{j-1}\wedge \eta $ at the $j$th step, which is smooth and closed. After $p$ steps the integral becomes $\int _ X\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p\wedge \eta $. $\square$ Lemma 13.5.2 . 05FB10FAF0D8 Let $R$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(1,1)$ on $X$, and let $a,b$ be bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$, or differences of such functions. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bR)$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(aR)$ are finite signed measures, and \[  \int _ X a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R =\int _ X b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R =-\int _ X\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge R.  \] Here the mixed gradient \[  \mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge R=\tfrac 12\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(abR)-a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R-b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R\bigr )  \] is a finite signed measure on $X$, symmetric in $a$ and $b$. It is the exterior product of $\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b$ with $R$ when $a$ and $b$ are smooth, and on an open set where $a=b$ is plurisubharmonic it is the gradient measure $E_ R(a)$ of ( 7.14.4 ). Proof. The measures. Near each point of $X$, a bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic function $b$ is the difference $b_1-b_2$ of two bounded plurisubharmonic functions: if $b+g$ is plurisubharmonic on a coordinate ball with $g$ smooth, and $q=C|z|^2$ with $C$ so large that $g+q$ is plurisubharmonic on a smaller ball, take $b_1=b+g+q$ and $b_2=g+q$. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge R-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_2\wedge R$ is locally the difference of two Bedford–Taylor products, which are positive measures. Covering the compact manifold $X$ by finitely many such neighborhoods, we see that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bR)$ is a finite signed measure; the same holds for $a$. For bounded plurisubharmonic functions $A$ and $B$ on an open set, additivity of Bedford–Taylor products (proposition 7.2.2 ) and the formula ( 7.14.4 ) give, after expanding $(A+B)^2$, \[  E_ R(A+B)=E_ R(A)+E_ R(B)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ABR)-A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B\wedge R-B\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A\wedge R,  \] so that $\frac12(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ABR)-A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B\wedge R-B\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A\wedge R)=\frac12(E_ R(A+B)-E_ R(A)-E_ R(B))$ is a signed measure, by lemma 7.14.3 . Since the expression defining the mixed gradient is bilinear in $(a,b)$, writing $a=a_1-a_2$ and $b=b_1-b_2$ locally shows that the mixed gradient is a signed measure near each point, hence a finite signed measure on $X$. It is symmetric by definition. For $a=b$ plurisubharmonic it equals $\frac12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a^2R)-a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R=E_ R(a)$. For smooth $a$ and $b$ we have $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ab)=a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b+b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a+\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b+\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}a$, and the $(1,1)$-parts of $\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b$ and $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}a$ both equal $\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }(\partial a\wedge \bar\partial b+\partial b\wedge \bar\partial a)$; since only $(1,1)$-parts contribute in products with $R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(abR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ab)\wedge R$, the mixed gradient is $\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge R$. A local identity. Let $\chi $ be a test function with support in a coordinate ball $W$, and let $A$ and $B$ be bounded plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline W$. We claim that 81F1166426A9 13.5.3 \begin{equation}  \int \chi A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(BR)-\int \chi B\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(AR)=-\int AB\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge R-2\, \mathrm d(BR)(A\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi ), \end{equation} where $\mathrm d(BR)$ is the current of order zero of lemma 7.14.3 and its value on the bounded Borel one-form $A\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi $ with compact support is computed with its coefficient measures. Suppose first that $A$ is smooth. Then $\int \chi A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(BR)=(BR)(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi A))$ and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi A)=\chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A+A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi +\mathrm d\chi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}A+\mathrm dA\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi .  \] The first term contributes $\int \chi B\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A\wedge R$. Since $BR$ has bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, it sees only the $(1,1)$-parts of the last two terms, which agree as above; so these terms contribute $2(BR)(\mathrm dA\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi )$. Finally $\mathrm dA\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi =\mathrm d(A\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi )-A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $, and $(BR)(\mathrm d\psi )=-\mathrm d(BR)(\psi )$ for one-forms $\psi $, because $BR$ has even degree. Collecting terms gives ( 13.5.3 ). In general, let $A_ l$ be smooth plurisubharmonic functions decreasing to $A$ on a neighborhood of $\overline W$, for instance mollifications (proposition 5.9.2 (2)). Then ( 13.5.3 ) holds for $A_ l$, and every term converges to the corresponding term for $A$. For the first, third and last terms this follows by dominated convergence against the fixed signed measures $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(BR)$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge R$ and the coefficient measures of $\mathrm d(BR)$, since the $A_ l$ are uniformly bounded on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ and converge pointwise to $A$. For the second term it follows from the weighted form of theorem 7.3.7 , with the constant sequence of weights $B$. This proves the claim. Since both sides of ( 13.5.3 ) are bilinear in $(A,B)$, the identity also holds for differences of bounded plurisubharmonic functions, and in particular for $A=a$ and $B=b$ near $\overline W$. Conclusion. Let $(\chi _ i)$ be a finite smooth partition of unity on $X$ subordinate to coordinate balls as above (proposition 5.2.6 ). Summing ( 13.5.3 ) for $\chi =\chi _ i$, $A=a$ and $B=b$ over $i$, and using that $abR$, $\mathrm d(bR)$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(aR)$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bR)$ are global currents, we obtain \[  \int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R-\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R=-\int _ Xab\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Bigl (\sum _ i\chi _ i\Bigr )\wedge R-2\, \mathrm d(bR)\Bigl (a\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\sum _ i\chi _ i\Bigr )=0,  \] because $\sum _ i\chi _ i=1$. This is the first equality. For the second, note that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(abR)$ is a finite signed measure, being a combination of the mixed gradient and the measures $a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R$ and $b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R$, and that its total integral is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(abR)(1)=(abR)(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}1)=0$, because the constant function $1$ is a test function on the compact manifold $X$. Integrating the definition of the mixed gradient over $X$ and using the first equality, we get $\int _ X\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge R=-\int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R$. $\square$ Theorem 13.5.4 . 3783DE0B4D00 Let $T_1,\ldots ,T_ p$, $1\leq p\leq n$, be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on the compact Kähler manifold $X$. Then their non-pluripolar product is finite. More precisely, write $T_ j=\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$ with $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$, and choose $C\geq 0$ such that the forms $\tau _ j=\theta _ j+C\omega $ are semipositive. Then 896BDD434F7F 13.5.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p} \leq \int _ X\tau _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \tau _ p\wedge \omega ^{n-p}. \end{equation} In particular, if the forms $\theta _ j$ are semipositive, we may take $C=0$. Proof. The decomposition $T_ j=\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$ exists by theorem 10.2.15 . Since $\tau _ j\geq \theta _ j$ and $\tau _ j\geq 0$, $\varphi _ j$ is $\tau _ j$-plurisubharmonic, and so is every constant; hence $\max \{ \varphi _ j,-k\} $ is a bounded $\tau _ j$-plurisubharmonic function, and \[  R_{j,k}=\tau _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ \varphi _ j,-k\}   \] is a closed positive current. By proposition 13.5.1 , the total mass $\int _ XR_{1,k}\wedge \cdots \wedge R_{p,k}\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$ equals the right side of ( 13.5.5 ) for every $k$. Local finiteness. Let $W$ be a relatively compact coordinate chart, and choose smooth functions $h_ j$ and $h$ near $\overline W$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ j=\theta _ j$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\omega $. Then $u_ j=\varphi _ j+h_ j$ is a plurisubharmonic potential of $T_ j$ on $W$. Let $B$ be an integer with $h_ j\leq B$ on $W$ for all $j$, fix an integer $l\geq 1$, and put $O_ l(u)=\bigcap _ j\{ u_ j>-l\} $. On $W\cap O_ l(u)$ we have $\varphi _ j>-l-B$, so for every integer $k\geq l+B$ the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $\max \{ u_ j,-l\} +Ch$ and $\max \{ \varphi _ j,-k\} +h_ j+Ch$ both equal $u_ j+Ch$ there; the second is a local potential of $R_{j,k}$. By plurifine locality, \[  \mathbf1_{O_ l(u)}\bigwedge _ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u_ j,-l\} +C\omega )=\mathbf1_{O_ l(u)}\bigwedge _ jR_{j,k}\quad \text{on }W.  \] Expanding the left side into positive terms gives \[  \mathbf1_{O_ l(u)}\bigwedge _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u_ j,-l\}  \leq \mathbf1_{O_ l(u)}\bigwedge _ j R_{j,k}\leq \bigwedge _ jR_{j,k}.  \] Let $K\subset W$ be compact. On a neighborhood of $K$ in $W$ we have $\beta \leq c\, \omega $ for some $c>0$ (lemma 6.14.1 ), so by the last display and ( 13.2.8 ), the trace masses on $K$ of the truncated local products are at most $c^{n-p}$ times the right side of ( 13.5.5 ), uniformly in $l$. Hence the non-pluripolar product is locally finite everywhere, and $\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle $ is a closed positive current by theorem 13.3.1 . Mass bound. By the same argument, the currents $T_ j+C\omega =\tau _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$, with local potentials $u_ j+Ch$, have a locally finite non-pluripolar product. The sets $G_ k=\bigcap _ j\{ \varphi _ j>-k\} $ increase and exhaust the complement of the union of the pole sets of the $\varphi _ j$. On $G_ k$ the global truncations $\max \{ \varphi _ j,-k\} $ coincide with $\varphi _ j$. If $B'$ is an integer with $h_ j+Ch\geq -B'$ on $W$ for all $j$, then on $G_ k\cap W$ all local potentials satisfy $u_ j+Ch>-k-B'$, so they coincide there with their truncations at level $k+B'$, and also with the local potentials $\max \{ \varphi _ j,-k\} +h_ j+Ch$ of $R_{j,k}$. By plurifine locality and lemma 13.2.2 , $\mathbf1_{G_ k}\bigwedge _ jR_{j,k}=\mathbf1_{G_ k}\langle \bigwedge _ j(T_ j+C\omega )\rangle $, and these restrictions increase to $\langle \bigwedge _ j(T_ j+C\omega )\rangle $. Their total masses against $\omega ^{n-p}$ are at most the right side of ( 13.5.5 ), hence so is that of the limit. Finally, expanding $\langle \bigwedge _ j(T_ j+C\omega )\rangle $ by multilinearity (proposition 13.2.6 ) into a sum of positive currents, one of which is $\langle \bigwedge _ jT_ j\rangle $, we obtain $\langle \bigwedge _ j T_ j\rangle \leq \langle \bigwedge _ j(T_ j+C\omega )\rangle $, which proves ( 13.5.5 ). $\square$ Example 13.5.6 . 3D09B5B530AA On $\mathbb P^1$, the current of integration $[0]$ at the point $0$ satisfies $\langle [0]\rangle =0$. Indeed, near $0$ it has the potential $\log |z|^2$ (theorem 5.5.6 ), whose pole set is $\{ 0\} $, so $\langle [0]\rangle =\mathbf1_{\{ z\neq 0\} }[0]=0$ there by proposition 13.4.7 ; away from $0$ the current vanishes. Thus $[0]$ has mass one while $\langle [0]\rangle $ has mass zero: discarding the poles can change the cohomology class, even in degree one.

title: Proposition 13.5.1
section: 13.5 Global finiteness and bounded cohomological mass
text: Proposition 13.5.1 . 06A36B9354A5 Let $1\leq p\leq n$, let $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ be locally bounded for $1\leq j\leq p$, and let $\eta $ be a smooth closed $(n-p,n-p)$-form on $X$. Then \[  \int _ X\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\wedge \eta =\int _ X\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p\wedge \eta .  \] Proof. Fix $j$, let $R$ be the closed positive current $\bigwedge _{i>j}(\theta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i)$, and let $\eta '$ be a smooth closed form of pure complementary bidegree. Locally $\theta _ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ j$ with $h_ j$ smooth, and since $R$ is closed, the recursion gives \[  (\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\wedge R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((h_ j+\varphi _ j)R)=\theta _ j\wedge R+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi _ jR).  \] Here $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_ jR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ j\wedge R$ because $h_ j$ is smooth and $R$ is closed of pure bidegree, so that $\partial R=\bar\partial R=0$. Both sides are globally defined, because $\varphi _ j$ is a global bounded function. Moreover $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi _ jR)\wedge \eta '=\int _ X\varphi _ jR\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta '=0$, since $\eta '$ is closed of pure bidegree, so that $\partial \eta '=\bar\partial \eta '=0$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta '=0$. Hence $\int _ X(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\wedge R\wedge \eta '=\int _ X\theta _ j\wedge R\wedge \eta '$. Apply this successively for $j=1,2,\ldots ,p$, with $\eta '=\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{j-1}\wedge \eta $ at the $j$th step, which is smooth and closed. After $p$ steps the integral becomes $\int _ X\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p\wedge \eta $. $\square$

title: Lemma 13.5.2
section: 13.5 Global finiteness and bounded cohomological mass
text: Lemma 13.5.2 . 05FB10FAF0D8 Let $R$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(1,1)$ on $X$, and let $a,b$ be bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$, or differences of such functions. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bR)$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(aR)$ are finite signed measures, and \[  \int _ X a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R =\int _ X b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R =-\int _ X\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge R.  \] Here the mixed gradient \[  \mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge R=\tfrac 12\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(abR)-a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R-b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R\bigr )  \] is a finite signed measure on $X$, symmetric in $a$ and $b$. It is the exterior product of $\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b$ with $R$ when $a$ and $b$ are smooth, and on an open set where $a=b$ is plurisubharmonic it is the gradient measure $E_ R(a)$ of ( 7.14.4 ). Proof. The measures. Near each point of $X$, a bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic function $b$ is the difference $b_1-b_2$ of two bounded plurisubharmonic functions: if $b+g$ is plurisubharmonic on a coordinate ball with $g$ smooth, and $q=C|z|^2$ with $C$ so large that $g+q$ is plurisubharmonic on a smaller ball, take $b_1=b+g+q$ and $b_2=g+q$. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge R-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_2\wedge R$ is locally the difference of two Bedford–Taylor products, which are positive measures. Covering the compact manifold $X$ by finitely many such neighborhoods, we see that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bR)$ is a finite signed measure; the same holds for $a$. For bounded plurisubharmonic functions $A$ and $B$ on an open set, additivity of Bedford–Taylor products (proposition 7.2.2 ) and the formula ( 7.14.4 ) give, after expanding $(A+B)^2$, \[  E_ R(A+B)=E_ R(A)+E_ R(B)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ABR)-A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B\wedge R-B\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A\wedge R,  \] so that $\frac12(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ABR)-A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B\wedge R-B\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A\wedge R)=\frac12(E_ R(A+B)-E_ R(A)-E_ R(B))$ is a signed measure, by lemma 7.14.3 . Since the expression defining the mixed gradient is bilinear in $(a,b)$, writing $a=a_1-a_2$ and $b=b_1-b_2$ locally shows that the mixed gradient is a signed measure near each point, hence a finite signed measure on $X$. It is symmetric by definition. For $a=b$ plurisubharmonic it equals $\frac12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a^2R)-a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R=E_ R(a)$. For smooth $a$ and $b$ we have $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ab)=a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b+b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a+\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b+\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}a$, and the $(1,1)$-parts of $\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b$ and $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}a$ both equal $\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }(\partial a\wedge \bar\partial b+\partial b\wedge \bar\partial a)$; since only $(1,1)$-parts contribute in products with $R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(abR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ab)\wedge R$, the mixed gradient is $\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge R$. A local identity. Let $\chi $ be a test function with support in a coordinate ball $W$, and let $A$ and $B$ be bounded plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline W$. We claim that 81F1166426A9 13.5.3 \begin{equation}  \int \chi A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(BR)-\int \chi B\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(AR)=-\int AB\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge R-2\, \mathrm d(BR)(A\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi ), \end{equation} where $\mathrm d(BR)$ is the current of order zero of lemma 7.14.3 and its value on the bounded Borel one-form $A\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi $ with compact support is computed with its coefficient measures. Suppose first that $A$ is smooth. Then $\int \chi A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(BR)=(BR)(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi A))$ and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi A)=\chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A+A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi +\mathrm d\chi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}A+\mathrm dA\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi .  \] The first term contributes $\int \chi B\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A\wedge R$. Since $BR$ has bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, it sees only the $(1,1)$-parts of the last two terms, which agree as above; so these terms contribute $2(BR)(\mathrm dA\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi )$. Finally $\mathrm dA\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi =\mathrm d(A\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\chi )-A\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $, and $(BR)(\mathrm d\psi )=-\mathrm d(BR)(\psi )$ for one-forms $\psi $, because $BR$ has even degree. Collecting terms gives ( 13.5.3 ). In general, let $A_ l$ be smooth plurisubharmonic functions decreasing to $A$ on a neighborhood of $\overline W$, for instance mollifications (proposition 5.9.2 (2)). Then ( 13.5.3 ) holds for $A_ l$, and every term converges to the corresponding term for $A$. For the first, third and last terms this follows by dominated convergence against the fixed signed measures $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(BR)$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge R$ and the coefficient measures of $\mathrm d(BR)$, since the $A_ l$ are uniformly bounded on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ and converge pointwise to $A$. For the second term it follows from the weighted form of theorem 7.3.7 , with the constant sequence of weights $B$. This proves the claim. Since both sides of ( 13.5.3 ) are bilinear in $(A,B)$, the identity also holds for differences of bounded plurisubharmonic functions, and in particular for $A=a$ and $B=b$ near $\overline W$. Conclusion. Let $(\chi _ i)$ be a finite smooth partition of unity on $X$ subordinate to coordinate balls as above (proposition 5.2.6 ). Summing ( 13.5.3 ) for $\chi =\chi _ i$, $A=a$ and $B=b$ over $i$, and using that $abR$, $\mathrm d(bR)$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(aR)$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bR)$ are global currents, we obtain \[  \int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R-\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R=-\int _ Xab\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Bigl (\sum _ i\chi _ i\Bigr )\wedge R-2\, \mathrm d(bR)\Bigl (a\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\sum _ i\chi _ i\Bigr )=0,  \] because $\sum _ i\chi _ i=1$. This is the first equality. For the second, note that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(abR)$ is a finite signed measure, being a combination of the mixed gradient and the measures $a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R$ and $b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R$, and that its total integral is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(abR)(1)=(abR)(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}1)=0$, because the constant function $1$ is a test function on the compact manifold $X$. Integrating the definition of the mixed gradient over $X$ and using the first equality, we get $\int _ X\mathrm da\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge R=-\int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R$. $\square$

title: 13.6 Fiber integration and modifications
text: We now pass the fiber formula of lemma 13.4.5 through the truncations that define non-pluripolar products on a product of compact Kähler manifolds. The resulting identity, weighted by a bounded difference of potentials, is the form needed for relative energy in section 17.1 . We also show that non-pluripolar products commute with modifications. Corollary 13.6.1 . BEC54934FC2C Let $X$ and $Z$ be connected compact Kähler manifolds of dimensions $r$ and $m$, with projections $p_ X,p_ Z$ from $X\times Z$. Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $\gamma \geq 0$ be a smooth closed $(1,1)$-form on $Z$. Put \[  \Theta =p_ X^*\theta +p_ Z^*\gamma ,\qquad \Phi =p_ X^*\varphi ,\qquad T=\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W,\quad S=\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi ,  \] where $W\in \mathrm{PSH}(X\times Z,\Theta )$ satisfies $\Phi -C\leq W\leq \Phi +C$ for a constant $C\geq 0$. Then for every $z\in Z$ the function $W_ z=W(\, \cdot \, ,z)$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and for every integer $0\leq j\leq r$ and every smooth real $(m,m)$-form $\eta $ on $Z$, F6B4982710D8 13.6.2 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned} & \int _{X\times Z}(W-\Phi )\, p_ Z^*\eta \wedge \langle T^ j\wedge S^{r-j}\rangle \\ & \qquad =\int _ Z\left(\int _ X(W_ z-\varphi ) \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W_ z)^ j\wedge (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^{r-j}\rangle \right)\eta (z). \end{aligned} \end{equation} The same identity holds with both difference weights replaced by $1$. The weights are undefined only on the common pole set of the two potentials involved, where they may be given any bounded values. Proof. In product charts choose smooth local potentials $a(x)$ of $\theta $ and $b(z)$ of $\gamma $. Then $W+a+b$ is plurisubharmonic, so by proposition 5.9.3 its restriction $W_ z+a+b(z)$ to a fiber is plurisubharmonic in $x$ or identically $-\infty $; the second alternative is excluded, because $W_ z\geq \varphi -C$ and $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $ on any open set. Hence $W_ z$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W_ z\geq 0$, that is, $W_ z\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. All the products in ( 13.6.2 ) are finite by theorem 13.5.4 , and ( 13.5.5 ) bounds the fiber masses uniformly in $z$, because the shifted background can be chosen from the fixed form $\theta $, independently of $W_ z$. Put $w=W+a+b$, $v=\Phi +a+b$ and $O_ k=\{ w>-k\} \cap \{ v>-k\} $ in a product chart. Let $\rho \geq 0$ be a smooth function with compact support in the chart, let $G\geq 0$ be bounded and Borel, and let $\eta \geq 0$. Apply ( 13.4.6 ) to the bounded functions $\max \{ w,-k\} $ and $\max \{ v,-k\} $, with multiplicities $j$ and $r-j$, and to the weight $\rho G\mathbf1_{O_ k}$. The set $O_ k$ is contained in the level-$k$ set of the tuple formed by $j$ copies of $w$ and $r-j$ copies of $v$ (if $j=0$ or $j=r$, one of the two conditions defining $O_ k$ concerns a potential that does not occur in the tuple). Hence, by lemma 13.2.2 , the restriction to $O_ k$ of the bounded mixed product equals the restriction to $O_ k$ of the non-pluripolar product, on the total space and, with $(O_ k)_ z$ in place of $O_ k$, on every fiber. These restrictions increase with $k$, and they increase to the non-pluripolar products, because the complements of $\bigcup _ kO_ k$ and of $\bigcup _ k(O_ k)_ z$ are contained in the pole sets of $w,v$ and of $w_ z,v_ z$, which are pluripolar and carry no mass. Monotone convergence, on the total space and in $z$, therefore gives the fiber formula for the non-pluripolar products with weight $\rho G$. Taking $G=1$ gives the unweighted identity. Since $\Phi -C\leq W\leq \Phi +C$, the potentials $W$ and $\Phi $ have the same pole set, and so do $W_ z$ and $\varphi $; take $G=W-\Phi +C\in [0,2C]$ off this set and $G=C$ on it, and subtract $C$ times the unweighted identity. Summing over a finite partition of unity by such functions $\rho $ (proposition 5.2.6 ), and writing a signed $\eta $ as a difference of nonnegative forms, gives ( 13.6.2 ). All integrals are finite by the uniform mass bound and $|W-\Phi |\leq C$, and the values assigned on the common pole set do not matter, because this set is pluripolar and carries no mass for any of the products. $\square$ Proposition 13.6.3 . 0811FFDF15B7 Let $\pi \colon \widetilde X\to X$ be a modification between compact Kähler manifolds, that is, a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map, and let $1\leq p\leq \dim X$. For closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_1,\ldots ,T_ p$ on $X$, \[  \pi _*\langle \pi ^*T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \pi ^*T_ p\rangle =\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle ,  \] and for closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $R_1,\ldots ,R_ p$ on $\widetilde X$, \[  \pi _*\langle R_1\wedge \cdots \wedge R_ p\rangle =\langle \pi _*R_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \pi _*R_ p\rangle .  \] In particular, in top degree the corresponding total masses agree. Proof. The pullback $\pi ^*T_ j$ is the closed positive current of proposition 5.6.5 , defined by pulling back local plurisubharmonic potentials; a pulled-back potential is not identically $-\infty $ on any open set, because $\pi $ is biholomorphic over a dense open set whose preimage is dense (proposition 9.8.3 and the definition of bimeromorphic maps in section 9.4 ). The pushforward $\pi _*R$ of a closed positive current is closed and positive, since pullback of smooth forms commutes with $\mathrm d$ and preserves strong positivity (proposition 5.3.2 ). All products in the statement are therefore defined, and they are finite by theorem 13.5.4 . Choose a nowhere dense analytic subset $A\subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense and $\pi $ restricts to a biholomorphism $\pi ^{-1}(X\setminus A)\to X\setminus A$. Both $A$ and $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ are pluripolar: near each point, a nowhere dense analytic set is contained in the zero set of a holomorphic function $f$ that does not vanish identically on a connected neighborhood, hence in the pole set of $\log |f|^2$. For a point $\widetilde x\in \pi ^{-1}(X\setminus A)$, use on a neighborhood of $\widetilde x$ the coordinates $z\circ \pi $, where $z$ are coordinates near $\pi (\widetilde x)$. In these coordinates $\pi $ is the identity, and the local potentials $u_ j\circ \pi $ of $\pi ^*T_ j$ are the local potentials $u_ j$ of $T_ j$. Since non-pluripolar products do not depend on the choice of coordinates or of local potentials, the two sides of the first identity agree on $X\setminus A$. It remains to show that neither side charges $A$. The right side gives the pluripolar set $A$ zero mass. The product $S=\langle \pi ^*T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \pi ^*T_ p\rangle $ gives $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ zero mass, and hence $\pi _*S$ gives $A$ zero mass. Indeed, in a chart of $X$, the trace measure of $\pi _*S$ is the image under $\pi $ of the positive measure $S\wedge \pi ^*\beta ^{n-p}$, which does not charge $\pi ^{-1}(A)$, and the coefficient measures of $\pi _*S$ are bounded by a multiple of this trace measure (theorem 5.3.7 ). Hence the two sides of the first identity have the same coefficient measures on $X\setminus A$ and on $A$, and they are equal. The same argument on $X\setminus A$, where now the local potentials of $\pi _*R_ j$ are those of $R_ j$ in the coordinates $z\circ \pi $, proves the second identity. In top degree, the total mass of $\pi _*S$ is $(\pi _*S)(1)=S(\pi ^*1)=S(1)$, which proves the assertion on masses. $\square$
