text: Lemma 13.8.1 . 663159428707 Let $\varphi _ j,\psi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ for $1\leq j\leq p\leq n$, and put $T_ j=\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$ and $T'_ j=\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j$. Suppose that $\varphi _ j\geq \psi _ j-O(1)$ for every $j$. Assume moreover that there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\tau $ on $X$ such that $A=\{ \tau =-\infty \} $ is closed and $\tau $ and all the $\varphi _ j,\psi _ j$ are locally bounded on $X\setminus A$. Then \[  \int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p} \geq \int _ X\langle T'_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T'_ p\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}.  \] If every difference $\varphi _ j-\psi _ j$ is bounded, equality holds. Proof. We replace the factors $T_ j$ by $T'_ j$ one at a time; the intermediate tuples satisfy the same hypotheses, so it suffices to treat one step, in which a single factor changes. Write it as $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ before and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ after the change, and let $\Theta $ be the non-pluripolar product of the remaining factors (some primed, some not) wedged with $\omega ^{n-p}$. By theorem 13.5.4 , theorem 13.3.1 , $\Theta $ is a closed positive current of bidimension $(1,1)$, and it gives zero mass to the set $A$, which is pluripolar and Borel, being closed and locally contained in the pole sets of plurisubharmonic functions. On the open set $X\setminus A$ all potentials are locally bounded, so there the non-pluripolar products of the remaining factors are Bedford–Taylor products, and by proposition 13.4.3 the products of the two tuples, wedged with $\omega ^{n-p}$, are the Bedford–Taylor products $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge \Theta $ and $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )\wedge \Theta $ with base $\Theta $; here $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge \Theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h+\varphi )\wedge \Theta $ for smooth local potentials $h$ of $\theta $. More generally, if $\Omega '$ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form and $\varrho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Omega ')$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus A$, then the measure $(\Omega '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varrho )\wedge \Theta $ on $X\setminus A$ is the restriction of a global non-pluripolar product wedged with $\omega ^{n-p}$, so it has finite mass by theorem 13.5.4 . Since none of these products charges $A$, it suffices to prove \[  \int _{X\setminus A}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )\wedge \Theta \leq \int _{X\setminus A}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge \Theta .  \] We prove it by applying Stokes' formula on $X\setminus A$ to functions that equal $\varphi -k$ near $A$. After adding constants we may assume $\varphi \geq \psi $ and $\tau \leq 0$. Since $\tau $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic and $X$ is compact, there is $C_\tau \geq 0$ with $C_\tau \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau \geq 0$ (lemma 6.14.4 (4)). Put $\Omega =(C_\tau +1)\omega $. Fix $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$ and put $f_ k=\max \{ \psi +\varepsilon \tau ,\varphi -k\} $. Since $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq 0$ and $\varepsilon (C_\tau \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau )\geq 0$, both $\psi +\varepsilon \tau $ and $\varphi -k$ are $(\theta +\Omega )$-plurisubharmonic, hence so is $f_ k$, and $f_ k$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus A$. Since $\psi +\varepsilon \tau -\varphi \leq \varepsilon \tau $, we have $f_ k=\varphi -k$ on the open neighborhood $\{ \tau <-k/\varepsilon \} $ of $A$. Hence on $X\setminus A$ the function $g_ k=f_ k-\varphi +k=\max \{ \psi +\varepsilon \tau -\varphi +k,0\} $ takes values in $[0,k]$, and it vanishes outside the compact set $L_ k=\{ \tau \geq -k/\varepsilon \} \subset X\setminus A$. Stokes' formula. With a smooth local potential $h$ of $\theta +\Omega $, the Bedford–Taylor recursion gives, on $X\setminus A$, \[  (\theta +\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ k)\wedge \Theta -(\theta +\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge \Theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((f_ k+h)\Theta \bigr )-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((\varphi +h)\Theta \bigr )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g_ k\Theta ),  \] because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k\Theta )=0$. The signed measure $\lambda _ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g_ k\Theta )$ vanishes outside $L_ k$. Let $\kappa $ be a smooth function with compact support in $X\setminus A$ that equals one on a neighborhood of $L_ k$. Then $\lambda _ k(X\setminus A)=\int \kappa \, \mathrm d\lambda _ k=(g_ k\Theta )(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa )=0$, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa $ vanishes near the support of $g_ k\Theta $. Since the measures on the left have finite mass, we obtain \[  \int _{X\setminus A}(\theta +\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ k)\wedge \Theta =\int _{X\setminus A}(\theta +\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge \Theta .  \] Passage to the limit. On $X\setminus A$ the functions $f_ k$ decrease to the locally bounded function $\psi +\varepsilon \tau $ as $k\to \infty $. By decreasing continuity with the fixed base $\Theta $ (theorem 7.3.7 ), applied locally, the positive measures $(\theta +\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ k)\wedge \Theta $ converge weakly on $X\setminus A$ to $(\theta +\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi +\varepsilon \tau ))\wedge \Theta $. The mass of the limit on the open set $X\setminus A$ is at most the lower limit of the masses, because it is the supremum of the integrals of test functions $0\leq \kappa \leq 1$ supported in $X\setminus A$, and each such integral is the limit of the corresponding integrals for the approximating measures. Therefore \[  \int _{X\setminus A}(\theta +\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi +\varepsilon \tau ))\wedge \Theta \leq \int _{X\setminus A}(\theta +\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge \Theta .  \] By additivity of Bedford–Taylor products, the measure on the left is the sum of the positive measures $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )\wedge \Theta $, $\varepsilon (C_\tau \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau )\wedge \Theta $ and $(\Omega -\varepsilon C_\tau \omega )\wedge \Theta $, and the measure on the right is the sum of $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge \Theta $ and $\Omega \wedge \Theta $; all these measures have finite mass on $X\setminus A$. Dropping the second term on the left, we get \[  \int _{X\setminus A}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )\wedge \Theta \leq \int _{X\setminus A}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge \Theta +\varepsilon C_\tau \int _ X\omega \wedge \Theta ,  \] and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the desired inequality. If the differences are bounded, the same argument with the roles of $\varphi $ and $\psi $ exchanged gives equality. $\square$

title: Lemma 13.8.2
text:
Lemma 13.8.2 . 984FFB015C24 Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $u$ be smooth and plurisubharmonic and $v$ plurisubharmonic on $U$, and let $N\geq 1$ be an integer. Put $\Sigma _ N=\{ x\in \mathbb R^ N:x_ i\geq 0,\  t(x)=\sum _ i x_ i\leq 1\} $, and define on $U	imes \mathbb C^ N$, with coordinates $(w,z)$, \[  F=\sup _{x\in \Sigma _ N} \left((1-t(x))u+t(x)v+ \sum _ i x_ i\log |z_ i|^2-\sum _ i x_ i^2ight),  \] with the convention that a zero coefficient times $-\infty $ is zero. Then $F$ is plurisubharmonic and locally bounded on $U	imes \mathbb C^ N$, and $F\geq u$. If $v$ is locally bounded, then, with $p\colon U	imes \mathbb C^ N	o U$ the projection, FE05CF9EAD76 13.8.3  egin{equation}  p_*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N} = inom {n+N}{n}N\int _0^1 (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)u+tv))^ n t^{N-1}\, \mathrm dt, \end{equation} in the sense that both sides have the same integral against every bounded Borel function with compact support in $U$; in particular the pushforward is locally finite. Moreover, for such $v$, if $v-u\geq -C$ on an open set $E\subset U$, then over $E$ the measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ is carried by $\{ |z_ i|\leq \mathrm e^{1+C/2}	ext{ for all }i\} $. Proof. After showing that $F$ is plurisubharmonic, we compute $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ explicitly for smooth $v$, and we treat locally bounded $v$ by decreasing approximation. Points of $U	imes \mathbb C^ N$ are also denoted by $q$. Step 1: $F$ is plurisubharmonic. For fixed $x\in \Sigma _ N$, the function \[  \phi _ x=(1-t(x))u+t(x)v+\sum _ ix_ i\log |z_ i|^2-|x|^2  \] is plurisubharmonic on $U	imes \mathbb C^ N$, as a sum of nonnegative multiples of plurisubharmonic functions and a constant (proposition 5.9.5 ). Since $\phi _0=u$ and $\phi _ x\leq \max \{ u,v\} +\sum _ i\max \{ \log |z_ i|^2,0\} $ for all $x$, the family $(\phi _ x)$ is locally uniformly bounded above, and $F$ lies between $u$ and the right side of this inequality; hence $F$ is locally bounded. The function $(x,q)\mapsto \phi _ x(q)$ on $\Sigma _ N	imes (U	imes \mathbb C^ N)$ is upper semicontinuous. Indeed, if $c\geq 0$ is a continuous function of $x$ and $f$ is an upper semicontinuous function of $q$ with values in $[-\infty ,M]$ for some $M\in \mathbb R$, then $cf$ is upper semicontinuous, with the convention $0\cdot (-\infty )=0$: at a point where $c=0$, we have $cf\leq cM^+	o 0$ nearby, and at a point where $c>0$ this follows from the upper semicontinuity of $f$. This applies to the terms $(1-t(x))u$, $t(x)v$ and $x_ i\log |z_ i|^2$, and a finite sum of upper semicontinuous functions with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$ is upper semicontinuous. Since $\Sigma _ N$ is compact, $F$ is upper semicontinuous: if $q_ k	o q$ and $x_ k\in \Sigma _ N$ satisfy $\phi _{x_ k}(q_ k)\geq F(q_ k)-1/k$, then along a subsequence with $\varlimsup _ kF(q_ k)$ as limit, $x_ k	o x$, and $\varlimsup _ kF(q_ k)\leq \phi _ x(q)\leq F(q)$. Hence $F$ coincides with its upper semicontinuous regularization, which is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.10.2 . Step 2: regularity of $F$ for smooth $v$. Let $v$ be smooth, and work on $G=U	imes (\mathbb C^*)^ N$. Put $a=v-u$, $y_ i=\log |z_ i|^2$ and $b_ i=(y_ i+a)/2$. Since \[  (1-t(x))u+t(x)v+\sum _ ix_ iy_ i-\sum _ ix_ i^2=u+|b|^2-|x-b|^2,  \] we have $F=u+\gamma (b)$ with $\gamma (b)=\max _{x\in \Sigma _ N}(2x\cdot b-|x|^2)=|b|^2-|b-P(b)|^2$, where $P(b)$ is the closest point of $\Sigma _ N$ to $b$; it exists by compactness and is unique because $x\mapsto |x-b|^2$ is strictly convex on the convex set $\Sigma _ N$. Differentiating $\sigma \mapsto |b-P(b)-\sigma (x'-P(b))|^2$ at $\sigma =0^+$ for $x'\in \Sigma _ N$ gives the variational inequality $(b-P(b))\cdot (x'-P(b))\leq 0$. Applying it to $b$ with $x'=P(b')$ and to $b'$ with $x'=P(b)$ and adding, we get $|P(b)-P(b')|^2\leq (b-b')\cdot (P(b)-P(b'))$, so $P$ is $1$-Lipschitz. Moreover $\gamma (b')\geq 2P(b)\cdot b'-|P(b)|^2=\gamma (b)+2P(b)\cdot (b'-b)$, and symmetrically, so that \[  0\leq \gamma (b')-\gamma (b)-2P(b)\cdot (b'-b)\leq 2(P(b')-P(b))\cdot (b'-b)\leq 2|b'-b|^2.  \] Hence $\gamma $ is differentiable, with the Lipschitz gradient $2P$. Consequently $F$ is of class $C^1$ on $G$ with locally Lipschitz first derivatives, and 4EF00D8CA3C9 13.8.4  egin{equation}  \mathrm dF=\mathrm du+\sum _ iP_ i(b)\, (\mathrm dy_ i+\mathrm da)=(1-t)\, \mathrm du+t\, \mathrm dv+\sum _ ix_ i\, \mathrm dy_ i,\qquad x=P(b),\  t=t(x). \end{equation} The projection is explicit. Let $\lambda (b)=0$ if $\sum _ i\max \{ b_ i,0\} \leq 1$; otherwise let $\lambda (b)>0$ be the unique solution of $\sum _ i\max \{ b_ i-\lambda ,0\} =1$, which exists because the left side is continuous, nonincreasing, and strictly decreasing where it is positive. The point $x$ with coordinates $\max \{ b_ i-\lambda (b),0\} $ lies in $\Sigma _ N$ and satisfies the variational inequality: if $I$ is the set of indices with $b_ i>\lambda (b)$, then for $x'\in \Sigma _ N$ the left side of the inequality is $\sum _{i\in I}\lambda (b)(x'_ i-x_ i)+\sum _{i
otin I}b_ ix'_ i\leq \lambda (b)(t(x')-t(x))\leq 0$, since $t(x)=1$ when $\lambda (b)>0$. A point $x\in \Sigma _ N$ satisfying the variational inequality for all $x'\in \Sigma _ N$ is the closest point, because $|b-x'|^2=|b-x|^2+|x'-x|^2-2(b-x)\cdot (x'-x)\geq |b-x|^2$; hence $P_ i(b)=\max \{ b_ i-\lambda (b),0\} $. For a nonempty set $I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,N\} $ put $\lambda _ I(b)=(\sum _{i\in I}b_ i-1)/|I|$, and consider the open sets \[   egin{aligned}  \Omega _{I,0}& =\{ b:\  b_ i>0\  (i\in I),\  b_ i<0\  (i
otin I),\  	extstyle \sum _{i\in I}b_ i<1\} ,\  \Omega _{I,+}& =\{ b:\  \lambda _ I(b)>0,\  b_ i>\lambda _ I(b)\  (i\in I),\  b_ i<\lambda _ I(b)\  (i
otin I)\} , \end{aligned}  \] and $\Omega _{\varnothing ,0}=\{ b:b_ i<0	ext{ for all }i\} $. On $\Omega _{I,0}$ we have $\lambda (b)=0$ and $P(b)=(b_ i\mathbf1_ I(i))_ i$, and on $\Omega _{I,+}$ we have $\lambda (b)=\lambda _ I(b)$, by the uniqueness of $\lambda $, and $P_ i(b)=(b_ i-\lambda _ I(b))\mathbf1_ I(i)$; in either case $P$ is affine there. Let $\mathcal H$ be the finite family of affine hyperplanes $\{ b_ i=0\} $, $\{ \sum _{i\in I}b_ i=1\} $ and $\{ b_ i=\lambda _ I(b)\} $, for $1\leq i\leq N$ and nonempty $I$, omitting the empty sets $\{ b_ i=\lambda _{\{ i\} }(b)\} $. Every $b$ outside $ igcup \mathcal H$ lies in one of the sets $\Omega _{I,0}$, $\Omega _{I,+}$: if $\lambda (b)=0$, it lies in $\Omega _{I,0}$ with $I=\{ i:b_ i>0\} $, and if $\lambda (b)>0$, then $\lambda (b)=\lambda _ I(b)$ for $I=\{ i:b_ i>\lambda (b)\} $, and $b\in \Omega _{I,+}$ because no $b_ i$ equals $\lambda _ I(b)$. Let $Z\subset G$ be the closed set of points with $b\in  igcup \mathcal H$. For a fixed base point, each hyperplane of $\mathcal H$ is given by a nonconstant affine equation in $y=(\log |z_ i|^2)_ i$; in polar coordinates $z_ i=r_ i\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\alpha _ i}$, the corresponding set is the product of the image of a hyperplane of $\mathbb R^ N$ under the diffeomorphism $y\mapsto (\mathrm e^{y_ i/2})_ i$ with the torus of angles, so it is a Lebesgue null set. By Fubini's theorem, $Z$ is a Lebesgue null set. On $G\setminus Z$ the function $F=u+|b|^2-|b-P(b)|^2$ is smooth, because $P$ is locally affine there. Step 3: for smooth $v$, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ is carried by the interior region. On the interior region $\Omega _{\{ 1,\ldots ,N\} ,0}=\{ b:b_ i>0,\  \sum _ ib_ i<1\} $, the interior of $\Sigma _ N$, we have $x=P(b)=b$ and $F=u+\sum _ ix_ i^2$. On every other region $\Omega $, the complex Hessian of $F$, which is positive semidefinite by proposition 5.9.2 (1), has a vertical null vector, and hence zero determinant. Indeed, if $j
otin I$, then $x_ j=P_ j(b)=0$ on $\Omega $, so $\partial F/\partial z_ j=x_ j/z_ j=0$ there by ( 13.8.4 ), and all second derivatives $\partial ^2F/\partial z_ j\partial  ar z_ k$ vanish. If instead $I=\{ 1,\ldots ,N\} $ and $\lambda >0$, then $\lambda = ar b-1/N$ with $ ar b=N^{-1}\sum _ ib_ i$, and since $|b|^2=\sum _ i(b_ i- ar b)^2+N ar b^2$, \[  F=u+|b|^2-N\lambda ^2=v+ rac1N\sum _ iy_ i- rac1N+\sum _ i(b_ i- ar b)^2.  \] For $\zeta \in \mathbb C$ near $0$, the point $(w,\mathrm e^\zeta z_1,\ldots ,\mathrm e^\zeta z_ N)$ stays in the region, every $y_ i$ increases by $2\operatorname{Re}\zeta $, and the differences $b_ i- ar b=(y_ i- ar y)/2$ do not change, so $F(w,\mathrm e^\zeta z)=F(w,z)+2\operatorname{Re}\zeta $ is harmonic in $\zeta $. Its Laplacian at $\zeta =0$ is a positive multiple of the value of the complex Hessian of $F$ on the vector $\xi =\sum _ iz_ i\, \partial /\partial z_ i$, which therefore vanishes; since the Hessian is positive semidefinite, $\xi $ is a null vector by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. We now identify $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ on $G$. Let $D$ be a first derivative of $F$ with respect to a real coordinate; by Step 2 it has a Lipschitz constant $L$ on a given ball $B\Subset G$. For a test function $\chi \geq 0$ supported in a smaller ball and a real coordinate $q_ l$, \[  |\langle \partial _{q_ l}D,\chi angle |=\Bigl |\lim _{h	o 0}\int  rac{D(q+he_ l)-D(q)}{h}\chi (q)\, \mathrm dq\Bigr |\leq L\int \chi \, \mathrm dq,  \] so by corollary 2.8.2 the distributional derivative $\partial _{q_ l}D$ is a locally bounded function. Hence the distributional second derivatives of $F$ are locally bounded functions on $G$, and on the open set $G\setminus Z$ they coincide almost everywhere with the classical ones, since $F$ is smooth there. As $Z$ is a null set, the Hessian determinant $\det (F_{j ar k})$, formed with these functions, is a locally bounded function that equals the classical determinant on $G\setminus Z$. Let $F_\varepsilon =F*ho _\varepsilon $ be the mollifications, defined, smooth and plurisubharmonic on a relatively compact open set $G'\Subset G$ for small $\varepsilon $ (proposition 5.9.2 (2)). Their second derivatives are the mollifications of those of $F$ (proposition 2.5.3 ); by lemma 2.5.1 they converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(G')$ and are locally uniformly bounded. Since the determinant is a polynomial in the entries, $\det (F_{\varepsilon ,j ar k})	o \det (F_{j ar k})$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(G')$. On the other hand $F_\varepsilon 	o F$ locally uniformly, because $F$ is continuous, so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F_\varepsilon )^{n+N}	o (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ weakly by proposition 7.2.6 . With ( 7.2.4 ) for the smooth functions $F_\varepsilon $, we conclude that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}= rac{(n+N)!}{\pi ^{n+N}}\det (F_{j ar k})\, \mathrm dV$ on $G$. In particular this measure does not charge the null set $Z$, and it vanishes on all regions except the interior one. It does not charge the pluripolar complement of $G$ either (corollary 5.47.11 ), so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ is carried by the set $G_0=\{ (w,z)\in G:b(w,z)\in \operatorname{Int}\Sigma _ N\} $ over the interior region. Step 4: the formula for smooth $v$. On $G_0$ we have $F=u+\sum _ ix_ i^2$ with $x_ i=(y_ i+a)/2$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(x_ i^2)=2x_ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}x_ i+2\, \mathrm dx_ i\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x_ i$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}x_ i=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a/2$, the functions $y_ i$ being pluriharmonic on $G$, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F=(1-t)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+\sum _ i\Gamma _ i,\qquad \Gamma _ i=2\, \mathrm dx_ i\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x_ i,  \] with $t=t(x)$. The form $\Lambda =(1-t)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ contains only differentials of the base variables, so $\Lambda ^{n+1}=0$, and $\Gamma _ i\wedge \Gamma _ i=0$. Since forms of even degree commute, the binomial expansion leaves only the term $ inom {n+N}{n}\Lambda ^ n\wedge (\sum _ i\Gamma _ i)^ N$, and $(\sum _ i\Gamma _ i)^ N=N!\, \Gamma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \Gamma _ N$. The map $(w,z)\mapsto (w,x,\alpha )$, with $\alpha _ i=\arg z_ i$, is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $G_0$ onto $U	imes \operatorname{Int}\Sigma _ N	imes (\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)^ N$, with inverse $z_ i=\mathrm e^{x_ i-a(w)/2}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\alpha _ i}$. With our normalization, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}y_ i=\mathrm d\alpha _ i/(2\pi )$, so $\Gamma _ i=\mathrm dx_ i\wedge \mathrm d\alpha _ i/(2\pi )+\mathrm dx_ i\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}a$, and the second term contains a differential of the base variables and disappears in the product with $\Lambda ^ n$. Hence, in these coordinates, \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}= inom {n+N}{n}N!\,  igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t(x))u+t(x)v) igr )^ n(w)\wedge  igwedge _ i\Bigl (\mathrm dx_ i\wedge  rac{\mathrm d\alpha _ i}{2\pi }\Bigr ).  \] Let $g\geq 0$ be a bounded Borel function with compact support in $U$. Since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ is carried by $G_0$, integrating $g(w)$ against this measure in the coordinates $(w,x,\alpha )$, first over the angles by Fubini's theorem, we obtain \[  \int (g\circ p)\, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}= inom {n+N}{n}N!\int _{\Sigma _ N}\Phi (t(x))\, \mathrm dx,  \] where $\Phi (t)=\int _ Ug\, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)u+tv))^ n$. By multilinearity of Bedford–Taylor products, $\Phi $ is a polynomial in $t$. The image of Lebesgue measure on $\Sigma _ N$ under $t$ is $t^{N-1}\, \mathrm dt/(N-1)!$ on $[0,1]$, because $\{ x\in \Sigma _ N:t(x)\leq t_0\} =t_0\Sigma _ N$ has volume $t_0^ N|\Sigma _ N|$ and $|\Sigma _ N|=1/N!$ by iterated integration, and finite measures on $[0,1]$ that agree on the intervals $[0,t_0]$ agree (lemma 2.2.6 ). This proves ( 13.8.3 ) for smooth $v$; for signed bounded Borel $g$ split $g$ into its positive and negative parts. Step 5: support for smooth $v$. If $a\geq -C$ at a base point, then at the points of $G_0$ over it we have $y_ i=2x_ i-a\leq 2+C$, because $x_ i<1$; hence $|z_ i|\leq \mathrm e^{1+C/2}$. Since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ is carried by $G_0$, this proves the support assertion for smooth $v$. Step 6: general $v$. Let $v$ be locally bounded, let $U'\Subset U$ be open, and let $v_ l$ be smooth plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline{U'}$ decreasing to $v$, for instance mollifications (proposition 5.9.2 (2)). Let $F_ l$ be the corresponding functions. For each $x$, the branch of $F_ l$ exceeds that of $F$ by $t(x)(v_ l-v)\in [0,v_ l-v]$, so $F\leq F_ l\leq F+(v_ l-v)$, and the $F_ l$ decrease pointwise to $F$; by Step 1 they are locally uniformly bounded. By theorem 7.3.7 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F_ l)^{n+N}	o (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ weakly on $U'	imes \mathbb C^ N$. If $v-u\geq -C$ on an open set $E$, then also $v_ l-u\geq -C$ there, so by Step 5 the measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F_ l)^{n+N}$ give no mass to the open set of points over $E\cap U'$ at which some $|z_ i|>\mathrm e^{1+C/2}$. The weak limit gives no mass to this open set either, since the mass of an open set is the supremum of the integrals of test functions $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ supported in it. This proves the support assertion. Now let $g$ be continuous with compact support in $U'$. Since $v$ is bounded below and $u$ is bounded above on a relatively compact neighborhood $E$ of $\operatorname{Supp}g$, there is $C$ with $v-u\geq -C$ on $E$, so all the measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F_ l)^{n+N}$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ over $E$ are carried by $E	imes \{ |z_ i|\leq \mathrm e^{1+C/2}\} $. Multiplying $g\circ p$ by a test function of $z$ equal to one on this polydisc, we see that $\int (g\circ p)(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F_ l)^{n+N}	o \int (g\circ p)(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$; here we use that weakly convergent positive measures with locally bounded masses converge against continuous functions with compact support. On the right side of ( 13.8.3 ), the functions $(1-t)u+tv_ l$ decrease to $(1-t)u+tv$ for each $t$, so $\int g\, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)u+tv_ l))^ n	o \int g\, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)u+tv))^ n$ by theorem 7.3.7 ; these integrals are bounded uniformly in $t\in [0,1]$ and $l$ by theorem 7.2.5 , and dominated convergence in $t$ applies. Hence ( 13.8.3 ) holds on $U'$ when tested against continuous functions with compact support. Both sides are positive measures that are finite on compact subsets of $U'$, so they agree as measures by the uniqueness in theorem 2.5.6 , and therefore also against bounded Borel functions with compact support. Exhausting $U$ by such sets $U'$ proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.8.5
text:
Proposition 13.8.5 . A00B4940B406 Let $\varphi _0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and assume that its pole set $P=\{ \varphi _0=-\infty \} $ is closed and that $\varphi _0$ is smooth on $X\setminus P$. Fix an integer $N\geq 1$, let $p_ X,p_{\mathbb P^ N}$ be the projections of $X	imes \mathbb P^ N$, and let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form of example 10.6.7 . For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ N]$ put \[  s_ i=\log  rac{|Z_ i|^2}{\sum _{l=0}^ N|Z_ l|^2},\qquad \widetilde	heta =p_ X^*	heta +p_{\mathbb P^ N}^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}},  \] and let $\Phi $ be the upper semicontinuous regularization of \[  \Phi _0=\sup _{x\in \Sigma _ N} \left((1-t(x))(\varphi _0+s_0)+t(x)\varphi +\sum _{i=1}^ N x_ i s_ i-\sum _{i=1}^ N x_ i^2ight),  \] with the convention that a zero coefficient times $-\infty $ is zero. Then $\Phi $ is $\widetilde	heta $-plurisubharmonic and locally bounded outside the closed set $A=(P	imes \mathbb P^ N)\cup (X	imes \{ Z_0=0\} )$, which is the pole set of the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi _0+s_0$, and 56FDDE3E50E0 13.8.6  egin{equation}   egin{aligned} & \int _{X	imes \mathbb P^ N}\langle (\widetilde	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )^{n+N}angle \ & \quad = inom {n+N}{n}N\int _0^1 \left(\int _ X\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi ))^ nangle ight) t^{N-1}\, \mathrm dt. \end{aligned} \end{equation} If $\{ 	heta \} $ is big, a potential $\varphi _0$ with these properties exists. Proof. The potential $\Phi $. Each function in the supremum is quasi-plurisubharmonic and $\widetilde	heta $-plurisubharmonic: its coefficients of the $	heta $-plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi _0$ and $\varphi $ are nonnegative and add up to one, and so do its coefficients of the functions $s_ i$, since $(1-t(x))+\sum _ ix_ i=1$. The $s_ i$ are $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic: in the standard chart $\{ Z_ l
eq 0\} $, where $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _ m|Z_ m/Z_ l|^2$ as in example 10.6.7 , the function $s_ i+\log \sum _ m|Z_ m/Z_ l|^2=\log |Z_ i/Z_ l|^2$ is plurisubharmonic. The family is uniformly bounded above, because $\varphi _0$ and $\varphi $ are bounded above on the compact manifold $X$ and $s_ i\leq 0$. Hence, by theorem 5.10.2 applied after adding smooth local potentials of $\widetilde	heta $, its regularized supremum $\Phi $ is $\widetilde	heta $-plurisubharmonic. The branch $x=0$ is $	au =\varphi _0+s_0$, which is quasi-plurisubharmonic, equal to $-\infty $ exactly on $A$, and locally bounded outside $A$, because $\varphi _0$ is smooth on $X\setminus P$ and $s_0$ is smooth on $\{ Z_0
eq 0\} $. Since $\Phi \geq \Phi _0\geq 	au $ and $\Phi $ is bounded above, $\Phi $ is locally bounded outside $A$; the set $A$ is closed because $P$ is. Local form. Let $W\subset X\setminus P$ be a coordinate chart, choose a smooth function $h$ on $W$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $, and use the affine coordinates $z_ i=Z_ i/Z_0$ on $\{ Z_0
eq 0\} =\mathbb C^ N$. There $s_0=-\log (1+|z|^2)$ and $s_ i=\log |z_ i|^2-\log (1+|z|^2)$, and $\log (1+|z|^2)$ is a potential of $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. Since the coefficients of the $s_ i$ add up to one, adding the smooth function $h+\log (1+|z|^2)$ to each function in the supremum turns $\Phi _0$ into the function $F$ of lemma 13.8.2 , formed with $u=\varphi _0+h$, which is smooth and plurisubharmonic on $W$, and $v=\varphi +h$, which is plurisubharmonic on $W$. By that lemma, $F$ is plurisubharmonic, hence upper semicontinuous, so $\Phi _0$ is upper semicontinuous on the open set $(X\setminus P)	imes \{ Z_0
eq 0\} =(X	imes \mathbb P^ N)\setminus A$, and $\Phi =\Phi _0$ there. Thus $F$ is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic potential of $\widetilde	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi $ on $W	imes \mathbb C^ N$, and the non-pluripolar product $\langle (\widetilde	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )^{n+N}angle $ is the Bedford–Taylor measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ there. The mass formula. For $C>0$ put $v_ C=\max \{ v,u-C\} $, a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $W$, and let $F_ C$ be the function of lemma 13.8.2 formed with $u$ and $v_ C$. At base points $w$ with $v(w)>u(w)-C$ we have $v_ C(w)=v(w)$, so $F_ C=F$ on the set $Y_ C=\{ (w,z):v(w)>u(w)-C\} $. This set is plurifine open in $W	imes \mathbb C^ N$, because $(w,z)\mapsto v(w)$ is plurisubharmonic and $u$ is continuous. By plurifine locality (theorem 5.47.22 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F_ C)^{n+N}$ agree on $Y_ C$. Similarly, for $0\leq t\leq 1$, the function $(1-t)u+tv$ is a local potential of the closed positive current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi )$, whose non-pluripolar products are finite by theorem 13.5.4 , and on the plurifine open set $\{ v>u-C\} $ it coincides with the bounded function $(1-t)u+tv_ C$; so by proposition 13.2.6 , \[  \mathbf1_{\{ v>u-C\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)u+tv_ C))^ n=\mathbf1_{\{ v>u-C\} }\langle (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)u+tv))^ nangle .  \] Let $g\geq 0$ be a bounded Borel function with compact support in $W$. Applying lemma 13.8.2 to $F_ C$ with the Borel weight $g\mathbf1_{\{ v>u-C\} }$, we obtain \[   egin{aligned} & \int _{Y_ C}(g\circ p_ X)(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}\ & \qquad = inom {n+N}{n}N\int _0^1\Bigl (\int _ Wg\, \mathbf1_{\{ v>u-C\} }\langle (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)u+tv))^ nangle \Bigr )t^{N-1}\, \mathrm dt. \end{aligned}  \] Let $C	o \infty $. The sets $\{ v>u-C\} $ increase to $\{ v>-\infty \} $, whose complement is the pole set of $v$; this set and its product with $\mathbb C^ N$ are pluripolar Borel sets, which carry no mass for the non-pluripolar products on $W$ and for the Bedford–Taylor measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^{n+N}$ (corollary 5.47.11 ). By monotone convergence, first in the inner integrals and then in $t$, \[   egin{aligned} & \int _{W	imes \mathbb C^ N}(g\circ p_ X)\, \langle (\widetilde	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )^{n+N}angle \ & \qquad = inom {n+N}{n}N\int _0^1\Bigl (\int _ Xg\, \langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi ))^ nangle \Bigr )t^{N-1}\, \mathrm dt. \end{aligned}  \] The non-pluripolar product on $X	imes \mathbb P^ N$ gives zero mass to the pluripolar Borel set $A$, and the products on $X$ give zero mass to $P$. Hence the left side is the integral of $g\circ p_ X$ over $X	imes \mathbb P^ N$. Now cover $X\setminus P$ by countably many compact sets $K_ k$, each contained in a chart $W_ k\subset X\setminus P$, and put $B_ k=K_ k\setminus  igcup _{j<k}K_ j$. For a nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $X$, applying the identity to the functions $\min \{ g,M\} \mathbf1_{B_ k}$ and using monotone convergence in $M$ and in the sum over $k$, we obtain the identity for $g\mathbf1_{X\setminus P}$, and hence for $g$, since both sides give $P$ zero mass. Taking $g=1$ gives ( 13.8.6 ). Existence of $\varphi _0$. If $\{ 	heta \} $ is big, it contains a Kähler current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$, that is, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )$. By lemma 6.17.1 (1), applied to $\psi $ with the background $	heta -\delta \omega $, for every integer $m\geq 1$ there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $G_ m=m^{-1}\log R_ m$ with $R_ m$ smooth and $	heta -\delta \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq -(c'/m)\omega $, where the constant $c'>0$ does not depend on $m$. For $m\geq c'/\delta $, the function $\varphi _0=G_ m$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic; its pole set $\{ R_ m=0\} $ is closed, and $\varphi _0$ is smooth on its complement, where $R_ m>0$. $\square$

title: Equation 13.8.6
text: 56FDDE3E50E0 13.8.6 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned} & \int _{X\times \mathbb P^ N}\langle (\widetilde\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )^{n+N}\rangle \\ & \quad =\binom {n+N}{n}N\int _0^1 \left(\int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi ))^ n\rangle \right) t^{N-1}\, \mathrm dt. \end{aligned} \end{equation}

title: Theorem 13.8.7
text: Theorem 13.8.7 . 60DE4F681F75 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\varphi \geq \psi -O(1)$. Then \[  \int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n\rangle .  \] Proof. Suppose first that $\{ \theta \} $ is big. Choose a reference potential $\varphi _0$ as in proposition 13.8.5 , which exists because the class is big, and construct the corresponding potentials $\Phi _ N$ from $\varphi $ and $\Psi _ N$ from $\psi $. If $\varphi \geq \psi -C$, then for every $x\in \Sigma _ N$ the branch defining $\Phi _ N$ is at least the branch defining $\Psi _ N$ minus $t(x)C\leq C$; hence the suprema and their regularizations satisfy $\Phi _ N\geq \Psi _ N-C$, with a constant independent of $N$. By proposition 13.8.5 , both are locally bounded outside the same closed set $A$, which is the pole set of the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi _0+s_0$, and this function is locally bounded outside $A$. The product $X\times \mathbb P^ N$ is a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n+N$, with the Kähler form $p_ X^*\omega +p_{\mathbb P^ N}^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, so the results of this section apply to it. For $0\leq t\leq 1$ put \[  f_\varphi (t)=\int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi ))^ n\rangle ,  \] and define $f_\psi $ in the same way. Applying lemma 13.8.1 on $X\times \mathbb P^ N$, with all $n+N$ factors equal to $\widetilde\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ N$, respectively $\widetilde\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi _ N$, and cancelling the common binomial coefficient in ( 13.8.6 ), we obtain \[  \int _0^1f_\varphi (t)\, Nt^{N-1}\, \mathrm dt\geq \int _0^1f_\psi (t)\, Nt^{N-1}\, \mathrm dt.  \] Writing $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi )=(1-t)T_0+tT_\varphi $ with $T_0=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _0$ and $T_\varphi =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $, multilinearity shows that $f_\varphi $ is a polynomial in $t$, in particular continuous on $[0,1]$, and $f_\varphi (1)$ is the mass of $\varphi $. The probability measures $Nt^{N-1}\, \mathrm dt$ concentrate at $1$ as $N\to \infty $, since their mass on $[0,1-\delta ]$ is $(1-\delta )^ N$. By uniform continuity the two integrals tend to $f_\varphi (1)$ and $f_\psi (1)$, which proves the theorem for big classes. In general, $\{ \theta \} $ is pseudo-effective, because it contains $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $. For $\varepsilon >0$ the class of $\theta +\varepsilon \omega $ is big, since it contains the Kähler current $\theta +\varepsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \varepsilon \omega $, and $\varphi ,\psi $ are $(\theta +\varepsilon \omega )$-plurisubharmonic. By the big case, the mass of $\varphi $ with respect to $\theta +\varepsilon \omega $ is at least that of $\psi $. By multilinearity and theorem 13.5.4 , both masses are polynomials in $\varepsilon $ with finite coefficients, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the theorem. $\square$

title: Corollary 13.8.8
text: Corollary 13.8.8 . A8BA63307F6C Let $u_ j,v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ for $1\leq j\leq p\leq n$, and put $T_ j=\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ and $T'_ j=\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j$. If every difference $u_ j-v_ j$ is bounded, then \[  \int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p} =\int _ X\langle T'_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T'_ p\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}.  \] If only $u_ j\geq v_ j-O(1)$ for every $j$, then the left side is at least the right side. Proof. Bounded differences. For real numbers $a_0,a_1,\ldots ,a_ p>0$, apply theorem 13.8.7 in both directions to the potentials $\sum _ ja_ ju_ j$ and $\sum _ ja_ jv_ j$, whose difference is bounded, with respect to the background $a_0\omega +\sum _ ja_ j\theta _ j$. The two resulting masses are equal. By multilinearity, both are homogeneous polynomials of degree $n$ in $(a_0,\ldots ,a_ p)$, and they agree on an open set; fixing all but one variable and using the uniqueness of polynomials in one variable successively, we see that their coefficients agree. By proposition 13.4.3 , the coefficient of $a_0^{n-p}a_1\cdots a_ p$ is $n!/(n-p)!$ times the mixed mass in the statement, which proves equality. The ordered case. Put $v_{j,k}=\max \{ u_ j-k,v_ j\} $. Since $v_ j\leq u_ j+C_ j$ for constants $C_ j$, we have $u_ j-k\leq v_{j,k}\leq u_ j+C_ j$, so each tuple $(v_{j,k})_ j$ has the same mixed mass as $(u_ j)_ j$, by the first part. As $k\to \infty $, $v_{j,k}$ decreases to $v_ j$ and therefore converges to it in extended capacity (lemma 13.7.3 ). The lower inequality of theorem 13.7.5 , with test form $\omega ^{n-p}$, bounds the mixed mass of the $v_ j$ by these equal masses. $\square$

title: Corollary 13.8.9
text: Corollary 13.8.9 . 56037F3B58D7 Suppose that $u_{j,k}\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ increase almost everywhere to $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ as $k\to \infty $, for $1\leq j\leq p\leq n$. Then the non-pluripolar products $\langle \bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{j,k})\rangle $ converge weakly to $\langle \bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\rangle $, and their mixed masses against $\omega ^{n-p}$ converge. Proof. The inequality $u_{j,k}\leq u_ j$ holds almost everywhere, hence everywhere, since $\max \{ u_{j,k},u_ j\} $ and $u_ j$ are quasi-plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere. On coordinate charts add smooth local potentials and truncate below at a fixed level $-C$. The resulting locally uniformly bounded plurisubharmonic sequences increase almost everywhere to the truncations of the limits, so they converge in capacity by theorem 7.6.1 ; by lemma 13.7.3 , the original sequences converge in extended capacity. Since $u_{j,k}\leq u_ j$, corollary 13.8.8 bounds every mixed mass of the sequence by that of the limit, and theorem 13.7.5 gives weak convergence and convergence of the masses. This applies in particular to the regularized supremum of an increasing sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ that is bounded above: it belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ by theorem 5.10.2 , and it differs from the pointwise supremum only on a pluripolar set, by corollary 5.47.11 , hence only on a Lebesgue null set, because plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable. $\square$

title: 13.9 Maximal mass and comparison
text: By the monotonicity just proved, potentials with minimal singularities have the largest non-pluripolar masses in a big class, and these maximal masses are invariants of the classes. We extend them to pseudo-effective classes by perturbing with a Kähler class, and then derive the comparison and domination principles for non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measures. Recall that $V_\theta $ denotes the extremal potential of definition 10.3.7 . Definition 13.9.1 . 4F64B29C315E For big classes $\alpha _ j=\{ \theta _ j\} $, $1\leq j\leq p\leq n$, the positive mixed intersection number relative to the Kähler class $\{ \omega \} $ is \[  I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p) =\int _ X\left\langle \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p (\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_{\theta _ j})\right\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}.  \] For pseudo-effective classes $\alpha _ j$ that are not all big, we define $I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)$ as the limit of the numbers $I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots ,\alpha _ p+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )$, which decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ (proposition 13.9.2 ); when all $\alpha _ j$ are big, the same limit equals the number defined by the display. In top degree we put $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )=I_\omega (\alpha ,\ldots ,\alpha )$, the volume of $\alpha $; the factor $\omega ^{n-p}$ is then absent. Proposition 13.9.2 . 44F242B6965F The numbers of definition 13.9.1 do not depend on the chosen smooth representatives or minimal potentials, nor on the Kähler form within its class. The limit in definition 13.9.1 exists for all pseudo-effective classes, does not depend on the Kähler class used for the perturbation, and equals the number defined by the display when all $\alpha _ j$ are big. For closed positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$, \[  \int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p} \leq I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p).  \] The numbers are positively homogeneous in each class and increase when a pseudo-effective class is added to any argument. For nef classes they equal the cohomological intersection numbers $\int _ X\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$. Big classes have positive volume. Proof. Big classes. Any two potentials with minimal singularities in a fixed big class differ by a bounded function, and a change of smooth representative changes each potential by a smooth function. Hence corollary 13.8.8 shows that $I_\omega $ does not depend on these choices. The same corollary and minimality give the upper bound for closed positive currents in big classes. If $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is another Kähler form in the class of $\omega $, with $f$ smooth, then $\omega '^{n-p}-\omega ^{n-p}=\mathrm d\bigl (\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \sum _{i=0}^{n-p-1}\omega '^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-p-1-i}\bigr )$ is a smooth exact form. Its integral against the closed current $\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle $ vanishes, because $S(\mathrm d\psi )=\pm (\mathrm dS)(\psi )=0$ for a closed current $S$ and a smooth form $\psi $ on the compact manifold $X$. Hence the numbers for big classes do not depend on $\omega $ within its class, and neither do their limits, since the perturbing classes $\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ are the same. Let $\alpha $ be big and $\gamma $ pseudo-effective, represented by a closed positive current $S$. Adding $S$ to a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $ gives a current in the big class $\alpha +\gamma $, which by the upper bound has mixed mass at most the number with $\alpha $ replaced by $\alpha +\gamma $. By multilinearity and positivity, its mixed mass is at least the number for $\alpha $. Hence, when all arguments are big, replacing an argument $\alpha $ by $\alpha +\gamma $ increases the number. Homogeneity for big classes follows by scaling a minimal potential together with its background: if $c>0$, then $cV_\theta $ has minimal singularities in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,c\theta )$, and the product is homogeneous in each factor by proposition 13.2.6 . Pseudo-effective classes. By this monotonicity for big classes, the perturbed numbers decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; they are nonnegative, so the limit exists. Every Kähler form $\kappa $ satisfies $c^{-1}\omega \leq \kappa \leq c\omega $ for some $c\geq 1$ (lemma 6.14.1 ), so monotonicity places the perturbation by $\varepsilon \kappa $ between the perturbations by $c^{-1}\varepsilon \omega $ and $c\varepsilon \omega $, with the same fixed test form $\omega ^{n-p}$; this proves independence of the perturbing class. The same comparison shows that perturbing the arguments by different fixed multiples of $\varepsilon \omega $ gives the same limit, which extends homogeneity to pseudo-effective classes. Monotonicity also extends: if $\gamma $ is pseudo-effective, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ the number with an argument $\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ replaced by $\alpha +\gamma +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is at least the original one, by the big case, and we let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. If all $\alpha _ j$ are big, choose $\delta >0$ such that each $\alpha _ j$ contains a Kähler current $R_ j\geq \delta \omega $. Then $(1+\varepsilon /\delta )\alpha _ j-(\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )=(\varepsilon /\delta )\{ R_ j-\delta \omega \} $ is pseudo-effective, so monotonicity and homogeneity give \[  I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)\leq I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots ,\alpha _ p+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )\leq (1+\varepsilon /\delta )^ pI_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p),  \] and the limit is $I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)$. For arbitrary closed positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$, the upper bound in the big classes $\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, applied to $T_ j+\varepsilon \omega $, and multilinearity give $\int _ X\langle \bigwedge _ jT_ j\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}\leq I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots )$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the upper bound. Nef and big classes. If the $\alpha _ j$ are nef, their perturbations are Kähler classes: $\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ contains $\theta _{j,\varepsilon /2}+\varepsilon \omega \geq \varepsilon \omega /2$, where $\theta _{j,\varepsilon /2}\geq -(\varepsilon /2)\omega $ is a smooth representative of $\alpha _ j$ given by definition 10.4.1 . If $\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is a Kähler form with $f$ smooth, then $f\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega )$, so $V_{\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }\geq f-\sup _ Xf$ by lemma 10.3.8 ; since also $V_{\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }\leq 0$ by the same lemma, the minimal potentials are bounded. By proposition 13.5.1 , the perturbed numbers are the integrals $\int _ X\bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega )\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$, and their limits are the cohomological intersection numbers. Finally, let $\alpha $ be big and $T_0\in \alpha $ a Kähler current with $T_0\geq \delta \omega $. Expanding $T_0=\delta \omega +(T_0-\delta \omega )$ by multilinearity gives $\langle T_0^ n\rangle \geq \delta ^ n\omega ^ n$, so $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )\geq \delta ^ n\int _ X\omega ^ n>0$ by the upper bound. $\square$ Conversely, a pseudo-effective class of positive volume is big. The proof requires the construction of a Kähler current in the class and is given in subsection 17.5.27 , after Monge–Ampère equations with prescribed measures have been solved. Definition 13.9.3 . 2AF01ACCF985 A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ has full Monge–Ampère mass if $\int _ X\langle T^ n\rangle =\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$. We write $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$ for the set of $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has full Monge–Ampère mass. For $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the class $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ consists of the potentials $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\leq \phi +O(1)$ and \[  \int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi )^ n\rangle ;  \] these potentials have full mass relative to $\phi $. In a big class, $\mathcal E(X,\theta )=\mathcal E(X,\theta ,V_\theta )$, because every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $u\leq V_\theta +\sup _ Xu$ and $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$ is the mass of $V_\theta $. The class $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$ should not be confused with the local Cegrell class $\mathcal E_0(B)$ of definition 7.11.1 , nor with the pseudo-effective cone of definition 10.4.1 , a cone of cohomology classes. Corollary 13.9.4 . 45601E7EC1EE Let $u_ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u_ k\leq \phi +C_ k$ for constants $C_ k$, let $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and suppose that $u_ k\to u$ in extended capacity. Then \[  \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k)^ n\rangle \longrightarrow \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle  \] weakly, and the masses converge. The same holds, without the constants $C_ k$, if $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta )$; in particular it holds for every sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ that decreases to an element of $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$. Proof. By theorem 13.8.7 , the mass of each $u_ k$ is at most that of $\phi $, which equals the mass of $u$. Hence theorem 13.7.5 , with $p=n$, gives weak convergence, and its lower inequality together with this bound gives convergence of the masses. If $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta )$, then by proposition 13.9.2 the mass of each $u_ k$ is at most $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$, which is the mass of $u$, and the same argument applies. Finally, decreasing sequences converge in extended capacity by lemma 13.7.3 . $\square$ Proposition 13.9.5 . FEA17FAE6BAA For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ write $\mu _ u=\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle $. Then for all $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ v \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ u+\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )-\mu _ u(X).  \] The last two terms may be omitted if $u$ has full mass or if $u\geq v-O(1)$. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$. The function $w=\max \{ u,v-\varepsilon \} $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ and $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ are disjoint and plurifine open. Indeed, near each point we have $u-v=(u+h)-(v+h)$ for a smooth local potential $h$ of $\theta $, and $u+h$, $v+h$ are plurisubharmonic, so by proposition 5.47.25 the function $u-v$ is plurifinely continuous off the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, which is disjoint from both sets. Moreover $w$ equals $v-\varepsilon $ on the first set and $u$ on the second. By plurifine locality (proposition 13.2.6 ), \[  \mu _ w(X)\geq \mu _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} )+\mu _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} ).  \] The left side is at most $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$ by proposition 13.9.2 . The complement of $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ consists of $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $, which is contained in $\{ u<v\} $ up to the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, and that pluripolar set carries no mass. Hence \[  \mu _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} )\leq \operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )-\mu _ u(X)+\mu _ u(\{ u<v\} ).  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ increase to $\{ u<v\} $, which proves the inequality. If $u$ has full mass, the last two terms cancel. If $u\geq v-O(1)$, then $w-u$ is bounded, so $\mu _ w(X)=\mu _ u(X)$ by corollary 13.8.8 , and the same computation with $\mu _ u(X)$ in place of the volume gives the inequality without these terms. $\square$ Corollary 13.9.6 . D91589CC5A89 Let $u,v,\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\geq v-O(1)$ and $u\geq \rho -O(1)$. If $u\geq v$ almost everywhere for $\mu _ u$, then $u\geq v$ almost everywhere for $\mu _\rho $. If, in addition, the class $\{ \theta \} $ is big and $u$ has minimal singularities, then $u\geq v$ everywhere on $X$. Proof. After adding a constant to $\rho $ we may assume $\rho \leq u$. For $0<t<1$ put $q_ t=(1-t)v+t\rho $. Then $u\geq q_ t-O(1)$, and $\{ u<q_ t\} \subset \{ u<v\} $, because $u<(1-t)v+t\rho \leq (1-t)v+tu$ forces $u<v$. Multilinearity and proposition 13.9.5 therefore give \[  t^ n\mu _\rho (\{ u<q_ t\} ) \leq \mu _{q_ t}(\{ u<q_ t\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<q_ t\} )\leq \mu _ u(\{ u<v\} )=0.  \] As $t\downarrow 0$, every point where $u<v$ and $\rho >-\infty $ eventually lies in $\{ u<q_ t\} $, so Fatou's lemma, applied along a sequence $t\downarrow 0$, gives $\mu _\rho (\{ u<v\} \cap \{ \rho >-\infty \} )=0$. Since $\mu _\rho $ gives no mass to the pole set of $\rho $, this proves the first assertion. Now let the class be big and $u$ have minimal singularities. The class contains a Kähler current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$. Then $u\geq \rho -O(1)$ by minimality, and $\mu _\rho \geq \delta ^ n\omega ^ n$, because multilinearity expands $\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n\rangle =\langle (\delta \omega +(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho -\delta \omega ))^ n\rangle $ into positive terms, one of which is $\delta ^ n\omega ^ n$. The first assertion gives $u\geq v$ almost everywhere with respect to $\omega ^ n$, that is, almost everywhere for Lebesgue measure in charts. Near each point, $u$ and $v$ become plurisubharmonic after adding a common smooth local potential $h$ of $\theta $, and then $\max \{ u,v\} +h$ and $u+h$ are plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere; by theorem 5.9.1 , theorem 3.4.12 they agree everywhere, that is, $u\geq v$ everywhere. $\square$

title: Definition 13.9.1
text: Definition 13.9.1 . 4F64B29C315E For big classes $\alpha _ j=\{ \theta _ j\} $, $1\leq j\leq p\leq n$, the positive mixed intersection number relative to the Kähler class $\{ \omega \} $ is \[  I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p) =\int _ X\left\langle \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p (\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_{\theta _ j})\right\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}.  \] For pseudo-effective classes $\alpha _ j$ that are not all big, we define $I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)$ as the limit of the numbers $I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots ,\alpha _ p+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )$, which decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ (proposition 13.9.2 ); when all $\alpha _ j$ are big, the same limit equals the number defined by the display. In top degree we put $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )=I_\omega (\alpha ,\ldots ,\alpha )$, the volume of $\alpha $; the factor $\omega ^{n-p}$ is then absent.

title: Proposition 13.9.2
text: Proposition 13.9.2 . 44F242B6965F The numbers of definition 13.9.1 do not depend on the chosen smooth representatives or minimal potentials, nor on the Kähler form within its class. The limit in definition 13.9.1 exists for all pseudo-effective classes, does not depend on the Kähler class used for the perturbation, and equals the number defined by the display when all $\alpha _ j$ are big. For closed positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$, \[  \int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p} \leq I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p).  \] The numbers are positively homogeneous in each class and increase when a pseudo-effective class is added to any argument. For nef classes they equal the cohomological intersection numbers $\int _ X\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$. Big classes have positive volume. Proof. Big classes. Any two potentials with minimal singularities in a fixed big class differ by a bounded function, and a change of smooth representative changes each potential by a smooth function. Hence corollary 13.8.8 shows that $I_\omega $ does not depend on these choices. The same corollary and minimality give the upper bound for closed positive currents in big classes. If $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is another Kähler form in the class of $\omega $, with $f$ smooth, then $\omega '^{n-p}-\omega ^{n-p}=\mathrm d\bigl (\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \sum _{i=0}^{n-p-1}\omega '^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-p-1-i}\bigr )$ is a smooth exact form. Its integral against the closed current $\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle $ vanishes, because $S(\mathrm d\psi )=\pm (\mathrm dS)(\psi )=0$ for a closed current $S$ and a smooth form $\psi $ on the compact manifold $X$. Hence the numbers for big classes do not depend on $\omega $ within its class, and neither do their limits, since the perturbing classes $\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ are the same. Let $\alpha $ be big and $\gamma $ pseudo-effective, represented by a closed positive current $S$. Adding $S$ to a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $ gives a current in the big class $\alpha +\gamma $, which by the upper bound has mixed mass at most the number with $\alpha $ replaced by $\alpha +\gamma $. By multilinearity and positivity, its mixed mass is at least the number for $\alpha $. Hence, when all arguments are big, replacing an argument $\alpha $ by $\alpha +\gamma $ increases the number. Homogeneity for big classes follows by scaling a minimal potential together with its background: if $c>0$, then $cV_\theta $ has minimal singularities in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,c\theta )$, and the product is homogeneous in each factor by proposition 13.2.6 . Pseudo-effective classes. By this monotonicity for big classes, the perturbed numbers decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; they are nonnegative, so the limit exists. Every Kähler form $\kappa $ satisfies $c^{-1}\omega \leq \kappa \leq c\omega $ for some $c\geq 1$ (lemma 6.14.1 ), so monotonicity places the perturbation by $\varepsilon \kappa $ between the perturbations by $c^{-1}\varepsilon \omega $ and $c\varepsilon \omega $, with the same fixed test form $\omega ^{n-p}$; this proves independence of the perturbing class. The same comparison shows that perturbing the arguments by different fixed multiples of $\varepsilon \omega $ gives the same limit, which extends homogeneity to pseudo-effective classes. Monotonicity also extends: if $\gamma $ is pseudo-effective, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ the number with an argument $\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ replaced by $\alpha +\gamma +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is at least the original one, by the big case, and we let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. If all $\alpha _ j$ are big, choose $\delta >0$ such that each $\alpha _ j$ contains a Kähler current $R_ j\geq \delta \omega $. Then $(1+\varepsilon /\delta )\alpha _ j-(\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )=(\varepsilon /\delta )\{ R_ j-\delta \omega \} $ is pseudo-effective, so monotonicity and homogeneity give \[  I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)\leq I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots ,\alpha _ p+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )\leq (1+\varepsilon /\delta )^ pI_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p),  \] and the limit is $I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)$. For arbitrary closed positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$, the upper bound in the big classes $\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, applied to $T_ j+\varepsilon \omega $, and multilinearity give $\int _ X\langle \bigwedge _ jT_ j\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}\leq I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots )$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the upper bound. Nef and big classes. If the $\alpha _ j$ are nef, their perturbations are Kähler classes: $\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ contains $\theta _{j,\varepsilon /2}+\varepsilon \omega \geq \varepsilon \omega /2$, where $\theta _{j,\varepsilon /2}\geq -(\varepsilon /2)\omega $ is a smooth representative of $\alpha _ j$ given by definition 10.4.1 . If $\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is a Kähler form with $f$ smooth, then $f\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega )$, so $V_{\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }\geq f-\sup _ Xf$ by lemma 10.3.8 ; since also $V_{\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }\leq 0$ by the same lemma, the minimal potentials are bounded. By proposition 13.5.1 , the perturbed numbers are the integrals $\int _ X\bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega )\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$, and their limits are the cohomological intersection numbers. Finally, let $\alpha $ be big and $T_0\in \alpha $ a Kähler current with $T_0\geq \delta \omega $. Expanding $T_0=\delta \omega +(T_0-\delta \omega )$ by multilinearity gives $\langle T_0^ n\rangle \geq \delta ^ n\omega ^ n$, so $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )\geq \delta ^ n\int _ X\omega ^ n>0$ by the upper bound. $\square$

title: Definition 13.9.3
text: Definition 13.9.3 . 2AF01ACCF985 A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ has full Monge–Ampère mass if $\int _ X\langle T^ n\rangle =\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$. We write $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$ for the set of $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has full Monge–Ampère mass. For $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the class $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ consists of the potentials $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\leq \phi +O(1)$ and \[  \int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi )^ n\rangle ;  \] these potentials have full mass relative to $\phi $. In a big class, $\mathcal E(X,\theta )=\mathcal E(X,\theta ,V_\theta )$, because every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $u\leq V_\theta +\sup _ Xu$ and $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$ is the mass of $V_\theta $.

title: Corollary 13.9.4
text: Corollary 13.9.4 . 45601E7EC1EE Let $u_ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u_ k\leq \phi +C_ k$ for constants $C_ k$, let $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and suppose that $u_ k\to u$ in extended capacity. Then \[  \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k)^ n\rangle \longrightarrow \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle  \] weakly, and the masses converge. The same holds, without the constants $C_ k$, if $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta )$; in particular it holds for every sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ that decreases to an element of $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$. Proof. By theorem 13.8.7 , the mass of each $u_ k$ is at most that of $\phi $, which equals the mass of $u$. Hence theorem 13.7.5 , with $p=n$, gives weak convergence, and its lower inequality together with this bound gives convergence of the masses. If $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta )$, then by proposition 13.9.2 the mass of each $u_ k$ is at most $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$, which is the mass of $u$, and the same argument applies. Finally, decreasing sequences converge in extended capacity by lemma 13.7.3 . $\square$

title: Proposition 13.9.5
text: Proposition 13.9.5 . FEA17FAE6BAA For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ write $\mu _ u=\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle $. Then for all $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ v \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ u+\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )-\mu _ u(X).  \] The last two terms may be omitted if $u$ has full mass or if $u\geq v-O(1)$. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$. The function $w=\max \{ u,v-\varepsilon \} $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ and $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ are disjoint and plurifine open. Indeed, near each point we have $u-v=(u+h)-(v+h)$ for a smooth local potential $h$ of $\theta $, and $u+h$, $v+h$ are plurisubharmonic, so by proposition 5.47.25 the function $u-v$ is plurifinely continuous off the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, which is disjoint from both sets. Moreover $w$ equals $v-\varepsilon $ on the first set and $u$ on the second. By plurifine locality (proposition 13.2.6 ), \[  \mu _ w(X)\geq \mu _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} )+\mu _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} ).  \] The left side is at most $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$ by proposition 13.9.2 . The complement of $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ consists of $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $, which is contained in $\{ u<v\} $ up to the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, and that pluripolar set carries no mass. Hence \[  \mu _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} )\leq \operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )-\mu _ u(X)+\mu _ u(\{ u<v\} ).  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ increase to $\{ u<v\} $, which proves the inequality. If $u$ has full mass, the last two terms cancel. If $u\geq v-O(1)$, then $w-u$ is bounded, so $\mu _ w(X)=\mu _ u(X)$ by corollary 13.8.8 , and the same computation with $\mu _ u(X)$ in place of the volume gives the inequality without these terms. $\square$

title: Corollary 13.9.6
text: Corollary 13.9.6 . D91589CC5A89 Let $u,v,\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\geq v-O(1)$ and $u\geq \rho -O(1)$. If $u\geq v$ almost everywhere for $\mu _ u$, then $u\geq v$ almost everywhere for $\mu _\rho $. If, in addition, the class $\{ \theta \} $ is big and $u$ has minimal singularities, then $u\geq v$ everywhere on $X$. Proof. After adding a constant to $\rho $ we may assume $\rho \leq u$. For $0<t<1$ put $q_ t=(1-t)v+t\rho $. Then $u\geq q_ t-O(1)$, and $\{ u<q_ t\} \subset \{ u<v\} $, because $u<(1-t)v+t\rho \leq (1-t)v+tu$ forces $u<v$. Multilinearity and proposition 13.9.5 therefore give \[  t^ n\mu _\rho (\{ u<q_ t\} ) \leq \mu _{q_ t}(\{ u<q_ t\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<q_ t\} )\leq \mu _ u(\{ u<v\} )=0.  \] As $t\downarrow 0$, every point where $u<v$ and $\rho >-\infty $ eventually lies in $\{ u<q_ t\} $, so Fatou's lemma, applied along a sequence $t\downarrow 0$, gives $\mu _\rho (\{ u<v\} \cap \{ \rho >-\infty \} )=0$. Since $\mu _\rho $ gives no mass to the pole set of $\rho $, this proves the first assertion. Now let the class be big and $u$ have minimal singularities. The class contains a Kähler current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$. Then $u\geq \rho -O(1)$ by minimality, and $\mu _\rho \geq \delta ^ n\omega ^ n$, because multilinearity expands $\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n\rangle =\langle (\delta \omega +(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho -\delta \omega ))^ n\rangle $ into positive terms, one of which is $\delta ^ n\omega ^ n$. The first assertion gives $u\geq v$ almost everywhere with respect to $\omega ^ n$, that is, almost everywhere for Lebesgue measure in charts. Near each point, $u$ and $v$ become plurisubharmonic after adding a common smooth local potential $h$ of $\theta $, and then $\max \{ u,v\} +h$ and $u+h$ are plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere; by theorem 5.9.1 , theorem 3.4.12 they agree everywhere, that is, $u\geq v$ everywhere. $\square$

title: 16.10 Envelopes and model potentials
text: Throughout this chapter $X$ is a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a fixed Kähler form $\omega $, and $\theta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, as in the two preceding chapters. Many potentials are defined as envelopes: given an obstacle $f$, one takes the largest $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function that lies below $f$ outside a pluripolar set. For instance, the extremal potential $V_\theta $ of definition 10.3.7 is the envelope of the obstacle $0$. Two features of the global setting require care. The obstacle is often only a Borel function, so we must keep track of which inequalities hold everywhere and which only quasi-everywhere. And there may be no $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function below the obstacle at all: two $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions need not have a common $\theta $-plurisubharmonic minorant (example 16.11.7 ). The basic property of an envelope is that its non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure is carried by the contact set, where the envelope touches the obstacle; for quasi-continuous obstacles in a big class this is theorem 16.13.4 . Away from the contact set, the envelope of a lower semicontinuous obstacle can be replaced locally by a maximal plurisubharmonic function, so its measure vanishes there, and quasi-continuity lets us approximate a general obstacle by lower semicontinuous ones. Regularity of the obstacles also passes to the envelope. If finitely many obstacles have bounded Laplacian with respect to the Riemannian metric of $\omega $, then so does the envelope of their minimum. For a Kähler background we prove this with an exponentially penalized Monge–Ampère equation (theorem 16.15.24 ), which also shows that envelopes of finite minima of $C^{1,1}$ obstacles are $C^{1,1}$ (theorem 16.16.7 ); in a big class the bound holds locally on the ample locus, the complement of the non-Kähler locus (theorem 16.19.1 ). On the contact set of such an obstacle with an arbitrary potential lying below it, the non-pluripolar measure of the potential is then computed from the second derivatives of the obstacle (theorem 16.20.2 ). The second half of the chapter studies envelopes that prescribe singularities rather than values. The singularity envelope $P_\theta [u]$ of a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$ is the upper envelope of all nonpositive $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions $v$ with $v\leq u+C$ for some constant $C$, which may depend on $v$. It has the same non-pluripolar masses as $u$ but may be less singular, and its fixed points of positive mass are called model potentials. The main tool is extrapolation (theorem 16.22.4 ): if $u$ is more singular than $v$ and has almost the same mass, then for some $a>1$ the function $v+a(u-v)$, which continues the segment from $v$ to $u$ beyond $u$, still has a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic minorant of positive mass. From this we derive the domination principle for potentials of full mass relative to a reference potential (theorem 16.22.10 ) and the characterization of $P_\theta [u]$, for $u$ of positive mass, as the largest nonpositive potential that is less singular than $u$ and has the same mass (theorem 16.22.11 ). Rooftop envelopes satisfy a mass inequality (theorem 16.23.5 ), and upper envelopes preserve the comparison of singularities through multiplier ideals (section 16.24 ). Finally we introduce the Monge–Ampère capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ relative to a reference potential $\phi $, prove that it is comparable with the capacity of a Kähler form when $\phi $ has positive mass (theorem 16.27.17 ), and use it to measure the deep sublevel sets $\{ u<\phi -s\} $ of potentials of full mass relative to $\phi $. These estimates are what the next chapter needs in order to integrate by parts with singular potentials. Singularity envelopes of potentials of zero mass, and contact concentration in arbitrary pseudo-effective classes, depend on the Monge–Ampère equations solved there (section 17.6 , subsection 17.5.27 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in subsection 25.1.16 .

title: 16.11 Obstacles and rooftops
text:
The fixed Kähler form $\omega $ serves as a reference: volumes, norms and the Laplacians of obstacles are taken with respect to $\omega $, also when an envelope is formed with respect to a different background. We call the elements of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ (definition 6.14.3 ) potentials ; they are pointwise defined functions, not identically $-\infty $. Recall from definition 10.3.7 that $u$ is more singular than $v$, written $u\preceq v$, if $u\leq v+C$ for some constant $C$. We write $u\sim v$, and say that $u$ and $v$ have the same singularity type , if $u\preceq v$ and $v\preceq u$. Two facts are used constantly. First, pluripolar sets have Lebesgue measure zero (see the remarks after definition 5.47.2 ). Second, if two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions satisfy $u\leq v$ almost everywhere, then $u\leq v$ everywhere, by lemma 6.14.4 (1). Consequently, an inequality between quasi-plurisubharmonic functions that holds quasi-everywhere, that is, outside a pluripolar set (definition 5.47.2 ), holds everywhere. In particular, if $u\sim v$, then $u$ and $v$ have the same pole set and $u-v$ is bounded outside it. Quasi-continuity on $X$ is the notion of definition 7.5.1 , read in local charts as in section 13.7 : a Borel function $f\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is quasi-continuous if its restriction to every coordinate chart, identified with a bounded open set $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$, is quasi-continuous for the Monge–Ampère capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ of definition 7.4.2 . The following lemma shows that it suffices to check this on the charts of one atlas; in proposition 16.27.18 we show that quasi-continuous functions are also continuous outside open sets of small global capacity. Lemma 16.11.1 . 33A40EB62C98 Let $D$ and $D'$ be coordinate charts of $X$, identified with bounded open subsets of $\mathbb C^ n$. For every compact set $L\subset D\cap D'$ there is a constant $c$ such that $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(E)\leq c\operatorname {Cap}_{D'}(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset L$. If $E\subset X$ is pluripolar, then $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(E\cap D)=0$. If a Borel function $f\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is quasi-continuous on each chart of an atlas of $X$, then it is quasi-continuous on every coordinate chart. Proof. Assertions (1) and (3) are contained in lemma 13.7.1 : (1) is its inequality for Borel sets, applied with the roles of $D$ and $D'$ exchanged, and (3) is its final assertion. For (2) we first observe that if $W\subset D$ is open, then every competitor $v$ for $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ restricts to a plurisubharmonic function on $W$ with values in $[0,1]$, and the restriction of the Bedford–Taylor measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ to $W$ is the Bedford–Taylor measure of this restriction. Hence $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(E)\leq \operatorname {Cap}_ W(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset W$, and, taking infima over the open sets $G$ with $A\subset G\subset W$, also $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(A)\leq \operatorname {Cap}_ W^*(A)$ for every set $A\subset W$. Now cover $D$ by countably many open balls $B_ k$, in the coordinates of $D$, with $\overline{B_ k}\subset D$. Since the condition in definition 5.47.2 is local, $E\cap B_ k$ is pluripolar in $B_ k$, so $\operatorname {Cap}_{B_ k}^*(E\cap B_ k)=0$ by theorem 5.47.8 . By the observation above, $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(E\cap B_ k)=0$, and the countable subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*$ (proposition 7.4.3 ) gives $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(E\cap D)=0$. $\square$ Quasi-plurisubharmonic functions are quasi-continuous, and quasi-continuity is preserved by the following operations. Lemma 16.11.2 . 1BA71B27F698 Let $	heta '$ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ')$ is quasi-continuous. In particular, every potential $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is quasi-continuous. Finite maxima and minima of quasi-continuous functions on $X$ are quasi-continuous. If $f$ is quasi-continuous on $X$ and $g\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is a Borel function that agrees with $f$ outside a pluripolar set, then $g$ is quasi-continuous. Proof. (1) By lemma 5.4.2 every point of $X$ has a neighborhood on which $	heta '=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ for a smooth function $h$, so $X$ is covered by finitely many coordinate balls $D_ i$ on which $	heta '=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ i$ with $h_ i$ smooth near $\overline{D_ i}$. On $D_ i$ the function $u+h_ i$ is plurisubharmonic by lemma 6.14.4 (2), hence quasi-continuous by theorem 7.5.2 , and so is $u=(u+h_ i)-h_ i$, because $h_ i$ is continuous and real. By lemma 16.11.1 (3), $u$ is quasi-continuous on every chart. (2) Let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ k$ be quasi-continuous, let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart $D$, and let $\varepsilon >0$. Choose open sets $G_ i\subset D$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G_ i)<\varepsilon /k$ such that $f_ i$ is continuous on $K\setminus G_ i$. By subadditivity, $G=G_1\cup \cdots \cup G_ k$ has capacity less than $\varepsilon $, and all the $f_ i$, hence also their maximum and minimum, are continuous on $K\setminus G$. (3) Let $D$ be a chart, $K\subset D$ compact and $\varepsilon >0$. The set $\{ f
e g\} $ is pluripolar, so by lemma 16.11.1 (2) its intersection with $D$ is contained in an open set $G'\subset D$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G')<\varepsilon /2$. If $G\subset D$ is an open set with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G)<\varepsilon /2$ such that $f$ is continuous on $K\setminus G$, then $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G\cup G')<\varepsilon $, and $g=f$ is continuous on $K\setminus (G\cup G')$. $\square$ Definition 16.11.3 . A4F165851008 Let $f\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ be a Borel function, called an obstacle , and put \[  \mathcal A_	heta (f)=\{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):v\leq f 	ext{ quasi-everywhere}\} .  \] The members of $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ are called the competitors for $f$. If $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, the obstacle envelope of $f$ is \[  P_	heta (f)= igl (\sup \mathcal A_	heta (f) igr )^*,  \] where ${}^*$ denotes the upper semicontinuous regularization. If $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is empty, we put $P_	heta (f)=-\infty $. If $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty but not uniformly bounded above, $P_	heta (f)$ is not defined, and whenever we use $P_	heta (f)$ for an obstacle that is not bounded above, we verify the upper bound first. If $f\leq b$ quasi-everywhere for a constant $b$, the upper bound is automatic: every competitor satisfies $v\leq b$ quasi-everywhere, hence almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere by lemma 6.14.4 (1). As for the capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ (definition 7.4.2 ) and the relative extremal functions of section 5.47 , a competitor is a member of the family whose supremum defines the object under consideration; we always say which obstacle, envelope or capacity is meant. Proposition 16.11.4 . 641F3FEC623D Let $f$ be a Borel obstacle. If $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, then $P_	heta (f)\in \mathcal A_	heta (f)$; thus $P_	heta (f)$ is the largest competitor for $f$. If $f$ is upper semicontinuous, then every competitor $v$ for $f$ satisfies $v\leq f$ everywhere. The envelope does not change when $f$ is modified on a pluripolar set, and $P_	heta (f+c)=P_	heta (f)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. Applying theorem 5.10.2 on each ball to the plurisubharmonic functions $v+h$, $v\in \mathcal A_	heta (f)$, and taking the union of the resulting countable subfamilies, we find competitors $v_1,v_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _ kv_ k)^*=P_	heta (f)$. Each $w_ k$ satisfies $w_ k\leq f$ outside a pluripolar set $N_ k$, and $N= igcup _ kN_ k$ is pluripolar by theorem 5.47.8 . Thus $P_	heta (f)$ is a competitor, and by construction it dominates every competitor. (2) Let $v$ be a competitor, let $x\in X$, and choose a coordinate ball $B(x,r)$ and a smooth function $h$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $ near its closure. Since $v+h$ is plurisubharmonic and $v\leq f$ outside a Lebesgue null set, the sub-mean value inequality gives \[  v(x)+h(x)\leq  rac1{|B(x,r)|}\int _{B(x,r)}(v+h)\, \mathrm dV_{2n} \leq \sup _{B(x,r)}(f+h).  \] As $r	o 0$, the right side tends to at most $f(x)+h(x)$, because $f+h$ is upper semicontinuous. Hence $v(x)\leq f(x)$. (3) A modification of $f$ on a pluripolar set does not change $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$, since the union of two pluripolar sets is pluripolar. Moreover $\mathcal A_	heta (f+c)=\mathcal A_	heta (f)+c$, and $\mathcal A_	heta (f)\subset \mathcal A_	heta (g)$ if $f\leq g$ quasi-everywhere. These relations between the families of competitors give the three assertions. (4) By (3), $\mathcal A_	heta (f)-c\subset \mathcal A_	heta (g)\subset \mathcal A_	heta (f)+c$. Thus $v$ is a competitor for $f$ and $v\leq P_	heta (f)$; the reverse inequality follows from $P_	heta (f)\leq P_	heta (f_ j)$. Suppose next that $v\equiv -\infty $. A competitor $w$ for $f$ would be a competitor for every $f_ j$, so $w\leq P_	heta (f_ j)$ for all $j$ and $w\leq v$, which is impossible. Hence $\mathcal A_	heta (f)=\varnothing $ and $P_	heta (f)=-\infty =v$. $\square$ Definition 16.11.5 . F80B4C1B3032 For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, the rooftop envelope of $u$ and $v$ is \[  P_	heta (u,v)=P_	heta (\min \{ u,v\} ).  \] We also put $P_	heta (u,-\infty )=P_	heta (-\infty ,u)=-\infty $ for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $. The obstacle $\min \{ u,v\} $ is upper semicontinuous and bounded above. By proposition 16.11.4 , a potential is therefore a competitor for it exactly when it lies below both $u$ and $v$ everywhere. Thus $P_	heta (u,v)$ is the largest common minorant of $u$ and $v$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ if they have one, and $P_	heta (u,v)=-\infty $ if they have none. For a constant $c$, $P_	heta (u+c,v+c)=P_	heta (u,v)+c$. Commutativity, monotonicity and idempotence follow directly from the description of $P_	heta (u,v)$ as the largest common minorant. For associativity, let also $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $. A potential lies below $P_	heta (u,v)$ and $w$ if and only if it lies below $u$, $v$ and $w$: when $P_	heta (u,v)
e -\infty $ this is the maximality of $P_	heta (u,v)$, and otherwise neither condition can be satisfied. Hence $P_	heta (P_	heta (u,v),w)$ and $P_	heta (u,P_	heta (v,w))$ are both the largest common minorant of $u$, $v$ and $w$, or both equal $-\infty $ if there is none. If $u$ or $v$ is identically $-\infty $, this limit obstacle has no competitor, in accordance with our convention. For the last assertion put $B=\max \{ \sup _ Xu,-C\} $. Then $u-B\leq 0$, so $u-B\leq V_	heta $, and also $u-B\leq u+C$. Hence $u-B$ is a common minorant of $u+C$ and $V_	heta $, and \[  u-B\leq P_	heta (u+C,V_	heta )\leq u+C.  \] $\square$ Example 16.11.7 . 908479CB91B3 On $\mathbb P^1$ let $	heta =\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$ be the Fubini–Study form of example 10.6.7 , in the affine coordinate $z$, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^1}	heta =1$.
