title: 16.22 Extrapolation and model singularities
text: Throughout this section $\{ \theta \} $ is big, and all potentials belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Mass is monotone with respect to $\preceq $, but two potentials with the same mass need not have bounded difference (example 16.22.12 ). The basic step reverses a convex combination: if $u\preceq v$ and the mass lost from $v$ to $u$ is small, then $u\geq a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v$ for some $a>1$ and some potential $\eta $ of positive mass. The contact concentration of section 16.13 prevents the envelopes used to construct $\eta $ from collapsing. This extrapolation yields the domination principle and identifies the singularity envelopes of potentials of positive mass as model potentials. Lemma 16.22.1 . 7420706BAE2F Let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\psi \leq 0$ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle >0$. Then there is a model potential $\phi \geq \psi $ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle $. Proof. Fix a smooth probability volume form $\mathrm dV$ on $X$, put $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle $, and consider \[  \mathcal S=\{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\psi \leq v\leq 0, \  \int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle =m\} , \qquad H(v)=\int _ Xv\, \mathrm dV.  \] The set $\mathcal S$ contains $\psi $, and $H$ takes values in $[H(\psi ),0]$ on it. We construct an increasing sequence in $\mathcal S$ that almost maximizes $H$ at every stage. Put $v_0=\psi $. Given $v_ k\in \mathcal S$, let \[  s_ k=\sup \{ H(w):w\in \mathcal S,\  w\geq v_ k\} ,  \] and choose $v_{k+1}\in \mathcal S$ with $v_{k+1}\geq v_ k$ and $H(v_{k+1})\geq s_ k-2^{-k}$. The regularized limit $\phi =(\sup _ kv_ k)^*$ is a potential with $\psi \leq \phi \leq 0$, and $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =m$ by corollary 13.8.9 ; thus $\phi \in \mathcal S$. Since $v_ k$ increases to $\phi $ almost everywhere, between the integrable bounds $\psi $ and $0$, dominated convergence gives $H(v_ k)\to H(\phi )$. Let $w\in \mathcal S$ with $w\geq \phi $. Then $w\geq v_ k$ for every $k$, so \[  H(w)\leq s_ k\leq H(v_{k+1})+2^{-k},  \] and letting $k\to \infty $ gives $H(w)\leq H(\phi )$. Since $w\geq \phi $, it follows that $w=\phi $ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. Now $P_\theta [\phi ]$ lies between $\phi $ and $0$, because $\phi \leq 0$ is a competitor for it, and it has mass $m$ by proposition 16.21.2 . Thus $P_\theta [\phi ]\in \mathcal S$ and $P_\theta [\phi ]\geq \phi $, so $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $. Since $m>0$, $\phi $ is a model potential. $\square$ Lemma 16.22.2 . 4D5FAF80D021 Let $\phi ,\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $ and $\tau \preceq \phi $. Then \[  \sup _{\{ \phi > -\infty \} }(\tau -\phi )=\sup _ X\tau .  \] In particular, if $\tau \leq 0$, then $\tau \leq \phi $. Proof. The potential $\tau -\sup _ X\tau $ is nonpositive and more singular than $\phi $, so it is a competitor for $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $. Hence $\tau -\phi \leq \sup _ X\tau $ wherever $\phi $ is finite. Conversely, $\phi \leq 0$, so $\tau -\phi \geq \tau $ wherever $\phi $ is finite. The pole set of $\phi $ is pluripolar, and removing a pluripolar set does not change the supremum of the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\tau $: an upper bound for $\tau $ off a Lebesgue null set holds everywhere. This proves the reverse inequality. $\square$ The envelopes used for extrapolation have obstacles of the form $au+(1-a)v$ with $a>1$. The following lemma collects their basic properties. Lemma 16.22.3 . B36FB6000F3B Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\leq v$, let $a>1$, and put $f=au+(1-a)v$, where $f=-\infty $ on the pole set of $u$, which contains that of $v$. The obstacle $f$ is quasi-continuous, and $f\leq u$. A potential $\eta $ satisfies \[  a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u  \] if and only if $\eta \leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Suppose that $f$ has a competitor. Then $\eta =P_\theta (f)$ is the largest potential satisfying this inequality, and $\eta \leq u$. Moreover, if $\gamma =a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v$ and $D=\{ \gamma =u>-\infty \} $, then \[  \mu _\eta \leq a^ n\mathbf1_ D\mu _ u.  \] Proof. (1) Off the pole set of $u$, the functions $u$ and $v$ are finite and $f=u+(a-1)(u-v)\leq u$, because $u\leq v$; on the pole set, $f=-\infty $. Thus $f$ is a Borel function with $f\leq u$. Let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart. Since $u$ and $v$ are quasi-continuous (lemma 16.11.2 (1)), there are open sets of arbitrarily small capacity outside which both are continuous on $K$, as functions with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. On the complement in $K$ of such a set, $f$ is continuous at every point where $u$ is finite, because $v\geq u$ is finite near such a point, and at a pole of $u$ it is continuous with value $-\infty $, because $f\leq u$. Hence $f$ is quasi-continuous. Off the pole set of $u$, the inequalities $\eta \leq f$ and $a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u$ are equivalent. Since the pole set is pluripolar, and an inequality between quasi-plurisubharmonic functions that holds quasi-everywhere holds everywhere, this proves the equivalence. (2) By (1), the potentials satisfying the inequality are exactly the competitors for $f$; since $f\leq u$, they lie below $u$ quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere. Thus $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ is nonempty, by assumption, and uniformly bounded above, and proposition 16.11.4 shows that $\eta $ is its largest member; in particular $\eta \leq u$ and $\gamma \leq u$. By theorem 16.13.4 , $\mu _\eta $ is carried by $\{ \eta =f\} $. At a point of this set at which $u$ is finite, $\eta =au+(1-a)v$ means $\gamma =u$; since $\mu _\eta $ does not charge the pole set of $u$, it is carried by $D$. Moreover $\mu _\gamma \geq a^{-n}\mu _\eta $, and lemma 16.13.1 , applied to $\gamma \leq u$, gives $\mathbf1_ D\mu _\gamma \leq \mathbf1_ D\mu _ u$. Hence \[  \mu _\eta =\mathbf1_ D\mu _\eta \leq a^ n\mathbf1_ D\mu _\gamma \leq a^ n\mathbf1_ D\mu _ u.  \] $\square$ Theorem 16.22.4 . FCFA7EB59B34 Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq v$ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$, and let $a>1$ satisfy 4801296ED5A2 16.22.5 \begin{equation}  a^ n\left(\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \right)<\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle . \end{equation} Then there exists $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _\eta ^ n\rangle >0$ such that C646467A8FDD 16.22.6 \begin{equation}  a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u. \end{equation} The largest such $\eta $ is the obstacle envelope $E_ a(u,v)=P_\theta (au+(1-a)v)$; here the obstacle $au+(1-a)v$ is defined to be $-\infty $ on the pole set of $u$, which contains that of $v$. If $u$ and $v$ have the same mass, then ( 16.22.5 ) holds for every $a>1$, and $E_ a(u,v)$ also has this mass. Proof. We first construct one potential satisfying ( 16.22.6 ) as the limit of a decreasing sequence of envelopes, and then show that $E_ a(u,v)$ is the largest solution and has positive mass. Reduction. Since $u\preceq v$, there are constants $A,B$ with $u-A\leq v-B\leq 0$. If $\eta '$ satisfies ( 16.22.6 ) for the pair $u-A$, $v-B$, then $\eta '+aA+(1-a)B$ satisfies it for $u$, $v$; the envelopes of the two pairs differ by the same constant, and masses do not change. We may therefore assume that $u\leq v\leq 0$. Then $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$, and lemma 16.22.1 provides a model potential $\phi \geq v$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =m$. Since $1-a<0$, we have $au+(1-a)\phi \leq au+(1-a)v$; we first construct a potential below $au+(1-a)\phi $. A decreasing sequence of envelopes. For $j\geq 1$ put $u_ j=\max \{ u,\phi -j\} $, so that $\phi -j\leq u_ j\leq \phi $; in particular, $u_ j$ and $\phi $ have the same pole set. Put \[  f_ j=au_ j+(1-a)\phi ,\qquad \eta _ j=P_\theta (f_ j),  \] where $f_ j=-\infty $ on the pole set of $\phi $, as in lemma 16.22.3 for the pair $u_ j\leq \phi $. Outside this pole set, $f_ j=\phi +a(u_ j-\phi )$ lies between $\phi -aj$ and $\phi $. Hence the potential $\phi -aj$ is a competitor, and every competitor is at most $\phi $, so $\eta _ j$ is a potential with \[  \phi -aj\leq \eta _ j\leq \phi ,\qquad \int _ X\langle \theta _{\eta _ j}^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _{u_ j}^ n\rangle =m,  \] where the masses agree because $\eta _ j\sim \phi \sim u_ j$. Since $u_ j$ decreases with $j$, so do $f_ j$ and $\eta _ j$. A contact bound. Put $\gamma _ j=a^{-1}\eta _ j+(1-a^{-1})\phi $ and $D_ j=\{ \gamma _ j=u_ j>-\infty \} $. By lemma 16.22.3 (2), applied to the pair $u_ j\leq \phi $, we have $\gamma _ j\leq u_ j$ and B2A56AF9922E 16.22.7 \begin{equation}  \mu _{\eta _ j}\leq a^ n\mathbf1_{D_ j}\mu _{u_ j}. \end{equation} A tail estimate. Fix $k>0$ and let $j>k$. On $D_ j$ we have $\eta _ j=\phi +a(u_ j-\phi )$, so there $\eta _ j\leq \phi -ak$ if and only if $u_ j\leq \phi -k$, that is, if and only if $u\leq \phi -k$. The plurifine open set $\{ u>\phi -k\} $ is contained in $\{ u>\phi -j\} $, on which $u_ j=u$; hence $\mu _{u_ j}=\mu _ u$ on $\{ u>\phi -k\} $, and $\mu _{u_ j}(\{ u\leq \phi -k\} )=m-\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )$, pole sets having measure zero. Together with ( 16.22.7 ) this gives 246B560461D1 16.22.8 \begin{equation}  \mu _{\eta _ j}(\{ \eta _ j\leq \phi -ak\} ) \leq a^ n\left(m-\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )\right). \end{equation} The envelopes do not collapse. Suppose that $\eta _ j$ decreases to $-\infty $ identically. Then $\sup _ X\eta _ j\to -\infty $ by corollary 10.3.6 . Since $\eta _ j\preceq \phi $ and $\phi $ is a model potential, lemma 16.22.2 gives $\eta _ j-\phi \leq \sup _ X\eta _ j$ off the pole set of $\phi $. Hence, for each $k$, $\eta _ j\leq \phi -ak$ everywhere once $j$ is large, and the left side of ( 16.22.8 ) equals $\int _ X\langle \theta _{\eta _ j}^ n\rangle =m$. Since $\phi $ is finite wherever $u$ is, $\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )\to \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $ as $k\to \infty $, and ( 16.22.8 ) yields $m\leq a^ n\bigl (m-\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \bigr )$, which contradicts ( 16.22.5 ). Consequently $\eta _ j$ decreases to a potential $\eta $. Letting $j\to \infty $ in $\gamma _ j\leq u_ j$ gives $a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})\phi \leq u$, and since $v\leq \phi $, also ( 16.22.6 ). The largest solution. By lemma 16.22.3 (1), applied to the pair $u\leq v$, the potentials satisfying ( 16.22.6 ) are exactly the competitors for the obstacle $f=au+(1-a)v$. The potential $\eta $ constructed above is one of them, so part (2) of the lemma shows that $E_ a=E_ a(u,v)=P_\theta (f)$ is the largest potential satisfying ( 16.22.6 ), and that $E_ a\leq u$. Positive mass. Choose $b>a$ that still satisfies ( 16.22.5 ). The preceding steps, applied to $b$, give $E_ b=E_ b(u,v)$. The potential \[  q=\frac abE_ b+\left(1-\frac ab\right)u  \] is a competitor for the obstacle $f$ of $E_ a$: quasi-everywhere, $E_ b\leq bu+(1-b)v$, and therefore \[  q\leq au+(1-a)v+\left(1-\frac ab\right)(u-v)\leq au+(1-a)v.  \] Hence $q\leq E_ a$, and the monotonicity of mass together with $\mu _ q\geq (1-a/b)^ n\mu _ u$ yields \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _{E_ a}^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _ q^ n\rangle \geq \left(1-\frac ab\right)^ n\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0.  \] If $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle $, then ( 16.22.5 ) holds for every $a>1$, so $b$ can be taken arbitrarily large, and we obtain $\int _ X\langle \theta _{E_ a}^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $. The reverse inequality follows from $E_ a\leq u$. $\square$ Lemma 16.22.9 . 52ED2F2B0A63 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$. Then there are $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\leq u$ and $\delta >0$ such that $\theta _ v\geq \delta \omega $. Proof. Put $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _{V_\theta }^ n\rangle $. Since $u\preceq V_\theta $ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$, we can choose $a>1$ so close to one that $a^ n\bigl (m-\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \bigr )<m$. Theorem 16.22.4 gives $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})V_\theta \leq u$. Since the class is big, it contains a closed current $T\geq \delta _0\omega $ for some $\delta _0>0$, and by theorem 10.2.15 we can write $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ with $\psi $ quasi-plurisubharmonic; after subtracting a constant, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $\psi \leq 0$ and $\theta _\psi \geq \delta _0\omega $, and $\psi \leq V_\theta $ because $\psi $ is a competitor for $V_\theta $. Therefore \[  v=a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})\psi \leq u,\qquad \theta _ v=a^{-1}\theta _\eta +(1-a^{-1})\theta _\psi \geq (1-a^{-1})\delta _0\omega .  \] $\square$ Recall from definition 13.9.3 that, for $\chi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the class $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\chi )$ of potentials of full mass relative to $\chi $ consists of the potentials $u\preceq \chi $ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\chi ^ n\rangle $. Theorem 16.22.10 (Domination principle) . 0F4D01059518 Let $\chi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _\chi ^ n\rangle >0$, and let $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\chi )$. If $\mu _ u(\{ u<v\} )=0$, then $u\geq v$ everywhere on $X$. Proof. After reducing to the case $u\leq v$, we show that the extrapolation envelopes $E_ a(u,v)$ agree with $u$ almost everywhere for $\mu _ u$. Hence they do not collapse as $a\to \infty $, while their limit equals $-\infty $ quasi-everywhere on $\{ u<v\} $, so that this set is pluripolar. The potential $\max \{ u,v\} $ is more singular than $\chi $ and less singular than $u$, so \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _\chi ^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\chi ^ n\rangle ;  \] thus $\max \{ u,v\} \in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\chi )$. Since $\{ u<\max \{ u,v\} \} =\{ u<v\} $, we may replace $v$ by $\max \{ u,v\} $ and assume that $u\leq v$. Subtracting the same constant from $u$ and $v$, we may also assume $v\leq 0$. Let $m>0$ be the common mass of $u$, $v$ and $\chi $. For $a>1$ let $\eta _ a=E_ a(u,v)$, $\gamma _ a=a^{-1}\eta _ a+(1-a^{-1})v$ and $D_ a=\{ \gamma _ a=u>-\infty \} $. By theorem 16.22.4 , $\eta _ a$ is a potential of mass $m$; in particular its obstacle $au+(1-a)v$ has a competitor, and lemma 16.22.3 (2), applied to the pair $u\leq v$, gives $\eta _ a\leq u$, $\gamma _ a\leq u$ and \[  \mu _{\eta _ a}\leq a^ n\mathbf1_{D_ a}\mu _ u.  \] Since $u\leq v$, the hypothesis means that $\mu _ u$ is carried by $\{ u=v\} $, so $\mu _{\eta _ a}$ is carried by $D_ a\cap \{ u=v\} $. At a point of this set, $a^{-1}\eta _ a+(1-a^{-1})u=u$, that is, $\eta _ a=u$. Hence $\mu _{\eta _ a}$ is carried by $\{ \eta _ a=u\} $, and lemma 16.13.1 , applied to $\eta _ a\leq u$, gives $\mu _{\eta _ a}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ \eta _ a=u\} }\mu _ u\leq \mu _ u$. Both measures have mass $m$, so they are equal, and $\eta _ a=u$ holds $\mu _ u$-almost everywhere. In particular \[  \int _ X\mathrm e^{\eta _ a}\, \mu _ u =\int _ X\mathrm e^ u\, \mu _ u>0,  \] where the last integral is positive because $m>0$ and $\mu _ u$ does not charge the pole set of $u$. As $a$ increases, the obstacle $v+a(u-v)$ decreases, so $\eta _ a$ decreases. If $\eta _ a$ decreased to $-\infty $ identically as $a\to \infty $ through the integers, dominated convergence, with $0\leq \mathrm e^{\eta _ a}\leq 1$, would make the left side of the last display tend to zero, a contradiction. Hence the limit $\eta $ along the integers is a potential. Each $\eta _ a$ satisfies $\eta _ a\leq v+a(u-v)$ outside a pluripolar set; let $N$ be the union of these sets over the integers $a\geq 2$. At a point outside $N$ where $u$ is finite and $u<v$, we get $\eta \leq v+a(u-v)$ for every integer $a$, hence $\eta =-\infty $. Thus $\{ u<v\} $ is contained in the union of $N$ and the pole sets of $u$ and $\eta $, which is pluripolar. Therefore $u\geq v$ quasi-everywhere, and hence everywhere. $\square$ Theorem 16.22.11 . 4A1DC8C4E020 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$. Then \[  P_\theta [u]=\max \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):v\leq 0, \  u\preceq v,\  \int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \} .  \] In particular $P_\theta [P_\theta [u]]=P_\theta [u]$, so $P_\theta [u]$ is a model potential of mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $. Proof. Write $w=P_\theta [u]$, and let $v$ belong to the displayed family. By proposition 16.21.2 , $w\leq P_\theta [v]$, and the potentials $w$, $u$, $v$ and $P_\theta [v]$ all have the same positive mass. Moreover $v\leq P_\theta [v]$, because $v\leq 0$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [v]$. Hence $w$ and $v$ both belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,P_\theta [v])$, a class whose reference potential has positive mass. By proposition 16.21.3 , $\mu _ w$ is carried by $\{ w=0\} $, and since $v\leq 0$, it gives no mass to $\{ w<v\} $. The domination principle, theorem 16.22.10 , yields $w\geq v$. Finally, $w$ itself belongs to the family: it is nonpositive, it satisfies $u-\sup _ Xu\leq w$, and it has the same mass as $u$ by proposition 16.21.2 . This proves the formula. The potential $P_\theta [w]$ is nonpositive, satisfies $u\preceq w\preceq P_\theta [w]$, and has the same mass as $u$ by proposition 16.21.2 . Hence it belongs to the family, and the formula gives $P_\theta [w]\leq w$. Conversely, $w\leq 0$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [w]$, so $P_\theta [w]=w$. Since the mass of $w$ is positive, $w$ is a model potential. $\square$ Example 16.22.12 . 246496245694 On $\mathbb P^1$ let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$ in the affine coordinate $z$, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega =1$; since $\omega $ is Kähler, $V_\omega =0$. Define \[  F(r)=\begin{cases}  \max \{ -\log (-r),r+2\} ,& r\leq -1,\\  r+2,& r\geq -1, \end{cases} \qquad u(z)=F(\log |z|^2)-\log (1+|z|^2).  \] The function $F$ is continuous and nondecreasing. Since $-\log (-r)<r+2$ at $r=-1$, there is $\delta >0$ with $F(r)=r+2$ for $r\geq -1-\delta $, and since $r+2+\log (-r)\to -\infty $ as $r\to -\infty $, we have $F(r)=-\log (-r)$ for all sufficiently negative $r$. We first show that $F(\log |z|^2)$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $. On the open set $\{ |z|^2>\mathrm e^{-1-\delta }\} $ it equals the harmonic function $\log |z|^2+2$. On the open set $\{ 0<|z|^2<\mathrm e^{-1}\} $ it equals $\max \{ g(\log |z|^2),\log |z|^2+2\} $, where $g(t)=-\log (-t)$ for $t<0$. Since $g''(t)=t^{-2}>0$, the function $g$ is convex, so it is the supremum of its tangent lines $t\mapsto g(s)+g'(s)(t-s)$, $s<0$, whose slopes $g'(s)=-1/s$ are positive. Hence $g(\log |z|^2)$ is a continuous supremum of the harmonic functions $g(s)+g'(s)(\log |z|^2-s)$; it therefore satisfies the submean inequality and is subharmonic, and so is its maximum with $\log |z|^2+2$. Since subharmonicity is a local property, $F(\log |z|^2)$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $; it tends to $-\infty $ at $0$ and extends subharmonically across the polar set $\{ 0\} $ by theorem 3.4.27 . Next we check that $u$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic. For $|z|^2\geq \mathrm e^{-1}$ we have $u=2-\log (1+|z|^{-2})$. In the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$ near $\infty $ this reads $u=2-\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$, while $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$, because $\log (1+|z|^2)=\log (1+|\zeta |^2)-\log |\zeta |^2$ and $\log |\zeta |^2$ is pluriharmonic for $\zeta \ne 0$; thus $u$ is smooth near $\infty $, with $u(\infty )=2$ and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=0$ there. Hence $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,\omega )$, with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(\log |z|^2)$ on $\mathbb C$, and its only pole is $0$. To compute the mass of $u$, note that its Lelong number at $0$ is that of the subharmonic function $F(\log |z|^2)$, which differs from $u$ by a smooth function, and since $F$ is continuous and nondecreasing, $\sup _{|z|<\mathrm e^{t/2}}F(\log |z|^2)=F(t)$. By proposition 6.7.1 , the Lelong number is therefore \[  \lim _{t\to -\infty }\frac{F(t)}t=\lim _{t\to -\infty }\frac{-\log (-t)}t=0.  \] By theorem 6.7.6 , in one variable the mass that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(\log |z|^2)$ gives to $0$ is this Lelong number, namely the limit of the masses of the discs $B(0,r)$ as $r\downarrow 0$, so the current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has no atom at its pole. By proposition 13.4.7 , $\mu _ u$ is the restriction of $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ to $\{ u>-\infty \} $, hence the mass of $u$ is $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\langle \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\rangle =\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega =1$. The potential $0$ is nonpositive, less singular than $u$, and has the same mass $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega =1$, so theorem 16.22.11 gives $P_\omega [u]\geq 0$; since also $P_\omega [u]\leq V_\omega =0$, we obtain $P_\omega [u]=0$. Near $0$, however, $u=-\log (-\log |z|^2)+O(1)$ is unbounded below. Thus the singularity envelope can change the singularity type of a potential while preserving its full mass. Definition 16.22.13 . D3EBF9A66D06 Let $u,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $. The singularity envelope of $u$ relative to $\phi $ is \[  P_\theta [u](\phi ) =\left(\lim _{C\to \infty }P_\theta (u+C,\phi )\right)^*.  \] Choose $C_0$ with $u-C_0\leq \phi $. For $C\geq -C_0$, the potential $u-C_0$ is a common minorant of $u+C$ and $\phi $, so the rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u+C,\phi )$ lies between $u-C_0$ and $u+C$ and has the singularity type of $u$. These rooftop envelopes increase with $C$ and are bounded above by $\phi $, so the regularized limit is a potential between $u-C_0$ and $\phi $. Proposition 16.22.14 . 7E199392108C Let $u,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle >0$. Then the following are equivalent: $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$; $P_\theta [u](\phi )=\phi $; $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\phi ]$. Furthermore, the relative envelope $w=P_\theta [u](\phi )$ has the same mass as $u$, and \[  \mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=\phi \} }\mu _\phi .  \] Proof. Write $w_ C=P_\theta (u+C,\phi )$. Each $w_ C$ with $C$ large has the singularity type of $u$, hence mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $, and $w_ C$ increases almost everywhere to $w$; by corollary 13.8.9 , $\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $. By corollary 16.13.5 , together with $w_ C\leq \phi $ and $w_ C\leq w\leq \phi $, \[  \mu _{w_ C}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ u+C\leq \phi \} }\mu _ u +\mathbf1_{\{ w=\phi \} }\mu _\phi .  \] As $C\to \infty $, the sets $\{ u+C\leq \phi \} $ decrease to the pole set of $u$, which is $\mu _ u$-null, because $\phi $ is bounded above; so the first term tends to zero in total variation by dominated convergence. Moreover $\mu _{w_ C}\to \mu _ w$ weakly by corollary 13.8.9 . Integrating continuous functions $\chi \geq 0$ and applying lemma 16.12.1 , we obtain the asserted measure bound. If (1) holds, then $w$ and $\phi $ have the same positive mass and both belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. By the measure bound, $\mu _ w$ gives no mass to $\{ w<\phi \} $, and the domination principle, theorem 16.22.10 , gives $w\geq \phi $; hence (2). Conversely, if (2) holds, then $u$ has the mass of $w=\phi $, which is (1). To prove that (2) implies (3), normalize $\phi \leq 0$. This is harmless: replacing $\phi $ by $\phi +c$ replaces $w_ C$ by $P_\theta (u+C-c,\phi )+c$, hence $w$ by $w+c$, so (2) is preserved, and $P_\theta [u]$ and $P_\theta [\phi ]$ do not change. Every $w_ C$ is then a nonpositive potential with the singularity type of $u$, hence a competitor for $P_\theta [u]$, so $\phi =w\leq P_\theta [u]$. Since (2) implies (1), $u$ has the positive mass of $\phi $, so $P_\theta [u]$ is a model potential by theorem 16.22.11 . Monotonicity and $u\preceq \phi $ now give \[  P_\theta [\phi ]\leq P_\theta [P_\theta [u]]=P_\theta [u] \leq P_\theta [\phi ].  \] Finally, if (3) holds, then by proposition 16.21.2 the potential $u$ has the mass of $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\phi ]$, which is the mass of $\phi $; this is (1). $\square$

title: Lemma 16.22.1
text: Lemma 16.22.1 . 7420706BAE2F Let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\psi \leq 0$ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle >0$. Then there is a model potential $\phi \geq \psi $ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle $. Proof. Fix a smooth probability volume form $\mathrm dV$ on $X$, put $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle $, and consider \[  \mathcal S=\{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\psi \leq v\leq 0, \  \int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle =m\} , \qquad H(v)=\int _ Xv\, \mathrm dV.  \] The set $\mathcal S$ contains $\psi $, and $H$ takes values in $[H(\psi ),0]$ on it. We construct an increasing sequence in $\mathcal S$ that almost maximizes $H$ at every stage. Put $v_0=\psi $. Given $v_ k\in \mathcal S$, let \[  s_ k=\sup \{ H(w):w\in \mathcal S,\  w\geq v_ k\} ,  \] and choose $v_{k+1}\in \mathcal S$ with $v_{k+1}\geq v_ k$ and $H(v_{k+1})\geq s_ k-2^{-k}$. The regularized limit $\phi =(\sup _ kv_ k)^*$ is a potential with $\psi \leq \phi \leq 0$, and $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =m$ by corollary 13.8.9 ; thus $\phi \in \mathcal S$. Since $v_ k$ increases to $\phi $ almost everywhere, between the integrable bounds $\psi $ and $0$, dominated convergence gives $H(v_ k)\to H(\phi )$. Let $w\in \mathcal S$ with $w\geq \phi $. Then $w\geq v_ k$ for every $k$, so \[  H(w)\leq s_ k\leq H(v_{k+1})+2^{-k},  \] and letting $k\to \infty $ gives $H(w)\leq H(\phi )$. Since $w\geq \phi $, it follows that $w=\phi $ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. Now $P_\theta [\phi ]$ lies between $\phi $ and $0$, because $\phi \leq 0$ is a competitor for it, and it has mass $m$ by proposition 16.21.2 . Thus $P_\theta [\phi ]\in \mathcal S$ and $P_\theta [\phi ]\geq \phi $, so $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $. Since $m>0$, $\phi $ is a model potential. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.22.2
text: Lemma 16.22.2 . 4D5FAF80D021 Let $\phi ,\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $ and $\tau \preceq \phi $. Then \[  \sup _{\{ \phi > -\infty \} }(\tau -\phi )=\sup _ X\tau .  \] In particular, if $\tau \leq 0$, then $\tau \leq \phi $. Proof. The potential $\tau -\sup _ X\tau $ is nonpositive and more singular than $\phi $, so it is a competitor for $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $. Hence $\tau -\phi \leq \sup _ X\tau $ wherever $\phi $ is finite. Conversely, $\phi \leq 0$, so $\tau -\phi \geq \tau $ wherever $\phi $ is finite. The pole set of $\phi $ is pluripolar, and removing a pluripolar set does not change the supremum of the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\tau $: an upper bound for $\tau $ off a Lebesgue null set holds everywhere. This proves the reverse inequality. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.22.3
text: Lemma 16.22.3 . B36FB6000F3B Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\leq v$, let $a>1$, and put $f=au+(1-a)v$, where $f=-\infty $ on the pole set of $u$, which contains that of $v$. The obstacle $f$ is quasi-continuous, and $f\leq u$. A potential $\eta $ satisfies \[  a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u  \] if and only if $\eta \leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Suppose that $f$ has a competitor. Then $\eta =P_\theta (f)$ is the largest potential satisfying this inequality, and $\eta \leq u$. Moreover, if $\gamma =a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v$ and $D=\{ \gamma =u>-\infty \} $, then \[  \mu _\eta \leq a^ n\mathbf1_ D\mu _ u.  \] Proof. (1) Off the pole set of $u$, the functions $u$ and $v$ are finite and $f=u+(a-1)(u-v)\leq u$, because $u\leq v$; on the pole set, $f=-\infty $. Thus $f$ is a Borel function with $f\leq u$. Let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart. Since $u$ and $v$ are quasi-continuous (lemma 16.11.2 (1)), there are open sets of arbitrarily small capacity outside which both are continuous on $K$, as functions with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. On the complement in $K$ of such a set, $f$ is continuous at every point where $u$ is finite, because $v\geq u$ is finite near such a point, and at a pole of $u$ it is continuous with value $-\infty $, because $f\leq u$. Hence $f$ is quasi-continuous. Off the pole set of $u$, the inequalities $\eta \leq f$ and $a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u$ are equivalent. Since the pole set is pluripolar, and an inequality between quasi-plurisubharmonic functions that holds quasi-everywhere holds everywhere, this proves the equivalence. (2) By (1), the potentials satisfying the inequality are exactly the competitors for $f$; since $f\leq u$, they lie below $u$ quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere. Thus $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ is nonempty, by assumption, and uniformly bounded above, and proposition 16.11.4 shows that $\eta $ is its largest member; in particular $\eta \leq u$ and $\gamma \leq u$. By theorem 16.13.4 , $\mu _\eta $ is carried by $\{ \eta =f\} $. At a point of this set at which $u$ is finite, $\eta =au+(1-a)v$ means $\gamma =u$; since $\mu _\eta $ does not charge the pole set of $u$, it is carried by $D$. Moreover $\mu _\gamma \geq a^{-n}\mu _\eta $, and lemma 16.13.1 , applied to $\gamma \leq u$, gives $\mathbf1_ D\mu _\gamma \leq \mathbf1_ D\mu _ u$. Hence \[  \mu _\eta =\mathbf1_ D\mu _\eta \leq a^ n\mathbf1_ D\mu _\gamma \leq a^ n\mathbf1_ D\mu _ u.  \] $\square$

title: Theorem 16.22.4
text: Theorem 16.22.4 . FCFA7EB59B34 Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq v$ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$, and let $a>1$ satisfy 4801296ED5A2 16.22.5 \begin{equation}  a^ n\left(\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \right)<\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle . \end{equation} Then there exists $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _\eta ^ n\rangle >0$ such that C646467A8FDD 16.22.6 \begin{equation}  a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u. \end{equation} The largest such $\eta $ is the obstacle envelope $E_ a(u,v)=P_\theta (au+(1-a)v)$; here the obstacle $au+(1-a)v$ is defined to be $-\infty $ on the pole set of $u$, which contains that of $v$. If $u$ and $v$ have the same mass, then ( 16.22.5 ) holds for every $a>1$, and $E_ a(u,v)$ also has this mass. Proof. We first construct one potential satisfying ( 16.22.6 ) as the limit of a decreasing sequence of envelopes, and then show that $E_ a(u,v)$ is the largest solution and has positive mass. Reduction. Since $u\preceq v$, there are constants $A,B$ with $u-A\leq v-B\leq 0$. If $\eta '$ satisfies ( 16.22.6 ) for the pair $u-A$, $v-B$, then $\eta '+aA+(1-a)B$ satisfies it for $u$, $v$; the envelopes of the two pairs differ by the same constant, and masses do not change. We may therefore assume that $u\leq v\leq 0$. Then $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$, and lemma 16.22.1 provides a model potential $\phi \geq v$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =m$. Since $1-a<0$, we have $au+(1-a)\phi \leq au+(1-a)v$; we first construct a potential below $au+(1-a)\phi $. A decreasing sequence of envelopes. For $j\geq 1$ put $u_ j=\max \{ u,\phi -j\} $, so that $\phi -j\leq u_ j\leq \phi $; in particular, $u_ j$ and $\phi $ have the same pole set. Put \[  f_ j=au_ j+(1-a)\phi ,\qquad \eta _ j=P_\theta (f_ j),  \] where $f_ j=-\infty $ on the pole set of $\phi $, as in lemma 16.22.3 for the pair $u_ j\leq \phi $. Outside this pole set, $f_ j=\phi +a(u_ j-\phi )$ lies between $\phi -aj$ and $\phi $. Hence the potential $\phi -aj$ is a competitor, and every competitor is at most $\phi $, so $\eta _ j$ is a potential with \[  \phi -aj\leq \eta _ j\leq \phi ,\qquad \int _ X\langle \theta _{\eta _ j}^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _{u_ j}^ n\rangle =m,  \] where the masses agree because $\eta _ j\sim \phi \sim u_ j$. Since $u_ j$ decreases with $j$, so do $f_ j$ and $\eta _ j$. A contact bound. Put $\gamma _ j=a^{-1}\eta _ j+(1-a^{-1})\phi $ and $D_ j=\{ \gamma _ j=u_ j>-\infty \} $. By lemma 16.22.3 (2), applied to the pair $u_ j\leq \phi $, we have $\gamma _ j\leq u_ j$ and B2A56AF9922E 16.22.7 \begin{equation}  \mu _{\eta _ j}\leq a^ n\mathbf1_{D_ j}\mu _{u_ j}. \end{equation} A tail estimate. Fix $k>0$ and let $j>k$. On $D_ j$ we have $\eta _ j=\phi +a(u_ j-\phi )$, so there $\eta _ j\leq \phi -ak$ if and only if $u_ j\leq \phi -k$, that is, if and only if $u\leq \phi -k$. The plurifine open set $\{ u>\phi -k\} $ is contained in $\{ u>\phi -j\} $, on which $u_ j=u$; hence $\mu _{u_ j}=\mu _ u$ on $\{ u>\phi -k\} $, and $\mu _{u_ j}(\{ u\leq \phi -k\} )=m-\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )$, pole sets having measure zero. Together with ( 16.22.7 ) this gives 246B560461D1 16.22.8 \begin{equation}  \mu _{\eta _ j}(\{ \eta _ j\leq \phi -ak\} ) \leq a^ n\left(m-\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )\right). \end{equation} The envelopes do not collapse. Suppose that $\eta _ j$ decreases to $-\infty $ identically. Then $\sup _ X\eta _ j\to -\infty $ by corollary 10.3.6 . Since $\eta _ j\preceq \phi $ and $\phi $ is a model potential, lemma 16.22.2 gives $\eta _ j-\phi \leq \sup _ X\eta _ j$ off the pole set of $\phi $. Hence, for each $k$, $\eta _ j\leq \phi -ak$ everywhere once $j$ is large, and the left side of ( 16.22.8 ) equals $\int _ X\langle \theta _{\eta _ j}^ n\rangle =m$. Since $\phi $ is finite wherever $u$ is, $\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )\to \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $ as $k\to \infty $, and ( 16.22.8 ) yields $m\leq a^ n\bigl (m-\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \bigr )$, which contradicts ( 16.22.5 ). Consequently $\eta _ j$ decreases to a potential $\eta $. Letting $j\to \infty $ in $\gamma _ j\leq u_ j$ gives $a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})\phi \leq u$, and since $v\leq \phi $, also ( 16.22.6 ). The largest solution. By lemma 16.22.3 (1), applied to the pair $u\leq v$, the potentials satisfying ( 16.22.6 ) are exactly the competitors for the obstacle $f=au+(1-a)v$. The potential $\eta $ constructed above is one of them, so part (2) of the lemma shows that $E_ a=E_ a(u,v)=P_\theta (f)$ is the largest potential satisfying ( 16.22.6 ), and that $E_ a\leq u$. Positive mass. Choose $b>a$ that still satisfies ( 16.22.5 ). The preceding steps, applied to $b$, give $E_ b=E_ b(u,v)$. The potential \[  q=\frac abE_ b+\left(1-\frac ab\right)u  \] is a competitor for the obstacle $f$ of $E_ a$: quasi-everywhere, $E_ b\leq bu+(1-b)v$, and therefore \[  q\leq au+(1-a)v+\left(1-\frac ab\right)(u-v)\leq au+(1-a)v.  \] Hence $q\leq E_ a$, and the monotonicity of mass together with $\mu _ q\geq (1-a/b)^ n\mu _ u$ yields \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _{E_ a}^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _ q^ n\rangle \geq \left(1-\frac ab\right)^ n\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0.  \] If $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle $, then ( 16.22.5 ) holds for every $a>1$, so $b$ can be taken arbitrarily large, and we obtain $\int _ X\langle \theta _{E_ a}^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $. The reverse inequality follows from $E_ a\leq u$. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.22.9
text: Lemma 16.22.9 . 52ED2F2B0A63 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$. Then there are $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\leq u$ and $\delta >0$ such that $\theta _ v\geq \delta \omega $. Proof. Put $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _{V_\theta }^ n\rangle $. Since $u\preceq V_\theta $ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$, we can choose $a>1$ so close to one that $a^ n\bigl (m-\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \bigr )<m$. Theorem 16.22.4 gives $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})V_\theta \leq u$. Since the class is big, it contains a closed current $T\geq \delta _0\omega $ for some $\delta _0>0$, and by theorem 10.2.15 we can write $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ with $\psi $ quasi-plurisubharmonic; after subtracting a constant, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $\psi \leq 0$ and $\theta _\psi \geq \delta _0\omega $, and $\psi \leq V_\theta $ because $\psi $ is a competitor for $V_\theta $. Therefore \[  v=a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})\psi \leq u,\qquad \theta _ v=a^{-1}\theta _\eta +(1-a^{-1})\theta _\psi \geq (1-a^{-1})\delta _0\omega .  \] $\square$

title: Theorem 16.22.10 (Domination principle)
text: Theorem 16.22.10 (Domination principle) . 0F4D01059518 Let $\chi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _\chi ^ n\rangle >0$, and let $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\chi )$. If $\mu _ u(\{ u<v\} )=0$, then $u\geq v$ everywhere on $X$. Proof. After reducing to the case $u\leq v$, we show that the extrapolation envelopes $E_ a(u,v)$ agree with $u$ almost everywhere for $\mu _ u$. Hence they do not collapse as $a\to \infty $, while their limit equals $-\infty $ quasi-everywhere on $\{ u<v\} $, so that this set is pluripolar. The potential $\max \{ u,v\} $ is more singular than $\chi $ and less singular than $u$, so \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _\chi ^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\chi ^ n\rangle ;  \] thus $\max \{ u,v\} \in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\chi )$. Since $\{ u<\max \{ u,v\} \} =\{ u<v\} $, we may replace $v$ by $\max \{ u,v\} $ and assume that $u\leq v$. Subtracting the same constant from $u$ and $v$, we may also assume $v\leq 0$. Let $m>0$ be the common mass of $u$, $v$ and $\chi $. For $a>1$ let $\eta _ a=E_ a(u,v)$, $\gamma _ a=a^{-1}\eta _ a+(1-a^{-1})v$ and $D_ a=\{ \gamma _ a=u>-\infty \} $. By theorem 16.22.4 , $\eta _ a$ is a potential of mass $m$; in particular its obstacle $au+(1-a)v$ has a competitor, and lemma 16.22.3 (2), applied to the pair $u\leq v$, gives $\eta _ a\leq u$, $\gamma _ a\leq u$ and \[  \mu _{\eta _ a}\leq a^ n\mathbf1_{D_ a}\mu _ u.  \] Since $u\leq v$, the hypothesis means that $\mu _ u$ is carried by $\{ u=v\} $, so $\mu _{\eta _ a}$ is carried by $D_ a\cap \{ u=v\} $. At a point of this set, $a^{-1}\eta _ a+(1-a^{-1})u=u$, that is, $\eta _ a=u$. Hence $\mu _{\eta _ a}$ is carried by $\{ \eta _ a=u\} $, and lemma 16.13.1 , applied to $\eta _ a\leq u$, gives $\mu _{\eta _ a}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ \eta _ a=u\} }\mu _ u\leq \mu _ u$. Both measures have mass $m$, so they are equal, and $\eta _ a=u$ holds $\mu _ u$-almost everywhere. In particular \[  \int _ X\mathrm e^{\eta _ a}\, \mu _ u =\int _ X\mathrm e^ u\, \mu _ u>0,  \] where the last integral is positive because $m>0$ and $\mu _ u$ does not charge the pole set of $u$. As $a$ increases, the obstacle $v+a(u-v)$ decreases, so $\eta _ a$ decreases. If $\eta _ a$ decreased to $-\infty $ identically as $a\to \infty $ through the integers, dominated convergence, with $0\leq \mathrm e^{\eta _ a}\leq 1$, would make the left side of the last display tend to zero, a contradiction. Hence the limit $\eta $ along the integers is a potential. Each $\eta _ a$ satisfies $\eta _ a\leq v+a(u-v)$ outside a pluripolar set; let $N$ be the union of these sets over the integers $a\geq 2$. At a point outside $N$ where $u$ is finite and $u<v$, we get $\eta \leq v+a(u-v)$ for every integer $a$, hence $\eta =-\infty $. Thus $\{ u<v\} $ is contained in the union of $N$ and the pole sets of $u$ and $\eta $, which is pluripolar. Therefore $u\geq v$ quasi-everywhere, and hence everywhere. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.22.11
text: Theorem 16.22.11 . 4A1DC8C4E020 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$. Then \[  P_\theta [u]=\max \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):v\leq 0, \  u\preceq v,\  \int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \} .  \] In particular $P_\theta [P_\theta [u]]=P_\theta [u]$, so $P_\theta [u]$ is a model potential of mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $. Proof. Write $w=P_\theta [u]$, and let $v$ belong to the displayed family. By proposition 16.21.2 , $w\leq P_\theta [v]$, and the potentials $w$, $u$, $v$ and $P_\theta [v]$ all have the same positive mass. Moreover $v\leq P_\theta [v]$, because $v\leq 0$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [v]$. Hence $w$ and $v$ both belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,P_\theta [v])$, a class whose reference potential has positive mass. By proposition 16.21.3 , $\mu _ w$ is carried by $\{ w=0\} $, and since $v\leq 0$, it gives no mass to $\{ w<v\} $. The domination principle, theorem 16.22.10 , yields $w\geq v$. Finally, $w$ itself belongs to the family: it is nonpositive, it satisfies $u-\sup _ Xu\leq w$, and it has the same mass as $u$ by proposition 16.21.2 . This proves the formula. The potential $P_\theta [w]$ is nonpositive, satisfies $u\preceq w\preceq P_\theta [w]$, and has the same mass as $u$ by proposition 16.21.2 . Hence it belongs to the family, and the formula gives $P_\theta [w]\leq w$. Conversely, $w\leq 0$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [w]$, so $P_\theta [w]=w$. Since the mass of $w$ is positive, $w$ is a model potential. $\square$

title: Example 16.22.12
text: Example 16.22.12 . 246496245694 On $\mathbb P^1$ let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$ in the affine coordinate $z$, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega =1$; since $\omega $ is Kähler, $V_\omega =0$. Define \[  F(r)=\begin{cases}  \max \{ -\log (-r),r+2\} ,& r\leq -1,\\  r+2,& r\geq -1, \end{cases} \qquad u(z)=F(\log |z|^2)-\log (1+|z|^2).  \] The function $F$ is continuous and nondecreasing. Since $-\log (-r)<r+2$ at $r=-1$, there is $\delta >0$ with $F(r)=r+2$ for $r\geq -1-\delta $, and since $r+2+\log (-r)\to -\infty $ as $r\to -\infty $, we have $F(r)=-\log (-r)$ for all sufficiently negative $r$. We first show that $F(\log |z|^2)$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $. On the open set $\{ |z|^2>\mathrm e^{-1-\delta }\} $ it equals the harmonic function $\log |z|^2+2$. On the open set $\{ 0<|z|^2<\mathrm e^{-1}\} $ it equals $\max \{ g(\log |z|^2),\log |z|^2+2\} $, where $g(t)=-\log (-t)$ for $t<0$. Since $g''(t)=t^{-2}>0$, the function $g$ is convex, so it is the supremum of its tangent lines $t\mapsto g(s)+g'(s)(t-s)$, $s<0$, whose slopes $g'(s)=-1/s$ are positive. Hence $g(\log |z|^2)$ is a continuous supremum of the harmonic functions $g(s)+g'(s)(\log |z|^2-s)$; it therefore satisfies the submean inequality and is subharmonic, and so is its maximum with $\log |z|^2+2$. Since subharmonicity is a local property, $F(\log |z|^2)$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $; it tends to $-\infty $ at $0$ and extends subharmonically across the polar set $\{ 0\} $ by theorem 3.4.27 . Next we check that $u$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic. For $|z|^2\geq \mathrm e^{-1}$ we have $u=2-\log (1+|z|^{-2})$. In the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$ near $\infty $ this reads $u=2-\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$, while $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$, because $\log (1+|z|^2)=\log (1+|\zeta |^2)-\log |\zeta |^2$ and $\log |\zeta |^2$ is pluriharmonic for $\zeta \ne 0$; thus $u$ is smooth near $\infty $, with $u(\infty )=2$ and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=0$ there. Hence $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,\omega )$, with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(\log |z|^2)$ on $\mathbb C$, and its only pole is $0$. To compute the mass of $u$, note that its Lelong number at $0$ is that of the subharmonic function $F(\log |z|^2)$, which differs from $u$ by a smooth function, and since $F$ is continuous and nondecreasing, $\sup _{|z|<\mathrm e^{t/2}}F(\log |z|^2)=F(t)$. By proposition 6.7.1 , the Lelong number is therefore \[  \lim _{t\to -\infty }\frac{F(t)}t=\lim _{t\to -\infty }\frac{-\log (-t)}t=0.  \] By theorem 6.7.6 , in one variable the mass that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(\log |z|^2)$ gives to $0$ is this Lelong number, namely the limit of the masses of the discs $B(0,r)$ as $r\downarrow 0$, so the current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has no atom at its pole. By proposition 13.4.7 , $\mu _ u$ is the restriction of $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ to $\{ u>-\infty \} $, hence the mass of $u$ is $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\langle \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\rangle =\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega =1$. The potential $0$ is nonpositive, less singular than $u$, and has the same mass $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega =1$, so theorem 16.22.11 gives $P_\omega [u]\geq 0$; since also $P_\omega [u]\leq V_\omega =0$, we obtain $P_\omega [u]=0$. Near $0$, however, $u=-\log (-\log |z|^2)+O(1)$ is unbounded below. Thus the singularity envelope can change the singularity type of a potential while preserving its full mass.

title: Definition 16.22.13
text: Definition 16.22.13 . D3EBF9A66D06 Let $u,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $. The singularity envelope of $u$ relative to $\phi $ is \[  P_\theta [u](\phi ) =\left(\lim _{C\to \infty }P_\theta (u+C,\phi )\right)^*.  \] Choose $C_0$ with $u-C_0\leq \phi $. For $C\geq -C_0$, the potential $u-C_0$ is a common minorant of $u+C$ and $\phi $, so the rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u+C,\phi )$ lies between $u-C_0$ and $u+C$ and has the singularity type of $u$. These rooftop envelopes increase with $C$ and are bounded above by $\phi $, so the regularized limit is a potential between $u-C_0$ and $\phi $.

title: Proposition 16.22.14
text: Proposition 16.22.14 . 7E199392108C Let $u,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle >0$. Then the following are equivalent: $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$; $P_\theta [u](\phi )=\phi $; $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\phi ]$. Furthermore, the relative envelope $w=P_\theta [u](\phi )$ has the same mass as $u$, and \[  \mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=\phi \} }\mu _\phi .  \] Proof. Write $w_ C=P_\theta (u+C,\phi )$. Each $w_ C$ with $C$ large has the singularity type of $u$, hence mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $, and $w_ C$ increases almost everywhere to $w$; by corollary 13.8.9 , $\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $. By corollary 16.13.5 , together with $w_ C\leq \phi $ and $w_ C\leq w\leq \phi $, \[  \mu _{w_ C}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ u+C\leq \phi \} }\mu _ u +\mathbf1_{\{ w=\phi \} }\mu _\phi .  \] As $C\to \infty $, the sets $\{ u+C\leq \phi \} $ decrease to the pole set of $u$, which is $\mu _ u$-null, because $\phi $ is bounded above; so the first term tends to zero in total variation by dominated convergence. Moreover $\mu _{w_ C}\to \mu _ w$ weakly by corollary 13.8.9 . Integrating continuous functions $\chi \geq 0$ and applying lemma 16.12.1 , we obtain the asserted measure bound. If (1) holds, then $w$ and $\phi $ have the same positive mass and both belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. By the measure bound, $\mu _ w$ gives no mass to $\{ w<\phi \} $, and the domination principle, theorem 16.22.10 , gives $w\geq \phi $; hence (2). Conversely, if (2) holds, then $u$ has the mass of $w=\phi $, which is (1). To prove that (2) implies (3), normalize $\phi \leq 0$. This is harmless: replacing $\phi $ by $\phi +c$ replaces $w_ C$ by $P_\theta (u+C-c,\phi )+c$, hence $w$ by $w+c$, so (2) is preserved, and $P_\theta [u]$ and $P_\theta [\phi ]$ do not change. Every $w_ C$ is then a nonpositive potential with the singularity type of $u$, hence a competitor for $P_\theta [u]$, so $\phi =w\leq P_\theta [u]$. Since (2) implies (1), $u$ has the positive mass of $\phi $, so $P_\theta [u]$ is a model potential by theorem 16.22.11 . Monotonicity and $u\preceq \phi $ now give \[  P_\theta [\phi ]\leq P_\theta [P_\theta [u]]=P_\theta [u] \leq P_\theta [\phi ].  \] Finally, if (3) holds, then by proposition 16.21.2 the potential $u$ has the mass of $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\phi ]$, which is the mass of $\phi $; this is (1). $\square$

title: 16.23 Rooftops and mass inequalities
text:
Two potentials need not have a common minorant, as example 16.11.7 shows. We prove that a strict mass inequality guarantees one, and that the masses of $u$, $v$, $\max \{ u,v\} $ and $P_	heta (u,v)$ satisfy the inequality of theorem 16.23.5 . Contact concentration for model potentials gives these results for model potentials, and extrapolation transfers them to arbitrary potentials of full mass relative to model potentials. As in the preceding section, $\{ 	heta \} $ is big. Proposition 16.23.1 . 3499B9FD713C Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy \[  \int _ X\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle +\int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle >\int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ nangle .  \] Then $P_	heta (u,v)
e -\infty $. Proof. Subtracting the same constant from $u$ and $v$ changes neither the hypothesis nor the conclusion, so we may assume that $u,v\leq 0$. Put $m=\int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ nangle $ and $\phi =P_	heta [\max \{ u,v\} ]$. By monotonicity $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle \leq m$ and $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle \leq m$, so the strict inequality forces both masses to be positive. Hence $m>0$, and by theorem 16.22.11 , $\phi $ is a model potential of mass $m$. Moreover $u,v\leq \max \{ u,v\} \leq \phi $, because the nonpositive potential $\max \{ u,v\} $ is a competitor for $\phi $. Since $\mu _ u$ and $\mu _ v$ do not charge pole sets, $\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )	o \int _ X\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle $ and $\mu _ v(\{ v>\phi -k\} )	o \int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle $ as $k	o \infty $. Choose $k>0$ so large that \[  \mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )+\mu _ v(\{ v>\phi -k\} )>m.  \] For $C>k$ put \[  u_ C=\max \{ u,\phi -C\} ,\quad v_ C=\max \{ v,\phi -C\} ,\quad w_ C=P_	heta (u_ C,v_ C).  \] Since $\phi -C$ is a common minorant, all three potentials have the singularity type of $\phi $ and mass $m$. As $C	o \infty $, $w_ C$ decreases to $P_	heta (u,v)$ by proposition 16.11.6 . Suppose that $P_	heta (u,v)=-\infty $, so that $w_ C$ decreases to $-\infty $ identically. Then $\sup _ Xw_ C	o -\infty $ by corollary 10.3.6 , and lemma 16.22.2 gives $w_ C\leq \phi -k$ for all large $C$. On $\{ w_ C=u_ C\} $ we then have $u_ C\leq \phi -k$, and similarly for $v_ C$, so corollary 16.13.5 gives \[   egin{split}  m=\int _ X\langle 	heta _{w_ C}^ nangle & \leq \mu _{u_ C}(\{ u_ C\leq \phi -k\} ) +\mu _{v_ C}(\{ v_ C\leq \phi -k\} )\ & =2m-\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )-\mu _ v(\{ v>\phi -k\} )<m. \end{split}  \] For the equality we used that, since $C>k$, $u_ C=u$ on the plurifine open set $\{ u>\phi -k\} $, so $\mu _{u_ C}=\mu _ u$ there, and similarly for $v$. This contradiction shows that $P_	heta (u,v)
e -\infty $. $\square$ Proposition 16.23.2 . E33C504A684F Let $\phi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $P_	heta [\phi ]=\phi $ and $P_	heta [\psi ]=\psi $, and suppose that $w=P_	heta (\phi ,\psi )
e -\infty $. Then $P_	heta [w]=w$. Thus the rooftop envelope of two model potentials is a model potential whenever its mass is positive. Proof. Since $w\leq \phi $, monotonicity gives $P_	heta [w]\leq P_	heta [\phi ]=\phi $, and likewise $P_	heta [w]\leq \psi $. Thus $P_	heta [w]$ is a common minorant of $\phi $ and $\psi $, and $P_	heta [w]\leq w$. Conversely, $w\leq \phi \leq 0$, so $w$ is a competitor for $P_	heta [w]$. $\square$ Proposition 16.23.3 . 37241FAAC9EF Let $\phi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be such that their rooftop envelope $w=P_	heta (\phi ,\psi )$ is a potential of positive mass. If $u\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and $v\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\psi )$, then $P_	heta (u,v)$ is a potential with the same mass as $w$. Proof. Shifting $u$ and $v$ by constants affects neither the existence of a common minorant nor the mass of $P_	heta (u,v)$. Indeed, a common minorant can be shifted down by the largest absolute change, and by proposition 16.11.4 (4) the rooftop envelopes of the original and of the shifted pair differ by a bounded amount, because their obstacles do. We may therefore assume that $u\leq \phi $ and $v\leq \psi $. We first replace $\phi $ by $u$, and then $\psi $ by $v$; both steps combine extrapolation with proposition 16.23.1 . Since $w\leq \phi $ and $w\leq \psi $, the masses of $\phi $ and $\psi $ are at least that of $w$, hence positive. For $a>1$ let $u_ a=E_ a(u,\phi )$. Since $u$ and $\phi $ have the same positive mass, theorem 16.22.4 shows that $u_ a$ also has this mass and that $a^{-1}u_ a+(1-a^{-1})\phi \leq u$; moreover $u_ a\leq u\leq \phi $, because the obstacle $u+(a-1)(u-\phi )$ of $u_ a$ is at most $u$. Since $\max \{ u_ a,w\} \leq \phi $ and $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle >0$, \[  \int _ X\langle 	heta _{u_ a}^ nangle +\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle >\int _ X\langle 	heta _\phi ^ nangle \geq \int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ u_ a,w\} }^ nangle .  \] By proposition 16.23.1 , the rooftop envelope $P_	heta (u_ a,w)$ is a potential. By associativity and $u_ a\leq \phi $, it equals $P_	heta (u_ a,\psi )$. The potential \[  a^{-1}P_	heta (u_ a,\psi )+(1-a^{-1})w  \] lies below $a^{-1}u_ a+(1-a^{-1})\phi \leq u$ and below $\psi $, so it is a common minorant of $u$ and $\psi $. Hence $z=P_	heta (u,\psi )$ is a potential, and positivity and monotonicity of mass give $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ z^ nangle \geq (1-a^{-1})^ n\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle $. On the other hand $z\leq P_	heta (\phi ,\psi )=w$, so the mass of $z$ is at most that of $w$. Letting $a	o \infty $, we see that $z$ and $w$ have the same positive mass. Now let $v_ a=E_ a(v,\psi )$. In the same way, $v_ a\leq v\leq \psi $, the mass of $v_ a$ is that of $\psi $, and $a^{-1}v_ a+(1-a^{-1})\psi \leq v$. Since $\max \{ v_ a,z\} \leq \psi $ and $z$ has positive mass, we have \[  \int _ X\langle 	heta _{v_ a}^ nangle +\int _ X\langle 	heta _ z^ nangle >\int _ X\langle 	heta _\psi ^ nangle \geq \int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ v_ a,z\} }^ nangle ,  \] so proposition 16.23.1 shows that $P_	heta (z,v_ a)$ is a potential, and by associativity and $v_ a\leq \psi $ it equals $P_	heta (u,v_ a)$. The potential \[  a^{-1}P_	heta (u,v_ a)+(1-a^{-1})z  \] lies below $u$ and below $a^{-1}v_ a+(1-a^{-1})\psi \leq v$, and its mass is at least $(1-a^{-1})^ n\int _ X\langle 	heta _ z^ nangle $. Hence $P_	heta (u,v)$ is a potential whose mass is at least $(1-a^{-1})^ n\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle $, for every $a>1$. Since $P_	heta (u,v)\leq w$, its mass is at most that of $w$, and letting $a	o \infty $ completes the proof. $\square$ The proof of the mass inequality for rooftop envelopes passes to the limit along a decreasing sequence of potentials. The following lemma shows that the mass that nonpositive potentials put on their zero sets can only increase in such a limit. Lemma 16.23.4 . F4294ED919CC Let $q_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be nonpositive potentials decreasing to a potential $q$. Then \[  \varlimsup _{j	o \infty }\mu _{q_ j}(\{ q_ j=0\} )\leq \mu _ q(\{ q=0\} ).  \] Proof. Put $\lambda _ j=\mathbf1_{\{ q_ j=0\} }\mu _{q_ j}$. Since $q_ j\leq V_	heta \leq 0$, the set $\{ q_ j=0\} $ is contained in $\{ q_ j=V_	heta \} $, and lemma 16.13.1 gives $\lambda _ j\leq \mu _{V_	heta }$. Let $A$ be the proper analytic subset of lemma 16.13.2 : potentials with minimal singularities are locally bounded on $X\setminus A$, and $\mu _{V_	heta }(A)=0$. For $t>0$ put $b_ j=\max \{ 1+tq_ j,0\} $ and $b=\max \{ 1+tq,0\} $, with value zero at the poles. Fix a coordinate ball $D\Subset X\setminus A$ with a smooth potential $ho $ of $	heta $ near $\overline D$ (lemma 5.4.2 ) and a number $L>1/t$, and put $\widetilde q_ j=\max \{ q_ j,V_	heta -L\} $ and $\widetilde q=\max \{ q,V_	heta -L\} $. On $D$ the functions $\widetilde q_ j$ are uniformly bounded and decrease to $\widetilde q$, so they converge in capacity (proposition 7.5.6 ). Since $V_	heta -L<-1/t$, the weight $b_ j$ vanishes on $\{ q_ j\leq V_	heta -L\} $, and on the complementary plurifine open set $\widetilde q_ j=q_ j$; hence $b_ j\mu _{q_ j}=b_ j\mu _{\widetilde q_ j}$ by plurifine locality, and likewise $b\mu _ q=b\mu _{\widetilde q}$. Moreover $b_ j=\max \{ 1+t\widetilde q_ j,0\} $ and $b=\max \{ 1+t\widetilde q,0\} $ on $D$, so the weights are bounded and quasi-continuous and converge in capacity to $b$. The weighted form of theorem 7.5.8 , applied to the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $ho +\widetilde q_ j$, therefore gives \[  b_ j\mu _{q_ j}=b_ j\mu _{\widetilde q_ j} \longrightarrow b\mu _{\widetilde q}=b\mu _ q \quad 	ext{weakly on }D.  \] Let $\delta >0$. Since $\mu _{V_	heta }(A)=0$, lemma 16.12.1 (1) gives a compact set $K\subset X\setminus A$ with $\mu _{V_	heta }(X\setminus K)<\delta $; choose a continuous function $0\leq \zeta \leq 1$ with compact support in $X\setminus A$ and $\zeta =1$ on $K$ (proposition 5.2.6 ). Since $b_ j=1$ on $\{ q_ j=0\} $ and $\lambda _ j\leq \mu _{V_	heta }$, \[  \lambda _ j(X)\leq \int _ X\zeta b_ j\, \mu _{q_ j}+\delta .  \] Cover the support of $\zeta $ by finitely many balls $D_ l$ as above, and write $\zeta =\sum _ l\zeta _ l$ with continuous functions $\zeta _ l\geq 0$ with compact support in $D_ l$ (for instance $\zeta _ l=\zeta \psi _ l/\sum _ k\psi _ k$, where $\psi _ l\geq 0$ is continuous with compact support in $D_ l$ and $\sum _ k\psi _ k>0$ on the support of $\zeta $). The weak convergence on each $D_ l$ gives $\int _ X\zeta b_ j\, \mu _{q_ j}	o \int _ X\zeta b\, \mu _ q\leq \int _ Xb\, \mu _ q$, and letting then $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $\varlimsup _ j\lambda _ j(X)\leq \int _ Xb\, \mu _ q$. Finally, as $t	o \infty $ the weights $b$, which depend on $t$, decrease to $\mathbf1_{\{ q=0\} }$, because $q\leq 0$; dominated convergence for the finite measure $\mu _ q$ proves the lemma. $\square$ Theorem 16.23.5 . 641CB44C78E9 Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $w=P_	heta (u,v)
e -\infty $. Then \[  \int _ X\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle +\int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle \leq \int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ nangle +\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle .  \] Proof. We first reduce to model potentials, and then apply contact concentration to the rooftop envelopes of their truncations. If $u$ has mass zero, the inequality follows from the monotonicity of mass, $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle \leq \int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ nangle $, and similarly if $v$ has mass zero. Otherwise, subtracting the same constant from $u$ and $v$, which subtracts it from $\max \{ u,v\} $ and $w$ and changes no mass, we may assume that $u,v\leq 0$. Put $\phi =P_	heta [u]$ and $\psi =P_	heta [v]$; by theorem 16.22.11 , these are model potentials with the same masses as $u$ and $v$, respectively, and $u\leq \phi $, $v\leq \psi $, since $u$ and $v$ are competitors for their own singularity envelopes. Put also $\gamma =\max \{ \phi ,\psi \} $ and $r=P_	heta (\phi ,\psi )$. The four masses in the inequality do not change when $u,v$ are replaced by $\phi ,\psi $. Indeed, for every integer $C$ the potential $\max \{ P_	heta (u+C,V_	heta ),P_	heta (v+C,V_	heta )\} $ has the singularity type of $\max \{ u,v\} $, by proposition 16.11.6 , and by proposition 16.21.2 (2) these potentials increase almost everywhere to $\gamma $ as $C	o \infty $; so $\gamma $ has the same mass as $\max \{ u,v\} $, by corollary 13.8.9 . Moreover $w$ is a common minorant of $\phi $ and $\psi $, so $r\geq w$ is a potential. If $r$ has mass zero, then so has $w$, by monotonicity. If the mass of $r$ is positive, then $w$ has the same mass as $r$ by proposition 16.23.3 , applied to $u\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and $v\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\psi )$. It therefore suffices to prove the theorem for the model potentials $\phi $ and $\psi $, whose maximum is $\gamma $ and whose rooftop envelope is $r$. Put $m=\int _ X\langle 	heta _\gamma ^ nangle $, and for $C>0$ let \[  \phi _ C=\max \{ \phi ,\gamma -C\} ,\quad \psi _ C=\max \{ \psi ,\gamma -C\} ,\quad r_ C=P_	heta (\phi _ C,\psi _ C).  \] These potentials have the singularity type of $\gamma $, hence mass $m$, and $r_ C$ decreases to $r$ as $C	o \infty $. By proposition 16.21.3 , the measure $\mu _\phi $ is carried by $\{ \phi =0\} $, which is contained in the plurifine open set $\{ \phi >\gamma -C\} $, where $\phi _ C=\phi $. Plurifine locality therefore gives \[  \mu _{\phi _ C}=\mu _\phi + \mathbf1_{\{ \phi \leq \gamma -C\} }\mu _{\phi _ C},  \] and the last summand has mass $m-\int _ X\langle 	heta _\phi ^ nangle $; the analogous decomposition holds for $\psi _ C$. By corollary 16.13.5 , $\mu _{r_ C}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ r_ C=\phi _ C\} }\mu _{\phi _ C}+\mathbf1_{\{ r_ C=\psi _ C\} }\mu _{\psi _ C}$. On the set $\{ r_ C<0\} $, the summand $\mu _\phi $ of $\mu _{\phi _ C}$ contributes nothing to this bound, because at a point of $\{ \phi =0\} \cap \{ r_ C=\phi _ C\} $ we have $r_ C=\phi _ C=0$; the same holds for $\mu _\psi $. Consequently \[  \mu _{r_ C}(\{ r_ C<0\} )\leq 2m-\int _ X\langle 	heta _\phi ^ nangle -\int _ X\langle 	heta _\psi ^ nangle .  \] Since $r_ C\leq 0$ and $\int _ X\langle 	heta _{r_ C}^ nangle =m$, it follows that \[  \mu _{r_ C}(\{ r_ C=0\} )\geq \int _ X\langle 	heta _\phi ^ nangle +\int _ X\langle 	heta _\psi ^ nangle -m.  \] Applying lemma 16.23.4 along the integers $C	o \infty $ to the potentials $r_ C$, which decrease to $r$, we find that \[  \int _ X\langle 	heta _ r^ nangle \geq \mu _ r(\{ r=0\} ) \geq \int _ X\langle 	heta _\phi ^ nangle +\int _ X\langle 	heta _\psi ^ nangle -m,  \] which is the assertion for $\phi $ and $\psi $. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.23.1
text: Proposition 16.23.1 . 3499B9FD713C Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle +\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle >\int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle .  \] Then $P_\theta (u,v)\ne -\infty $. Proof. Subtracting the same constant from $u$ and $v$ changes neither the hypothesis nor the conclusion, so we may assume that $u,v\leq 0$. Put $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle $ and $\phi =P_\theta [\max \{ u,v\} ]$. By monotonicity $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \leq m$ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle \leq m$, so the strict inequality forces both masses to be positive. Hence $m>0$, and by theorem 16.22.11 , $\phi $ is a model potential of mass $m$. Moreover $u,v\leq \max \{ u,v\} \leq \phi $, because the nonpositive potential $\max \{ u,v\} $ is a competitor for $\phi $. Since $\mu _ u$ and $\mu _ v$ do not charge pole sets, $\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )\to \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $ and $\mu _ v(\{ v>\phi -k\} )\to \int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle $ as $k\to \infty $. Choose $k>0$ so large that \[  \mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )+\mu _ v(\{ v>\phi -k\} )>m.  \] For $C>k$ put \[  u_ C=\max \{ u,\phi -C\} ,\quad v_ C=\max \{ v,\phi -C\} ,\quad w_ C=P_\theta (u_ C,v_ C).  \] Since $\phi -C$ is a common minorant, all three potentials have the singularity type of $\phi $ and mass $m$. As $C\to \infty $, $w_ C$ decreases to $P_\theta (u,v)$ by proposition 16.11.6 . Suppose that $P_\theta (u,v)=-\infty $, so that $w_ C$ decreases to $-\infty $ identically. Then $\sup _ Xw_ C\to -\infty $ by corollary 10.3.6 , and lemma 16.22.2 gives $w_ C\leq \phi -k$ for all large $C$. On $\{ w_ C=u_ C\} $ we then have $u_ C\leq \phi -k$, and similarly for $v_ C$, so corollary 16.13.5 gives \[  \begin{split}  m=\int _ X\langle \theta _{w_ C}^ n\rangle & \leq \mu _{u_ C}(\{ u_ C\leq \phi -k\} ) +\mu _{v_ C}(\{ v_ C\leq \phi -k\} )\\ & =2m-\mu _ u(\{ u>\phi -k\} )-\mu _ v(\{ v>\phi -k\} )<m. \end{split}  \] For the equality we used that, since $C>k$, $u_ C=u$ on the plurifine open set $\{ u>\phi -k\} $, so $\mu _{u_ C}=\mu _ u$ there, and similarly for $v$. This contradiction shows that $P_\theta (u,v)\ne -\infty $. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.23.2
text: Proposition 16.23.2 . E33C504A684F Let $\phi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $ and $P_\theta [\psi ]=\psi $, and suppose that $w=P_\theta (\phi ,\psi )\ne -\infty $. Then $P_\theta [w]=w$. Thus the rooftop envelope of two model potentials is a model potential whenever its mass is positive. Proof. Since $w\leq \phi $, monotonicity gives $P_\theta [w]\leq P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $, and likewise $P_\theta [w]\leq \psi $. Thus $P_\theta [w]$ is a common minorant of $\phi $ and $\psi $, and $P_\theta [w]\leq w$. Conversely, $w\leq \phi \leq 0$, so $w$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [w]$. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.23.3
text: Proposition 16.23.3 . 37241FAAC9EF Let $\phi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be such that their rooftop envelope $w=P_\theta (\phi ,\psi )$ is a potential of positive mass. If $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\psi )$, then $P_\theta (u,v)$ is a potential with the same mass as $w$. Proof. Shifting $u$ and $v$ by constants affects neither the existence of a common minorant nor the mass of $P_\theta (u,v)$. Indeed, a common minorant can be shifted down by the largest absolute change, and by proposition 16.11.4 (4) the rooftop envelopes of the original and of the shifted pair differ by a bounded amount, because their obstacles do. We may therefore assume that $u\leq \phi $ and $v\leq \psi $. We first replace $\phi $ by $u$, and then $\psi $ by $v$; both steps combine extrapolation with proposition 16.23.1 . Since $w\leq \phi $ and $w\leq \psi $, the masses of $\phi $ and $\psi $ are at least that of $w$, hence positive. For $a>1$ let $u_ a=E_ a(u,\phi )$. Since $u$ and $\phi $ have the same positive mass, theorem 16.22.4 shows that $u_ a$ also has this mass and that $a^{-1}u_ a+(1-a^{-1})\phi \leq u$; moreover $u_ a\leq u\leq \phi $, because the obstacle $u+(a-1)(u-\phi )$ of $u_ a$ is at most $u$. Since $\max \{ u_ a,w\} \leq \phi $ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle >0$, \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _{u_ a}^ n\rangle +\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle >\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u_ a,w\} }^ n\rangle .  \] By proposition 16.23.1 , the rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u_ a,w)$ is a potential. By associativity and $u_ a\leq \phi $, it equals $P_\theta (u_ a,\psi )$. The potential \[  a^{-1}P_\theta (u_ a,\psi )+(1-a^{-1})w  \] lies below $a^{-1}u_ a+(1-a^{-1})\phi \leq u$ and below $\psi $, so it is a common minorant of $u$ and $\psi $. Hence $z=P_\theta (u,\psi )$ is a potential, and positivity and monotonicity of mass give $\int _ X\langle \theta _ z^ n\rangle \geq (1-a^{-1})^ n\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle $. On the other hand $z\leq P_\theta (\phi ,\psi )=w$, so the mass of $z$ is at most that of $w$. Letting $a\to \infty $, we see that $z$ and $w$ have the same positive mass. Now let $v_ a=E_ a(v,\psi )$. In the same way, $v_ a\leq v\leq \psi $, the mass of $v_ a$ is that of $\psi $, and $a^{-1}v_ a+(1-a^{-1})\psi \leq v$. Since $\max \{ v_ a,z\} \leq \psi $ and $z$ has positive mass, we have \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _{v_ a}^ n\rangle +\int _ X\langle \theta _ z^ n\rangle >\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ v_ a,z\} }^ n\rangle ,  \] so proposition 16.23.1 shows that $P_\theta (z,v_ a)$ is a potential, and by associativity and $v_ a\leq \psi $ it equals $P_\theta (u,v_ a)$. The potential \[  a^{-1}P_\theta (u,v_ a)+(1-a^{-1})z  \] lies below $u$ and below $a^{-1}v_ a+(1-a^{-1})\psi \leq v$, and its mass is at least $(1-a^{-1})^ n\int _ X\langle \theta _ z^ n\rangle $. Hence $P_\theta (u,v)$ is a potential whose mass is at least $(1-a^{-1})^ n\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle $, for every $a>1$. Since $P_\theta (u,v)\leq w$, its mass is at most that of $w$, and letting $a\to \infty $ completes the proof. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.23.4
text: Lemma 16.23.4 . F4294ED919CC Let $q_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be nonpositive potentials decreasing to a potential $q$. Then \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\mu _{q_ j}(\{ q_ j=0\} )\leq \mu _ q(\{ q=0\} ).  \] Proof. Put $\lambda _ j=\mathbf1_{\{ q_ j=0\} }\mu _{q_ j}$. Since $q_ j\leq V_\theta \leq 0$, the set $\{ q_ j=0\} $ is contained in $\{ q_ j=V_\theta \} $, and lemma 16.13.1 gives $\lambda _ j\leq \mu _{V_\theta }$. Let $A$ be the proper analytic subset of lemma 16.13.2 : potentials with minimal singularities are locally bounded on $X\setminus A$, and $\mu _{V_\theta }(A)=0$. For $t>0$ put $b_ j=\max \{ 1+tq_ j,0\} $ and $b=\max \{ 1+tq,0\} $, with value zero at the poles. Fix a coordinate ball $D\Subset X\setminus A$ with a smooth potential $\rho $ of $\theta $ near $\overline D$ (lemma 5.4.2 ) and a number $L>1/t$, and put $\widetilde q_ j=\max \{ q_ j,V_\theta -L\} $ and $\widetilde q=\max \{ q,V_\theta -L\} $. On $D$ the functions $\widetilde q_ j$ are uniformly bounded and decrease to $\widetilde q$, so they converge in capacity (proposition 7.5.6 ). Since $V_\theta -L<-1/t$, the weight $b_ j$ vanishes on $\{ q_ j\leq V_\theta -L\} $, and on the complementary plurifine open set $\widetilde q_ j=q_ j$; hence $b_ j\mu _{q_ j}=b_ j\mu _{\widetilde q_ j}$ by plurifine locality, and likewise $b\mu _ q=b\mu _{\widetilde q}$. Moreover $b_ j=\max \{ 1+t\widetilde q_ j,0\} $ and $b=\max \{ 1+t\widetilde q,0\} $ on $D$, so the weights are bounded and quasi-continuous and converge in capacity to $b$. The weighted form of theorem 7.5.8 , applied to the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $\rho +\widetilde q_ j$, therefore gives \[  b_ j\mu _{q_ j}=b_ j\mu _{\widetilde q_ j} \longrightarrow b\mu _{\widetilde q}=b\mu _ q \quad \text{weakly on }D.  \] Let $\delta >0$. Since $\mu _{V_\theta }(A)=0$, lemma 16.12.1 (1) gives a compact set $K\subset X\setminus A$ with $\mu _{V_\theta }(X\setminus K)<\delta $; choose a continuous function $0\leq \zeta \leq 1$ with compact support in $X\setminus A$ and $\zeta =1$ on $K$ (proposition 5.2.6 ). Since $b_ j=1$ on $\{ q_ j=0\} $ and $\lambda _ j\leq \mu _{V_\theta }$, \[  \lambda _ j(X)\leq \int _ X\zeta b_ j\, \mu _{q_ j}+\delta .  \] Cover the support of $\zeta $ by finitely many balls $D_ l$ as above, and write $\zeta =\sum _ l\zeta _ l$ with continuous functions $\zeta _ l\geq 0$ with compact support in $D_ l$ (for instance $\zeta _ l=\zeta \psi _ l/\sum _ k\psi _ k$, where $\psi _ l\geq 0$ is continuous with compact support in $D_ l$ and $\sum _ k\psi _ k>0$ on the support of $\zeta $). The weak convergence on each $D_ l$ gives $\int _ X\zeta b_ j\, \mu _{q_ j}\to \int _ X\zeta b\, \mu _ q\leq \int _ Xb\, \mu _ q$, and letting then $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $\varlimsup _ j\lambda _ j(X)\leq \int _ Xb\, \mu _ q$. Finally, as $t\to \infty $ the weights $b$, which depend on $t$, decrease to $\mathbf1_{\{ q=0\} }$, because $q\leq 0$; dominated convergence for the finite measure $\mu _ q$ proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.23.5
text: Theorem 16.23.5 . 641CB44C78E9 Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w=P_\theta (u,v)\ne -\infty $. Then \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle +\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle \leq \int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle +\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle .  \] Proof. We first reduce to model potentials, and then apply contact concentration to the rooftop envelopes of their truncations. If $u$ has mass zero, the inequality follows from the monotonicity of mass, $\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle \leq \int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle $, and similarly if $v$ has mass zero. Otherwise, subtracting the same constant from $u$ and $v$, which subtracts it from $\max \{ u,v\} $ and $w$ and changes no mass, we may assume that $u,v\leq 0$. Put $\phi =P_\theta [u]$ and $\psi =P_\theta [v]$; by theorem 16.22.11 , these are model potentials with the same masses as $u$ and $v$, respectively, and $u\leq \phi $, $v\leq \psi $, since $u$ and $v$ are competitors for their own singularity envelopes. Put also $\gamma =\max \{ \phi ,\psi \} $ and $r=P_\theta (\phi ,\psi )$. The four masses in the inequality do not change when $u,v$ are replaced by $\phi ,\psi $. Indeed, for every integer $C$ the potential $\max \{ P_\theta (u+C,V_\theta ),P_\theta (v+C,V_\theta )\} $ has the singularity type of $\max \{ u,v\} $, by proposition 16.11.6 , and by proposition 16.21.2 (2) these potentials increase almost everywhere to $\gamma $ as $C\to \infty $; so $\gamma $ has the same mass as $\max \{ u,v\} $, by corollary 13.8.9 . Moreover $w$ is a common minorant of $\phi $ and $\psi $, so $r\geq w$ is a potential. If $r$ has mass zero, then so has $w$, by monotonicity. If the mass of $r$ is positive, then $w$ has the same mass as $r$ by proposition 16.23.3 , applied to $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\psi )$. It therefore suffices to prove the theorem for the model potentials $\phi $ and $\psi $, whose maximum is $\gamma $ and whose rooftop envelope is $r$. Put $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _\gamma ^ n\rangle $, and for $C>0$ let \[  \phi _ C=\max \{ \phi ,\gamma -C\} ,\quad \psi _ C=\max \{ \psi ,\gamma -C\} ,\quad r_ C=P_\theta (\phi _ C,\psi _ C).  \] These potentials have the singularity type of $\gamma $, hence mass $m$, and $r_ C$ decreases to $r$ as $C\to \infty $. By proposition 16.21.3 , the measure $\mu _\phi $ is carried by $\{ \phi =0\} $, which is contained in the plurifine open set $\{ \phi >\gamma -C\} $, where $\phi _ C=\phi $. Plurifine locality therefore gives \[  \mu _{\phi _ C}=\mu _\phi + \mathbf1_{\{ \phi \leq \gamma -C\} }\mu _{\phi _ C},  \] and the last summand has mass $m-\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $; the analogous decomposition holds for $\psi _ C$. By corollary 16.13.5 , $\mu _{r_ C}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ r_ C=\phi _ C\} }\mu _{\phi _ C}+\mathbf1_{\{ r_ C=\psi _ C\} }\mu _{\psi _ C}$. On the set $\{ r_ C<0\} $, the summand $\mu _\phi $ of $\mu _{\phi _ C}$ contributes nothing to this bound, because at a point of $\{ \phi =0\} \cap \{ r_ C=\phi _ C\} $ we have $r_ C=\phi _ C=0$; the same holds for $\mu _\psi $. Consequently \[  \mu _{r_ C}(\{ r_ C<0\} )\leq 2m-\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle .  \] Since $r_ C\leq 0$ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _{r_ C}^ n\rangle =m$, it follows that \[  \mu _{r_ C}(\{ r_ C=0\} )\geq \int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle +\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle -m.  \] Applying lemma 16.23.4 along the integers $C\to \infty $ to the potentials $r_ C$, which decrease to $r$, we find that \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _ r^ n\rangle \geq \mu _ r(\{ r=0\} ) \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle +\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle -m,  \] which is the assertion for $\phi $ and $\psi $. $\square$

title: 16.24 Divisorial constraints under envelopes
text:

By the valuative criterion of theorem 6.12.16 , inclusions between multiplier ideals are governed by generic Lelong numbers along divisors over $X$. We identify the resulting order and show that it is preserved by upper envelopes, which requires pulling envelopes back to smooth models. u (u,E)$ denotes its generic Lelong number (proposition 6.9.7 ). Since multiplier ideals are local, the valuative criterion uses prime divisors over small neighborhoods of a point; accordingly, in this section a prime divisor over $X$ may also be a prime divisor over an open subset $U\subset X$, that is, a prime divisor on a smooth model of $U$, and $
u (u,E)$ then refers to the restriction of $u$ to $U$. FFB5A7083041 Let $(v_ j)_{j\in J}$ be a nonempty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ that is uniformly bounded above, and let $v=(\sup _ jv_ j)^*$. Then \[  
u (v,E)=\inf _ j
u (v_ j,E)  \] for every prime divisor $E$ over $X$. Consequently, maxima, sums and positive multiples preserve the relation $\sim _{\mathcal I}$; and if two such families are termwise equivalent for $\sim _{\mathcal I}$, their upper envelopes are equivalent as well. Proof. Let $\pi \colon Y	o U$ be a smooth model of an open subset $U\subset X$ (possibly $U=X$) on which $E$ is a divisor, and let $Z\subset Y$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset outside which $\pi $ is a biholomorphism onto an open subset of $U$; such a set exists by the definition of a smooth model, and it has Lebesgue measure zero. We first show that $v\circ \pi $ is the regularized supremum of the family $(v_ j\circ \pi )$. By theorem 5.10.2 , a countable subfamily has the same regularized supremum $v$, and its increasing finite maxima $w_ k$ satisfy $\sup _ kw_ k=v$ almost everywhere. The functions $w_ k\circ \pi $ are $\pi ^*	heta $-plurisubharmonic, increase with $k$, and are locally uniformly bounded above; let $W$ be their regularized supremum, so that $W=\sup _ kw_ k\circ \pi $ almost everywhere by theorem 5.10.2 . If $N\subset U$ is a Lebesgue null set outside which $\sup _ kw_ k=v$, then $\pi ^{-1}(N)\setminus Z$ is a null set, because $\pi $ restricts to a biholomorphism of $Y\setminus Z$ onto an open set; hence $\sup _ kw_ k\circ \pi =v\circ \pi $ outside the null set $(\pi ^{-1}(N)\setminus Z)\cup Z$. It remains to compare Lelong numbers. Near a point $y\in E$, adding to all these functions the pullback of a smooth local potential of $	heta $ near $\pi (y)$ makes them plurisubharmonic, so proposition 6.7.9 gives $
u (v\circ \pi ,y)=\inf _ j
u (v_ j\circ \pi ,y)$ at every point $y\in E$. Taking the infimum over $y\in E$, which defines the generic Lelong number (proposition 6.9.7 ) and commutes with the infimum over $j$, we obtain the formula. For the remaining assertions, let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$, and recall from proposition 6.7.9 that Lelong numbers at a point are additive and positively homogeneous, and that the Lelong number of a maximum is the minimum of the Lelong numbers. Taking infima over $y\in E$, we obtain $
u (c\varphi ,E)=c
u (\varphi ,E)$ for $c>0$ and $
u (\max \{ \varphi ,\psi \} ,E)=\min \{ 
u (\varphi ,E),
u (\psi ,E)\} $. For sums we use that, by proposition 6.9.7 , the infima defining $
u (\varphi ,E)$, $
u (\psi ,E)$ and $
u (\varphi +\psi ,E)$ are attained at every point of $E$ outside a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $E$. Such a point exists, since by the same proposition the complement in $E$ of such a union is dense in $E$, and in particular nonempty. At a point of $E$ where the three infima are attained, the additivity at a point gives $
u (\varphi +\psi ,E)=
u (\varphi ,E)+
u (\psi ,E)$. By these three rules and proposition 16.24.1 , maxima, sums and positive multiples preserve $\sim _{\mathcal I}$, and by the formula just proved, so do upper envelopes of termwise equivalent families. $\square$
