title: 16.25 Singularity constraints and relative capacity
text: We now combine a singularity constraint with an obstacle. For a bounded obstacle the resulting envelope stays within a bounded distance of the singularity envelope $P_\theta [u]$, and it satisfies a contact bound. We then introduce the capacity relative to a reference potential $\phi $, defined through the potentials in the strip $\phi -1\leq v\leq \phi $, and use it to measure the deep sublevel sets of potentials of full mass relative to $\phi $. Throughout this section $\{ \theta \} $ is big. Definition 16.25.1 . 3558A6E66BA8 For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a Borel obstacle $f$, define \[  P_\theta [u](f)=\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): v\preceq u,\  v\leq f\text{ quasi-everywhere}\} \right)^*  \] when this family is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, and put $P_\theta [u](f)=-\infty $ when it is empty. For Borel obstacles $g$ and $f$ we write $P_\theta (g,f)=P_\theta (\min \{ g,f\} )$, under the same conditions on the family of competitors. By the rooftop representation in proposition 16.25.2 below, this is consistent with definition 16.22.13 when $f$ is a potential $\phi $ with $u\preceq \phi $. Proposition 16.25.2 . 467197AADC50 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $f$ be a Borel obstacle for which the family in definition 16.25.1 is nonempty and uniformly bounded above. $P_\theta [u](f)\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. The envelope increases with $f$ and with the singularity type of $u$, does not change when $f$ is modified on a pluripolar set, and satisfies $P_\theta [u](f+c)=P_\theta [u](f)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. For all sufficiently large $k$, the rooftop envelopes $P_\theta (u+k,f)$ are potentials, and \[  P_\theta [u](f)=\left(\lim _{k\to \infty }P_\theta (u+k,f)\right)^*.  \] If $|f|\leq C$ quasi-everywhere, then \[  P_\theta [u]-C\leq P_\theta [u](f)\leq P_\theta [u]+C,  \] and $P_\theta [u](f)$ has the same mass as $u$. In particular, $P_\theta [u](0)=P_\theta [u]$ and $P_\theta [V_\theta ](f)=P_\theta (f)$ whenever these envelopes are defined. Proof. We begin with the final identities. A competitor for $P_\theta [u](0)$ is a nonpositive potential more singular than $u$, exactly as in definition 16.21.1 ; and every potential is more singular than $V_\theta $, by minimality, so the families defining $P_\theta [V_\theta ](f)$ and $P_\theta (f)$ coincide. (1) The maximum of two members of the family in definition 16.25.1 is again a member. By theorem 5.10.2 , applied on finitely many coordinate balls on which $\theta $ has smooth local potentials, there are members $v_1,v_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _ kv_ k)^*=P_\theta [u](f)$, and the maxima $w_ k=\max \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_ k\} $ form an increasing sequence of members with the same regularized supremum. By corollary 5.47.11 , $\sup _ kw_ k=P_\theta [u](f)$ outside a pluripolar set, and each $w_ k$ lies below $f$ outside a pluripolar set; since countable unions of pluripolar sets are pluripolar (theorem 5.47.8 ), $P_\theta [u](f)\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. (The envelope itself need not be more singular than $u$; see example 16.22.12 .) The other assertions follow from the corresponding properties of the families of competitors. (2) A competitor $h$ for the obstacle $\min \{ u+k,f\} $ satisfies $h\leq u+k$ quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere, and $h\leq f$ quasi-everywhere; so it belongs to the family of definition 16.25.1 . In particular these competitors are uniformly bounded above, $P_\theta (u+k,f)$ is defined, and when it is a potential, it belongs to the family. Conversely, every member $v$ of the family satisfies $v\leq u+k$ for all sufficiently large integers $k$, hence $v\leq \min \{ u+k,f\} $ quasi-everywhere and $v\leq P_\theta (u+k,f)$. Thus a fixed member shows that the rooftop envelopes, which increase with $k$, are potentials for all large $k$, and the family and the rooftop envelopes have the same supremum. This proves the representation. (3) Normalize $u\leq 0$. If $|f|\leq C$ quasi-everywhere, then $u-C$ is a competitor, and for large $k$ each rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u+k,f)$ lies between $u-C$ and $u+k$, so it has the singularity type of $u$ and mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $. By (2) and corollary 13.8.9 , $P_\theta [u](f)$ also has this mass. Comparing $f$ with the constants $-C$ and $C$, and using (1) together with $P_\theta [u](0)=P_\theta [u]$, gives the two bounds. $\square$ Proposition 16.25.3 . 4338492503DC Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $f$ be a bounded quasi-continuous obstacle. Then $w=P_\theta [u](f)$ is a potential, and \[  \mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=P_\theta (f)\} }\mu _{P_\theta (f)}, \qquad \mu _ w(X\setminus \{ w=f\} )=0.  \] In particular $\int _ X(f-w)\, \mu _ w=0$, where the integrand may be given any value at the poles of $w$. Proof. Write $p=P_\theta (f)$ and choose $C$ with $|f|\leq C$. Then $V_\theta -C$ is a competitor for $f$, and every competitor $v$ satisfies $v-C\leq 0$, hence $v\leq V_\theta +C$; thus $V_\theta -C\leq p\leq V_\theta +C$. Consequently $p$ has minimal singularities, and its mass is that of $V_\theta $, namely $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )>0$, by definition 13.9.1 , proposition 13.9.2 . A potential lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere if and only if it lies below $p$: one direction is the maximality of $p$, the other holds because $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Hence the two constrained families coincide, and $w=P_\theta [u](p)$. Since $u\preceq p$, this is the relative envelope of definition 16.22.13 , by proposition 16.25.2 . The measure bound in proposition 16.22.14 , which applies because $p$ has positive mass, gives the first inequality. By theorem 16.13.4 , $\mu _ p$ is carried by $\{ p=f\} $, so $\mu _ w$ is carried by $\{ w=p\} \cap \{ p=f\} \subset \{ w=f\} $. Finally, $f-w$ is nonnegative quasi-everywhere and vanishes $\mu _ w$-almost everywhere, which gives the integral identity. $\square$ Proposition 16.25.4 . C32431185924 Let $u,v,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, let $p$ be an integer with $1\leq p\leq n$, and let $T_1,\ldots ,T_{n-p}$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. For $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ put \[  \lambda _ q=\left\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ p \wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-p}\right\rangle .  \] If $u,v\preceq \phi $, then \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v\} )\leq \lambda _ u(\{ u<v\} ) +\lambda _\phi (X)-\lambda _ u(X).  \] If moreover $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle >0$ and $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\lambda _ u(X)=\lambda _\phi (X)$, and the inequality also holds with $\{ u\leq v\} $ in place of $\{ u<v\} $. Proof. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $q=\max \{ u,v-\varepsilon \} $. Write $T_ i=\theta _ i'+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ with smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ i'$ and $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i')$ (theorem 10.2.15 ). Since $q\preceq \phi $, the monotonicity of mixed masses in corollary 13.8.8 , applied with $n$ factors to the potentials $q,\ldots ,q,\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _{n-p}$ and $\phi ,\ldots ,\phi ,\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _{n-p}$, gives $\lambda _ q(X)\leq \lambda _\phi (X)$. On the disjoint plurifine open sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ and $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $, $q$ equals $v-\varepsilon $ and $u$ respectively, so plurifine locality gives \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} ) \leq \lambda _\phi (X)-\lambda _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} ).  \] Writing $\lambda _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} )=\lambda _ u(X)-\lambda _ u(\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} )$, enlarging $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $ to $\{ u<v\} $ up to the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, which carries no mass, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain the first inequality. Now let $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle >0$ and $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. By proposition 16.22.14 , $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [v]=P_\theta [\phi ]$. With the potentials $\varphi _ i$ of the currents $T_ i$ chosen above, the preservation of mixed masses in proposition 16.21.2 , applied to the $n$ potentials $u,\ldots ,u,\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _{n-p}$ and to the corresponding tuples for $v$ and $\phi $, gives $\lambda _ u(X)=\lambda _ v(X)=\lambda _\phi (X)$. Thus the last two terms in the inequality cancel. Applying the inequality with $u$ and $v$ interchanged, we get $\lambda _ u(\{ v<u\} )\leq \lambda _ v(\{ v<u\} )$, and subtracting this from $\lambda _ v(X)=\lambda _ u(X)$ gives $\lambda _ v(\{ u\leq v\} )\leq \lambda _ u(\{ u\leq v\} )$. $\square$ Definition 16.25.5 . E9BD67F94210 For a reference potential $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a Borel set $A\subset X$, the Monge–Ampère capacity relative to $\phi $ is \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A) =\sup \{ \mu _ v(A):v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),\  \phi -1\leq v\leq \phi \} .  \] The potentials $v$ in this supremum are called competitors for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$. For $\phi =V_\theta $ we obtain the $\theta $-capacity . Proposition 16.25.6 . 1587DBB4654F Let $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The relative capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ is monotone, countably subadditive, zero on pluripolar Borel sets and continuous along increasing sequences of Borel sets. Its total value is $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(X)=\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $, and it is inner regular on Borel sets: \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A) =\sup _{K\subset A\text{ compact}}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K).  \] It does not change when a constant is added to $\phi $. If $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $|\phi -\psi |\leq C$ outside the pole sets of $\phi $ and $\psi $, for a constant $C\geq 0$, then \[  (2C+1)^{-n}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(A) \leq \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A) \leq (2C+1)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(A).  \] Replacing $(\theta ,\phi )$ by $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g,\phi -g)$ for a smooth real function $g$ leaves the capacity unchanged. Proof. Every competitor has the singularity type of $\phi $ and hence mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $; since $\phi $ itself is a competitor, the capacity is finite and $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(X)=\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $. Monotonicity, countable subadditivity and continuity along increasing sequences hold for each measure $\mu _ v$ and pass to the supremum; for the last property, interchange the supremum over the sequence with the supremum over competitors. Inner regularity follows in the same way from the inner regularity of each finite measure $\mu _ v$ (lemma 16.12.1 ): $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A)=\sup _ v\sup _ K\mu _ v(K)=\sup _ K\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K)$, the inner suprema being taken over the compact sets $K\subset A$. Each $\mu _ v$ gives no mass to pluripolar sets. Adding a constant $c$ to $\phi $ corresponds to the bijection $v\mapsto v+c$ of competitors, which does not change $\mu _ v$. For the comparison, note first that $\phi \leq \psi +C$ and $\psi \leq \phi +C$ hold almost everywhere, hence everywhere; in particular $\phi $ and $\psi $ have the same pole set. Put $t=(2C+1)^{-1}$. If $\phi -1\leq v\leq \phi $, the potential $q=(1-t)\psi +tv-tC$ satisfies \[  q\leq (1-t)\psi +t(\psi +C)-tC=\psi ,\qquad q\geq (1-t)\psi +t(\psi -C-1)-tC=\psi -1,  \] so it is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$, and $\mu _ q\geq t^ n\mu _ v$. This proves the upper comparison, and exchanging $\phi $ and $\psi $ proves the lower one. The last assertion follows from the bijection $v\mapsto v-g$ between the two families of competitors, which preserves the current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. $\square$ Proposition 16.25.7 . CDA70099F425 Let $u,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $, and let $s\in \mathbb R$ and $0<t\leq 1$. Then \[  t^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(\{ u<\phi -s-t\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<\phi -s\} )+\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle .  \] In particular, if $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(\{ u<\phi -s\} )\to 0$ as $s\to \infty $. Proof. Let $v$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$, and put $q=(1-t)\phi +tv-s$. Then $\phi -s-t\leq q\leq \phi -s$, so \[  \{ u<\phi -s-t\} \subset \{ u<q\} \subset \{ u<\phi -s\} .  \] Moreover $q\sim \phi $ and $\mu _ q\geq t^ n\mu _ v$. Proposition 16.25.4 , with $p=n$, applied to $u$ and $q$, gives \[  t^ n\mu _ v(\{ u<\phi -s-t\} )\leq \mu _ q(\{ u<q\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<\phi -s\} )+\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle ,  \] and taking the supremum over $v$ proves the inequality. If $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $. With $t=1$, the right side tends to zero as $s\to \infty $ by dominated convergence, because the sets $\{ u<\phi -s\} $ decrease to the pole set of $u$, which is $\mu _ u$-null. $\square$

title: Definition 16.25.1
text: Definition 16.25.1 . 3558A6E66BA8 For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a Borel obstacle $f$, define \[  P_\theta [u](f)=\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): v\preceq u,\  v\leq f\text{ quasi-everywhere}\} \right)^*  \] when this family is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, and put $P_\theta [u](f)=-\infty $ when it is empty. For Borel obstacles $g$ and $f$ we write $P_\theta (g,f)=P_\theta (\min \{ g,f\} )$, under the same conditions on the family of competitors.

title: Proposition 16.25.2
text: Proposition 16.25.2 . 467197AADC50 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $f$ be a Borel obstacle for which the family in definition 16.25.1 is nonempty and uniformly bounded above. $P_\theta [u](f)\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. The envelope increases with $f$ and with the singularity type of $u$, does not change when $f$ is modified on a pluripolar set, and satisfies $P_\theta [u](f+c)=P_\theta [u](f)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. For all sufficiently large $k$, the rooftop envelopes $P_\theta (u+k,f)$ are potentials, and \[  P_\theta [u](f)=\left(\lim _{k\to \infty }P_\theta (u+k,f)\right)^*.  \] If $|f|\leq C$ quasi-everywhere, then \[  P_\theta [u]-C\leq P_\theta [u](f)\leq P_\theta [u]+C,  \] and $P_\theta [u](f)$ has the same mass as $u$. In particular, $P_\theta [u](0)=P_\theta [u]$ and $P_\theta [V_\theta ](f)=P_\theta (f)$ whenever these envelopes are defined. Proof. We begin with the final identities. A competitor for $P_\theta [u](0)$ is a nonpositive potential more singular than $u$, exactly as in definition 16.21.1 ; and every potential is more singular than $V_\theta $, by minimality, so the families defining $P_\theta [V_\theta ](f)$ and $P_\theta (f)$ coincide. (1) The maximum of two members of the family in definition 16.25.1 is again a member. By theorem 5.10.2 , applied on finitely many coordinate balls on which $\theta $ has smooth local potentials, there are members $v_1,v_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _ kv_ k)^*=P_\theta [u](f)$, and the maxima $w_ k=\max \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_ k\} $ form an increasing sequence of members with the same regularized supremum. By corollary 5.47.11 , $\sup _ kw_ k=P_\theta [u](f)$ outside a pluripolar set, and each $w_ k$ lies below $f$ outside a pluripolar set; since countable unions of pluripolar sets are pluripolar (theorem 5.47.8 ), $P_\theta [u](f)\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. (The envelope itself need not be more singular than $u$; see example 16.22.12 .) The other assertions follow from the corresponding properties of the families of competitors. (2) A competitor $h$ for the obstacle $\min \{ u+k,f\} $ satisfies $h\leq u+k$ quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere, and $h\leq f$ quasi-everywhere; so it belongs to the family of definition 16.25.1 . In particular these competitors are uniformly bounded above, $P_\theta (u+k,f)$ is defined, and when it is a potential, it belongs to the family. Conversely, every member $v$ of the family satisfies $v\leq u+k$ for all sufficiently large integers $k$, hence $v\leq \min \{ u+k,f\} $ quasi-everywhere and $v\leq P_\theta (u+k,f)$. Thus a fixed member shows that the rooftop envelopes, which increase with $k$, are potentials for all large $k$, and the family and the rooftop envelopes have the same supremum. This proves the representation. (3) Normalize $u\leq 0$. If $|f|\leq C$ quasi-everywhere, then $u-C$ is a competitor, and for large $k$ each rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u+k,f)$ lies between $u-C$ and $u+k$, so it has the singularity type of $u$ and mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $. By (2) and corollary 13.8.9 , $P_\theta [u](f)$ also has this mass. Comparing $f$ with the constants $-C$ and $C$, and using (1) together with $P_\theta [u](0)=P_\theta [u]$, gives the two bounds. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.25.3
text: Proposition 16.25.3 . 4338492503DC Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $f$ be a bounded quasi-continuous obstacle. Then $w=P_\theta [u](f)$ is a potential, and \[  \mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=P_\theta (f)\} }\mu _{P_\theta (f)}, \qquad \mu _ w(X\setminus \{ w=f\} )=0.  \] In particular $\int _ X(f-w)\, \mu _ w=0$, where the integrand may be given any value at the poles of $w$. Proof. Write $p=P_\theta (f)$ and choose $C$ with $|f|\leq C$. Then $V_\theta -C$ is a competitor for $f$, and every competitor $v$ satisfies $v-C\leq 0$, hence $v\leq V_\theta +C$; thus $V_\theta -C\leq p\leq V_\theta +C$. Consequently $p$ has minimal singularities, and its mass is that of $V_\theta $, namely $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )>0$, by definition 13.9.1 , proposition 13.9.2 . A potential lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere if and only if it lies below $p$: one direction is the maximality of $p$, the other holds because $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Hence the two constrained families coincide, and $w=P_\theta [u](p)$. Since $u\preceq p$, this is the relative envelope of definition 16.22.13 , by proposition 16.25.2 . The measure bound in proposition 16.22.14 , which applies because $p$ has positive mass, gives the first inequality. By theorem 16.13.4 , $\mu _ p$ is carried by $\{ p=f\} $, so $\mu _ w$ is carried by $\{ w=p\} \cap \{ p=f\} \subset \{ w=f\} $. Finally, $f-w$ is nonnegative quasi-everywhere and vanishes $\mu _ w$-almost everywhere, which gives the integral identity. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.25.4
text: Proposition 16.25.4 . C32431185924 Let $u,v,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, let $p$ be an integer with $1\leq p\leq n$, and let $T_1,\ldots ,T_{n-p}$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. For $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ put \[  \lambda _ q=\left\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ p \wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-p}\right\rangle .  \] If $u,v\preceq \phi $, then \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v\} )\leq \lambda _ u(\{ u<v\} ) +\lambda _\phi (X)-\lambda _ u(X).  \] If moreover $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle >0$ and $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\lambda _ u(X)=\lambda _\phi (X)$, and the inequality also holds with $\{ u\leq v\} $ in place of $\{ u<v\} $. Proof. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $q=\max \{ u,v-\varepsilon \} $. Write $T_ i=\theta _ i'+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ with smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ i'$ and $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i')$ (theorem 10.2.15 ). Since $q\preceq \phi $, the monotonicity of mixed masses in corollary 13.8.8 , applied with $n$ factors to the potentials $q,\ldots ,q,\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _{n-p}$ and $\phi ,\ldots ,\phi ,\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _{n-p}$, gives $\lambda _ q(X)\leq \lambda _\phi (X)$. On the disjoint plurifine open sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ and $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $, $q$ equals $v-\varepsilon $ and $u$ respectively, so plurifine locality gives \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} ) \leq \lambda _\phi (X)-\lambda _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} ).  \] Writing $\lambda _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} )=\lambda _ u(X)-\lambda _ u(\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} )$, enlarging $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $ to $\{ u<v\} $ up to the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, which carries no mass, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain the first inequality. Now let $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle >0$ and $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. By proposition 16.22.14 , $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [v]=P_\theta [\phi ]$. With the potentials $\varphi _ i$ of the currents $T_ i$ chosen above, the preservation of mixed masses in proposition 16.21.2 , applied to the $n$ potentials $u,\ldots ,u,\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _{n-p}$ and to the corresponding tuples for $v$ and $\phi $, gives $\lambda _ u(X)=\lambda _ v(X)=\lambda _\phi (X)$. Thus the last two terms in the inequality cancel. Applying the inequality with $u$ and $v$ interchanged, we get $\lambda _ u(\{ v<u\} )\leq \lambda _ v(\{ v<u\} )$, and subtracting this from $\lambda _ v(X)=\lambda _ u(X)$ gives $\lambda _ v(\{ u\leq v\} )\leq \lambda _ u(\{ u\leq v\} )$. $\square$

text: Proposition 16.25.7 . CDA70099F425 Let $u,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $, and let $s\in \mathbb R$ and $0<t\leq 1$. Then \[  t^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(\{ u<\phi -s-t\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<\phi -s\} )+\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle .  \] In particular, if $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(\{ u<\phi -s\} )\to 0$ as $s\to \infty $. title: 16.26 Quantitative rooftop extrapolation
text: In theorem 16.22.4 the potentials are ordered by $u\preceq v$. We now show that it suffices to order their singularity envelopes, $P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [v]$. The obstacle $au+(1-a)v$ may then be unbounded above near the poles of $v$, so we must show separately that its competitors are uniformly bounded above. This follows from the uniform $L^1$ bound for normalized potentials, applied on a set of positive volume on which the obstacle is bounded. As before, $\{ \theta \} $ is big. Theorem 16.26.1 . 64513E83F854 Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$ and $P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [v]$, and let $a>1$ satisfy \[  a^ n\left(\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \right)<\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle .  \] Consider the obstacle $au+(1-a)v$, evaluated where $u$ and $v$ are both finite and given arbitrary Borel values on the remaining pluripolar set. Then $\eta =P_\theta (au+(1-a)v)$ is a potential of positive mass, and \[  a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u, \qquad P_\theta [\eta ]\leq P_\theta [u].  \] If $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [v]$, then every $a>1$ is allowed, $P_\theta [\eta ]=P_\theta [u]$, and $\eta $ has the same mass as $u$. Proof. Write $\phi =P_\theta [u]$ and $\psi =P_\theta [v]$. Then $u\preceq \phi \leq \psi $, and by proposition 16.21.2 and the monotonicity of mass, \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0.  \] Hence theorem 16.22.4 , applied to $u$ and $\psi $, gives a potential $\eta '=P_\theta (au+(1-a)\psi )$ of positive mass. Choose $C$ with $v\leq \psi +C$. Since $1-a<0$, we have $\eta '-(a-1)C\leq au+(1-a)v$ quasi-everywhere, so $\eta '-(a-1)C$ is a competitor for the obstacle $au+(1-a)v$. We show that the competitors are uniformly bounded above. Since $u$ and $v$ are finite almost everywhere, there is a Borel set $K$ of positive $\omega ^ n$-volume on which both are bounded; the obstacle is then bounded above on $K$ by a constant $D$. Let $h$ be a competitor. By proposition 10.3.1 , there is a constant $B$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $ and $\omega $, such that \[  \int _ X|h-\sup _ Xh|\, \omega ^ n\leq B.  \] Since $h\leq D$ almost everywhere on $K$, integration over $K$ gives $\sup _ Xh\leq D+B/\int _ K\omega ^ n$. Hence the envelope $\eta $ is a potential. It dominates $\eta '-(a-1)C$, so it has positive mass. The inequality $\eta \leq au+(1-a)v$, which holds quasi-everywhere, is equivalent there to $a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u$; this inequality between quasi-plurisubharmonic functions therefore holds everywhere. Next we compare singularity envelopes. Put $t=a^{-1}$. For all sufficiently large integers $k$, the potential $tP_\theta (\eta +k,0)+(1-t)P_\theta (v+k,0)$ is nonpositive and more singular than $t\eta +(1-t)v\leq u$; here $P_\theta (\eta +k,0)=P_\theta (\min \{ \eta +k,0\} )$, as in definition 16.25.1 , and similarly for $v$. It is therefore a competitor for $\phi $. By proposition 16.25.2 , $P_\theta (\eta +k,0)$ and $P_\theta (v+k,0)$ increase almost everywhere to $P_\theta [\eta ]$ and $\psi $ as $k\to \infty $. Hence \[  tP_\theta [\eta ]+(1-t)\psi \leq \phi  \] almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere. Since $\phi \leq \psi $, subtracting $(1-t)\psi $ where $\phi $ is finite gives $P_\theta [\eta ]\leq \phi $ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. Suppose finally that $\phi =\psi $. Then $u$ and $v$ have the same mass, so every $a>1$ is allowed, and theorem 16.22.4 shows that $\eta '$ also has this mass. Since $\eta \geq \eta '-(a-1)C$, the mass of $\eta $ is at least that of $u$, by monotonicity. Conversely, $P_\theta [\eta ]\leq \phi $ and the preservation of mass by singularity envelopes show that the mass of $\eta $ is at most that of $\phi $, which is the mass of $u$. Thus $\phi $ is nonpositive, has the same mass as $\eta $, and is less singular than $\eta $, because $\eta \preceq P_\theta [\eta ]\leq \phi $. The characterization of $P_\theta [\eta ]$ in theorem 16.22.11 therefore gives $\phi \leq P_\theta [\eta ]$, so $P_\theta [\eta ]=\phi $. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.26.1
text: Theorem 16.26.1 . 64513E83F854 Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$ and $P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [v]$, and let $a>1$ satisfy \[  a^ n\left(\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \right)<\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle .  \] Consider the obstacle $au+(1-a)v$, evaluated where $u$ and $v$ are both finite and given arbitrary Borel values on the remaining pluripolar set. Then $\eta =P_\theta (au+(1-a)v)$ is a potential of positive mass, and \[  a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u, \qquad P_\theta [\eta ]\leq P_\theta [u].  \] If $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [v]$, then every $a>1$ is allowed, $P_\theta [\eta ]=P_\theta [u]$, and $\eta $ has the same mass as $u$. Proof. Write $\phi =P_\theta [u]$ and $\psi =P_\theta [v]$. Then $u\preceq \phi \leq \psi $, and by proposition 16.21.2 and the monotonicity of mass, \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0.  \] Hence theorem 16.22.4 , applied to $u$ and $\psi $, gives a potential $\eta '=P_\theta (au+(1-a)\psi )$ of positive mass. Choose $C$ with $v\leq \psi +C$. Since $1-a<0$, we have $\eta '-(a-1)C\leq au+(1-a)v$ quasi-everywhere, so $\eta '-(a-1)C$ is a competitor for the obstacle $au+(1-a)v$. We show that the competitors are uniformly bounded above. Since $u$ and $v$ are finite almost everywhere, there is a Borel set $K$ of positive $\omega ^ n$-volume on which both are bounded; the obstacle is then bounded above on $K$ by a constant $D$. Let $h$ be a competitor. By proposition 10.3.1 , there is a constant $B$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $ and $\omega $, such that \[  \int _ X|h-\sup _ Xh|\, \omega ^ n\leq B.  \] Since $h\leq D$ almost everywhere on $K$, integration over $K$ gives $\sup _ Xh\leq D+B/\int _ K\omega ^ n$. Hence the envelope $\eta $ is a potential. It dominates $\eta '-(a-1)C$, so it has positive mass. The inequality $\eta \leq au+(1-a)v$, which holds quasi-everywhere, is equivalent there to $a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u$; this inequality between quasi-plurisubharmonic functions therefore holds everywhere. Next we compare singularity envelopes. Put $t=a^{-1}$. For all sufficiently large integers $k$, the potential $tP_\theta (\eta +k,0)+(1-t)P_\theta (v+k,0)$ is nonpositive and more singular than $t\eta +(1-t)v\leq u$; here $P_\theta (\eta +k,0)=P_\theta (\min \{ \eta +k,0\} )$, as in definition 16.25.1 , and similarly for $v$. It is therefore a competitor for $\phi $. By proposition 16.25.2 , $P_\theta (\eta +k,0)$ and $P_\theta (v+k,0)$ increase almost everywhere to $P_\theta [\eta ]$ and $\psi $ as $k\to \infty $. Hence \[  tP_\theta [\eta ]+(1-t)\psi \leq \phi  \] almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere. Since $\phi \leq \psi $, subtracting $(1-t)\psi $ where $\phi $ is finite gives $P_\theta [\eta ]\leq \phi $ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. Suppose finally that $\phi =\psi $. Then $u$ and $v$ have the same mass, so every $a>1$ is allowed, and theorem 16.22.4 shows that $\eta '$ also has this mass. Since $\eta \geq \eta '-(a-1)C$, the mass of $\eta $ is at least that of $u$, by monotonicity. Conversely, $P_\theta [\eta ]\leq \phi $ and the preservation of mass by singularity envelopes show that the mass of $\eta $ is at most that of $\phi $, which is the mass of $u$. Thus $\phi $ is nonpositive, has the same mass as $\eta $, and is less singular than $\eta $, because $\eta \preceq P_\theta [\eta ]\leq \phi $. The characterization of $P_\theta [\eta ]$ in theorem 16.22.11 therefore gives $\phi \leq P_\theta [\eta ]$, so $P_\theta [\eta ]=\phi $. $\square$

title: 16.27 Comparison of relative capacities
text: We now compare the relative capacities $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ with each other and with the capacity of a Kähler form. The main tool is the envelope $S$ of lemma 16.27.5 , an increasing limit of envelopes of smooth penalties that vanish exactly on a compact set $K$. Its Monge–Ampère measure is carried by $K$, and its height $\sup _ XS$ controls the relative capacity of $K$ from both sides. All backgrounds are smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms. In each statement, $\mu _ q$ denotes the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of $q$ for the background indicated there, and the mass of $q$ is $\mu _ q(X)$; when two backgrounds occur, we write the measures explicitly, as in $\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n\rangle $. For a Kähler form $\kappa $ we have $V_\kappa =0$, since the constant $0$ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic and $V_\kappa \leq 0$; we write $\Omega =\int _ X\kappa ^ n$ and $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa =\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,0}$. The capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $ is the Monge–Ampère capacity $c_\kappa $ of section 10.9 . Indeed, $v\mapsto v+1$ maps the competitors for $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $ onto the functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ with values in $[0,1]$, and non-pluripolar products of bounded potentials are Bedford–Taylor products (definition 13.2.4 ). Since $\kappa $ is closed, the form $\sigma $ in ( 10.9.2 ) is closed, hence locally $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a smooth function (lemma 5.4.2 ), and the multilinearity of Bedford–Taylor products identifies the products defined there with the Bedford–Taylor products of local potentials. Lemma 16.27.1 . 49691FF58A24 Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ be bounded. Then $p$ is the pointwise limit of smooth functions $p_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ with $\sup _ j\sup _ X|p_ j|<\infty $. Proof. Apply theorem 6.17.6 with $\kappa $ as the Kähler form of reference. It gives potentials $\Phi _ j$ decreasing to $p$ with $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ j\geq -\varepsilon _ j\kappa $, where $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, and with gentle analytic singularities of type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ jp))$. Since $p$ is bounded, $\mathrm e^{-2^ jp}$ is bounded, so $\mathcal I(2^ jp)$ is the unit ideal. In the local presentations $\Phi _ j=2^{-j}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+b$ of definition 6.14.5 , the functions $g_ i$ therefore generate the unit ideal and have no common zero, so $\Phi _ j$ is bounded. Hence the smooth function $\exp (2^ j\Phi _ j)$ has no zeros, and $\Phi _ j=2^{-j}\log \exp (2^ j\Phi _ j)$ is smooth. Put $p_ j=\Phi _ j/(1+\varepsilon _ j)$. Then \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_ j=\frac{(1+\varepsilon _ j)\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ j}{1+\varepsilon _ j}\geq 0.  \] The bounds $p\leq \Phi _ j\leq \Phi _1$ give $|p_ j|\leq |\Phi _ j|\leq \max \{ \sup _ X|p|,\sup _ X|\Phi _1|\} $, and $p_ j\to p$ pointwise because $\Phi _ j\to p$ and $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$ (unlike the $\Phi _ j$, the $p_ j$ need not decrease). $\square$ Lemma 16.27.2 . A73E0CBD9FAB Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form, let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ satisfy $v\leq u\leq v+B$ for a constant $B\geq 0$, and let $p$ be a bounded function in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$. Then E0D5BEEFADA4 16.27.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ Xp\, \mu _ u\geq \int _ Xp\, \mu _ v-nB\Omega . \end{equation} Moreover, there is a constant $C_\kappa $, depending only on $X$ and $\kappa $, such that for every model potential $\phi $ for the background $\kappa $, every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ with $\phi -1\leq v\leq \phi $, and every $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ with $\sup _ Xp=0$, bounded or not, E22DEE0D88EE 16.27.4 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(-p)\, \mu _ v\leq C_\kappa . \end{equation} Proof. Write $\kappa _ q=\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$. We first prove ( 16.27.3 ) when $u=v$ near the poles of $v$ and then reduce to this case; the second assertion follows from the first. A special case. Assume first that there are $l_0>0$ and an open set $U\supset \{ v<-l_0\} $ on which $u=v$. For $l>l_0$ put $u_ l=\max \{ u,-l\} $ and $v_ l=\max \{ v,-l\} $; these are bounded functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ with $0\leq u_ l-v_ l\leq B$. On $U$ we have $u_ l=v_ l$ and $u=v$, so $\mu _{u_ l}=\mu _{v_ l}$ and $\mu _ u=\mu _ v$ there. The complement of $U$ lies in the plurifine open set $\{ v>-l\} $, on which $u_ l=u$ and $v_ l=v$, because $u\geq v$; by plurifine locality, $\mu _{u_ l}=\mu _ u$ and $\mu _{v_ l}=\mu _ v$ on this set. Hence $\mu _{u_ l}-\mu _{v_ l}=\mu _ u-\mu _ v$. Expanding $\kappa _{u_ l}^ n-\kappa _{v_ l}^ n$ and integrating by parts with lemma 13.5.2 , we obtain \[  \begin{split}  \int _ Xp\, (\mu _ u-\mu _ v)=\int _ Xp(\mu _{u_ l}-\mu _{v_ l}) & =\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}\int _ X(u_ l-v_ l)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p \wedge \kappa _{u_ l}^{j}\wedge \kappa _{v_ l}^{n-1-j}\\ & \geq -nB\Omega . \end{split}  \] For the last inequality write $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)-\kappa $: the first part contributes a nonnegative amount, since $u_ l-v_ l\geq 0$, and the second contributes at least $-B\int _ X\kappa \wedge \kappa _{u_ l}^ j\wedge \kappa _{v_ l}^{n-1-j}=-B\Omega $, by proposition 13.5.1 . The general case. Subtracting a common constant, we may assume $v\leq 0$. For $0<a<1$ put $v_ a=av$ and $u_ a=\max \{ u,av\} $; these belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ because $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(av)=(1-a)\kappa +a\kappa _ v$. Since $v\leq av$, we have $v_ a\leq u_ a\leq v_ a+B$. On the open set $U_ a=\{ v<-B/(1-a)\} $ we have $av-v>B\geq u-v$, so $u_ a=v_ a$ there. With $l_0=aB/(1-a)+1$, the set $\{ v_ a<-l_0\} =\{ v<-l_0/a\} $ is contained in $U_ a$, so the special case applies to $u_ a$ and $v_ a$. As $a\uparrow 1$, $v_ a$ and $u_ a$ decrease to $v$ and $u$. The masses of $u_ a$ and $v_ a$ agree, and by multilinearity $\int _ X\langle \kappa _{v_ a}^ n\rangle $ is a polynomial in $a$ that tends to $\int _ X\langle \kappa _ v^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \kappa _ u^ n\rangle $. Decreasing sequences converge in extended capacity (lemma 13.7.3 ), so theorem 13.7.5 shows that $\mu _{u_ a}\to \mu _ u$ and $\mu _{v_ a}\to \mu _ v$ weakly along every sequence $a\uparrow 1$. Passing to the limit in ( 16.27.3 ) for $u_ a$ and $v_ a$, we obtain ( 16.27.3 ) for every continuous, in particular every smooth, $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$. For a bounded $p$, take the approximations $p_ j$ of lemma 16.27.1 ; they converge pointwise with a common bound, and dominated convergence with respect to the finite measures $\mu _ u$ and $\mu _ v$ proves ( 16.27.3 ). The second assertion. Let $\phi $ be a model potential for $\kappa $. Since $V_\kappa =0$, proposition 16.21.3 gives $\mu _\phi \leq \kappa ^ n$. If $\phi -1\leq v\leq \phi $, the first assertion, applied to $\phi \leq v+1\leq \phi +1$, gives for every bounded $p$ with $\sup _ Xp=0$ \[  \int _ X(-p)\, \mu _ v\leq \int _ X(-p)\, \mu _\phi +n\Omega \leq \int _ X(-p)\, \kappa ^ n+n\Omega .  \] By proposition 10.3.1 , applied on the compact Kähler manifold $(X,\kappa )$ with background $\kappa $, the last integral is bounded by a constant depending only on $X$ and $\kappa $. For an unbounded $p$ with $\sup _ Xp=0$, apply this bound to the truncations $\max \{ p,-l\} $, which are bounded, belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ and have supremum zero, and let $l\to \infty $ by monotone convergence. $\square$ Lemma 16.27.5 . 48CC217E0795 Suppose that $\{ \theta \} $ is big, let $\phi $ be a model potential of mass $m>0$, and let $K\subset X$ be a compact non-pluripolar set. There is a smooth function $g\geq 0$ on $X$ whose zero set is $K$. For every such $g$, the envelopes $q_ j=P_\theta (\phi +jg)$, $j\geq 1$, are potentials that increase with $j$, and their regularized limit $S=(\sup _ jq_ j)^*$ is a potential such that $L=\sup _ XS\geq 0$ and \[  \begin{gathered} \phi \leq S\leq \phi +L,\qquad S=\phi \text{ quasi-everywhere on }K,\\ \int _ X\langle \theta _ S^ n\rangle =m,\qquad \mu _ S(X\setminus K)=0. \end{gathered}  \] In particular, 6B1343C4F9ED 16.27.6 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K) \geq \frac{m}{\max \{ 1,L\} ^{n}}. \end{equation} If $\theta =\kappa $ is a Kähler form, then also 7D6FB72AF287 16.27.7 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(K) \leq \frac{C}{\max \{ 1,L\} }, \end{equation} where $C$ depends only on $X$ and $\kappa $. Proof. We first construct $g$. If $K=X$, take $g=0$. Otherwise fix finitely many coordinate charts $D_ i$ and compact sets $K_ i\subset D_ i$ whose interiors cover $X$, and measure derivatives on $K_ i$ in the coordinates of $D_ i$. Each point of $X\setminus K$ is the center of a coordinate ball whose closure lies in $X\setminus K$; since $X\setminus K$ has a countable basis, countably many of the concentric balls of half the radius, say $B_1',B_2',\ldots $, cover $X\setminus K$. Let $B_ l$ be the corresponding ball of full radius, and choose a smooth function $g_ l\geq 0$ with compact support in $B_ l$ that is positive on $\overline{B_ l'}$ (a smooth cutoff function, lemma 2.5.1 ). Multiplying $g_ l$ by a small positive constant, we may assume that all its derivatives of order at most $l$ are bounded by $2^{-l}$ on every $K_ i$. Then the series $g=\sum _ lg_ l$ converges uniformly on every $K_ i$ together with all its derivatives, so $g$ is smooth on the interior of every $K_ i$, hence on $X$; it vanishes on $K$, and it is positive on $X\setminus K$, because every point there lies in some $B_ l'$. Now let $g$ be any smooth nonnegative function with zero set $K$, and put $q_ j=P_\theta (\phi +jg)$. Since $\phi $ is a competitor and every competitor is at most $\phi +j\sup _ Xg$, we have $\phi \leq q_ j\leq \phi +j\sup _ Xg$, so $q_ j\sim \phi $. The obstacle $\phi +jg$ is upper semicontinuous, so $q_ j\leq \phi +jg$ everywhere by proposition 16.11.4 , and therefore $q_ j=\phi $ on $K$. In particular $\sup _ Kq_ j\leq 0$, and corollary 10.3.5 bounds $\sup _ Xq_ j$ uniformly in $j$. The envelopes $q_ j$ increase with $j$, since $g\geq 0$, so $S=(\sup _ jq_ j)^*$ is a potential; put $L=\sup _ XS$. Then $L\geq 0$, because $S\geq \phi $ and $\sup _ X\phi =0$. Since $q_ j\preceq \phi $ and $\sup _ Xq_ j\leq \sup _ XS=L$, lemma 16.22.2 gives $q_ j\leq \phi +L$, hence $\phi \leq S\leq \phi +L$. By corollary 5.47.11 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, the regularization changes $\sup _ jq_ j$ only on a pluripolar set, so $S=\phi $ quasi-everywhere on $K$. Since $S\sim \phi $, $\int _ X\langle \theta _ S^ n\rangle =m$. The obstacle $\phi +jg$ is quasi-continuous, and its family of competitors is nonempty and bounded above by $j\sup _ Xg$, so theorem 16.13.4 shows that $\mu _{q_ j}$ is carried by the contact set $\{ q_ j=\phi +jg\} $. At a point of this set where $\phi $ is finite, the bound $q_ j\leq \phi +L$ gives $jg\leq L$. Thus $\mu _{q_ j}$ is carried by $\{ g\leq L/j\} $. By corollary 13.8.9 , $\mu _{q_ j}\to \mu _ S$ weakly. If $\chi \geq 0$ is continuous with compact support in $X\setminus K$, then $g$ has a positive lower bound $c$ on the support of $\chi $, so $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _{q_ j}=0$ for $j>L/c$, and in the limit $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _ S=0$. By lemma 16.12.1 (2), applied on $W=X\setminus K$ with the zero measure, $\mu _ S(X\setminus K)=0$. Set $t=1/\max \{ 1,L\} $ and $h=(1-t)\phi +tS-tL$. Then $\phi -1\leq \phi -tL\leq h\leq \phi $, so $h$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$, and $\mu _ h\geq t^ n\mu _ S$. Hence $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K)\geq t^ n\mu _ S(K)=t^ nm$, which is ( 16.27.6 ). In the Kähler case apply ( 16.27.4 ) to the potential $p=S-L$, which has supremum zero. Quasi-everywhere on $K$ we have $-p=L-\phi \geq L$, so $L\mu _ v(K)\leq C_\kappa $ for every competitor $v$ for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }$. If $L\geq 1$, this gives ( 16.27.7 ) with $C=C_\kappa $. If $L<1$, use $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(K)\leq \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(X)=m\leq \Omega $; the last inequality is the monotonicity of mass, because $\phi \preceq V_\kappa =0$ and the mass of $0$ is $\int _ X\kappa ^ n=\Omega $. Thus $C=\max \{ C_\kappa ,\Omega \} $ works. $\square$ The capacity of a compact set controls the height $L$ of its penalized envelope, and the uniform exponential integrability of normalized potentials converts this height into a volume estimate. The resulting constants do not depend on the model potential. Proposition 16.27.8 . C745DD03819C Suppose that $\{ \theta \} $ is big, and let $\phi $ be a model potential of mass $m>0$. There are $\alpha ,C>0$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $ and $\omega $, such that every Borel set $E\subset X$ satisfies 7D19131D8004 16.27.9 \begin{equation}  \int _ E\omega ^ n\leq C\exp \left[-\alpha \left(\frac{m}{\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)}\right)^{1/n}\right], \end{equation} where the right side is interpreted as zero when the capacity is zero. Proof. Let $\alpha $ and $C_0$ be the constants of corollary 10.3.3 . First let $K$ be compact and non-pluripolar, and let $S,L$ be as in lemma 16.27.5 . The potential $p=S-L$ has supremum zero and satisfies $p\leq -L$ quasi-everywhere on $K$, because $S=\phi \leq 0$ there. Since pluripolar sets have zero volume, ( 10.3.4 ) gives \[  \int _ K\omega ^ n\leq \int _ K\mathrm e^{-\alpha p-\alpha L}\, \omega ^ n\leq C_0\mathrm e^{-\alpha L}.  \] Write $c=\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K)$, which is positive by ( 16.27.6 ). By the same inequality, \[  \left(\frac mc\right)^{1/n}\leq \max \{ 1,L\} \leq 1+L,  \] so ( 16.27.9 ) holds for $K$ with $C=C_0\mathrm e^\alpha $. If $K$ is pluripolar, its volume and its capacity both vanish. Now let $E$ be a Borel set. If $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)>0$, the estimate for compact subsets $K\subset E$, together with the monotonicity of capacity and the inner regularity of the smooth volume, gives ( 16.27.9 ). If $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)=0$, every compact subset of $E$ has zero capacity, hence is pluripolar by ( 16.27.6 ) and has zero volume; by inner regularity, $E$ has zero volume. $\square$ Corollary 16.27.10 . 9C70131AD005 Under the hypotheses of proposition 16.27.8 , let $p>1$, $0\leq f\in L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$ and $r>0$. There is $B_ r>0$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $, $\omega $, $p$ and $r$, such that every Borel set $E$ satisfies 8CF36AE13615 16.27.11 \begin{equation}  \int _ E f\omega ^ n\leq B_ r\| f\| _{L^ p} \left(\frac{\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)}m\right)^ r. \end{equation} In particular, for every $r>1$ the measure $f\omega ^ n$ is dominated by a constant multiple of $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }^ r$. Proof. If $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)=0$, then $E$ has zero volume by proposition 16.27.8 , and both sides vanish. Otherwise let $q=p/(p-1)$. By Hölder's inequality and ( 16.27.9 ), the integral is at most \[  \| f\| _{L^ p}C^{1/q}\exp \left[-\frac\alpha q \left(\frac{m}{\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)}\right)^{1/n}\right].  \] Put $t=(m/\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E))^{1/n}$; then $t\geq 1$, since the capacity is at most $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =m$. The function $t^{nr}\mathrm e^{-\alpha t/q}$ is bounded on $[1,\infty )$: its logarithmic derivative is $nr/t-\alpha /q$, so its maximum is attained at $1$ or at $nrq/\alpha $. Hence $\mathrm e^{-\alpha t/q}\leq A\, t^{-nr}$ for a constant $A$ depending only on $n,r,q,\alpha $, and this proves ( 16.27.11 ). $\square$ Proposition 16.27.12 . 04DE884FD6DB Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form and $\phi $ a model potential for $\kappa $ of mass $m>0$. There is $A\geq 1$ such that every Borel set $E\subset X$ satisfies 3F70CF1B1F96 16.27.13 \begin{equation}  A^{-1}\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (E)^ n \leq \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(E) \leq A\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (E)^{1/n}. \end{equation} More generally, if $\theta \leq \kappa $, $\{ \theta \} $ is big and $\phi $ is a model potential for $\theta $ of mass $m>0$, then 391CDC0D1779 16.27.14 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (E)^ n \leq \frac{C^ n}{m}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E), \end{equation} where $C$ depends only on $X$ and $\kappa $. Proof. All capacities involved are inner regular (proposition 16.25.6 ), so it suffices to treat compact sets $K$: the inequalities for a Borel set $E$ follow by applying them to the compact subsets of $E$ and taking suprema. If $K$ is pluripolar, all capacities of $K$ vanish. Otherwise fix a smooth function $g\geq 0$ with zero set $K$, and apply lemma 16.27.5 with this $g$ to $(\theta ,\phi )$ and to $(\kappa ,0)$; here $0=V_\kappa $ is a model potential for $\kappa $ of mass $\Omega $, by proposition 16.21.2 (4). Denote the resulting envelopes by $S_\phi $ and $S_0$ and their suprema by $L_\phi $ and $L_0$. Every competitor for $P_\theta (\phi +jg)$ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic, because $\theta \leq \kappa $, and it is at most $\phi +jg\leq jg$ quasi-everywhere, so $P_\theta (\phi +jg)\leq P_\kappa (jg)$ for every $j$; hence $S_\phi \leq S_0$ and $L_\phi \leq L_0$. The two estimates of lemma 16.27.5 give \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (K)^ n \leq \frac{C^ n}{\max \{ 1,L_0\} ^ n} \leq \frac{C^ n}{\max \{ 1,L_\phi \} ^ n} \leq \frac{C^ n}{m}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K).  \] This proves ( 16.27.14 ) and, for $\theta =\kappa $, the first inequality in ( 16.27.13 ). For the upper bound let $\theta =\kappa $, and choose $b>1$ with $b^ n(\Omega -m)<\Omega $. By theorem 16.22.4 , applied to $\phi \preceq 0$, where the mass of $0$ is $\int _ X\kappa ^ n=\Omega $, the envelope $\eta =E_ b(\phi ,0)=P_\kappa (b\phi )$ is a potential, and it satisfies $b^{-1}\eta \leq \phi $; in particular $\eta =-\infty $ at the poles of $\phi $. Write $c=1-b^{-1}>0$. For fixed $j$ and $\delta >0$ consider \[  v_ j=c\, P_\kappa (jg)+b^{-1}\eta -\delta ,  \] a convex combination of $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic functions minus a constant. The function $P_\kappa (jg)$ is upper semicontinuous and vanishes on $K$, because $0\leq P_\kappa (jg)\leq jg$. Hence $P_\kappa (jg)<\delta /c$ on a neighborhood $U$ of $K$, and there $v_ j<b^{-1}\eta \leq \phi $. Outside the poles of $\phi $, the difference $v_ j-\phi $ is bounded above by $cj\sup _ Xg$, and $g$ has a positive minimum on $X\setminus U$. Therefore $v_ j\leq \phi +lg$ for a sufficiently large integer $l$, so $v_ j\leq P_\kappa (\phi +lg)\leq S_\phi $. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ and then $j\to \infty $, and using that the increasing limit of $P_\kappa (jg)$ equals $S_0$ almost everywhere, we obtain \[  cS_0+b^{-1}\eta \leq S_\phi  \] almost everywhere, hence everywhere. Choose a Borel set $G$ of positive volume on which $b^{-1}\eta \geq -D$ for a constant $D$; such a set exists because $\eta $ is finite almost everywhere. By proposition 10.3.1 , there is a constant $B$, independent of $K$, with $\int _ X|S_0-L_0|\, \kappa ^ n\leq B$. Hence $S_0\geq L_0-B/\int _ G\kappa ^ n$ at some point $x\in G$, for otherwise $\int _ G(L_0-S_0)\, \kappa ^ n>B$. At this point the last display gives $L_\phi \geq S_\phi (x)\geq cL_0-D'$ with $D'=cB/\int _ G\kappa ^ n+D$, which does not depend on $K$. If $L_0\geq \max \{ 1,2D'/c\} $, then $L_\phi \geq cL_0/2$, and lemma 16.27.5 gives \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(K)\leq \frac{2C}{cL_0} \leq \frac{2C}{c\, \Omega ^{1/n}}\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (K)^{1/n};  \] the last inequality is the lower bound ( 16.27.6 ) for the construction with reference potential $0$, which gives $\Omega /L_0^ n\leq \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (K)$. In the remaining range $L_0<\max \{ 1,2D'/c\} $, the same lower bound shows that $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (K)$ is bounded below by a positive constant independent of $K$, and we use $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(K)\leq m$, enlarging $A$ if necessary. The constant $A$ in the upper bound depends on $\phi $. $\square$ Lemma 16.27.15 . A285A0B9F4B7 Suppose that $\{ \theta \} $ is big, let $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have positive mass, and let $\psi \in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. There is a continuous nondecreasing function $F\colon [0,\infty )\to [0,\infty )$ with $F(0)=0$, which may depend on $\psi $ and $\phi $, such that \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E) \leq F(\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E))  \] for every Borel set $E\subset X$. Proof. Since $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ does not change when a constant is added to $\phi $ (proposition 16.25.6 ), we may assume that $\psi \leq \phi $. Let $u$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$, so that $\psi -1\leq u\leq \psi $, and let $t\geq 1$. We estimate $\mu _ u(E)$ separately on $\{ u>\phi -2t\} $ and on $\{ u\leq \phi -2t\} $. Put $u_ t=\max \{ u,\phi -2t\} $, so that $\phi -2t\leq u_ t\leq \phi $. The potential $(1-(2t)^{-1})\phi +(2t)^{-1}u_ t$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$, and its measure is at least $(2t)^{-n}\mu _{u_ t}$. Since $u_ t=u$ on the plurifine open set $\{ u>\phi -2t\} $, it follows that \[  \mu _ u(E\cap \{ u>\phi -2t\} ) \leq (2t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E).  \] The potentials $\psi $, $u$ and $\psi -1$ belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. So does the midpoint $q=(u+\phi )/2$: by proposition 16.22.14 , $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\phi ]$, so by proposition 16.21.2 each mixed mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ k\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-k}\rangle $ equals the mass of $\phi $. Expanding $\mu _ q$ by multilinearity, we see that $q$ also has the mass of $\phi $. On the set $\{ u\leq \phi -2t\} $ we have $q-t\geq u\geq \psi -1$, and on $\{ \psi -1\leq q-t\} $ we have $\psi -1\leq (\psi +\phi )/2-t$, that is, $\psi \leq \phi -2t+2\leq \phi -t+1$. Thus \[  \{ u\leq \phi -2t\} \subset \{ \psi -1\leq q-t\}  \subset \{ \psi \leq \phi -t+1\} .  \] The non-strict comparison in proposition 16.25.4 , applied with $p=n$ to $\psi -1$ and $q-t$, together with $\mu _ q\geq 2^{-n}\mu _ u$, gives \[  \begin{split}  \mu _ u(\{ u\leq \phi -2t\} )& \leq 2^ n\mu _ q(\{ \psi -1\leq q-t\} ) \leq 2^ n\mu _\psi (\{ \psi -1\leq q-t\} )\\ & \leq 2^ n\mu _\psi (\{ \psi \leq \phi -t+1\} ). \end{split}  \] Adding the two estimates and taking the supremum over $u$, we obtain 106A989F297D 16.27.16 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E) \leq (2t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E) +2^ n\mu _\psi (\{ \psi \leq \phi -t+1\} ) \qquad (t\geq 1). \end{equation} The last term tends to zero as $t\to \infty $, since $\psi $ and $\phi $ are finite outside a $\mu _\psi $-null set. It remains to replace the right side by a continuous function of the capacity. Put $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle $, and let $H(s)$ be the minimum of $m$ and of the infimum over $t\geq 1$ of the right side of ( 16.27.16 ) with $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)$ replaced by $s$. Since $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }\leq \int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle =m$, we have $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E)\leq H(\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E))$. The function $H$ is nondecreasing, and $H(s)\to 0$ as $s\downarrow 0$. Choose a strictly decreasing sequence $s_ k\downarrow 0$ with $H(s_ k)\leq m2^{-k}$. Define $F(0)=0$, $F(s_ k)=m2^{1-k}$, $F$ linear on each interval $[s_{k+1},s_ k]$, and $F=m$ on $[s_1,\infty )$. On $[s_{k+1},s_ k]$ we have $H(s)\leq H(s_ k)\leq m2^{-k}=F(s_{k+1})\leq F(s)$, and $H\leq m=F$ on $[s_1,\infty )$. Thus $F$ is a continuous nondecreasing majorant of $H$ with $F(0)=0$. $\square$ Theorem 16.27.17 . 337360EF765B Suppose that $\{ \theta \} $ is big and that $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has positive mass. There are continuous nondecreasing functions $F,G\colon [0,\infty )\to [0,\infty )$, vanishing at zero, such that every Borel set $E\subset X$ satisfies \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E)\leq F(\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)), \qquad \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq G(\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E)).  \] Consequently, any two capacities of this kind, for possibly different big backgrounds and potentials of positive mass, are bounded by such functions of each other. In particular, they define the same notion of convergence in capacity , in which Borel functions $f_ j$ converge to $f$ if the capacities of the sets $\{ |f_ j-f|>\varepsilon \} $ tend to zero for every $\varepsilon >0$. They also define the same notion of uniform absolute continuity of a family of positive Borel measures: $\lambda (A)$ is small, uniformly over the members $\lambda $ of the family, whenever the Borel set $A$ has small capacity. Proof. Choose $A\geq 1$ with $\theta \leq \kappa =A\omega $. Every competitor $v$ for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\psi }$, and its measure for $\kappa $ dominates its measure for $\theta $: since $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(\kappa -\theta )$ with a smooth closed semipositive form $\kappa -\theta $, multilinearity and positivity of non-pluripolar products give $\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\rangle \geq \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\rangle $; hence $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }\leq \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\psi }$, and the mass of $\psi $ for $\kappa $ is at least its mass for $\theta $, hence positive. Adding a constant to $\psi $ does not change the capacities, so we may assume $\psi \leq 0$. Let $\Phi =P_\kappa [\psi ]$. By theorem 16.22.11 , $\Phi $ is a model potential for $\kappa $ with $\psi \leq \Phi $ and with the same mass for $\kappa $ as $\psi $. Thus $\psi \in \mathcal E(X,\kappa ,\Phi )$, and lemma 16.27.15 and proposition 16.27.12 bound $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\psi }$ by a continuous nondecreasing function, vanishing at zero, of $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $. Finally, rescaling the competitors gives \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa \leq A^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega :  \] every competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ is one for $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $, with a larger measure by the same argument, and if $v$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $, then $v/A$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ with measure $A^{-n}(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$. This proves the first inequality. For the second inequality use the model potential $\phi =P_\theta [\psi ]$ for $\theta $, which has the same positive mass $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle $ as $\psi $. By ( 16.27.14 ), $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa ^ n\leq (C^ n/m)\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$. By theorem 16.26.1 with $a=2$, applied to $\psi $ and $\phi $, whose singularity envelopes agree, the potential $\eta =P_\theta (2\psi -\phi )$ has mass $m$ and satisfies $P_\theta [\eta ]=\phi $ and $(\eta +\phi )/2\leq \psi $. It remains to bound $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ by a function of $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$. Put $u=(\eta +\phi )/2$. Since $P_\theta [\eta ]=P_\theta [\phi ]$, the preservation of mixed masses in proposition 16.21.2 shows that $u$ also has mass $m$. Since $u\leq \psi $, this means that $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\psi )$, and lemma 16.27.15 bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,u}$ by a continuous nondecreasing function, vanishing at zero, of $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$. If $v$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$, then $h=(v+\eta )/2$ satisfies $u-1/2\leq h\leq u$, so it is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,u}$, and $\mu _ h\geq 2^{-n}\mu _ v$. Thus \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }\leq 2^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,u}.  \] Combining these inequalities with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $ gives $G$; compositions, positive multiples and $n$th roots preserve continuity, monotonicity and the value zero at the origin. The remaining assertions follow by comparing both capacities with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $. $\square$ Proposition 16.27.18 . 7EC4B0FF8858 Let $B_\alpha \Subset B'_\alpha $ be finitely many pairs of concentric coordinate balls such that each $\overline{B'_\alpha }$ lies in a coordinate chart and the balls $B_\alpha $ cover $X$, and let $\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }$ be the capacities of definition 7.4.2 in these coordinates. Then there is a constant $c\geq 1$ such that every Borel set $E\subset X$ satisfies \[  c^{-1}\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E\cap B_\alpha ) \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E) \leq c\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E\cap B_\alpha ),  \] and moreover $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq c\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$ for every $\alpha $ and every Borel set $E\subset B'_\alpha $. Consequently, every relative capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$ as in theorem 16.27.17 has the following properties. A compact set has capacity zero if and only if it is pluripolar. Hence a Borel set has capacity zero if and only if all its compact subsets are pluripolar. If real Borel functions $f_ j$ converge to a real Borel function $f$ locally in capacity on every ball $B'_\alpha $ (definition 7.5.5 ), then $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(\{ |f_ j-f|>\delta \} )\to 0$ for every $\delta >0$. Every quasi-continuous function on $X$ is continuous outside open sets of arbitrarily small capacity. Moreover, let $\theta '$ be any smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ and every $\varepsilon >0$ there is an open set $G$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(G)<\varepsilon $ which contains the pole set of $u$ and such that $u$ is finite and continuous on $X\setminus G$. Proof. Let $v$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $, so that $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $-1\leq v\leq 0$. Fix $\alpha $ and write $B'_\alpha =B(0,R_\alpha )$ in its coordinates. Since $\overline{B'_\alpha }$ is a compact subset of a chart, there is $A_\alpha >0$ with $\omega \leq A_\alpha \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ on $B'_\alpha $ (lemma 6.14.1 ). Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+A_\alpha |z|^2)=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(A_\alpha \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2-\omega )\geq 0$, so $v+A_\alpha |z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $B'_\alpha $, by lemma 6.14.4 (2), applied on $B'_\alpha $ to the form $A_\alpha \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_\alpha |z|^2)$, and the multilinearity and positivity of Bedford–Taylor products give $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+A_\alpha |z|^2))^ n\geq (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ on $B'_\alpha $. Put $c_\alpha =1+A_\alpha R_\alpha ^2$. The function $w=(v+A_\alpha |z|^2+1)/c_\alpha $ is plurisubharmonic on $B'_\alpha $ with values in $[0,1]$, and $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\leq c_\alpha ^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ there. Hence $\mu _ v(E)\leq c_\alpha ^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset B'_\alpha $, and taking the supremum over $v$ gives $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq c_\alpha ^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$. Applying this to the sets $E\cap B_\alpha $ and using the subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ (proposition 16.25.6 ), we obtain the upper bound. For the lower bound fix $\alpha $ and write $B_\alpha =B(0,r)$ and $B'_\alpha =B(0,R)$ in the coordinates, with $r<R$. Choose $L>0$ with $L(R^2-r^2)>1$, and then $b>0$ so small that $\omega \geq bL\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ on $B(0,R)$ (lemma 6.14.1 ) and that we can choose a number $a$ with \[  b(1+Lr^2)<a<bLR^2,\qquad a\leq 1.  \] Let $w$ be plurisubharmonic on $B(0,R)$ with $-1\leq w\leq 0$, and put $q=bw-bL|z|^2$. Then $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq b\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0$ on $B(0,R)$. At the points of $B(0,R)$ where $|z|^2>a/(bL)$, which include a neighborhood of the boundary sphere because $a<bLR^2$, we have $q\leq -bL|z|^2<-a$. Define $v$ to be $\max \{ q,-a\} $ on $B(0,R)$ and $-a$ elsewhere. Then $v=-a$ on the open set $U$ formed by $X\setminus \overline{B(0,R)}$ and the points of the chart where $|z|^2>a/(bL)$. Since $U$ and $B(0,R)$ cover $X$, and $v$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic on each of them, $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. It takes values in $[-1,0]$, and on $B(0,r)$ we have $q\geq -b(1+Lr^2)>-a$, so $v=q$ there. Since $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$ is the sum of the semipositive form $\omega -bL\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and $b\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$, positivity of the mixed terms gives $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq b^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ on $B(0,r)$. The capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{B(0,R)}$ may equally be computed with competitors taking values in $[-1,0]$, so it follows that \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\geq b^ n \operatorname {Cap}_{B(0,R)}(E) \qquad (E\subset B(0,r)\text{ Borel}).  \] Summing over the finitely many balls gives the lower bound. It remains to prove (1)–(3). Let $F$ and $G$ be the functions of theorem 16.27.17 for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$; since they are continuous and vanish at zero, a sequence of Borel sets has capacities $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$ tending to zero if and only if their capacities $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ tend to zero. (1) Pluripolar Borel sets have capacity zero by proposition 16.25.6 . Conversely, let $K$ be a compact set that is not pluripolar. Since $\omega $ is Kähler, $0=V_\omega $ is a model potential for $\omega $ of mass $\int _ X\omega ^ n>0$, by proposition 16.21.2 , and ( 16.27.6 ) for this model potential gives $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (K)>0$. Since $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (K)\leq G(\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(K))$ and $G(0)=0$, it follows that $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(K)>0$. The assertion about Borel sets follows from the inner regularity in proposition 16.25.6 . (2) Let $\delta >0$ and $A_ j=\{ |f_ j-f|>\delta \} $. By the upper bound, $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (A_ j)\leq c\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(A_ j\cap B_\alpha )$. Each term is at most the outer capacity $\operatorname {Cap}^*_{B'_\alpha }(\overline{B_\alpha }\cap A_ j)$, which tends to zero because $\overline{B_\alpha }$ is a compact subset of $B'_\alpha $. Hence $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (A_ j)\to 0$, and therefore $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(A_ j)\to 0$. (3) Let $f$ be quasi-continuous on $X$ and $\eta >0$. For each $\alpha $ there is an open set $W_\alpha \subset B'_\alpha $ with $\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(W_\alpha )<\eta $ such that $f$ is continuous on the compact set $\overline{B_\alpha }\setminus W_\alpha $. Put $W=\bigcup _\alpha W_\alpha $. Then $X\setminus W$ is the union of the finitely many closed sets $\overline{B_\alpha }\setminus W$, on each of which $f$ is continuous, so $f$ is continuous on $X\setminus W$; and $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (W)\leq \sum _\alpha c\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(W_\alpha )<Nc\eta $, where $N$ is the number of balls. Now let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$. By lemma 16.11.2 (1), $u$ is quasi-continuous. Its pole set $P$ is pluripolar, because near each point $u$ is a plurisubharmonic function plus a smooth one (definition 6.14.3 ). Hence, by lemma 16.11.1 (2) there are open sets $W'_\alpha \subset B'_\alpha $ with $P\cap B'_\alpha \subset W'_\alpha $ and $\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(W'_\alpha )<\eta $. Replacing $W_\alpha $, chosen as above for $f=u$, by $W_\alpha \cup W'_\alpha $, we obtain an open set $W$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (W)<2Nc\eta $ which contains $P$, such that $u$ is continuous on $X\setminus W$ and finite there. In both cases $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(W)\leq F(\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (W))\leq F(2Nc\eta )$, which is arbitrarily small when $\eta $ is small. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.27.1
text: Lemma 16.27.1 . 49691FF58A24 Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ be bounded. Then $p$ is the pointwise limit of smooth functions $p_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ with $\sup _ j\sup _ X|p_ j|<\infty $. Proof. Apply theorem 6.17.6 with $\kappa $ as the Kähler form of reference. It gives potentials $\Phi _ j$ decreasing to $p$ with $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ j\geq -\varepsilon _ j\kappa $, where $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, and with gentle analytic singularities of type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ jp))$. Since $p$ is bounded, $\mathrm e^{-2^ jp}$ is bounded, so $\mathcal I(2^ jp)$ is the unit ideal. In the local presentations $\Phi _ j=2^{-j}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+b$ of definition 6.14.5 , the functions $g_ i$ therefore generate the unit ideal and have no common zero, so $\Phi _ j$ is bounded. Hence the smooth function $\exp (2^ j\Phi _ j)$ has no zeros, and $\Phi _ j=2^{-j}\log \exp (2^ j\Phi _ j)$ is smooth. Put $p_ j=\Phi _ j/(1+\varepsilon _ j)$. Then \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_ j=\frac{(1+\varepsilon _ j)\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ j}{1+\varepsilon _ j}\geq 0.  \] The bounds $p\leq \Phi _ j\leq \Phi _1$ give $|p_ j|\leq |\Phi _ j|\leq \max \{ \sup _ X|p|,\sup _ X|\Phi _1|\} $, and $p_ j\to p$ pointwise because $\Phi _ j\to p$ and $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$ (unlike the $\Phi _ j$, the $p_ j$ need not decrease). $\square$

title: Lemma 16.27.2
text: Lemma 16.27.2 . A73E0CBD9FAB Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form, let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ satisfy $v\leq u\leq v+B$ for a constant $B\geq 0$, and let $p$ be a bounded function in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$. Then E0D5BEEFADA4 16.27.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ Xp\, \mu _ u\geq \int _ Xp\, \mu _ v-nB\Omega . \end{equation} Moreover, there is a constant $C_\kappa $, depending only on $X$ and $\kappa $, such that for every model potential $\phi $ for the background $\kappa $, every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ with $\phi -1\leq v\leq \phi $, and every $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ with $\sup _ Xp=0$, bounded or not, E22DEE0D88EE 16.27.4 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(-p)\, \mu _ v\leq C_\kappa . \end{equation} Proof. Write $\kappa _ q=\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$. We first prove ( 16.27.3 ) when $u=v$ near the poles of $v$ and then reduce to this case; the second assertion follows from the first. A special case. Assume first that there are $l_0>0$ and an open set $U\supset \{ v<-l_0\} $ on which $u=v$. For $l>l_0$ put $u_ l=\max \{ u,-l\} $ and $v_ l=\max \{ v,-l\} $; these are bounded functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ with $0\leq u_ l-v_ l\leq B$. On $U$ we have $u_ l=v_ l$ and $u=v$, so $\mu _{u_ l}=\mu _{v_ l}$ and $\mu _ u=\mu _ v$ there. The complement of $U$ lies in the plurifine open set $\{ v>-l\} $, on which $u_ l=u$ and $v_ l=v$, because $u\geq v$; by plurifine locality, $\mu _{u_ l}=\mu _ u$ and $\mu _{v_ l}=\mu _ v$ on this set. Hence $\mu _{u_ l}-\mu _{v_ l}=\mu _ u-\mu _ v$. Expanding $\kappa _{u_ l}^ n-\kappa _{v_ l}^ n$ and integrating by parts with lemma 13.5.2 , we obtain \[  \begin{split}  \int _ Xp\, (\mu _ u-\mu _ v)=\int _ Xp(\mu _{u_ l}-\mu _{v_ l}) & =\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}\int _ X(u_ l-v_ l)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p \wedge \kappa _{u_ l}^{j}\wedge \kappa _{v_ l}^{n-1-j}\\ & \geq -nB\Omega . \end{split}  \] For the last inequality write $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)-\kappa $: the first part contributes a nonnegative amount, since $u_ l-v_ l\geq 0$, and the second contributes at least $-B\int _ X\kappa \wedge \kappa _{u_ l}^ j\wedge \kappa _{v_ l}^{n-1-j}=-B\Omega $, by proposition 13.5.1 . The general case. Subtracting a common constant, we may assume $v\leq 0$. For $0<a<1$ put $v_ a=av$ and $u_ a=\max \{ u,av\} $; these belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ because $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(av)=(1-a)\kappa +a\kappa _ v$. Since $v\leq av$, we have $v_ a\leq u_ a\leq v_ a+B$. On the open set $U_ a=\{ v<-B/(1-a)\} $ we have $av-v>B\geq u-v$, so $u_ a=v_ a$ there. With $l_0=aB/(1-a)+1$, the set $\{ v_ a<-l_0\} =\{ v<-l_0/a\} $ is contained in $U_ a$, so the special case applies to $u_ a$ and $v_ a$. As $a\uparrow 1$, $v_ a$ and $u_ a$ decrease to $v$ and $u$. The masses of $u_ a$ and $v_ a$ agree, and by multilinearity $\int _ X\langle \kappa _{v_ a}^ n\rangle $ is a polynomial in $a$ that tends to $\int _ X\langle \kappa _ v^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \kappa _ u^ n\rangle $. Decreasing sequences converge in extended capacity (lemma 13.7.3 ), so theorem 13.7.5 shows that $\mu _{u_ a}\to \mu _ u$ and $\mu _{v_ a}\to \mu _ v$ weakly along every sequence $a\uparrow 1$. Passing to the limit in ( 16.27.3 ) for $u_ a$ and $v_ a$, we obtain ( 16.27.3 ) for every continuous, in particular every smooth, $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$. For a bounded $p$, take the approximations $p_ j$ of lemma 16.27.1 ; they converge pointwise with a common bound, and dominated convergence with respect to the finite measures $\mu _ u$ and $\mu _ v$ proves ( 16.27.3 ). The second assertion. Let $\phi $ be a model potential for $\kappa $. Since $V_\kappa =0$, proposition 16.21.3 gives $\mu _\phi \leq \kappa ^ n$. If $\phi -1\leq v\leq \phi $, the first assertion, applied to $\phi \leq v+1\leq \phi +1$, gives for every bounded $p$ with $\sup _ Xp=0$ \[  \int _ X(-p)\, \mu _ v\leq \int _ X(-p)\, \mu _\phi +n\Omega \leq \int _ X(-p)\, \kappa ^ n+n\Omega .  \] By proposition 10.3.1 , applied on the compact Kähler manifold $(X,\kappa )$ with background $\kappa $, the last integral is bounded by a constant depending only on $X$ and $\kappa $. For an unbounded $p$ with $\sup _ Xp=0$, apply this bound to the truncations $\max \{ p,-l\} $, which are bounded, belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$ and have supremum zero, and let $l\to \infty $ by monotone convergence. $\square$
