title: 17.4 Continuity and compactness
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text:
We keep $	heta $ and the model potential $\phi $ of mass $m$. Convergence in $L^1(X)$ refers to the volume form $\omega ^ n$, and a $	heta $-psh potential is determined by its class in $L^1(X)$. The energy is continuous along increasing nets and upper semicontinuous for $L^1$ convergence, so that normalized potentials with energy bounded below form compact sets (corollary 17.4.5 ), as the variational method of section 17.5 requires. The finite-energy class is also stable under rooftop envelopes, which gives finite energy along the Perron segments of section 17.7 . Proposition 17.4.1 . 049F75F5547D Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be an increasing net in $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ which is uniformly bounded above on $X$. Then its regularized upper envelope $u=(\sup _ i u_ i)^*$ belongs to $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and \[  E_	heta ^\phi (u_ i)\uparrow E_	heta ^\phi (u).  \] Proof. By lemma 16.22.2 , $u_ i\leq \phi +\sup _ Xu_ i$, and the suprema $\sup _ Xu_ i$ are bounded above by hypothesis; hence $u\preceq \phi $. Since $u$ dominates every $u_ i$, monotonicity of the energy and theorem 17.3.14 show that $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Bounded differences. Consider first an increasing sequence $(u_ j)$ and a constant $C\geq 1$ such that $\phi -C\leq u_ j\leq u\leq \phi $ for all $j$. The pole sets of $u_ j$ and $u$ coincide with that of $\phi $. Let $f_ j$ be the function equal to $u-u_ j$ outside this pole set and to $0$ on it; it is a Borel function with values in $[0,C]$. By the tangent bound ( 17.3.10 ), \[  0\leq E_	heta ^\phi (u)-E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \int _ X(u-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j}=\int _ Xf_ j\, \mu _{u_ j},  \] and we show that the right side tends to zero by applying lemma 17.2.2 with $
u _ j=\mu _{u_ j}$, $
u =\mu _ u$, the weights $f_ j$ and the limit weight $0$. For each $j$ the potential $C^{-1}u_ j+(1-C^{-1})\phi $ lies between $\phi -1$ and $\phi $ and its measure is at least $C^{-n}\mu _{u_ j}$; hence $\mu _{u_ j}\leq C^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }$ on Borel sets, and likewise $\mu _ u\leq C^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }$. By theorem 16.27.17 , the measures $\mu _{u_ j}$ and $\mu _ u$ are therefore uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $. They converge weakly by corollary 13.8.9 , since $u_ j$ increases to $u$ quasi-everywhere (corollary 5.47.11 ). It remains to show that $f_ j	o 0$ in capacity. Fix finitely many pairs of concentric coordinate balls $B_\alpha \Subset B'_\alpha $ as in proposition 16.27.18 , chosen so that $	heta $ has a smooth potential $h_\alpha $ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B'_\alpha }$ (this is possible by lemma 6.14.2 , applied on slightly larger concentric balls), and let $c$ be the constant of that proposition. Let $\delta ,\eta >0$. By proposition 16.27.18 (3) there is an open set $G$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (G)<\eta $ which contains the pole set of $\phi $ and such that $\phi $ is finite and continuous on the compact set $X\setminus G$. Let $L$ be a common bound for $|\phi |$ on $X\setminus G$ and for the functions $|h_\alpha |$ on $B'_\alpha $. The functions \[  w_{\alpha ,j}=\max \{ u_ j+h_\alpha ,-2L-C\} ,\qquad w_\alpha =\max \{ u+h_\alpha ,-2L-C\}   \] are bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $B'_\alpha $, and $w_{\alpha ,j}$ increases to $w_\alpha $ almost everywhere, because $u_ j$ increases to $u$ quasi-everywhere and pluripolar sets have Lebesgue measure zero. By theorem 7.6.1 , $w_{\alpha ,j}	o w_\alpha $ locally in capacity on $B'_\alpha $. On $B_\alpha \setminus G$ we have $u_ j+h_\alpha \geq \phi -C-L\geq -2L-C$, so the truncations are inactive there and $w_\alpha -w_{\alpha ,j}=u-u_ j$. Since the balls $B_\alpha $ cover $X$, \[  \{ f_ j>\delta \} \subset G\cup  igcup _\alpha  igl (B_\alpha \cap \{ w_{\alpha ,j}<w_\alpha -\delta \}  igr ).  \] By the countable subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ (proposition 16.25.6 ) and the bound $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq c\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$ for Borel sets $E\subset B'_\alpha $ in proposition 16.27.18 , \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ f_ j>\delta \} )\leq \eta +c\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}^*_{B'_\alpha } igl (\overline{B_\alpha }\cap \{ w_{\alpha ,j}<w_\alpha -\delta \}  igr ),  \] where we also used that the capacity of a Borel set is at most its outer capacity. By definition 7.5.5 , the sum tends to zero as $j	o \infty $. Hence $\varlimsup _ j\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ f_ j>\delta \} )\leq \eta $, and since $\eta $ is arbitrary, $f_ j	o 0$ in capacity. Lemma 17.2.2 now gives $\int _ Xf_ j\, \mu _{u_ j}	o 0$, and hence $E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j)	o E_	heta ^\phi (u)$. Sequences. Now let $(u_ j)$ be an arbitrary increasing sequence; subtracting a common constant, we may assume $u_ j\leq u\leq \phi $. Put $u_{j,k}=\max \{ u_ j,\phi -k\} $ and $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $. For fixed $k$, the sequence $u_{j,k}$ increases to $\max \{ \sup _ ju_ j,\phi -k\} $, whose upper semicontinuous regularization is $\max \{ (\sup _ ju_ j)^*,\phi -k\} =u_ k$, because $\phi -k$ is upper semicontinuous; moreover $\phi -k\leq u_{j,k}\leq u_ k\leq \phi $. The preceding case, with $\max \{ k,1\} $ in place of $C$, gives $E_	heta ^\phi (u_{j,k})	o E_	heta ^\phi (u_ k)$ as $j	o \infty $. We bound the truncation error uniformly in $j$. The tangent bound of proposition 17.3.19 gives \[  0\leq E_	heta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \int _ X(u_{j,k}-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j} =\int _ k^\infty \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} )\, \mathrm dt.  \] For $t\geq k$ put $q_ t=(u_ j+\phi -t)/2$. On $\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} $ we have $u_1\leq u_ j<q_ t$, and $q_ t\leq \phi -t/2$ on $X$. Since $\mu _{q_ t}\geq 2^{-n}\mu _{u_ j}$ by multilinearity, and $q_ t,u_1\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, the comparison principle of proposition 16.25.4 gives \[   egin{aligned}  \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} ) & \leq 2^ n\mu _{q_ t}(\{ u_1<q_ t\} )\ & \leq 2^ n\mu _{u_1}(\{ u_1<q_ t\} ) \leq 2^ n\mu _{u_1}(\{ u_1<\phi -t/2\} ). \end{aligned}  \] Consequently D1604CAB7F82 17.4.2  egin{equation}   egin{aligned}  0& \leq E_	heta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j)\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\int _ X(\phi -u_1-k/2)_+\, \mu _{u_1}\longrightarrow 0 \end{aligned} \end{equation} as $k	o \infty $, uniformly in $j$; the limit is zero by dominated convergence, since $\phi -u_1$ is $\mu _{u_1}$-integrable. Since $E_	heta ^\phi (u_ k)\geq E_	heta ^\phi (u)$, letting first $j	o \infty $ and then $k	o \infty $ gives $\lim _ jE_	heta ^\phi (u_ j)\geq E_	heta ^\phi (u)$, and monotonicity gives the reverse inequality. Nets. Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net as in the statement. Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts $D_ eta $ on which $	heta $ has smooth potentials $h_ eta $. By theorem 5.10.2 , applied to the functions $u_ i+h_ eta $ on $D_ eta $, there are countable sets $J_ eta \subset I$ such that $(\sup _{i\in J_ eta }u_ i)^*=u$ on $D_ eta $. The countable set $J= igcup _ eta J_ eta $ then satisfies $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=u$ on $X$, since on each $D_ eta $ this envelope lies between the envelopes over $J_ eta $ and over $I$. Since the index set is directed, we can choose indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ such that $i_ k$ dominates the first $k$ elements of an enumeration of $J$. Since the net is increasing, $\sup _ ku_{i_ k}\geq \sup _{i\in J}u_ i$, so the increasing sequence $(u_{i_ k})$ has regularized upper envelope $u$, and the sequence case gives $E_	heta ^\phi (u_{i_ k})	o E_	heta ^\phi (u)$. Each of these energies is at most $\sup _ iE_	heta ^\phi (u_ i)$, which in turn is at most $E_	heta ^\phi (u)$ by monotonicity. Hence $\sup _ iE_	heta ^\phi (u_ i)=E_	heta ^\phi (u)$, and since the net of energies is increasing, its limit is this supremum. (The selected indices need not be cofinal in $I$, which is why we compare suprema.) $\square$ Upper semicontinuity of the energy for $L^1$ convergence rests on the following description of $L^1$ limits of potentials by decreasing sequences. Lemma 17.4.3 . 369EDE8DEEC5 Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $q_ k,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $q_ k	o q$ in $L^1(X)$. Then the functions $q_ k$ are uniformly bounded above on $X$, the tail envelopes $a_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k)^*$ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and $a_ j$ decreases pointwise to $q$ as $j	o \infty $. In particular, if $\psi \colon X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ is upper semicontinuous and $q_ k\leq \psi $ for every $k$, then $q\leq \psi $. Proof. By proposition 10.3.1 the suprema $\sup _ Xq_ k$ converge to $\sup _ Xq$, so they are bounded. Hence the tail envelopes $a_ j$ are $	heta $-psh, by theorem 5.10.2 applied in charts after adding smooth local potentials of $	heta $, and they decrease as $j$ increases. A subsequence of $(q_ k)$ converges to $q$ almost everywhere, so $a_ j\geq q$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, since both functions are $	heta $-psh (section 16.11 ). Conversely, let $x\in X$ and $\varepsilon >0$, let $h$ be a smooth local potential of $	heta $ on a coordinate ball $\Omega $ around $x$, and let $M>q(x)+h(x)$ be a real number. By upper semicontinuity there is a closed coordinate ball $K\subset \Omega $ around $x$ on which $q+h<M$ and $|h-h(x)|<\varepsilon $. The plurisubharmonic functions $q_ k+h$ converge to $q+h$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so Hartogs' lemma in the form of theorem 5.10.4 , applied with the constant function $M$ on $K$, gives $q_ k+h<M$ on $K$ for all large $k$. For such $k$ we have $q_ k<M-h(x)+\varepsilon $ on $K$. Since $K$ is a neighborhood of $x$, it follows that $a_ j(x)\leq M-h(x)+\varepsilon $ for all large $j$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and $M\downarrow q(x)+h(x)$, or $M	o -\infty $ if $q(x)=-\infty $, we obtain $\lim _ ja_ j(x)\leq q(x)$. Thus $a_ j\downarrow q$. Finally, if $q_ k\leq \psi $ for all $k$ with $\psi $ upper semicontinuous, then $\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k\leq \psi $, so $a_ j\leq \psi $ for every $j$, and therefore $q=\lim _ ja_ j\leq \psi $. $\square$ Proposition 17.4.4 . 2FF0E77E9188 The set $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\preceq \phi \} $ is closed in $L^1(X)$, and $E_	heta ^\phi $ is upper semicontinuous on it, with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$: if $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1(X)$, then \[  E_	heta ^\phi (u)\geq \varlimsup _ j E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j).  \] Proof. Let $u_ j\preceq \phi $ converge to $u$ in $L^1(X)$. By lemma 17.4.3 , the $u_ j$ are uniformly bounded above, so lemma 16.22.2 gives a constant $C$ with $u_ j\leq \phi +C$ for all $j$. Since $\phi +C$ is upper semicontinuous, the same lemma gives $u\leq \phi +C$, which proves closedness. The lemma also shows that the tail envelopes $v_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}u_ k)^*$ are $	heta $-psh potentials which decrease pointwise to $u$; moreover $v_ j\leq \phi +C$, because $\phi +C$ is upper semicontinuous and dominates every $u_ k$. Since $u_ j\leq v_ j$, monotonicity and proposition 17.3.13 give \[  \varlimsup _ j E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \lim _ jE_	heta ^\phi (v_ j)=E_	heta ^\phi (u).  \] Since $L^1(X)$ is a metric space, sequential upper semicontinuity is upper semicontinuity. $\square$ Corollary 17.4.5 . 85CFF04E2CEC For $B\geq 0$, the set \[  \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\leq \phi ,\quad E_	heta ^\phi (u)\geq -B\}   \] is compact in $L^1(X)$ and is contained in $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. The set \[  K_\phi =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\leq \phi ,\quad \sup _ Xu=0\}   \] is also compact in $L^1(X)$. Proof. For $u$ in the first set, lemma 16.22.2 gives $u\leq \phi +\sup _ Xu$, so monotonicity and the shift formula give $-B\leq E_	heta ^\phi (u)\leq m\sup _ Xu$. Also $\sup _ Xu\leq \sup _ X\phi =0$. Hence the set lies in $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):-B/m\leq \sup _ Xu\leq 0\} $, which is compact in $L^1(X)$ by proposition 10.3.1 . The set is closed in $L^1(X)$: the inequality $u\leq \phi $ passes to $L^1$ limits by lemma 17.4.3 , since $\phi $ is upper semicontinuous, and the energy bound passes to limits by upper semicontinuity (proposition 17.4.4 ). It is therefore compact. Its members have finite energy, so they lie in $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ by theorem 17.3.14 . The set $K_\phi $ is contained in $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):\sup _ Xu=0\} $, which is compact in $L^1(X)$ by proposition 10.3.1 , and it is closed in $L^1(X)$, because the supremum is continuous for $L^1$ convergence of potentials (by the same proposition) and the inequality $u\leq \phi $ passes to $L^1$ limits by lemma 17.4.3 . Hence $K_\phi $ is compact. $\square$ Proposition 17.4.6 . 2FA1EC20E3A2 Let $\mathcal F$ be one of the three classes $\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and $\mathcal E^\infty (X,	heta ,\phi )$. The regularized upper envelope of a nonempty family in $\mathcal F$ which is uniformly bounded above on $X$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. Proof. By lemma 16.22.2 , every member of the family is bounded above by $\phi +C$ for a common constant $C$, and so is the regularized upper envelope $U$. Fix a member $u_0$ of the family; then $u_0\leq U\preceq \phi $. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, mass monotonicity gives $m=\int _ X\langle 	heta _{u_0}^ nangle \leq \int _ X\langle 	heta _ U^ nangle \leq m$. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, the last assertion of corollary 17.3.17 , applied to $u_0\leq U$, gives $U\in \mathcal F$. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E^\infty (X,	heta ,\phi )$, the member $u_0$ supplies a lower bound $U\geq u_0\geq \phi -C'$. $\square$ Proposition 17.4.7 . 1A67C7F5BE56 Let $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Then the rooftop envelope $w=P_	heta (u,v)$ of definition 16.11.5 is not identically $-\infty $, and it belongs to $\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$. If moreover $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, then $w\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, and if in addition $u,v\leq \phi $, then \[  \int _ X(\phi -w)\, \mu _ w \leq \int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u+\int _ X(\phi -v)\, \mu _ v.  \] Proof. Since $u\leq \max \{ u,v\} \preceq \phi $, mass monotonicity gives $\int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ nangle =m$. Thus $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle +\int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle =2m>\int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ nangle $, and proposition 16.23.1 shows that $w
eq -\infty $. Theorem 16.23.5 gives $2m\leq m+\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle $, while $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle \leq m$ by mass monotonicity, since $w\leq u$. Hence $w\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Now let $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. The rooftop commutes with adding a common constant to $u$ and $v$ (proposition 16.11.4 (3)), so we may assume $u,v\leq \phi $; then $w\leq \phi $. The contact inequality of corollary 16.13.5 gives \[  \mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=u\} }\mu _ u +\mathbf1_{\{ w=v\} }\mu _ v.  \] Integrate the nonnegative weight $\min \{ \phi -w,N\} $ against both sides. On the first contact set the weight equals $\min \{ \phi -u,N\} $, and on the second it equals $\min \{ \phi -v,N\} $; pole sets carry no mass. Letting $N	o \infty $ gives the displayed bound. Both terms on the right are finite, so $w\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. $\square$ Corollary 17.4.8 . 838D06267D86 For $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, the singularity-constrained envelope of definition 16.25.1 satisfies $P_	heta [u](v)=v$. Proof. By proposition 17.4.7 , the rooftop $w=P_	heta (u,v)$ belongs to $\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Since $w\preceq v$ and $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle =\int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle >0$, proposition 16.22.14 gives $P_	heta [w](v)=v$. Every competitor for $P_	heta [w](v)$ is more singular than $w$, hence than $u$, so it is a competitor for $P_	heta [u](v)$; and $P_	heta [u](v)\leq v$ quasi-everywhere by proposition 16.25.2 (1), hence everywhere. Therefore $v=P_	heta [w](v)\leq P_	heta [u](v)\leq v$. $\square$ Proposition 17.4.9 . 69A8D9FFB919 For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and $u_ t=(1-t)u+tv$, the function $t\mapsto E_	heta ^\phi (u_ t)$ is continuously differentiable on $[0,1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_	heta ^\phi (u_ t) =\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] The derivative is a polynomial in $t$. Proof. By lemma 17.3.18 every integral $\int _ X(v-u)\langle 	heta _ v^ a\wedge 	heta _ u^{n-a}angle $ is finite. Expanding $\mu _{u_ t}$ by multilinearity shows that the right side is a polynomial in $t$ with these integrals as coefficients. The potentials $u_ t$ lie in $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ by corollary 17.3.17 . Apply the cocycle formula of proposition 17.3.19 to $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$, with $s
eq 0$ and $t,t+s\in [0,1]$, and use $u_{t+s}-u_ t=s(v-u)$: \[   rac{E_	heta ^\phi (u_{t+s})-E_	heta ^\phi (u_ t)}s = rac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n\int _ X(v-u)\langle 	heta _{u_{t+s}}^ j\wedge 	heta _{u_ t}^{n-j}angle .  \] Each mixed integral on the right is a polynomial in $s$ with the finite coefficients above, and at $s=0$ each of the $n+1$ terms equals $\int _ X(v-u)\mu _{u_ t}$. Letting $s	o 0$ proves the formula for the derivative, including the one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and its continuity. $\square$ Lemma 17.4.10 . F62E3A64C1EE For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, \[  \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ v\leq E_	heta ^\phi (v)-E_	heta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u.  \] If moreover $u\leq v$, then \[   rac1{n+1}\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u\leq E_	heta ^\phi (v)-E_	heta ^\phi (u).  \] Proof. The first display is the tangent bound ( 17.3.10 ), which holds on $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ by proposition 17.3.19 . By the same proposition, the cocycle formula ( 17.3.6 ) holds for $u$ and $v$. If $u\leq v$, all its terms are nonnegative, and retaining the term $j=0$, whose measure is $\mu _ u$, gives the second display. $\square$ Example 17.4.11 . 27DF9596E862 The energy is not continuous for $L^1$ convergence, even for smooth potentials on $\mathbb P^1$. Let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$, which has mass one. For $0<a<1$ put $\varepsilon _ a=\exp (-a^{-2})$ and \[  u_ a(z)=a\log  rac{|z|^2+\varepsilon _ a}{1+|z|^2}.  \] These functions extend smoothly across infinity, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ a=(1-a)\omega +a\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (|z|^2+\varepsilon _ a)>0$. They tend to zero in $L^1$ as $a\downarrow 0$, since $a\log (|z|^2/(1+|z|^2))\leq u_ a\leq 0$ and the left side is $a$ times a fixed integrable function. We compute their Dirichlet energies. Write $r=\log |z|^2$ and $F(r)=\log (\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon )-\log (1+\mathrm e^ r)$ with $\varepsilon =\varepsilon _ a$, so that $u_ a=aF(\log |z|^2)$. For a smooth function $g=G(\log |z|^2)$ we have $\partial g=G'(r)\, \mathrm dz/z$, hence $\mathrm dg\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial g\wedge  ar\partial g=\pi ^{-1}G'(r)^2|z|^{-2}\, \mathrm dA$, where $\mathrm dA$ is Lebesgue measure; integration in polar coordinates gives $\int \mathrm dg\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g=\int _{-\infty }^\infty G'(r)^2\, \mathrm dr$. Therefore \[  \int _ X\mathrm du_ a\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u_ a =a^2\int _{-\infty }^\infty F'(r)^2\, \mathrm dr =a^2(-\log \varepsilon _ a+O(1))\longrightarrow 1.  \] The bound $O(1)$ is uniform in $a$. Indeed, we have \[  F'(r)= rac{\mathrm e^ r}{\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon }- rac{\mathrm e^ r}{1+\mathrm e^ r}\in [0,1],\qquad 1-F'(r)= rac{\varepsilon }{\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon }+ rac{\mathrm e^ r}{1+\mathrm e^ r}\leq \varepsilon \mathrm e^{-r}+\mathrm e^ r.  \] On $[\log \varepsilon ,0]$ the integral of $\varepsilon \mathrm e^{-r}+\mathrm e^ r$ is at most $2$, and $1\geq F'^2\geq 1-2(1-F')$, so $\int _{\log \varepsilon }^0F'^2\, \mathrm dr=-\log \varepsilon +O(1)$. On the left tail $F'(r)\leq \mathrm e^ r/\varepsilon $, and on the right tail $F'(r)\leq \mathrm e^{-r}$; the corresponding integrals of $F'^2$ are at most $ rac12$. Since $\int _ Xu_ a\, \omega 	o 0$, the formula of example 17.3.16 gives $E_\omega (u_ a)	o - rac12$, whereas $E_\omega (0)=0$.

title: Proposition 17.4.1
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Proposition 17.4.1 . 049F75F5547D Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be an increasing net in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ which is uniformly bounded above on $X$. Then its regularized upper envelope $u=(\sup _ i u_ i)^*$ belongs to $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)\uparrow E_\theta ^\phi (u).  \] Proof. By lemma 16.22.2 , $u_ i\leq \phi +\sup _ Xu_ i$, and the suprema $\sup _ Xu_ i$ are bounded above by hypothesis; hence $u\preceq \phi $. Since $u$ dominates every $u_ i$, monotonicity of the energy and theorem 17.3.14 show that $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Bounded differences. Consider first an increasing sequence $(u_ j)$ and a constant $C\geq 1$ such that $\phi -C\leq u_ j\leq u\leq \phi $ for all $j$. The pole sets of $u_ j$ and $u$ coincide with that of $\phi $. Let $f_ j$ be the function equal to $u-u_ j$ outside this pole set and to $0$ on it; it is a Borel function with values in $[0,C]$. By the tangent bound ( 17.3.10 ), \[  0\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u)-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \int _ X(u-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j}=\int _ Xf_ j\, \mu _{u_ j},  \] and we show that the right side tends to zero by applying lemma 17.2.2 with $\nu _ j=\mu _{u_ j}$, $\nu =\mu _ u$, the weights $f_ j$ and the limit weight $0$. For each $j$ the potential $C^{-1}u_ j+(1-C^{-1})\phi $ lies between $\phi -1$ and $\phi $ and its measure is at least $C^{-n}\mu _{u_ j}$; hence $\mu _{u_ j}\leq C^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ on Borel sets, and likewise $\mu _ u\leq C^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$. By theorem 16.27.17 , the measures $\mu _{u_ j}$ and $\mu _ u$ are therefore uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $. They converge weakly by corollary 13.8.9 , since $u_ j$ increases to $u$ quasi-everywhere (corollary 5.47.11 ). It remains to show that $f_ j\to 0$ in capacity. Fix finitely many pairs of concentric coordinate balls $B_\alpha \Subset B'_\alpha $ as in proposition 16.27.18 , chosen so that $\theta $ has a smooth potential $h_\alpha $ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B'_\alpha }$ (this is possible by lemma 6.14.2 , applied on slightly larger concentric balls), and let $c$ be the constant of that proposition. Let $\delta ,\eta >0$. By proposition 16.27.18 (3) there is an open set $G$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (G)<\eta $ which contains the pole set of $\phi $ and such that $\phi $ is finite and continuous on the compact set $X\setminus G$. Let $L$ be a common bound for $|\phi |$ on $X\setminus G$ and for the functions $|h_\alpha |$ on $B'_\alpha $. The functions \[  w_{\alpha ,j}=\max \{ u_ j+h_\alpha ,-2L-C\} ,\qquad w_\alpha =\max \{ u+h_\alpha ,-2L-C\}   \] are bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $B'_\alpha $, and $w_{\alpha ,j}$ increases to $w_\alpha $ almost everywhere, because $u_ j$ increases to $u$ quasi-everywhere and pluripolar sets have Lebesgue measure zero. By theorem 7.6.1 , $w_{\alpha ,j}\to w_\alpha $ locally in capacity on $B'_\alpha $. On $B_\alpha \setminus G$ we have $u_ j+h_\alpha \geq \phi -C-L\geq -2L-C$, so the truncations are inactive there and $w_\alpha -w_{\alpha ,j}=u-u_ j$. Since the balls $B_\alpha $ cover $X$, \[  \{ f_ j>\delta \} \subset G\cup \bigcup _\alpha \bigl (B_\alpha \cap \{ w_{\alpha ,j}<w_\alpha -\delta \} \bigr ).  \] By the countable subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ (proposition 16.25.6 ) and the bound $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq c\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$ for Borel sets $E\subset B'_\alpha $ in proposition 16.27.18 , \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ f_ j>\delta \} )\leq \eta +c\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}^*_{B'_\alpha }\bigl (\overline{B_\alpha }\cap \{ w_{\alpha ,j}<w_\alpha -\delta \} \bigr ),  \] where we also used that the capacity of a Borel set is at most its outer capacity. By definition 7.5.5 , the sum tends to zero as $j\to \infty $. Hence $\varlimsup _ j\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ f_ j>\delta \} )\leq \eta $, and since $\eta $ is arbitrary, $f_ j\to 0$ in capacity. Lemma 17.2.2 now gives $\int _ Xf_ j\, \mu _{u_ j}\to 0$, and hence $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\to E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. Sequences. Now let $(u_ j)$ be an arbitrary increasing sequence; subtracting a common constant, we may assume $u_ j\leq u\leq \phi $. Put $u_{j,k}=\max \{ u_ j,\phi -k\} $ and $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $. For fixed $k$, the sequence $u_{j,k}$ increases to $\max \{ \sup _ ju_ j,\phi -k\} $, whose upper semicontinuous regularization is $\max \{ (\sup _ ju_ j)^*,\phi -k\} =u_ k$, because $\phi -k$ is upper semicontinuous; moreover $\phi -k\leq u_{j,k}\leq u_ k\leq \phi $. The preceding case, with $\max \{ k,1\} $ in place of $C$, gives $E_\theta ^\phi (u_{j,k})\to E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)$ as $j\to \infty $. We bound the truncation error uniformly in $j$. The tangent bound of proposition 17.3.19 gives \[  0\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \int _ X(u_{j,k}-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j} =\int _ k^\infty \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} )\, \mathrm dt.  \] For $t\geq k$ put $q_ t=(u_ j+\phi -t)/2$. On $\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} $ we have $u_1\leq u_ j<q_ t$, and $q_ t\leq \phi -t/2$ on $X$. Since $\mu _{q_ t}\geq 2^{-n}\mu _{u_ j}$ by multilinearity, and $q_ t,u_1\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, the comparison principle of proposition 16.25.4 gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} ) & \leq 2^ n\mu _{q_ t}(\{ u_1<q_ t\} )\\ & \leq 2^ n\mu _{u_1}(\{ u_1<q_ t\} ) \leq 2^ n\mu _{u_1}(\{ u_1<\phi -t/2\} ). \end{aligned}  \] Consequently D1604CAB7F82 17.4.2 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  0& \leq E_\theta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\int _ X(\phi -u_1-k/2)_+\, \mu _{u_1}\longrightarrow 0 \end{aligned} \end{equation} as $k\to \infty $, uniformly in $j$; the limit is zero by dominated convergence, since $\phi -u_1$ is $\mu _{u_1}$-integrable. Since $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\geq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$, letting first $j\to \infty $ and then $k\to \infty $ gives $\lim _ jE_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\geq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$, and monotonicity gives the reverse inequality. Nets. Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net as in the statement. Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts $D_\beta $ on which $\theta $ has smooth potentials $h_\beta $. By theorem 5.10.2 , applied to the functions $u_ i+h_\beta $ on $D_\beta $, there are countable sets $J_\beta \subset I$ such that $(\sup _{i\in J_\beta }u_ i)^*=u$ on $D_\beta $. The countable set $J=\bigcup _\beta J_\beta $ then satisfies $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=u$ on $X$, since on each $D_\beta $ this envelope lies between the envelopes over $J_\beta $ and over $I$. Since the index set is directed, we can choose indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ such that $i_ k$ dominates the first $k$ elements of an enumeration of $J$. Since the net is increasing, $\sup _ ku_{i_ k}\geq \sup _{i\in J}u_ i$, so the increasing sequence $(u_{i_ k})$ has regularized upper envelope $u$, and the sequence case gives $E_\theta ^\phi (u_{i_ k})\to E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. Each of these energies is at most $\sup _ iE_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)$, which in turn is at most $E_\theta ^\phi (u)$ by monotonicity. Hence $\sup _ iE_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)=E_\theta ^\phi (u)$, and since the net of energies is increasing, its limit is this supremum. (The selected indices need not be cofinal in $I$, which is why we compare suprema.) $\square$

title: Equation 17.4.2
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: D1604CAB7F82 17.4.2 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  0& \leq E_\theta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\int _ X(\phi -u_1-k/2)_+\, \mu _{u_1}\longrightarrow 0 \end{aligned} \end{equation}

title: Lemma 17.4.3
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Lemma 17.4.3 . 369EDE8DEEC5 Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $q_ k,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $q_ k\to q$ in $L^1(X)$. Then the functions $q_ k$ are uniformly bounded above on $X$, the tail envelopes $a_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k)^*$ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $a_ j$ decreases pointwise to $q$ as $j\to \infty $. In particular, if $\psi \colon X\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ is upper semicontinuous and $q_ k\leq \psi $ for every $k$, then $q\leq \psi $. Proof. By proposition 10.3.1 the suprema $\sup _ Xq_ k$ converge to $\sup _ Xq$, so they are bounded. Hence the tail envelopes $a_ j$ are $\theta $-psh, by theorem 5.10.2 applied in charts after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, and they decrease as $j$ increases. A subsequence of $(q_ k)$ converges to $q$ almost everywhere, so $a_ j\geq q$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, since both functions are $\theta $-psh (section 16.11 ). Conversely, let $x\in X$ and $\varepsilon >0$, let $h$ be a smooth local potential of $\theta $ on a coordinate ball $\Omega $ around $x$, and let $M>q(x)+h(x)$ be a real number. By upper semicontinuity there is a closed coordinate ball $K\subset \Omega $ around $x$ on which $q+h<M$ and $|h-h(x)|<\varepsilon $. The plurisubharmonic functions $q_ k+h$ converge to $q+h$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so Hartogs' lemma in the form of theorem 5.10.4 , applied with the constant function $M$ on $K$, gives $q_ k+h<M$ on $K$ for all large $k$. For such $k$ we have $q_ k<M-h(x)+\varepsilon $ on $K$. Since $K$ is a neighborhood of $x$, it follows that $a_ j(x)\leq M-h(x)+\varepsilon $ for all large $j$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and $M\downarrow q(x)+h(x)$, or $M\to -\infty $ if $q(x)=-\infty $, we obtain $\lim _ ja_ j(x)\leq q(x)$. Thus $a_ j\downarrow q$. Finally, if $q_ k\leq \psi $ for all $k$ with $\psi $ upper semicontinuous, then $\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k\leq \psi $, so $a_ j\leq \psi $ for every $j$, and therefore $q=\lim _ ja_ j\leq \psi $. $\square$

title: Proposition 17.4.4
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Proposition 17.4.4 . 2FF0E77E9188 The set $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\preceq \phi \} $ is closed in $L^1(X)$, and $E_\theta ^\phi $ is upper semicontinuous on it, with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$: if $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1(X)$, then \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u)\geq \varlimsup _ j E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j).  \] Proof. Let $u_ j\preceq \phi $ converge to $u$ in $L^1(X)$. By lemma 17.4.3 , the $u_ j$ are uniformly bounded above, so lemma 16.22.2 gives a constant $C$ with $u_ j\leq \phi +C$ for all $j$. Since $\phi +C$ is upper semicontinuous, the same lemma gives $u\leq \phi +C$, which proves closedness. The lemma also shows that the tail envelopes $v_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}u_ k)^*$ are $\theta $-psh potentials which decrease pointwise to $u$; moreover $v_ j\leq \phi +C$, because $\phi +C$ is upper semicontinuous and dominates every $u_ k$. Since $u_ j\leq v_ j$, monotonicity and proposition 17.3.13 give \[  \varlimsup _ j E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \lim _ jE_\theta ^\phi (v_ j)=E_\theta ^\phi (u).  \] Since $L^1(X)$ is a metric space, sequential upper semicontinuity is upper semicontinuity. $\square$

title: Corollary 17.4.5
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Corollary 17.4.5 . 85CFF04E2CEC For $B\geq 0$, the set \[  \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\leq \phi ,\quad E_\theta ^\phi (u)\geq -B\}   \] is compact in $L^1(X)$ and is contained in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. The set \[  K_\phi =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\leq \phi ,\quad \sup _ Xu=0\}   \] is also compact in $L^1(X)$. Proof. For $u$ in the first set, lemma 16.22.2 gives $u\leq \phi +\sup _ Xu$, so monotonicity and the shift formula give $-B\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u)\leq m\sup _ Xu$. Also $\sup _ Xu\leq \sup _ X\phi =0$. Hence the set lies in $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):-B/m\leq \sup _ Xu\leq 0\} $, which is compact in $L^1(X)$ by proposition 10.3.1 . The set is closed in $L^1(X)$: the inequality $u\leq \phi $ passes to $L^1$ limits by lemma 17.4.3 , since $\phi $ is upper semicontinuous, and the energy bound passes to limits by upper semicontinuity (proposition 17.4.4 ). It is therefore compact. Its members have finite energy, so they lie in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by theorem 17.3.14 . The set $K_\phi $ is contained in $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\sup _ Xu=0\} $, which is compact in $L^1(X)$ by proposition 10.3.1 , and it is closed in $L^1(X)$, because the supremum is continuous for $L^1$ convergence of potentials (by the same proposition) and the inequality $u\leq \phi $ passes to $L^1$ limits by lemma 17.4.3 . Hence $K_\phi $ is compact. $\square$

title: Proposition 17.4.6
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Proposition 17.4.6 . 2FA1EC20E3A2 Let $\mathcal F$ be one of the three classes $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$. The regularized upper envelope of a nonempty family in $\mathcal F$ which is uniformly bounded above on $X$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. Proof. By lemma 16.22.2 , every member of the family is bounded above by $\phi +C$ for a common constant $C$, and so is the regularized upper envelope $U$. Fix a member $u_0$ of the family; then $u_0\leq U\preceq \phi $. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, mass monotonicity gives $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _{u_0}^ n\rangle \leq \int _ X\langle \theta _ U^ n\rangle \leq m$. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, the last assertion of corollary 17.3.17 , applied to $u_0\leq U$, gives $U\in \mathcal F$. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, the member $u_0$ supplies a lower bound $U\geq u_0\geq \phi -C'$. $\square$

title: Proposition 17.4.7
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Proposition 17.4.7 . 1A67C7F5BE56 Let $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Then the rooftop envelope $w=P_\theta (u,v)$ of definition 16.11.5 is not identically $-\infty $, and it belongs to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. If moreover $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $w\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and if in addition $u,v\leq \phi $, then \[  \int _ X(\phi -w)\, \mu _ w \leq \int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u+\int _ X(\phi -v)\, \mu _ v.  \] Proof. Since $u\leq \max \{ u,v\} \preceq \phi $, mass monotonicity gives $\int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle =m$. Thus $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle +\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle =2m>\int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle $, and proposition 16.23.1 shows that $w\neq -\infty $. Theorem 16.23.5 gives $2m\leq m+\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle $, while $\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle \leq m$ by mass monotonicity, since $w\leq u$. Hence $w\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Now let $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. The rooftop commutes with adding a common constant to $u$ and $v$ (proposition 16.11.4 (3)), so we may assume $u,v\leq \phi $; then $w\leq \phi $. The contact inequality of corollary 16.13.5 gives \[  \mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=u\} }\mu _ u +\mathbf1_{\{ w=v\} }\mu _ v.  \] Integrate the nonnegative weight $\min \{ \phi -w,N\} $ against both sides. On the first contact set the weight equals $\min \{ \phi -u,N\} $, and on the second it equals $\min \{ \phi -v,N\} $; pole sets carry no mass. Letting $N\to \infty $ gives the displayed bound. Both terms on the right are finite, so $w\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. $\square$

title: Corollary 17.4.8
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Corollary 17.4.8 . 838D06267D86 For $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, the singularity-constrained envelope of definition 16.25.1 satisfies $P_\theta [u](v)=v$. Proof. By proposition 17.4.7 , the rooftop $w=P_\theta (u,v)$ belongs to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Since $w\preceq v$ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle >0$, proposition 16.22.14 gives $P_\theta [w](v)=v$. Every competitor for $P_\theta [w](v)$ is more singular than $w$, hence than $u$, so it is a competitor for $P_\theta [u](v)$; and $P_\theta [u](v)\leq v$ quasi-everywhere by proposition 16.25.2 (1), hence everywhere. Therefore $v=P_\theta [w](v)\leq P_\theta [u](v)\leq v$. $\square$

title: Proposition 17.4.9
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Proposition 17.4.9 . 69A8D9FFB919 For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $u_ t=(1-t)u+tv$, the function $t\mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t)$ is continuously differentiable on $[0,1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t) =\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] The derivative is a polynomial in $t$. Proof. By lemma 17.3.18 every integral $\int _ X(v-u)\langle \theta _ v^ a\wedge \theta _ u^{n-a}\rangle $ is finite. Expanding $\mu _{u_ t}$ by multilinearity shows that the right side is a polynomial in $t$ with these integrals as coefficients. The potentials $u_ t$ lie in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by corollary 17.3.17 . Apply the cocycle formula of proposition 17.3.19 to $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$, with $s\neq 0$ and $t,t+s\in [0,1]$, and use $u_{t+s}-u_ t=s(v-u)$: \[  \frac{E_\theta ^\phi (u_{t+s})-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t)}s =\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n\int _ X(v-u)\langle \theta _{u_{t+s}}^ j\wedge \theta _{u_ t}^{n-j}\rangle .  \] Each mixed integral on the right is a polynomial in $s$ with the finite coefficients above, and at $s=0$ each of the $n+1$ terms equals $\int _ X(v-u)\mu _{u_ t}$. Letting $s\to 0$ proves the formula for the derivative, including the one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and its continuity. $\square$

text: Lemma 17.4.10 . F62E3A64C1EE For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, \[  \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ v\leq E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u.  \] If moreover $u\leq v$, then \[  \frac1{n+1}\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u\leq E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u).  \] Proof. The first display is the tangent bound ( 17.3.10 ), which holds on $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by proposition 17.3.19 . By the same proposition, the cocycle formula ( 17.3.6 ) holds for $u$ and $v$. If $u\leq v$, all its terms are nonnegative, and retaining the term $j=0$, whose measure is $\mu _ u$, gives the second display. $\square$

title: Example 17.4.11

text: Example 17.4.11 . 27DF9596E862 The energy is not continuous for $L^1$ convergence, even for smooth potentials on $\mathbb P^1$. Let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$, which has mass one. For $0<a<1$ put $\varepsilon _ a=\exp (-a^{-2})$ and \[  u_ a(z)=a\log \frac{|z|^2+\varepsilon _ a}{1+|z|^2}.  \] These functions extend smoothly across infinity, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ a=(1-a)\omega +a\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (|z|^2+\varepsilon _ a)>0$. They tend to zero in $L^1$ as $a\downarrow 0$, since $a\log (|z|^2/(1+|z|^2))\leq u_ a\leq 0$ and the left side is $a$ times a fixed integrable function. We compute their Dirichlet energies. Write $r=\log |z|^2$ and $F(r)=\log (\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon )-\log (1+\mathrm e^ r)$ with $\varepsilon =\varepsilon _ a$, so that $u_ a=aF(\log |z|^2)$. For a smooth function $g=G(\log |z|^2)$ we have $\partial g=G'(r)\, \mathrm dz/z$, hence $\mathrm dg\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial g\wedge \bar\partial g=\pi ^{-1}G'(r)^2|z|^{-2}\, \mathrm dA$, where $\mathrm dA$ is Lebesgue measure; integration in polar coordinates gives $\int \mathrm dg\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g=\int _{-\infty }^\infty G'(r)^2\, \mathrm dr$. Therefore \[  \int _ X\mathrm du_ a\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u_ a =a^2\int _{-\infty }^\infty F'(r)^2\, \mathrm dr =a^2(-\log \varepsilon _ a+O(1))\longrightarrow 1.  \] The bound $O(1)$ is uniform in $a$. Indeed, we have \[  F'(r)=\frac{\mathrm e^ r}{\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon }-\frac{\mathrm e^ r}{1+\mathrm e^ r}\in [0,1],\qquad 1-F'(r)=\frac{\varepsilon }{\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon }+\frac{\mathrm e^ r}{1+\mathrm e^ r}\leq \varepsilon \mathrm e^{-r}+\mathrm e^ r.  \] On $[\log \varepsilon ,0]$ the integral of $\varepsilon \mathrm e^{-r}+\mathrm e^ r$ is at most $2$, and $1\geq F'^2\geq 1-2(1-F')$, so $\int _{\log \varepsilon }^0F'^2\, \mathrm dr=-\log \varepsilon +O(1)$. On the left tail $F'(r)\leq \mathrm e^ r/\varepsilon $, and on the right tail $F'(r)\leq \mathrm e^{-r}$; the corresponding integrals of $F'^2$ are at most $\frac12$. Since $\int _ Xu_ a\, \omega \to 0$, the formula of example 17.3.16 gives $E_\omega (u_ a)\to -\frac12$, whereas $E_\omega (0)=0$.

title: Lemma 17.5.3
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Lemma 17.5.3 . B408410BD203 Let $\lambda $ and $\sigma $ be finite positive Borel measures on $X$. If $\int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\lambda \geq \int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\sigma $ for every continuous function $g\geq 0$ on $X$, then $\lambda (E)\geq \sigma (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset X$. In particular, two finite positive Borel measures on $X$ with the same integrals of all continuous functions coincide. If finite positive Borel measures $\lambda _ j$ converge weakly to $\lambda $ and satisfy $\lambda _ j\geq \sigma $ for every $j$, then $\lambda \geq \sigma $. Proof. (1) This is lemma 16.12.1 (2) with $W=X$; the second assertion follows by applying the first in both directions. (2) Since $X$ is compact, weak convergence of measures on $X$ is convergence of the integrals of all continuous functions (see the discussion following definition 5.3.5 ). Hence $\int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\lambda =\lim _ j\int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\lambda _ j\geq \int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\sigma $ for every continuous function $g\geq 0$ on $X$, and (1) gives $\lambda \geq \sigma $. $\square$

title: Proposition 17.5.4
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Proposition 17.5.4 . 2099099BAE21 Let $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $f\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, and put $u_ t=P_\theta (u+tf)$ for $t\in \mathbb R$, the envelope of definition 16.11.3 . Then $u_0=u$, and for every $t$ we have $u_ t\sim u$ and $u_ t\leq u+tf$ on $X$. Each $u_ t$ has finite energy, and \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E(u_ t)=\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] The derivative is continuous on $\mathbb R$. Proof. Let $B=\sup _ X|f|$. The potential $u-|t|B$ is a competitor for the obstacle $u+tf$, and every competitor lies below $u+|t|B$, so $u-|t|B\leq u_ t\leq u+|t|B$. Hence $u_ t\sim u$, and $E(u_ t)\geq E(u)-|t|Bm>-\infty $, so $u_ t\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by theorem 17.3.14 . The obstacle $u+tf$ is upper semicontinuous, so $u_ t\leq u+tf$ everywhere, by proposition 16.11.4 (1),(2). In particular $u_0\leq u$; since $u$ is itself a competitor for the obstacle $u$, also $u\leq u_0$, so $u_0=u$. Next we show that $\mu _{u_{t+s}}\to \mu _{u_ t}$ weakly as $s\to 0$. The obstacles $u+tf$ and $u+(t+s)f$ differ by at most $|s|B$, so proposition 16.11.4 (4) gives $u_ t-|s|B\leq u_{t+s}\leq u_ t+|s|B$. In particular all $u_ t$ have the pole set of $u$, and $|u_{t+s}-u_ t|\leq |s|B$ outside it. Since $|\arctan a-\arctan b|\leq |a-b|$ for real $a,b$, and adding the same smooth local potential of $\theta $ to $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$ does not change their difference, the distance $d_*$ of definition 13.7.2 between the local potentials of $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$ is at most $|s|B$ everywhere. Hence, for every $\delta >0$, the sets where it exceeds $\delta $ are empty once $|s|B<\delta $, and $u_{t+s}\to u_ t$ in extended capacity as $s\to 0$. These potentials have full mass relative to $\phi $, so corollary 13.9.4 , applied along every sequence $s_ k\to 0$, gives the asserted weak convergence; in particular $\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_{t+s}}\to \int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}$. The obstacle $u+tf$ is bounded above, and it is quasi-continuous, because $u$ is (section 16.11 ) and $f$ is continuous. Hence theorem 16.13.4 shows that $\mu _{u_ t}$ is carried by the contact set $\{ u_ t=u+tf\} $. On the contact set of $u_{t+s}$ we have $u_{t+s}=u+(t+s)f$ and $u_ t\leq u+tf$, so $u_{t+s}-u_ t\geq sf$ there. On the contact set of $u_ t$ we have $u_ t=u+tf$ and $u_{t+s}\leq u+(t+s)f$, so $u_{t+s}-u_ t\leq sf$ there. The differences are bounded and the pole sets carry no mass, so the tangent bounds of lemma 17.4.10 give, for every real $s$, \[  s\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_{t+s}} \leq E(u_{t+s})-E(u_ t) \leq s\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] Dividing by $s>0$, respectively $s<0$, and letting $s\to 0$, we obtain the right and left derivatives from the weak convergence just proved. Both equal $\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}$, which depends continuously on $t$ by the same weak convergence. $\square$

text: Lemma 17.5.10 . DD59ECAA0656 Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. If $q_ j,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $q_ j\to q$ in $L^1(X)$, then $\varlimsup _ jq_ j=q$ quasi-everywhere. Proof. By lemma 17.4.3 , the tail envelopes $a_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k)^*$ are $\theta $-psh and decrease pointwise to $q$. For each $j$, corollary 5.47.11 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, gives $a_ j=\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k$ outside a pluripolar set. The countable union of these sets is pluripolar (theorem 5.47.8 ), and outside it $q=\lim _ ja_ j=\varlimsup _ jq_ j$. $\square$

title: Corollary 17.5.12

text: Corollary 17.5.12 . F89C0E4EBAC2 Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $q_ j,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $q_ j\to q$ in $L^1(X)$, and let $\nu $ be a finite non-pluripolar measure on $X$. Then for every $\lambda >0$, \[  \mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}\longrightarrow \mathrm e^{\lambda q} \quad \text{in }L^1(\nu ).  \] Proof. By proposition 10.3.1 there is a constant $C$ with $q_ j,q\leq C$. We show that the functions $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}$ and $\mathrm e^{\lambda q}$, with value zero on the pole sets, are $C_1\omega $-psh for a constant $C_1$ independent of $j$; the preceding lemma then applies to them. Choose $C_0\geq 0$ with $\theta \leq C_0\omega $, and a finite cover of $X$ by coordinate balls $W'\Subset W$ such that the smaller balls $W'$ still cover $X$, together with smooth functions $h_ W$ near $\overline W$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ W=\theta $. The function $q_ j+h_ W$ is plurisubharmonic on $W$, so for every $\delta >0$ smaller than the distance from $W'$ to the boundary of $W$, its regularization $g_\delta =(q_ j+h_ W)*\rho _\delta $ by the radial mollifier is a smooth plurisubharmonic function on the ball $W'$, and $g_\delta $ decreases to $q_ j+h_ W$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$, by proposition 5.9.2 (2). Put $q_{j,\delta }=g_\delta -h_ W$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_{j,\delta }\geq -\theta \geq -C_0\omega $. Moreover $g_\delta (x)$ is an average of values of $q_ j+h_ W\leq C+h_ W$ at points within distance $\delta $ of $x$, so by uniform continuity of $h_ W$ on a compact neighborhood of $\overline{W'}$ in $W$ we have $q_{j,\delta }\leq C+1$ on $W'$ for all small $\delta $, independently of $j$. For a smooth real function $s$, the chain rule $\partial \bar\partial \, \mathrm e^{\lambda s}=\lambda \mathrm e^{\lambda s}\partial \bar\partial s+\lambda ^2\mathrm e^{\lambda s}\partial s\wedge \bar\partial s$ and the identity $\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial s\wedge \bar\partial s=\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s$, which follows from ( 5.2.10 ), give \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }} =\lambda \mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_{j,\delta } +\lambda ^2\mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }} \mathrm dq_{j,\delta }\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q_{j,\delta } \geq -\lambda C_0\mathrm e^{\lambda (C+1)}\omega ,  \] because $\mathrm dq_{j,\delta }\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q_{j,\delta }$ is a semipositive $(1,1)$-form. Thus $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }}$ is $C_1\omega $-psh on $W'$ with $C_1=\lambda C_0\mathrm e^{\lambda (C+1)}$, and so is its decreasing limit $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$, by theorem 5.10.1 applied after adding a smooth local potential of $C_1\omega $; the limit is not identically $-\infty $, since it is nonnegative. Since the balls $W'$ cover $X$, the function $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C_1\omega )$, and the same argument applies to $\mathrm e^{\lambda q}$. The exponential is Lipschitz with constant $\lambda \mathrm e^{\lambda C}$ on $(-\infty ,C]$, so $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}\to \mathrm e^{\lambda q}$ in $L^1(X)$. These functions take values in $[0,\mathrm e^{\lambda C}]$, and lemma 17.5.11 , with the background $C_1\omega $, gives the assertion. $\square$

title: 17.5.16 Uniqueness by concentration of mass
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: We now show that the solution given by theorem 17.5.15 is unique up to an additive constant. The proof uses existence once more. If two solutions $u,v$ with $\mu _ u=\mu _ v=\mu $ do not differ by a constant $\mu $-almost everywhere, then, after a shift of $v$, the set $U=\{ u<v\} $ carries a proper fraction of the mass of $\mu $. We solve the equation whose right-hand side is $\mu $ restricted to $U$ and rescaled to total mass $m$. Mixing this auxiliary solution into $v$ raises the density of the Monge–Ampère measure on $U$ (corollary 13.5.11 ), in contradiction with the comparison principle. The domination principle then turns equality $\mu $-almost everywhere into equality everywhere. Theorem 17.5.17 . 777B716B7208 Let $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ satisfy $\mu _ u=\mu _ v$. Then there is a constant $C\in \mathbb R$ such that $u=v+C$ everywhere on $X$. Consequently, every non-pluripolar measure of mass $m$ is the Monge–Ampère measure $\mu _ u$ of exactly one $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$. Proof. Put $\mu =\mu _ u=\mu _ v$. Since $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, this is a finite measure of mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =m$, and it is non-pluripolar, because non-pluripolar products give no mass to pluripolar sets (lemma 13.2.2 ). Hence the pole sets of $u$ and $v$ are $\mu $-null, and $u-v$ is defined and finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. We first show that $u-v$ is constant $\mu $-almost everywhere. Suppose not. Let $\lambda $ be the image of $\mu $ under $u-v$, a finite Borel measure on $\mathbb R$ of total mass $m>0$, and put \[  c_-=\sup \{ c\in \mathbb R:\lambda ((-\infty ,c))=0\} ,\qquad c_+=\inf \{ c\in \mathbb R:\lambda ((c,\infty ))=0\} ,  \] with $\sup \varnothing =-\infty $ and $\inf \varnothing =+\infty $. The sets $(-\infty ,c)$ increase to $\mathbb R$ as $c\to +\infty $, so $\lambda ((-\infty ,c))\to m>0$; hence $c_-<+\infty $, and similarly $c_+>-\infty $. If $c_->-\infty $, the $\lambda $-null sets $(-\infty ,c)$ with $c<c_-$ increase to $(-\infty ,c_-)$, so $\lambda ((-\infty ,c_-))=0$; similarly $\lambda ((c_+,\infty ))=0$ if $c_+<+\infty $. Hence $c_+<c_-$ is impossible, since $\mathbb R=(-\infty ,c_-)\cup (c_+,\infty )$ would then be $\lambda $-null. If $c_-=c_+$, then $\lambda $ is carried by the point $c_-$, that is, $u-v$ is constant $\mu $-almost everywhere, contrary to our assumption. Thus $c_-<c_+$, and every $c\in (c_-,c_+)$ satisfies $\lambda ((-\infty ,c))>0$ and $\lambda ((c,\infty ))>0$, that is, \[  \mu (\{ u-v<c\} )>0,\qquad \mu (\{ u-v>c\} )>0.  \] The singletons $\{ c\} $ with $\lambda (\{ c\} )>0$ are pairwise disjoint sets of positive measure, so there are only countably many of them by lemma 2.2.5 . Since the interval $(c_-,c_+)$ is uncountable, we may choose $c$ in it with $\mu (\{ u-v=c\} )=0$. Replacing $v$ by $v+c$ changes neither the class $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ nor the measure $\mu _ v$, so we may assume $c=0$. Then $\mu (\{ u<v\} )$ and $\mu (\{ u>v\} )$ are positive, and the set $U=\{ u<v\} $ satisfies \[  0<\mu (U)<m,\qquad \mu (\{ u=v\} )=0.  \] Set $q=(m/\mu (U))^{1/n}>1$. The measure $q^ n\mathbf1_ U\mu $ is non-pluripolar and has mass $m$, so theorem 17.5.15 gives $h\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ with \[  \mu _ h=q^ n\mathbf1_ U\mu .  \] For $0<t<1$ put $w_ t=(1-t)v+th$. By corollary 17.3.17 , $w_ t\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Since $\theta _{w_ t}=(1-t)\theta _ v+t\theta _ h$, corollary 13.5.11 , applied to the currents $\theta _ v,\theta _ h$, the common measure $\mu $ and the densities $1$ and $q^ n\mathbf1_ U$, gives \[  \mu _{w_ t}\geq \big ((1-t)+tq\mathbf1_ U\big )^ n\mu .  \] Let $U_ t=\{ u<w_ t\} $, and put \[  d_ t=(1-t)^ n,\qquad b_ t=(1-t+tq)^ n.  \] The comparison principle for relative full mass, proposition 16.25.4 , applied to $u$ and $w_ t$, and the preceding lower bound give \[  \mu (U_ t)=\mu _ u(U_ t)\geq \mu _{w_ t}(U_ t) \geq d_ t\mu (U_ t)+(b_ t-d_ t)\mu (U_ t\cap U).  \] Since $1-d_ t>0$, it follows that EAFAB682B4E1 17.5.18 \begin{equation}  \frac{b_ t-d_ t}{1-d_ t}\, \mu (U_ t\cap U)\leq \mu (U_ t). \end{equation} We let $t\downarrow 0$. At every point where $u,v,h$ are finite and $u\neq v$, we have $w_ t=v+t(h-v)$, so $\mathbf1_{U_ t}\to \mathbf1_ U$ there. These points have full $\mu $-measure, because the three pole sets and the level set $\{ u=v\} $ are $\mu $-null. By dominated convergence, \[  \mu (U_ t\cap U)\longrightarrow \mu (U),\qquad \mu (U_ t)\longrightarrow \mu (U).  \] Moreover $b_ t-d_ t=ntq+O(t^2)$ and $1-d_ t=nt+O(t^2)$, so $(b_ t-d_ t)/(1-d_ t)\to q$. Passing to the limit in ( 17.5.18 ) gives $q\mu (U)\leq \mu (U)$, which contradicts $q>1$ and $\mu (U)>0$. Hence, for the original pair, there is a finite constant $C$ such that $u=v+C$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. Both $u$ and $v+C$ belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and their common measure $\mu $ gives zero mass to $\{ u<v+C\} $ and to $\{ v+C<u\} $. The domination principle (theorem 16.22.10 ), applied in both directions, gives $u=v+C$ everywhere, including at the common poles. This proves the first assertion. For the second, theorem 17.5.15 provides a solution with supremum zero. If $u$ and $v$ are two such solutions, then $u=v+C$, and comparing suprema gives $C=0$. $\square$

Since $\theta _{w_ t}=(1-t)\theta _ v+t\theta _ h$, corollary 13.5.11 , applied to the currents $\theta _ v,\theta _ h$, the common measure $\mu $ and the densities $1$ and $q^ n\mathbf1_ U$, gives \[  \mu _{w_ t}\geq \big ((1-t)+tq\mathbf1_ U\big )^ n\mu .  \] Let $U_ t=\{ u<w_ t\} $, and put \[  d_ t=(1-t)^ n,\qquad b_ t=(1-t+tq)^ n.  \] The comparison principle for relative full mass, proposition 16.25.4 , applied to $u$ and $w_ t$, and the preceding lower bound give \[  \mu (U_ t)=\mu _ u(U_ t)\geq \mu _{w_ t}(U_ t) \geq d_ t\mu (U_ t)+(b_ t-d_ t)\mu (U_ t\cap U).  \] Since $1-d_ t>0$, it follows that EAFAB682B4E1 17.5.18 \begin{equation}  \frac{b_ t-d_ t}{1-d_ t}\, \mu (U_ t\cap U)\leq \mu (U_ t). \end{equation} We let $t\downarrow 0$. At every point where $u,v,h$ are finite and $u\neq v$, we have $w_ t=v+t(h-v)$, so $\mathbf1_{U_ t}\to \mathbf1_ U$ there. These points have full $\mu $-measure, because the three pole sets and the level set $\{ u=v\} $ are $\mu $-null. By dominated convergence, \[  \mu (U_ t\cap U)\longrightarrow \mu (U),\qquad \mu (U_ t)\longrightarrow \mu (U).  \] Moreover $b_ t-d_ t=ntq+O(t^2)$ and $1-d_ t=nt+O(t^2)$, so $(b_ t-d_ t)/(1-d_ t)\to q$. The domination principle (theorem 16.22.10 ), applied in both directions, gives $u=v+C$ everywhere, including at the common poles. This proves the first assertion. For the second, theorem 17.5.15 provides a solution with supremum zero. If $u$ and $v$ are two such solutions, then $u=v+C$, and comparing suprema gives $C=0$. $\square$

title: 17.5.27 Positive mass and bigness
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text:
So far the background class has been big, and big classes have positive volume by proposition 13.9.2 . The equations solved above give the converse for pseudo-effective classes. In this subsection $	heta $ denotes an arbitrary smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$; its class need not be big, and no model potential is fixed. Let $\alpha =\{ 	heta \} $ be a pseudo-effective class whose volume, in the sense of definition 13.9.1 , is positive. The classes $\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, $\varepsilon >0$, are big, and in each of them we solve the Monge–Ampère equation whose right-hand side is a fixed smooth measure rescaled to the total mass $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )$, which is at least $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$. A pointwise inequality between traces, integrated against these solutions, yields lower bounds for the pairings $\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au $ with strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-forms $	au $, uniformly in $\varepsilon $. Lamari's duality criterion, which we prove first, turns such bounds into a Kähler current in $\alpha $. Recall from section 5.3 that weak and strong positivity coincide for real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, so that we speak simply of positive forms, and that such a form is strictly positive if at every point it lies in the interior of the cone of positive forms. For instance, $\omega ^{n-1}$ is strictly positive: at a point $x$, choose linear coordinates on the tangent space in which $\omega (x)$ is the standard form $ eta $; then $\omega (x)^{n-1}= eta ^{n-1}$ is an interior point of the cone by proposition 5.3.2 , and complex-linear isomorphisms preserve positivity. For real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms we write $\eta \leq 	au $ if $	au -\eta $ is positive. Lemma 17.5.28 (Lamari's criterion) . D70C0784CA6E Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
eq \varnothing $ if and only if 99EE27FCDCB1 17.5.29  egin{equation}  \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq 0 \end{equation} for every smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $	au $ on $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$. Consequently, the class $\{ 	heta \} $ is big if and only if there is $\delta >0$ such that every such form $	au $ satisfies C39A9A97E83C 17.5.30  egin{equation}  \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq \delta \int _ X\omega \wedge 	au . \end{equation} Proof. Necessity. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, then $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. For $	au $ as in the statement, the definition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ as a current gives $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge 	au =\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$, hence $\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au =\int _ XT\wedge 	au $, which is nonnegative by the definition of a positive current, since $	au $ is positive, hence strongly positive. If $n\geq 2$, the form $	heta _\varepsilon +C\omega $ is positive definite, so theorem 13.5.4 gives \[  \int _ X\langle S_\varepsilon ^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega \leq \int _ X(	heta +(C+\varepsilon )\omega )^{n-1}\wedge \omega \leq C_0;  \] the last inequality holds because $	heta +(C+1)\omega =(	heta +(C+\varepsilon )\omega )+(1-\varepsilon )\omega $ and products of positive $(1,1)$-forms are positive. If $n=1$, the second factor equals $\int _ X\omega =C_0$. As the first factor is nonnegative, in both cases \[  \left(\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au +\varepsilon ight)C_0\geq  rac mn.  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq m/(nC_0)$. Removing the normalization of $	au $, we conclude that every smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-form $	au $ satisfies ( 17.5.30 ) with $\delta =m/(nC_0)>0$. By lemma 17.5.28 , the class $\alpha $ is big. $\square$ If $\{ 	heta \} $ is pseudo-effective but not big, the theorem shows that every $	heta $-psh potential has zero non-pluripolar mass. This allows us to extend the contact theorems of section 16.10 from big to pseudo-effective classes. Corollary 17.5.38 . C78DFCF82004 Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form, and let $f\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ be a quasi-continuous Borel function. Suppose that the family $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ of definition 16.11.3 is nonempty and uniformly bounded above. Then $u=P_	heta (f)$ satisfies \[  \mu _ u igl (X\setminus \{ u=f\}  igr )=0.  \] If $\{ 	heta \} $ is not big, then $\mu _ u=0$. Moreover, if $r\geq 1$ and $u_1,\ldots ,u_ r\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ have a rooftop $w=P_	heta (\min _{1\leq j\leq r}u_ j)$ that is not identically $-\infty $, then \[  \mu _ w\leq \sum _{j=1}^ r\mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _{u_ j}.  \] Proof. By proposition 16.11.4 (1), $u\in \mathcal A_	heta (f)$; that is, $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. If $\{ 	heta \} $ is not big, then $\mu _ u(X)=0$ by theorem 17.5.37 , since otherwise $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ would be a closed positive current of positive non-pluripolar mass in $\{ 	heta \} $. Hence $\mu _ u=0$, and in particular the first assertion holds. If $\{ 	heta \} $ is big, the first assertion is theorem 16.13.4 . For the rooftop, the function $\min _ ju_ j$ is quasi-continuous, as a finite minimum of potentials (see the beginning of section 16.11 ), and it is bounded above; its envelope is $w$. Since $w$ is not identically $-\infty $, the family $\mathcal A_	heta (\min _ ju_ j)$ is nonempty, and it is uniformly bounded above because the obstacle is. By the first assertion, $\mu _ w$ is carried by $\{ w=\min _ ju_ j\} \subset  igcup _ j\{ w=u_ j\} $. The obstacle is upper semicontinuous, so $w\leq u_ j$ everywhere by proposition 16.11.4 (1),(2), and lemma 16.13.1 gives $\mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _{u_ j}$ for every $j$. Summing over $j$ proves the rooftop inequality. $\square$ Corollary 17.5.39 . 92C6B04981BA Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form with $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
eq \varnothing $, and let $f$ be a continuous real function on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian. Then \[  \langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_	heta (f))^ nangle =\mathbf1_{\{ P_	heta (f)=f\} }(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n,  \] where the right side is understood as in theorem 16.20.2 . In particular $\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_	heta )^ nangle =\mathbf1_{\{ V_	heta =0\} }	heta ^ n$. If $\{ 	heta \} $ is not big, both sides of these two identities vanish. Proof. The potential $V_	heta +\min _ Xf$ lies below $f$, so $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty, and it is bounded above by $\max _ Xf$. Put $u=P_	heta (f)$. Since $f$ is continuous, $u\leq f$ everywhere by proposition 16.11.4 (1),(2). The scalar case of theorem 16.20.2 , with all $	heta _ j=	heta $, $u_ j=u$ and $f_ j=f$, gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=f\} }\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle =\mathbf1_{\{ u=f\} }(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n,  \] and corollary 17.5.38 shows that $\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle $ is carried by $\{ u=f\} $. This proves the first identity. For $f=0$ the envelope $P_	heta (0)$ is $V_	heta $, by definition 10.3.7 , which gives the second. If $\{ 	heta \} $ is not big, the left sides vanish by corollary 17.5.38 , and hence so do the right sides. $\square$

title: Lemma 17.5.28 (Lamari's criterion)
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text:
Lemma 17.5.28 (Lamari's criterion) . D70C0784CA6E Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
eq \varnothing $ if and only if 99EE27FCDCB1 17.5.29  egin{equation}  \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq 0 \end{equation} for every smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $	au $ on $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$. Consequently, the class $\{ 	heta \} $ is big if and only if there is $\delta >0$ such that every such form $	au $ satisfies C39A9A97E83C 17.5.30  egin{equation}  \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq \delta \int _ X\omega \wedge 	au . \end{equation} Proof. Necessity. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, then $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. For $	au $ as in the statement, the definition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ as a current gives $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge 	au =\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$, hence $\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au =\int _ XT\wedge 	au $, which is nonnegative by the definition of a positive current, since $	au $ is positive, hence strongly positive. Sufficiency. Conversely, assume ( 17.5.29 ) for all forms $	au $ as in the statement. We extend the functional $	au \mapsto \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au $ from $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed forms to a positive linear functional on all smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, regard the extension as a positive $(1,1)$-current $T$, and show that $T-	heta $ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution. A positive extension. Let $F$ be the real vector space of smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms on $X$, let $S=\{ 	au \in F:\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0\} $, and put $e=\omega ^{n-1}$, with $e=1$ if $n=1$. Since $\omega $ is closed, $e\in S$, and $e$ is strictly positive. Define $\ell _0(	au )=\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au $ for $	au \in S$. By hypothesis $\ell _0(	au )\geq 0$ when $	au \in S$ is strictly positive. If $	au \in S$ is merely positive, then $	au +te\in S$ is strictly positive for every $t>0$. Indeed, at each point $x$ the cone of positive forms contains a ball about $e(x)$, for some norm; since the cone is stable under sums and positive multiples, it also contains the ball of $t$ times that radius about $	au (x)+te(x)$. Hence $\ell _0(	au )+t\ell _0(e)\geq 0$, and letting $t\downarrow 0$ gives $\ell _0(	au )\geq 0$. We next compare the forms in $F$ with $e$. Fix finitely many holomorphic charts $U_1,\ldots ,U_ N$ and compact sets $K_ a\subset U_ a$ with $ igcup _ aK_ a=X$. In $U_ a$ write $\eta \in F$ as $\eta =\sum _{I,J}\eta ^ a_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ J$, the sum running over increasing multi-indices of length $n-1$, and put \[  \| \eta \| =\max _{1\leq a\leq N}\  \max _{I,J}\  \sup _{K_ a}|\eta ^ a_{IJ}|.  \] We claim that there is a constant $M>0$ such that 316C32F396FA 17.5.31  egin{equation}  -M\| \eta \| e\leq \eta \leq M\| \eta \| e\qquad 	ext{for every }\eta \in F. \end{equation} Let $Z$ be the finite-dimensional real vector space of real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms with constant coefficients on $\mathbb C^ n$, normed by the maximum modulus of the coefficients, and let $P\subset Z$ be the closed convex cone of positive forms (proposition 5.3.2 ). For $x\in U_ a$, the differential of the chart is a complex-linear isomorphism from the tangent space at $x$ onto $\mathbb C^ n$, under which $\mathrm dz_ j$ corresponds to the $j$th coordinate form. Since complex-linear isomorphisms preserve positivity, a real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\eta $ is positive at $x$ if and only if its coefficient form $\eta ^ a(x)=\sum _{I,J}\eta ^ a_{IJ}(x)\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ J\in Z$ lies in $P$. Because $e$ is strictly positive, the continuous map $x\mapsto e^ a(x)$ sends the compact set $K_ a$ into the interior of $P$; the complement of this interior is closed and disjoint from the compact image, so it has positive distance $r_ a$ from it. Put $r= rac12\min _ ar_ a$. If $\eta \in F$ satisfies $\| \eta \| \leq r$ and $x\in K_ a$, then $e^ a(x)\pm \eta ^ a(x)$ lies within distance $r<r_ a$ of $e^ a(x)$, hence in $P$; thus $e\pm \eta $ is positive at $x$. Since the sets $K_ a$ cover $X$, the forms $e\pm \eta $ are positive. Applying this to $r\eta /\| \eta \| $ for $\eta 
eq 0$ proves ( 17.5.31 ) with $M=1/r$. For $\eta \in F$, a form $	au \in S$ with $	au \geq \eta $ is called an $S$-majorant of $\eta $, and we put \[  p(\eta )=\inf \{ \ell _0(	au ):	au 	ext{ is an $S$-majorant of }\eta \} .  \] Let $\eta \in F$ and $C=M\| \eta \| $, so that $-Ce\leq \eta \leq Ce$ by ( 17.5.31 ). The form $Ce$ is an $S$-majorant of $\eta $, so $p(\eta )\leq C\ell _0(e)$. If $	au $ is an $S$-majorant of $\eta $, then $	au +Ce\geq \eta +Ce\geq 0$, so $	au +Ce\in S$ is positive and $\ell _0(	au )\geq -C\ell _0(e)$. Thus $p$ is finite. It is sublinear: the sum of $S$-majorants of $\eta _1$ and $\eta _2$ is an $S$-majorant of $\eta _1+\eta _2$, and for $\lambda >0$ the $S$-majorants of $\lambda \eta $ are $\lambda $ times those of $\eta $. If $\eta \in S$, then $\eta $ is its own $S$-majorant, and every $S$-majorant $	au $ of $\eta $ satisfies $\ell _0(	au )-\ell _0(\eta )=\ell _0(	au -\eta )\geq 0$ because $	au -\eta \in S$ is positive. Hence $p=\ell _0$ on $S$. Next we extend $\ell _0$ to a linear functional on $F$ dominated by $p$; this is the Hahn–Banach theorem, whose proof we recall. Let $\ell $ be a linear functional on a subspace $W\supset S$ which extends $\ell _0$ and satisfies $\ell \leq p$ on $W$, and let $\eta _0\in F\setminus W$. For $\eta _1,\eta _2\in W$, \[  \ell (\eta _1)+\ell (\eta _2)=\ell (\eta _1+\eta _2)\leq p(\eta _1+\eta _2)\leq p(\eta _1-\eta _0)+p(\eta _2+\eta _0),  \] so \[  \sup _{\eta _1\in W} igl (\ell (\eta _1)-p(\eta _1-\eta _0) igr ) \leq \inf _{\eta _2\in W} igl (p(\eta _2+\eta _0)-\ell (\eta _2) igr ).  \] Taking $\eta _1=\eta _2=0$ shows that the supremum is greater than $-\infty $ and the infimum is less than $+\infty $; hence both are finite, and we may choose a real number $c$ between them. Define $\ell (\eta +t\eta _0)=\ell (\eta )+tc$ for $\eta \in W$ and $t\in \mathbb R$. For $t>0$, the upper bound for $c$ with $\eta _2=\eta /t$, multiplied by $t$, gives $\ell (\eta )+tc\leq p(\eta +t\eta _0)$; for $t<0$, the lower bound for $c$ with $\eta _1=\eta /|t|$, multiplied by $|t|$, gives the same inequality. Thus the extension to $W+\mathbb R\eta _0$ is still dominated by $p$. The union of a chain of such extensions is again such an extension, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal one, and by the step just proved its domain is $F$. We denote it again by $\ell $. The functional $\ell $ is positive: if $\eta \in F$ is positive, then $0$ is an $S$-majorant of $-\eta $, so $\ell (-\eta )\leq p(-\eta )\leq 0$. It is also bounded: by ( 17.5.31 ), the form $M\| \eta \| e$ is an $S$-majorant of both $\eta $ and $-\eta $, so 1FC0F0E3114E 17.5.32  egin{equation}  |\ell (\eta )|\leq M\ell _0(e)\| \eta \| \qquad (\eta \in F). \end{equation} We now turn $\ell $ into a current. Every smooth form on the compact manifold $X$ is a test form. For a complex form $\varphi $ of degree $2n-2$, let $\varphi '$ be its component of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, and put $T(\varphi )=\ell (\operatorname{Re}\varphi ')+\mathrm i\, \ell (\operatorname{Im}\varphi ')$, where $\operatorname{Re}\varphi '=(\varphi '+\overline{\varphi '})/2$ and $\operatorname{Im}\varphi '=(\varphi '-\overline{\varphi '})/(2\mathrm i)$ are real forms in $F$. This is a complex-linear functional: replacing $\varphi $ by $\mathrm i\varphi $ replaces $(\operatorname{Re}\varphi ',\operatorname{Im}\varphi ')$ by $(-\operatorname{Im}\varphi ',\operatorname{Re}\varphi ')$. Moreover, $T$ has the continuity property of a current of degree $2$. Indeed, let $Q$ be a compact subset of a chart $U$, and let $\varphi $ be supported in $Q$, with coefficients $\varphi _ J$ in real coordinates on $U$. On the compact set $K_ a\cap Q$, the coefficients of $\operatorname{Re}\varphi '$ and $\operatorname{Im}\varphi '$ in the chart $U_ a$ are linear combinations of the functions $\varphi _ J$ and $\overline{\varphi _ J}$ with coefficients that are smooth on $U\cap U_ a$, and they vanish on $K_ a\setminus Q$. Hence $\| \operatorname{Re}\varphi '\| +\| \operatorname{Im}\varphi '\| \leq C_ Q\sum _ J\sup _ Q|\varphi _ J|$ with a constant $C_ Q$ independent of $\varphi $, and ( 17.5.32 ) gives $|T(\varphi )|\leq MC_ Q\ell _0(e)\sum _ J\sup _ Q|\varphi _ J|$. By construction $T$ vanishes on forms of bidegree other than $(n-1,n-1)$, so it is a current of bidegree $(1,1)$. It is real, because the $(n-1,n-1)$-component of $\overline\varphi $ is $\overline{\varphi '}=\operatorname{Re}\varphi '-\mathrm i\operatorname{Im}\varphi '$, so that $T(\overline\varphi )=\overline{T(\varphi )}$. It is positive, because a strongly positive test form $\varphi $ of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$ is real and positive, so that $T(\varphi )=\ell (\varphi )\geq 0$. Since $\ell $ extends $\ell _0$, the real $(1,1)$-current $R=T-	heta $ annihilates $S$. The current $R$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. We first show that $R$ is closed. If $\xi $ is a smooth form of bidegree $(n-2,n-1)$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\partial \xi = rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial \partial \xi =- rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \partial  ar\partial \xi =0$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} ar\partial \xi '= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial  ar\partial \xi '=0$ for $\xi '$ of bidegree $(n-1,n-2)$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is a real operator, the conjugate of a $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed complex $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\sigma $ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, so the real forms $\operatorname{Re}\sigma $ and $\operatorname{Im}\sigma $ lie in $S$; as $R$ is complex-linear and annihilates $S$, it annihilates $\sigma $. In particular $R(\partial \xi )=R( ar\partial \xi ')=0$. For a smooth $(2n-3)$-form $\gamma $, the $(n-1,n-1)$-component of $\mathrm d\gamma $ is $\partial \gamma ^{n-2,n-1}+ ar\partial \gamma ^{n-1,n-2}$; since $R$ has bidegree $(1,1)$, it follows that $R(\mathrm d\gamma )=0$. Therefore $\mathrm dR=0$. Since $e\in S$, we also have $\int _ XR\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=0$. Let $\Lambda $ denote contraction with $\omega $, as in lemma 10.2.12 ; the identity $R\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=(\Lambda R)\omega ^ n/n$ shows that the trace $\Lambda R$ has mean zero. By lemma 10.2.5 (2), applied to the Laplacian $L=\mathrm d^*\mathrm d$ of section 10.2 , there is a real distribution $f$ with $Lf=-4\pi \Lambda R$. By lemma 10.2.12 , $\Lambda \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\Lambda R$, so $R'=R-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is a closed real $(1,1)$-current with zero trace. By the last assertion of lemma 10.2.12 , $R'$ is harmonic, and by lemma 10.2.5 (1) it is smooth. If $n=1$, a $(1,1)$-form with zero trace vanishes, so $R'=0$. If $n\geq 2$, ( 10.2.13 ) gives $*R'=-R'\wedge \omega ^{n-2}/(n-2)!$, a smooth closed $(n-1,n-1)$-form; hence $*R'\in S$. Since $R$ annihilates $S$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}{*R'}=0$, \[  \| R'\| _{L^2}^2 =\int _ XR'\wedge *R' =R(*R')-\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}{*R'}=0.  \] Thus $R'=0$ and $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ in every dimension. Conclusion. The current $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is closed and positive, and it lies in the class $\{ 	heta \} $, since it differs from $	heta $ by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution. By corollary 10.2.19 , there is $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T$. This proves sufficiency. For the last assertion, $\{ 	heta \} $ is big exactly when $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )
eq \varnothing $ for some $\delta >0$. Indeed, if $T\geq \delta \omega $ is a Kähler current in $\{ 	heta \} $ (definition 10.4.1 ), then $T-\delta \omega $ is a closed positive current in the class $\{ 	heta -\delta \omega \} $, so $T-\delta \omega =	heta -\delta \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )$, by corollary 10.2.19 . Conversely, if $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )$, then $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta \omega $ is a Kähler current in $\{ 	heta \} $. Applying the first part to $	heta -\delta \omega $ shows that this holds if and only if ( 17.5.30 ) holds for that $\delta $. $\square$
