title: Lemma 17.5.33
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text:
Lemma 17.5.33 . EB970BD6E881 Let $A$ be a closed subset of $X$ of Lebesgue measure zero in every chart, and let $S$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$ whose local potentials are locally bounded on $X\setminus A$. Let $	au $ be a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form, and put $
u =\omega \wedge 	au $. If \[  \langle S^ nangle =m
u \qquad 	ext{for some }m\geq 0,  \] then 0511A794D8D0 17.5.34  egin{equation}  \left(\int _ X S\wedge 	au ight) \left(\int _ X\langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega ight) \geq  rac mn\left(\int _ X
u ight)^2. \end{equation} For $n=1$ the second factor is $\int _ X\omega $. Proof. We prove a pointwise inequality for smooth forms, apply it to regularizations of the potentials of $S$ on small balls in $X\setminus A$, and globalize with a partition of unity. Step 1: a pointwise inequality. Let $\sigma $ be a smooth positive definite real $(1,1)$-form. At a given point, choose linear coordinates on the tangent space that diagonalize the Hermitian matrices of $\omega $ and $\sigma $ simultaneously, so that $\omega =\sum _ j\gamma _ j$ and $\sigma =\sum _ j\lambda _ j\gamma _ j$ with $\lambda _ j>0$, where $\gamma _ j=\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$, and put $\mathrm dV=\gamma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma _ n$. Since $	au $ is strictly positive (section 5.3 ), the form $	au -c\, \omega ^{n-1}$ is positive at this point for some $c>0$. The product of the strongly positive form $\gamma _ j$ with this positive form is a nonnegative multiple of $\mathrm dV$ (proposition 5.3.2 ), and $\gamma _ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=(n-1)!\, \mathrm dV$, so $\gamma _ j\wedge 	au \geq c(n-1)!\, \mathrm dV$; thus $\gamma _ j\wedge 	au =t_ j\, \mathrm dV$ with $t_ j>0$. Expanding the products, we obtain \[   rac{\sigma \wedge 	au }{\omega \wedge 	au } = rac{\sum _ j\lambda _ jt_ j}{\sum _ jt_ j},\qquad  rac{\sigma ^{n-1}\wedge \omega }{\sigma ^ n} = rac1n\sum _ j\lambda _ j^{-1}.  \] Since $\lambda _ j\sum _ k\lambda _ k^{-1}\geq 1$ for every $j$, the product of these two ratios is at least $1/n$. If $\sigma $ is only semipositive, we apply this to $\sigma +s\omega $ and let $s\downarrow 0$. Thus, for every smooth semipositive real $(1,1)$-form $\sigma $, as densities with respect to any fixed smooth volume form, B73555CD9C1D 17.5.35  egin{equation}  (\sigma \wedge 	au )(\sigma ^{n-1}\wedge \omega ) \geq  rac1n\sigma ^ n
u . \end{equation} Step 2: regularization on a ball. Since the local potentials of $S$ are locally bounded on the open set $X\setminus A$, every point of $X\setminus A$ is the center of a coordinate ball $B\Subset X\setminus A$ on which $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ with $v$ plurisubharmonic and bounded. Fix such a ball, put $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ as in section 7.8 , and write $
u =g\eta ^ n$ with $g$ smooth and positive on $B$. Since $v$ is bounded on $B$, the non-pluripolar powers of $S$ on $B$ are the Bedford–Taylor powers of $v$ (see the remark following definition 13.2.4 ); in particular $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=mg\eta ^ n$. Let $v_\varepsilon =v*ho _\varepsilon $ be the regularizations of $v$ by the radial mollifiers of section 2.5 . On each ball $B'$ concentric with $B$ and of smaller radius, the functions $v_\varepsilon $ are defined for $\varepsilon $ smaller than the difference of the radii, and by proposition 5.9.2 (2) they are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $B'$ and decrease to $v$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. As recalled at the beginning of section 7.8 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n=\det \mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\, \eta ^ n$. The last assertion of proposition 7.8.3 , applied on $B$ to $v$ and the continuous density $mg$, therefore gives \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n=F_\varepsilon \eta ^ n, \qquad F_\varepsilon =\det \mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\geq  igl ((mg)^{1/n}*ho _\varepsilon  igr )^ n.  \] The right side converges to $mg$ uniformly on compact subsets of $B$, by lemma 2.5.1 (1) applied to the continuous function $(mg)^{1/n}$. Hence $\sqrt{F_\varepsilon g}$ is bounded below by functions converging uniformly to $\sqrt mg$ on compact sets, and for every nonnegative $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$, 93DD9AEE16DC 17.5.36  egin{equation}  \varliminf _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int \chi \sqrt{F_\varepsilon g}\, \eta ^ n \geq \sqrt m\int \chi 
u . \end{equation} Moreover, for every $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$, as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ along any sequence, \[  \int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon \wedge 	au \longrightarrow \int \chi \, S\wedge 	au , \qquad \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^{n-1}\wedge \omega \longrightarrow \int \chi \, \langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega .  \] For the first convergence, note that $\int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon \wedge 	au =\int v_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi 	au )$, by the definition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ on currents (section 5.3 ); since $v_\varepsilon 	o v$ in $L^1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 2.5.1 (2)), this tends to $\int v\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi 	au )=\int \chi \, S\wedge 	au $. For the second convergence, choose a ball $B'$ as above containing $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and a sequence $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. By theorem 7.3.7 , applied on $B'$ to the closed positive current $\omega $ of bidimension $(n-1,n-1)$ and to $n-1$ copies of the decreasing sequence $(v_{\varepsilon _ j})$, the currents $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{\varepsilon _ j})^{n-1}\wedge \omega $ converge weakly to the Bedford–Taylor product $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}\wedge \omega $. By proposition 7.2.2 (1) and (4), these products are the exterior products with $\omega $ of the smooth forms $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{\varepsilon _ j})^{n-1}$ and of the current $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}$, which equals $\langle S^{n-1}angle $ on $B$. title: Theorem 17.5.37
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Theorem 17.5.37 . F3340D970A43 A pseudo-effective class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is big if and only if $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )>0$. In particular, if a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ satisfies $\int _ X\langle T^ n\rangle >0$, then its class is big. Proof. By proposition 13.9.2 , big classes have positive volume, and every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ satisfies $\int _ X\langle T^ n\rangle \leq \operatorname {vol}(\{ T\} )$. It therefore suffices to show that a pseudo-effective class $\alpha $ with $m=\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )>0$ is big, and we do so by verifying Lamari's criterion (lemma 17.5.28 ). Write $\alpha =\{ \theta \} $ with $\theta $ smooth and closed, choose $C>0$ such that $\theta +C\omega $ is positive definite, and put \[  C_0=\int _ X(\theta +(C+1)\omega )^{n-1}\wedge \omega >0;  \] the integrand is a positive multiple of the volume form at every point, by the positivity of mixed discriminants of positive definite matrices (lemma 5.3.3 (2),(3)). For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$ let $\theta _\varepsilon =\theta +\varepsilon \omega $. Since $\alpha $ is pseudo-effective, there is $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ (corollary 10.2.19 ), and $\theta _\varepsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \varepsilon \omega $; thus $\{ \theta _\varepsilon \} =\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is big. By proposition 16.21.2 (4), $P_{\theta _\varepsilon }[V_{\theta _\varepsilon }]=V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$, and the mass of $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$ is \[  m_\varepsilon =\operatorname {vol}(\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ) \geq m>0;  \] the inequality holds because $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )$ decreases to $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by definition 13.9.1 , proposition 13.9.2 . Hence $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$ is a model potential of mass $m_\varepsilon $. Fix a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\tau $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau =0$, normalized by $\int _ X\omega \wedge \tau =1$. The measure $m_\varepsilon \omega \wedge \tau $ has a smooth density with respect to $\omega ^ n$ and total mass $m_\varepsilon $. By corollary 17.5.26 , applied in the big class $\{ \theta _\varepsilon \} $ with the reference $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$, there are $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _\varepsilon )$ and finite constants $B_\varepsilon $ such that \[  \begin{gathered} S_\varepsilon =\theta _\varepsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \geq 0, \qquad \langle S_\varepsilon ^ n\rangle =m_\varepsilon \omega \wedge \tau ,\\ V_{\theta _\varepsilon }-B_\varepsilon \leq u_\varepsilon \leq V_{\theta _\varepsilon }. \end{gathered}  \] The constants $B_\varepsilon $ need not be bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $; we only use that $u_\varepsilon $ is locally bounded outside a closed set of measure zero. By lemma 16.13.2 , applied to the big class $\{ \theta _\varepsilon \} $, there is a closed pluripolar set $A_\varepsilon \subset X$ such that $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus A_\varepsilon $; being pluripolar, $A_\varepsilon $ has Lebesgue measure zero in every chart (see the remarks after definition 5.47.2 ). Hence $u_\varepsilon $, which lies between $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }-B_\varepsilon $ and $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$, is locally bounded on $X\setminus A_\varepsilon $, and so are the local potentials of $S_\varepsilon $, which differ from $u_\varepsilon $ by smooth local potentials of $\theta _\varepsilon $ (lemma 5.4.2 ). We may thus apply lemma 17.5.33 to $S_\varepsilon $, with $A_\varepsilon $, $\nu =\omega \wedge \tau $ and $m_\varepsilon $ in place of $A$, $\nu $ and $m$: \[  \left(\int _ X S_\varepsilon \wedge \tau \right) \left(\int _ X\langle S_\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \wedge \omega \right) \geq \frac{m_\varepsilon }{n}\geq \frac mn.  \] We bound the two factors on the left. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau =0$, the first factor equals the cohomological pairing $\int _ X\theta _\varepsilon \wedge \tau =\int _ X\theta \wedge \tau +\varepsilon $. If $n\geq 2$, the form $\theta _\varepsilon +C\omega $ is positive definite, so theorem 13.5.4 gives \[  \int _ X\langle S_\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \wedge \omega \leq \int _ X(\theta +(C+\varepsilon )\omega )^{n-1}\wedge \omega \leq C_0;  \] the last inequality holds because $\theta +(C+1)\omega =(\theta +(C+\varepsilon )\omega )+(1-\varepsilon )\omega $ and products of positive $(1,1)$-forms are positive. If $n=1$, the second factor equals $\int _ X\omega =C_0$. As the first factor is nonnegative, in both cases \[  \left(\int _ X\theta \wedge \tau +\varepsilon \right)C_0\geq \frac mn.  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $\int _ X\theta \wedge \tau \geq m/(nC_0)$. Removing the normalization of $\tau $, we conclude that every smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\tau $ satisfies ( 17.5.30 ) with $\delta =m/(nC_0)>0$. By lemma 17.5.28 , the class $\alpha $ is big. $\square$

title: Corollary 17.5.38
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Corollary 17.5.38 . C78DFCF82004 Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form, and let $f\colon X\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ be a quasi-continuous Borel function. Suppose that the family $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ of definition 16.11.3 is nonempty and uniformly bounded above. Then $u=P_\theta (f)$ satisfies \[  \mu _ u\bigl (X\setminus \{ u=f\} \bigr )=0.  \] If $\{ \theta \} $ is not big, then $\mu _ u=0$. Moreover, if $r\geq 1$ and $u_1,\ldots ,u_ r\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have a rooftop $w=P_\theta (\min _{1\leq j\leq r}u_ j)$ that is not identically $-\infty $, then \[  \mu _ w\leq \sum _{j=1}^ r\mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _{u_ j}.  \] Proof. By proposition 16.11.4 (1), $u\in \mathcal A_\theta (f)$; that is, $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. If $\{ \theta \} $ is not big, then $\mu _ u(X)=0$ by theorem 17.5.37 , since otherwise $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ would be a closed positive current of positive non-pluripolar mass in $\{ \theta \} $. Hence $\mu _ u=0$, and in particular the first assertion holds. If $\{ \theta \} $ is big, the first assertion is theorem 16.13.4 . For the rooftop, the function $\min _ ju_ j$ is quasi-continuous, as a finite minimum of potentials (see the beginning of section 16.11 ), and it is bounded above; its envelope is $w$. Since $w$ is not identically $-\infty $, the family $\mathcal A_\theta (\min _ ju_ j)$ is nonempty, and it is uniformly bounded above because the obstacle is. By the first assertion, $\mu _ w$ is carried by $\{ w=\min _ ju_ j\} \subset \bigcup _ j\{ w=u_ j\} $. The obstacle is upper semicontinuous, so $w\leq u_ j$ everywhere by proposition 16.11.4 (1),(2), and lemma 16.13.1 gives $\mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _{u_ j}$ for every $j$. Summing over $j$ proves the rooftop inequality. $\square$

title: Corollary 17.5.39
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Corollary 17.5.39 . 92C6B04981BA Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form with $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\neq \varnothing $, and let $f$ be a continuous real function on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian. Then \[  \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_\theta (f))^ n\rangle =\mathbf1_{\{ P_\theta (f)=f\} }(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n,  \] where the right side is understood as in theorem 16.20.2 . In particular $\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\theta )^ n\rangle =\mathbf1_{\{ V_\theta =0\} }\theta ^ n$. If $\{ \theta \} $ is not big, both sides of these two identities vanish. Proof. The potential $V_\theta +\min _ Xf$ lies below $f$, so $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ is nonempty, and it is bounded above by $\max _ Xf$. Put $u=P_\theta (f)$. Since $f$ is continuous, $u\leq f$ everywhere by proposition 16.11.4 (1),(2). The scalar case of theorem 16.20.2 , with all $\theta _ j=\theta $, $u_ j=u$ and $f_ j=f$, gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=f\} }\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\mathbf1_{\{ u=f\} }(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n,  \] and corollary 17.5.38 shows that $\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $ is carried by $\{ u=f\} $. This proves the first identity. For $f=0$ the envelope $P_\theta (0)$ is $V_\theta $, by definition 10.3.7 , which gives the second. If $\{ \theta \} $ is not big, the left sides vanish by corollary 17.5.38 , and hence so do the right sides. $\square$

title: 17.5.40 Mixed masses and concavity

text:
We now compare the mixed non-pluripolar mass of $n$ closed positive currents, which may lie in different classes, with their individual masses. The idea is to replace each current by a solution of a Monge–Ampère equation with one and the same smooth right-hand side. Since singularity envelopes preserve mixed masses (proposition 16.21.2 (3)), such a replacement does not change the mixed mass, and for the solutions the pointwise mixed lower bound of proposition 13.5.8 integrates to the desired inequality. The equations can be solved because, by theorem 17.5.37 , every current of positive mass lies in a big class. Proof. All the masses involved are finite by theorem 13.5.4 . If one of the masses $\int _ X\langle T_ i^ nangle $ vanishes, the right side of ( 17.5.42 ) is zero and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise put $m_ i=\int _ X\langle T_ i^ nangle >0$. By theorem 17.5.37 , the class of each $T_ i$ is big. Let $	heta _ i$ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form in the class of $T_ i$ (definition 10.2.17 ). By corollary 10.2.19 we can write $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ with $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ i)$. Set $\phi _ i=P_{	heta _ i}[u_ i]$. By the mass preservation in proposition 16.21.2 (3) and by theorem 16.22.11 , $\phi _ i$ is a model potential of mass one. Let $
u =\omega ^ n/\int _ X\omega ^ n$. This smooth probability measure is non-pluripolar, as noted after definition 17.5.2 . In each big class $\{ 	heta _ i\} $, theorem 17.5.15 gives \[  w_ i\in \mathcal E(X,	heta _ i,\phi _ i),\qquad S_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ i\geq 0,\qquad \langle S_ i^ nangle =
u .  \] By proposition 16.22.14 , $P_{	heta _ i}[w_ i]=P_{	heta _ i}[\phi _ i]=\phi _ i$. Applying the mixed mass preservation of proposition 16.21.2 (3) first to the tuple $(w_1,\ldots ,w_ n)$ and then to the tuple $(u_1,\ldots ,u_ n)$, we obtain \[  \int _ X\langle S_1\wedge \cdots \wedge S_ nangle =\int _ X\left\langle  igwedge _{i=1}^ n (	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ i)ightangle =\int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ nangle .  \] On the other hand, proposition 13.5.8 , with all densities equal to one, gives $\langle S_1\wedge \cdots \wedge S_ nangle \geq 
u $. Hence the common value of these mixed masses is at least $

By multilinearity, \[  \int _ X\langle ((1-t)T+tS)^ nangle =\sum _{k=0}^ n inom nk(1-t)^ kt^{n-k} \int _ X\langle T^ k\wedge S^{n-k}angle .  \] For $1\leq k\leq n-1$, ( 17.5.42 ) with $k$ factors $T$ and $n-k$ factors $S$ gives $\int _ X\langle T^ k\wedge S^{n-k}angle \geq a^{k/n}b^{(n-k)/n}$; the terms with $k=n$ and $k=0$ are $a$ and $b$, also when one of them vanishes. The binomial formula therefore yields \[  \int _ X\langle ((1-t)T+tS)^ nangle \geq  ig ((1-t)a^{1/n}+tb^{1/n} ig )^ n.  \] Taking $n$th roots proves that the function $T\mapsto (\int _ X\langle T^ nangle )^{1/n}$ is concave. title: 17.6 Singularity envelopes at arbitrary mass
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text:
Throughout this section $	heta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ with big class, and we put $V=V_	heta $ and $\Omega =\int _ X\omega ^ n$; volumes of Borel sets are taken with respect to $\omega ^ n$. No model potential is fixed in this section. For a potential $u$ of positive mass, theorem 16.22.11 describes $P_	heta [u]$ as the largest potential $v\leq 0$ with $u\preceq v$ and $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle =\int _ X\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle $, and it shows that $P_	heta [P_	heta [u]]=P_	heta [u]$. Its proof relies on the domination principle, which requires positive mass. For arbitrary $u$ we replace the mass by the collection of all mixed masses of $u$ against $V$; this leads to the singularity ceiling of definition 17.6.4 . We prove that the ceiling equals $P_	heta [u]$ and that $P_	heta [\cdot ]$ is idempotent, without any assumption on the mass of $u$. The main step, proposition 17.6.1 , perturbs $u$ to $w_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )u+\varepsilon V$, which has positive mass $m_\varepsilon $, and shows that $P_	heta [w_\varepsilon ]$ decreases to $P_	heta [u]$. Since $m_\varepsilon $ tends to zero when $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle =0$, the estimates must not deteriorate as the mass degenerates. We therefore use a tail bound normalized by $m_\varepsilon $, which is uniform in $\varepsilon $, and convert it into a volume bound by means of constant-density solutions of Monge–Ampère equations. Proposition 17.6.1 . DC1056C1A4A1 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $u\leq 0$. For $0<\varepsilon <1$ put \[  w_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )u+\varepsilon V, \qquad \phi _\varepsilon =P_	heta [w_\varepsilon ].  \] Then $\phi _\varepsilon $ decreases to $P_	heta [u]$, pointwise and in $L^1(X)$, as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$.
