Outside this set every $\widetilde U\circ \gamma $ equals $U\circ \gamma =U$, so $\breve U=U$ on the open set $\{ \tau <r_1\} \cup \{ \tau >r_2\} $, because $U$ is upper semicontinuous. Therefore $\breve U$ is defined by a subgeodesic whose slices coincide with $G_ t$ for $t<r_1$ and for $t>r_2$; in particular its endpoint potentials are $u_0$ and $u_1$. It is a competitor for the Perron segment between $u_0$ and $u_1$, so $\breve U\leq U$. Consequently $\widetilde U\leq U$, so $v-a\leq U$ on $D$, that is, $v\leq h$. This is maximality in the sense of definition 7.7.6 . $\square$ Theorem 17.8.3 . 678A18D6D406 For $u_0,u_1\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, \[  E_\theta ^\phi (G_ t(u_0,u_1)) =(1-t)E_\theta ^\phi (u_0)+tE_\theta ^\phi (u_1), \qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] Proof. Step 1: setting up a compact extension. Assume first that $u_0,u_1\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, and write $G_ t=G_ t(u_0,u_1)$. Let $A=\{ \mathrm e^{-1}<|z|<1\} \subset \mathbb C\subset \mathbb P^1$, and let $U(x,z)=G_{-\log |z|}(x)$ be the complexification on $X\times A$. Choose a constant $C$ with $\phi -C\leq u_0,u_1\leq \phi +C$. Then $\phi -C$ is a competitor for the rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u_0,u_1)$, so the bounds of theorem 17.7.8 give $\phi -C\leq U\leq \phi +C$. Fix concentric annuli $A_0\Subset A_1\Subset A$. On $Y=X\times \mathbb P^1$, with projections $p_1\colon Y\to X$ and $p_2\colon Y\to \mathbb P^1$, let $\beta =p_2^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, where $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the Fubini–Study form of mass one, and put \[  \Theta =p_1^*\theta +B\beta ,\qquad \Phi =p_1^*\phi ,  \] with a constant $B>0$ chosen below. To glue $U$ to $\Phi $ we use a smooth function $q$ on $\mathbb P^1$ that is small on $A_0$ and large near the boundary of $A_1$. Write $A_0=\{ r_0<|z|<r_0'\} $ and $A_1=\{ r_1<|z|<r_1'\} $, so that $\mathrm e^{-1}<r_1<r_0<r_0'<r_1'<1$, and choose $\varepsilon >0$ with $r_1+\varepsilon <r_0$ and $r_0'<r_1'-\varepsilon $. Let $\chi _0$ be a smooth function on $\mathbb R$ such that $1-\chi _0$ is a smooth cutoff function for $[r_0,r_0']$ in $(r_1+\varepsilon ,r_1'-\varepsilon )$ (lemma 2.5.1 (4)); thus $\chi _0$ takes values in $[0,1]$, vanishes on $[r_0,r_0']$, and equals $1$ outside $(r_1+\varepsilon ,r_1'-\varepsilon )$. The function $q(z)=(2C+4)\chi _0(|z|)-(C+2)$, with $q(\infty )=C+2$, is smooth on $\mathbb P^1$, because $|z|$ is smooth on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $ and $q$ is constant near $0$ and near $\infty $. It equals $-C-2$ on $A_0$ and $C+2$ on a neighborhood of $\partial A_1$. Choose $B$ so large that $B\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq 0$. Then $\Phi +q$ is $\Theta $-psh, and so is $U$ on $X\times A_1$, since $\beta \geq 0$. Define $W=\max \{ U,\Phi +q\} $ on $X\times A_1$ and $W=\Phi +q$ on $Y\setminus (X\times A_1)$. Near $X\times \partial A_1$ we have $\Phi +q=\Phi +C+2>U$ outside the pole set of $\Phi $, on which both functions are $-\infty $; hence $W=\Phi +q$ on a collar inside $X\times A_1$. Thus, near every point of $Y$, $W$ is either the maximum of two $\Theta $-psh functions or equal to $\Phi +q$, and $W$ is $\Theta $-psh on $Y$. Moreover $W-\Phi $ is bounded, and $W=U$ on $X\times A_0$, since there $\Phi +q=\Phi -C-2<U$ outside the pole set of $\Phi $. Step 2: a current on $\mathbb P^1$. Put $T=\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W$ and $R=\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi $, and define the current of order zero on $\mathbb P^1$ \[  H=\frac1{n+1}(p_2)_* \left((W-\Phi )\sum _{j=0}^ n\langle T^ j\wedge R^{n-j}\rangle \right).  \] Let $\chi $ be a smooth function on $\mathbb P^1$. By theorem 17.2.5 on the compact Kähler manifold $Y$, applied to the bounded quasi-psh differences $W-\Phi $ and $\chi \circ p_2$, we may move $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ from $\chi \circ p_2$ to $W-\Phi $. By ( 17.2.1 ), $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(W-\Phi )\wedge \langle T^ j\wedge R^{n-j}\rangle =\langle T^{j+1}\wedge R^{n-j}\rangle -\langle T^ j\wedge R^{n-j+1}\rangle $, and the sum over $j$ telescopes. Therefore 2B3BEF6C25C1 17.8.4 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H=\frac1{n+1}(p_2)_* (\langle T^{n+1}\rangle -\langle R^{n+1}\rangle ). \end{equation} On the other hand, corollary 13.6.1 , with $Z=\mathbb P^1$ and $\gamma =B\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, shows that $H$ is given by the function $z\mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (W(\cdot ,z))$. In particular, on $A_0$, $H$ is the function $z\mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (G_{-\log |z|})$. Step 3: $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H$ vanishes on $A_0$. On $X\times A_0$ put $L=p_1^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U\geq 0$, so that $T=L+B\beta $ there. Locally $T$ has a plurisubharmonic potential which is the sum of a potential of $L$ and a smooth potential of $B\beta $. The product $\langle T^{n+1}\rangle $ is finite by theorem 13.5.4 , so multilinearity (proposition 13.2.6 ), compatibility with smooth factors (proposition 13.4.3 ) and $\beta \wedge \beta =0$ give, on $X\times A_0$, \[  \langle T^{n+1}\rangle =\langle L^{n+1}\rangle +(n+1)B\beta \wedge \langle L^ n\rangle , \qquad \beta \wedge \langle T^ n\rangle =\beta \wedge \langle L^ n\rangle ,  \] with all terms locally finite. Every point of $X\times A_0$ has a coordinate ball $D\subset X\times A_0$ on which $p_1^*\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ for a smooth function $a$ (lemma 6.14.2 ); there $L=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(U+a)$, and lemma 17.8.2 , lemma 17.8.1 give $\langle L^{n+1}\rangle =0$ on $D$. Hence $\langle L^{n+1}\rangle =0$ on $X\times A_0$, so that $\langle T^{n+1}\rangle =(n+1)B\beta \wedge \langle T^ n\rangle $ on $X\times A_0$. Every slice $W(\cdot ,z)$ has bounded difference from $\phi $ and hence mass $m$, so corollary 13.6.1 with weight one gives $(p_2)_*(\beta \wedge \langle T^ n\rangle )=m\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. The current $R$ is treated in the same way. We have $R=p_1^*\theta _\phi +B\beta $, and $\langle (p_1^*\theta _\phi )^{n+1}\rangle =0$. Indeed, the local potentials of $p_1^*\theta _\phi $ do not depend on the variable in $\mathbb P^1$, and so neither do their bounded truncations; each truncation is the decreasing limit of smooth plurisubharmonic functions of the $n$ variables of $X$ (proposition 5.9.2 (2)), whose $(n+1)$st powers of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ vanish, so the bounded products of the truncations vanish by theorem 7.3.7 , and with them the truncated products defining $\langle (p_1^*\theta _\phi )^{n+1}\rangle $. Hence $\langle R^{n+1}\rangle =(n+1)B\beta \wedge \langle R^ n\rangle $, and the same fiber formula, applied to $\Phi $ in place of $W$, gives $(p_2)_*\langle R^{n+1}\rangle =(n+1)Bm\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. Hence the right side of ( 17.8.4 ) vanishes on $A_0$, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H=0$ on $A_0$. Step 4: the energy is affine. The function $\tau \mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (G_\tau )$ is locally Lipschitz on $(0,1)$. Indeed, let $0<\delta <\frac12$. On the common finite locus the convex functions $\tau \mapsto G_\tau (x)-\phi (x)$ take values in $[-C,C]$, so by lemma 17.7.2 (4) their chord slopes on $[\delta ,1-\delta ]$ are bounded by $2C/\delta $. Thus $G_ s-(2C/\delta )|s-\tau |\leq G_\tau \leq G_ s+(2C/\delta )|s-\tau |$ for $s,\tau \in [\delta ,1-\delta ]$ on the common finite locus, hence everywhere, and monotonicity and the shift formula give $|E_\theta ^\phi (G_\tau )-E_\theta ^\phi (G_ s)|\leq (2Cm/\delta )|s-\tau |$. Writing $z=\xi +\mathrm i\eta $, we have $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=(4\pi )^{-1}\Delta f\, \mathrm d\xi \wedge \mathrm d\eta $ for smooth functions $f$, and hence for distributions, so $\Delta H=0$ on $A_0$ by Step 3, and Weyl's lemma (theorem 3.1.11 ) shows that $H$ is represented on $A_0$ by a harmonic function. By Step 2, $H$ is also represented on $A_0$ by the function $z\mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (G_{-\log |z|})$, which is continuous by the Lipschitz bound just proved. Two locally integrable functions defining the same distribution agree almost everywhere (proposition 2.5.3 (4)), and two continuous functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere, so this function is harmonic on $A_0$. A radial harmonic function on an annulus is an affine function of $\log |z|$: if $f(z)=g(\log |z|)$ is smooth, then $g$ is smooth and the Laplacian in polar coordinates gives $\Delta f=|z|^{-2}g''(\log |z|)$, so $g''=0$. Since $A_0$ was arbitrary, $\tau \mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (G_\tau )$ is affine on $(0,1)$. Finally, $|u_1-u_0|\leq 2C$ on the common finite locus, so proposition 17.7.9 (5) gives $|G_\tau -u_0|\leq 2C\tau $ and $|G_\tau -u_1|\leq 2C(1-\tau )$ there. By the Lipschitz bound of proposition 17.3.9 , the energies converge to $E_\theta ^\phi (u_0)$ and $E_\theta ^\phi (u_1)$ as $\tau \to 0$ and $\tau \to 1$. This proves the theorem for $u_0,u_1\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$. Step 5: finite energy. Let $u_0,u_1\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Adding the same constant $c$ to both endpoints adds $c$ to $G_ t$, by proposition 17.7.9 (2), and adds $cm$ to both sides of the asserted identity. We may therefore assume $u_0,u_1\leq \phi $. Put $u_{j,k}=\max \{ u_ j,\phi -k\} $ for $j=0,1$. By proposition 17.7.9 (3), $G_ t(u_{0,k},u_{1,k})\downarrow G_ t(u_0,u_1)$ as $k\to \infty $, and the limit has finite energy by theorem 17.7.8 . The identity holds for $u_{0,k},u_{1,k}$ by the preceding steps, and proposition 17.3.13 , applied at the endpoints and at each interior slice, passes it to the limit. $\square$

title: Lemma 17.8.1
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Lemma 17.8.1 . 950F051CF55A Let $h$ be a maximal plurisubharmonic function on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ d$, $d\geq 1$, in the sense of definition 7.7.6 . Then the top-degree non-pluripolar product $\langle (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ d\rangle $ is locally finite and vanishes. Here $h$ need not be locally bounded. Proof. Fix a ball $B\Subset \Omega $ and a concentric ball $B_1$ with $B\Subset B_1\Subset \Omega $. Put $h_ j=\max \{ h,-j\} $ and let $\widehat h_ j$ be the function supplied by corollary 7.7.5 for $h_ j$ and $B$. These are locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions with $\widehat h_ j\geq h_ j\geq h$, equal to $h_ j$ outside $B$, with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat h_ j)^ d=0$ on $B$; they decrease with $j$, because $\widehat h_ j$ is increasing in $h_ j$. Their decreasing limit $v$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.10.1 , since it dominates $h$, and it equals $h$ outside $B$. Maximality gives $v\leq h$, hence $v=h$. Fix $C>0$ and $\varepsilon >0$, and put \[  z_ j=\max \{ \widehat h_ j,-C\} ,\quad a_ j=\frac{z_ j+C}{z_ j+C+\varepsilon },\quad z=\max \{ h,-C\} ,\quad a=\frac{z+C}{z+C+\varepsilon }.  \] The functions $z_ j$ are plurisubharmonic, locally uniformly bounded (between $-C$ and $\widehat h_1$), and decrease to $z$, so they converge to $z$ locally in capacity on the bounded open set $B_1$ (proposition 7.5.6 ). The weights take values in $[0,1]$, and since $s\mapsto (s+C)/(s+C+\varepsilon )$ is Lipschitz with constant $\varepsilon ^{-1}$ on $[-C,\infty )$, we have $|a_ j-a|\leq \varepsilon ^{-1}|z_ j-z|$, so $a_ j\to a$ locally in capacity on $B_1$. The limit weight $a$ is quasi-continuous on $B_1$, because $z$ is (theorem 7.5.2 ) and $a$ is a continuous function of $z$. On $B$, the weight $a_ j$ vanishes where $\widehat h_ j\leq -C$, and on the plurifine open set $\{ \widehat h_ j>-C\} $ we have $z_ j=\widehat h_ j$; hence plurifine locality of Bedford–Taylor products (theorem 5.47.22 ) gives \[  a_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}z_ j)^ d=a_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat h_ j)^ d=0\quad \text{on }B.  \] The last assertion of theorem 7.5.8 , applied on $B_1$ with $d$ factors $z_ j$ and the weights $a_ j$, gives \[  a_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}z_ j)^ d\longrightarrow a(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}z)^ d\quad \text{weakly on }B_1,  \] so $a(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}z)^ d=0$ on $B$. Since $a>0$ exactly on $\{ h>-C\} $ and $z=\max \{ h,-C\} $, the measure $\mathbf1_{\{ h>-C\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}z)^ d$ vanishes on $B$. Taking $C=k$ for all integers $k$, the truncated products in the definition of $\langle (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ d\rangle $ all vanish on $B$; hence the non-pluripolar product is locally finite and zero on $B$. A cover of $\Omega $ by such balls proves the lemma. $\square$

In particular, on $A_0$, $H$ is the function $z\mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (G_{-\log |z|})$. Step 3: $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H$ vanishes on $A_0$. On $X\times A_0$ put $L=p_1^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U\geq 0$, so that $T=L+B\beta $ there. Locally $T$ has a plurisubharmonic potential which is the sum of a potential of $L$ and a smooth potential of $B\beta $. The product $\langle T^{n+1}\rangle $ is finite by theorem 13.5.4 , so multilinearity (proposition 13.2.6 ), compatibility with smooth factors (proposition 13.4.3 ) and $\beta \wedge \beta =0$ give, on $X\times A_0$, \[  \langle T^{n+1}\rangle =\langle L^{n+1}\rangle +(n+1)B\beta \wedge \langle L^ n\rangle , \qquad \beta \wedge \langle T^ n\rangle =\beta \wedge \langle L^ n\rangle ,  \] with all terms locally finite. Every point of $X\times A_0$ has a coordinate ball $D\subset X\times A_0$ on which $p_1^*\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ for a smooth function $a$ (lemma 6.14.2 ); there $L=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(U+a)$, and lemma 17.8.2 , lemma 17.8.1 give $\langle L^{n+1}\rangle =0$ on $D$. Hence $\langle L^{n+1}\rangle =0$ on $X\times A_0$, so that $\langle T^{n+1}\rangle =(n+1)B\beta \wedge \langle T^ n\rangle $ on $X\times A_0$. Every slice $W(\cdot ,z)$ has bounded difference from $\phi $ and hence mass $m$, so corollary 13.6.1 with weight one gives $(p_2)_*(\beta \wedge \langle T^ n\rangle )=m\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. The current $R$ is treated in the same way. We have $R=p_1^*\theta _\phi +B\beta $, and $\langle (p_1^*\theta _\phi )^{n+1}\rangle =0$. Indeed, the local potentials of $p_1^*\theta _\phi $ do not depend on the variable in $\mathbb P^1$, and so neither do their bounded truncations; each truncation is the decreasing limit of smooth plurisubharmonic functions of the $n$ variables of $X$ (proposition 5.9.2 (2)), whose $(n+1)$st powers of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ vanish, so the bounded products of the truncations vanish by theorem 7.3.7 , and with them the truncated products defining $\langle (p_1^*\theta _\phi )^{n+1}\rangle $. Hence $\langle R^{n+1}\rangle =(n+1)B\beta \wedge \langle R^ n\rangle $, and the same fiber formula, applied to $\Phi $ in place of $W$, gives $(p_2)_*\langle R^{n+1}\rangle =(n+1)Bm\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. Hence the right side of ( 17.8.4 ) vanishes on $A_0$, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H=0$ on $A_0$. Step 4: the energy is affine. The function $\tau \mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (G_\tau )$ is locally Lipschitz on $(0,1)$. Indeed, let $0<\delta <\frac12$. On the common finite locus the convex functions $\tau \mapsto G_\tau (x)-\phi (x)$ take values in $[-C,C]$, so by lemma 17.7.2 (4) their chord slopes on $[\delta ,1-\delta ]$ are bounded by $2C/\delta $. Thus $G_ s-(2C/\delta )|s-\tau |\leq G_\tau \leq G_ s+(2C/\delta )|s-\tau |$ for $s,\tau \in [\delta ,1-\delta ]$ on the common finite locus, hence everywhere, and monotonicity and the shift formula give $|E_\theta ^\phi (G_\tau )-E_\theta ^\phi (G_ s)|\leq (2Cm/\delta )|s-\tau |$. Writing $z=\xi +\mathrm i\eta $, we have $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=(4\pi )^{-1}\Delta f\, \mathrm d\xi \wedge \mathrm d\eta $ for smooth functions $f$, and hence for distributions, so $\Delta H=0$ on $A_0$ by Step 3, and Weyl's lemma (theorem 3.1.11 ) shows that $H$ is represented on $A_0$ by a harmonic function. A radial harmonic function on an annulus is an affine function of $\log |z|$: if $f(z)=g(\log |z|)$ is smooth, then $g$ is smooth and the Laplacian in polar coordinates gives $\Delta f=|z|^{-2}g''(\log |z|)$, so $g''=0$. Since $A_0$ was arbitrary, $\tau \mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (G_\tau )$ is affine on $(0,1)$. Finally, $|u_1-u_0|\leq 2C$ on the common finite locus, so proposition 17.7.9 (5) gives $|G_\tau -u_0|\leq 2C\tau $ and $|G_\tau -u_1|\leq 2C(1-\tau )$ there. By the Lipschitz bound of proposition 17.3.9 , the energies converge to $E_\theta ^\phi (u_0)$ and $E_\theta ^\phi (u_1)$ as $\tau \to 0$ and $\tau \to 1$. This proves the theorem for $u_0,u_1\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$. Step 5: finite energy. Let $u_0,u_1\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Adding the same constant $c$ to both endpoints adds $c$ to $G_ t$, by proposition 17.7.9 (2), and adds $cm$ to both sides of the asserted identity. We may therefore assume $u_0,u_1\leq \phi $. Put $u_{j,k}=\max \{ u_ j,\phi -k\} $ for $j=0,1$. By proposition 17.7.9 (3), $G_ t(u_{0,k},u_{1,k})\downarrow G_ t(u_0,u_1)$ as $k\to \infty $, and the limit has finite energy by theorem 17.7.8 . The identity holds for $u_{0,k},u_{1,k}$ by the preceding steps, and proposition 17.3.13 , applied at the endpoints and at each interior slice, passes it to the limit. $\square$

section: 17.9 Extremal slopes and long Perron segments
text: We close the chapter with two estimates on how a weak geodesic depends on its endpoints. The first, proposition 17.9.1 , shows that the essential supremum of $G_ t(u,v)-u$ is a linear function of $t$, and similarly for the essential infimum; essential suprema and infima are taken with respect to the volume form $\omega ^ n$. The second, proposition 17.9.2 , concerns long segments from $\phi $ to the truncations of a singular potential. Proposition 17.9.1 . 0583958ACA6D Let $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ with $v\preceq u$, and put $C=\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_ X(v-u)$. Then $C$ is finite and \[  \operatorname *{ess\, sup}_ X(G_ t(u,v)-u)=tC,\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] If moreover $u\sim v$ and $c=\operatorname *{ess\, inf}_ X(v-u)$, then $\operatorname *{ess\, inf}_ X(G_ t(u,v)-u)=tc$. These essential extrema equal the corresponding extrema over the common finite locus, and they do not change if a pluripolar set is removed. Proof. The function $v-u$ is finite almost everywhere, and $v\preceq u$ gives $v-u\leq C'$ for some constant $C'$; hence $C$ is finite. The inequality $v\leq u+C$ holds almost everywhere, hence everywhere, as recalled in section 16.11 . Thus the supremum of $v-u$ over the common finite locus is at most $C$; it is at least $C$ because the common finite locus has full measure. The same argument applies to an infimum, and to the complement of any pluripolar set, which still has full measure. The same remarks apply to $G_ t-u$. By theorem 17.7.8 , $G_ t\leq (1-t)u+tv\leq u+tC$. The affine curve $v-C(1-t)$ is a competitor, since $v-C\leq u$, so $G_ t\geq v-(1-t)C$. On the common finite locus $v-u=(v-G_ t)+(G_ t-u)$, and taking essential suprema gives $C\leq (1-t)C+\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_ X(G_ t-u)$. Together with the first bound, this proves the equality for the supremum. Now let $u\sim v$. The affine curve $u+ct$ is a competitor, since $u+c\leq v$, so $G_ t-u\geq ct$. Applying the equality for the supremum to the reversed segment, $G_ t(u,v)=G_{1-t}(v,u)$, gives $\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_ X(G_ t-v)=(1-t)\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_ X(u-v)=-(1-t)c$, that is, $\operatorname *{ess\, inf}_ X(v-G_ t)=(1-t)c$. Taking essential infima in $v-u=(v-G_ t)+(G_ t-u)$ gives $c\geq (1-t)c+\operatorname *{ess\, inf}_ X(G_ t-u)$, which proves the opposite bound. $\square$ We now turn to long segments. Given a potential $u\leq \phi $ and $T>0$, we join $\phi $ to the truncation $\max \{ u,\phi -T\} $ by a weak geodesic parametrized by $[0,T]$. Changing $u$ by at most a constant $C$ changes this segment at time $s$ by at most $Cs/T$, an error that tends to zero as $T\to \infty $. Hence the limits of these segments as $T\to \infty $ depend only on the singularity type of $u$. Proposition 17.9.2 . A6533ED6CC68 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\leq \phi $. For $T>0$ and $0\leq s\leq T$ put \[  u_ T=\max \{ u,\phi -T\} ,\qquad L_ s^{u,T}=G_{s/T}(\phi ,u_ T).  \] For fixed $s\geq 0$, the potentials $L_ s^{u,T}$ increase with $T\geq s$ and satisfy $\phi -s\leq L_ s^{u,T}\leq \phi $. Their regularized limit \[  R_ s^ u=\left(\sup _{T>s}L_ s^{u,T}\right)^*  \] is $\theta $-psh. If $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $v\leq \phi $, and $u\leq v+C$ for a constant $C\geq 0$, then \[  L_ s^{u,T}\leq L_ s^{v,T}+\frac{Cs}{T},\qquad R_ s^ u\leq R_ s^ v.  \] In particular, if $u\sim v$, then $R_ s^ u=R_ s^ v$ for every $s\geq 0$. Consequently, for an arbitrary $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $, the potentials $R_ s^{u-c}$ do not depend on the constant $c$ with $u-c\leq \phi $. Denoting them by $R_ s^ u$, we have $R_ s^ u\leq R_ s^ v$ whenever $u\preceq v\preceq \phi $. Proof. Since $\phi -T\leq u_ T\leq \phi $, the potential $u_ T$ has bounded difference from $\phi $; in particular $u_ T\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. By theorem 17.7.8 , the Perron segment from $\phi $ to $u_ T$ is a weak geodesic. We regard it as a curve on $[0,T]$, so that its slice at time $s$ is $L_ s^{u,T}$. Bounds. For $0\leq s\leq T$ put $q_ s=\max \{ u,\phi -s\} $. After the affine change of parameter, the complexification of the curve $(q_ s)_{0\leq s\leq T}$ is $(x,\zeta )\mapsto \max \{ u(x),\phi (x)-T\operatorname{Re}\zeta \} $. This is the maximum of two $p^*\theta $-psh functions, because $\operatorname{Re}\zeta $ is pluriharmonic, and hence it is $p^*\theta $-psh (proposition 5.9.5 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $p^*\theta $, which exist by lemma 5.4.2 ). Moreover $q_0=\phi $, since $u\leq \phi $, and $q_ T=u_ T$. As $|q_ s-q_ t|\leq |s-t|$ on the finite locus of $\phi $, the curve tends to $\phi $ and $u_ T$ in $L^1$ at the two ends. Thus $(q_ s)$ is a subgeodesic with endpoints $\phi $ and $u_ T$, and by the definition of the Perron segment, $L_ s^{u,T}\geq q_ s\geq \phi -s$. On the other hand, theorem 17.7.8 gives $L_ s^{u,T}\leq (1-s/T)\phi +(s/T)u_ T\leq \phi $. Monotonicity in $T$. Let $T'>T$. The same subgeodesic, now on $[0,T']$, shows that $L_ T^{u,T'}\geq q_ T=u_ T$. By the last assertion of theorem 17.7.8 , the restriction of the segment of length $T'$ to $[0,T]$ is the weak geodesic from $\phi $ to $L_ T^{u,T'}$. Since weak geodesics increase with their endpoints (proposition 17.7.9 (1)), this restriction dominates the weak geodesic from $\phi $ to $u_ T$. Hence $L_ s^{u,T'}\geq L_ s^{u,T}$ for $0\leq s\leq T$. The limit. Fix $s$. The family $(L_ s^{u,T})_{T>s}$ is increasing, bounded above by $\phi $ and bounded below by $\phi -s$. By theorem 5.10.2 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, its regularized supremum $R_ s^ u$ is $\theta $-psh, and $\phi -s\leq R_ s^ u\leq \phi $. Since the family is increasing, the supremum may be taken over $T\geq A$ for any $A>s$ without changing $R_ s^ u$. For $s=0$, all the potentials $L_0^{u,T}$ and $R_0^ u$ equal $\phi $. Comparison. Suppose that $v\leq \phi $ and $u\leq v+C$ with $C\geq 0$. Then \[  u_ T\leq \max \{ v+C,\phi -T\} \leq v_ T+C.  \] By the monotonicity of weak geodesics in their endpoints and the formula for constant shifts of the endpoints, proposition 17.7.9 (1) and (2), we have $G_ t(\phi ,u_ T)\leq G_ t(\phi ,v_ T+C)=G_ t(\phi ,v_ T)+tC$ for $0\leq t\leq 1$. Taking $t=s/T$ gives the bound $L_ s^{u,T}\leq L_ s^{v,T}+Cs/T$. Now fix $s$ and $A>s$. For $T\geq A$ we get $L_ s^{u,T}\leq R_ s^ v+Cs/A$, and taking the regularized supremum over $T\geq A$ gives \[  R_ s^ u\leq R_ s^ v+\frac{Cs}{A}.  \] Letting $A\to \infty $ yields $R_ s^ u\leq R_ s^ v$. If $u\sim v$, then $u\leq v+C$ and $v\leq u+C$ for some $C\geq 0$, and the comparison applied in both directions gives $R_ s^ u=R_ s^ v$. If $u\preceq \phi $ is arbitrary, any two constants $c,c'$ with $u-c\leq \phi $ and $u-c'\leq \phi $ give potentials $u-c\sim u-c'$, so $R_ s^{u-c}=R_ s^{u-c'}$. Finally, if $u\preceq v\preceq \phi $, choose constants $c,c'$ with $u-c\leq \phi $ and $v-c'\leq \phi $. Then $u-c\leq v-c'+C$ for some $C\geq 0$, and the comparison gives $R_ s^ u=R_ s^{u-c}\leq R_ s^{v-c'}=R_ s^ v$. $\square$

title: 21.1 Convex analysis and toric potentials
text: Let the compact torus $(S^1)^ n$ act on $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ by separate rotations of the coordinates, $(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)\mapsto (\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta _1}z_1,\ldots ,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta _ n}z_ n)$. A plurisubharmonic function on $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ that is invariant under this action depends only on the logarithmic radii $x_ j=\log |z_ j|^2$, and we show in corollary 21.2.9 that, as a function of $x\in \mathbb R^ n$, it is precisely a finite convex function. The complex Hessian accounts for the convexity; conversely, the supporting affine functions of a convex function give the submean inequality on complex lines. Questions about the growth and the Monge–Ampère mass of invariant potentials thus become questions about convex functions on a real vector space, and we answer them in terms of the slopes of supporting affine functions. The first part of the chapter develops the convex analysis that this requires. Separation of convex sets produces supporting affine functions, and Legendre duality identifies the closure of the set of slopes of a convex function $F$ with the closure of the set where its conjugate $F^*$ is finite. An upper bound of $F$, up to a constant, by the support function of a convex body $P$ holds exactly when all slopes of $F$ lie in $P$ (proposition 21.4.2 ); this leads to convex analogues of the classes of potentials with bounded growth, full mass and finite energy. The real Monge–Ampère measure of $F$ assigns to a set $E$ the volume of the set of slopes of $F$ at points of $E$, multiplied by $n!$. Since the subgradient map is multivalued, we construct this measure by pushing Lebesgue measure forward under the gradient of $F^*$, which is defined almost everywhere (theorem 21.5.1 ). Its total mass is $n!$ times the volume of the closed set of slopes, and it depends continuously on $F$ for local uniform convergence (theorem 21.5.2 ); when no mass escapes to infinity, the convergence also holds against bounded continuous functions. Finally, counting lattice points in the dilates $kP$ relates these volumes to dimensions of spaces of sections. The second part constructs, from a smooth lattice polytope $P$, a projective toric manifold $X_ P$ with a very ample line bundle $L$. Monomial charts at the vertices of $P$ make its geometry explicit, and we read off from them the correspondence between torus orbits and faces of $P$, the orders of characters along the boundary divisors, and a basis of $H^0(X_ P,L^ k)$ indexed by the lattice points of $kP$ (theorem 21.9.5 ). The potential of Guillemin's reference metric on $L$ is the Legendre transform of an explicit entropy function on $P$, whose gradient has logarithmic singularities along the facets. In the same charts we show that these singularities cancel after the transformation, so that the metric is smooth, with positive definite curvature, also along the boundary orbits (theorem 21.10.1 ). Throughout the chapter, $N_{\mathbb R}$ is a real vector space of finite dimension $n\geq 0$ and $M_{\mathbb R}$ is its dual space, with pairing $\langle p,x\rangle $ for $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$ and $x\in N_{\mathbb R}$; we identify the dual of $M_{\mathbb R}$ with $N_{\mathbb R}$. Whenever an estimate requires a norm, we fix a Euclidean norm on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and give $M_{\mathbb R}$ the dual norm $|p|=\max _{|x|\leq 1}\langle p,x\rangle $, so that $|\langle p,x\rangle |\leq |p||x|$; the open and closed balls $B(x,r)$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}$ of section 2.5 are taken with respect to these norms. When volumes are involved, we also fix a lattice $N\subset N_{\mathbb R}$, that is, the set of integral linear combinations of a basis of $N_{\mathbb R}$, and the dual lattice $M=\{ p\in M_{\mathbb R}:\langle p,x\rangle \in \mathbb Z\text{ for all }x\in N\} $. Lebesgue measure on $M_{\mathbb R}$, written $\mathrm dp$ or $\operatorname {vol}$, and Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dx$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ are normalized so that a fundamental parallelepiped of $M$, respectively of $N$, has volume one; equivalently, they are Lebesgue measure in the coordinates of a lattice basis. (This volume of subsets of $M_{\mathbb R}$ is not to be confused with the volume of a cohomology class in definition 13.9.1 .) In dimension zero both spaces are a point and both measures are the unit point mass. A convex body is a nonempty compact convex set, possibly with empty interior. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in subsection 25.1.20 .

section: 21.2 Closed convex functions and supporting slopes
text:
The conjugate of a finite convex function is in general finite only on a convex subset of the dual space. We therefore allow convex functions to take the value $+\infty $, and we impose lower semicontinuity as the regularity condition that controls their behavior at the boundary of the set where they are finite. The definitions and results of this section and the next are stated on $N_{\mathbb R}$; they apply equally to functions on $M_{\mathbb R}$, with the roles of the two spaces interchanged. Definition 21.2.1 . 4A9F1082E9C2 A function $F\colon N_{\mathbb R}	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is convex if its epigraph \[  \operatorname {epi}F=\{ (x,r)\in N_{\mathbb R}	imes \mathbb R:r\geq F(x)\}   \] is convex. A convex function is proper if it does not take the value $-\infty $ and its effective domain $\operatorname {dom}F=\{ x:F(x)<+\infty \} $ is nonempty; a proper convex function is closed if it is lower semicontinuous. The relative interior $\operatorname {ri}C$ of a convex set $C$ is its interior in its affine span, and $\overline C\setminus \operatorname {ri}C$ is its relative boundary . For a proper convex function $F$ and $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$, the subgradient set of $F$ at $x$ is \[  \partial F(x)=\{ p\in M_{\mathbb R}:F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p,y-xangle 	ext{ for every }y\in N_{\mathbb R}\} .  \] Its elements are the subgradients , or supporting slopes , of $F$ at $x$: they are the slopes of the affine functions that lie below $F$ and agree with $F$ at $x$. We set $\partial F(x)=\varnothing $ for $x
otin \operatorname {dom}F$ and $\partial F(E)= igcup _{x\in E}\partial F(x)$ for $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$. For a function $F$ with values in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$, the epigraph is convex if and only if $F((1-\lambda )x+\lambda y)\leq (1-\lambda )F(x)+\lambda F(y)$ for all $x,y\in N_{\mathbb R}$ and $0<\lambda <1$. Indeed, suppose that the epigraph is convex. If $F(x)$ and $F(y)$ are finite, the inequality expresses that the corresponding combination of $(x,F(x))$ and $(y,F(y))$ lies in $\operatorname {epi}F$; otherwise its right side is $+\infty $. Conversely, for $(x,r),(y,s)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ the inequality gives $F((1-\lambda )x+\lambda y)\leq (1-\lambda )r+\lambda s$. Thus definition 21.2.1 extends the usual notion of a convex function, with the sign convention fixed in the Conventions, to functions with values in $[-\infty ,+\infty ]$. The effective domain of a convex function is convex, being the image of its epigraph under the projection to $N_{\mathbb R}$. A convex set contains every convex combination $\sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ ix_ i$ of its points, where $\lambda _ i\geq 0$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ i=1$: for $q\geq 2$ and $\lambda _ q<1$ this follows by induction on $q$ from $\sum _ i\lambda _ ix_ i=(1-\lambda _ q)\sum _{i<q} rac{\lambda _ i}{1-\lambda _ q}x_ i+\lambda _ qx_ q$. Consequently, the convex hull of a set $S$, that is, the smallest convex set containing $S$, is the set of all convex combinations of points of $S$, since this set is convex and contains $S$. Applied to the epigraph, the same fact gives the finite form of Jensen's inequality \[  F\Bigl (\sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ ix_ i\Bigr )\leq \sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ iF(x_ i)  \] for every convex function $F$ with values in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$ and every convex combination. A function with values in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is lower semicontinuous if and only if its epigraph is closed in $N_{\mathbb R}	imes \mathbb R$. Indeed, if $F$ is lower semicontinuous and $(x_ k,r_ k)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ converge to $(x,r)$, then $F(x)\leq \varliminf _ kF(x_ k)\leq r$. Conversely, if the epigraph is closed and $x_ k	o x$ with $\varliminf _ kF(x_ k)<r<F(x)$ for some real $r$, then $(x_ k,r)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ for infinitely many $k$, and in the limit $(x,r)\in \operatorname {epi}F$, which is impossible. A finite convex function is a real-valued one. A finite convex function $F$ on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$ is identified with the proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$ that equals $F$ on $\Omega $ and $+\infty $ elsewhere; this extension is convex, since its convexity inequality is trivial when $x$ or $y$ lies outside $\Omega $. In particular, $\partial F(x)$ is defined for $x\in \Omega $. The subgradient notation $\partial F$ is unrelated to the boundary $\partial E$ of a set. We shall need a Lipschitz bound on cubes. Let $Q'\subset Q$ be closed cubes with a common center and half-sides $\delta $ and $2\delta $ in affine coordinates on an affine subspace of $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $|\cdot |$ be the Euclidean norm of these coordinates. If a convex function $F$ is finite on $Q$, with oscillation $\omega =\sup _ QF-\inf _ QF<\infty $, then C59E34BB3C43 21.2.2  egin{equation}  |F(z)-F(y)|\leq  rac{\omega }{\delta }|z-y|\qquad (y,z\in Q'). \end{equation} Indeed, for $y
eq z$ in $Q'$ the point $w=z+\delta (z-y)/|z-y|$ lies in $Q$, and $z=(1-\lambda )y+\lambda w$ with $\lambda =|z-y|/(|z-y|+\delta )\leq |z-y|/\delta $. Convexity gives $F(z)-F(y)\leq \lambda (F(w)-F(y))\leq (\omega /\delta )|z-y|$, and we may exchange $y$ and $z$. Lemma 21.2.3 . 34526AA883B2 Let $W$ be a real vector space of finite dimension $n$, and let $C\subset W$ be convex. If $C$ is closed and nonempty and $z\in W\setminus C$, there is a linear functional $\ell $ on $W$ with $\sup _ C\ell <\ell (z)$. If $C$ is closed and $z$ is a boundary point of $C$ in $W$, there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell $ on $W$ with $\sup _ C\ell =\ell (z)$; that is, $C$ has a supporting hyperplane at $z$. Every point of the convex hull of a set $S\subset W$ is a convex combination of affinely independent points of $S$, hence of at most $n+1$ points of $S$. If $C
eq \varnothing $, then $\operatorname {ri}C
eq \varnothing $, and $(1-t)x_0+ty\in \operatorname {ri}C$ whenever $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}C$, $y\in \overline C$ and $0\leq t<1$. Moreover, \[  \overline{\operatorname {ri}C}=\overline C,\qquad \operatorname {ri}C=\operatorname {ri}\overline C,  \] and the relative boundary of $C$ has Lebesgue measure zero in the affine span of $C$. Proof. Fix a Euclidean inner product $y\cdot w$ on $W$, with norm $|y|$. (1) Choose $y_ k\in C$ with $|z-y_ k|	o \inf _{w\in C}|z-w|$. The sequence $(y_ k)$ is bounded, so a subsequence converges to a point $y$, which lies in $C$ because $C$ is closed. Thus $y$ minimizes the distance to $z$ on $C$, and $y
eq z$. For $w\in C$ and $0\leq t\leq 1$ the point $y+t(w-y)$ lies in $C$, so the function $t\mapsto |z-y-t(w-y)|^2$ on $[0,1]$ is minimal at $t=0$, and its derivative there, $-2(z-y)\cdot (w-y)$, is nonnegative. Hence $\ell (w)=(z-y)\cdot w$ satisfies $\ell (w)\leq \ell (y)=\ell (z)-|z-y|^2<\ell (z)$ for every $w\in C$. (2) Since $z$ is a boundary point of $C$, there are points $z_ k
otin C$ with $z_ k	o z$. By (1) there are unit vectors $a_ k$ with $a_ k\cdot w<a_ k\cdot z_ k$ for all $w\in C$. A subsequence of $(a_ k)$ converges to a unit vector $a$, and in the limit $a\cdot w\leq a\cdot z$ for all $w\in C$. As $z\in C$, the functional $\ell (w)=a\cdot w$ has the required property. (3) Let $x=\sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ ix_ i$ with $x_ i\in S$, $\lambda _ i>0$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ i=1$. If the points $x_ i$ are affinely dependent, the vectors $(x_ i,1)\in W	imes \mathbb R$ are linearly dependent, say $\sum _ i\mu _ i(x_ i,1)=0$ with not all $\mu _ i$ zero. Since $\sum _ i\mu _ i=0$, some $\mu _ i$ is positive. Replacing each $\lambda _ i$ by $\lambda _ i-s\mu _ i$, where $s=\min \{ \lambda _ i/\mu _ i:\mu _ i>0\} $, preserves $\sum _ i\lambda _ i$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ ix_ i$, keeps all coefficients nonnegative and makes at least one of them zero. We discard the points with zero coefficient and repeat. Eventually the remaining points are affinely independent, and an affinely independent subset of $W$ has at most $n+1$ elements. (4) Let $A$ be the affine span of $C$, of dimension $k$, and write $B_ A(x,r)$ for the open ball of $A$ with center $x$ and radius $r$. If $k=0$, then $C$ is a point, equal to its relative interior and to its closure, and its relative boundary is empty; so assume $k\geq 1$. A maximal affinely independent subset of $C$ spans an affine subspace containing $C$, hence equal to $A$, so it consists of $k+1$ points $x_0',\ldots ,x_ k'$. Every point $y\in A$ has unique barycentric coordinates $\lambda _ i(y)$, which are affine functions of $y$ with $\sum _ i\lambda _ i(y)=1$ and $y=\sum _ i\lambda _ i(y)x_ i'$. At the barycenter $c$ of the simplex with vertices $x_ i'$ all of them equal $1/(k+1)$, so they are positive on a ball $B_ A(c,r)$; every point of this ball is then a convex combination of the $x_ i'$ and lies in $C$. Hence $c\in \operatorname {ri}C$. Now let $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}C$, choose $r>0$ with $B_ A(x_0,r)\subset C$, and let $y\in \overline C$ and $0\leq t<1$. If $y\in C$, convexity gives $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty,(1-t)r)=(1-t)B_ A(x_0,r)+ty\subset C$. In general choose $y_ k\in C$ with $y_ k	o y$; then $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty_ k,(1-t)r)\subset C$, and for large $k$ this ball contains $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty,(1-t)r/2)$. Thus $(1-t)x_0+ty\in \operatorname {ri}C$. Letting $t\uparrow 1$, we see that every point of $\overline C$ is a limit of points of $\operatorname {ri}C$, so $\overline{\operatorname {ri}C}=\overline C$. Next, $\operatorname {ri}C\subset \operatorname {ri}\overline C$, since both are interiors in the same affine space $A$. Conversely, if $x\in \operatorname {ri}\overline C$, then $y=x+\varepsilon (x-c)$ lies in $\overline C$ for small $\varepsilon >0$, and $x=(1-t)c+ty$ with $t=1/(1+\varepsilon )<1$; hence $x\in \operatorname {ri}C$. For the measure assertion, translate so that $c=0$ and identify $A$ with $\mathbb R^ k$ by a linear isomorphism, which changes Lebesgue measure on $A$ only by a constant factor. Let $Z=\overline C\setminus \operatorname {ri}C$ be the relative boundary; it is closed in $A$, because $\operatorname {ri}C$ is open in $A$, hence Borel, and $0
otin Z$. We claim that the dilates $sZ$, $s>0$, are pairwise disjoint. Indeed, suppose that $sz=s'z'$ with $z,z'\in Z$ and $0<s<s'$. Then $z'=(s/s')z$ is of the form $(1-t)\cdot 0+tz$ with $z\in \overline C$ and $0<t<1$, so $z'\in \operatorname {ri}C$ by what we have just shown, which is impossible. Now fix $R>0$ and put $Z_ R=Z\cap B(0,R)$. The sets $sZ_ R$ with $s$ rational in $[ rac12,1]$ are pairwise disjoint subsets of $B(0,R)$, and each has measure $s^ k|Z_ R|\geq 2^{-k}|Z_ R|$. Since infinitely many of them fit into a set of finite measure, $|Z_ R|=0$. Letting $R	o \infty $, we obtain $|Z|=0$. $\square$ Proposition 21.2.4 . 72D7B299EAB8 Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Then $F$ is locally Lipschitz on $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and $\partial F(x)
eq \varnothing $ for every $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Now let $F$ be a finite convex function on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$. Then the following hold. The sets $\partial F(x)$, $x\in \Omega $, are compact and bounded uniformly for $x$ in each compact subset of $\Omega $, and the graph $\{ (x,p):x\in \Omega ,\  p\in \partial F(x)\} $ is closed in $\Omega 	imes M_{\mathbb R}$. For $x\in \Omega $ and $v\in N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  F'(x;v)=\lim _{t\downarrow 0} rac{F(x+tv)-F(x)}t =\max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle .  \] $F$ is differentiable at $x\in \Omega $ if and only if $\partial F(x)$ is a singleton; in that case $\partial F(x)=\{ 
abla F(x)\} $, where $
abla F(x)\in M_{\mathbb R}$ denotes the differential of $F$ at $x$. $F$ is differentiable almost everywhere on $\Omega $. More precisely, the set $\Omega _ F$ of points of $\Omega $ at which $F$ is differentiable is a Borel set whose complement in $\Omega $ is a null set, and $
abla F\colon \Omega _ F	o M_{\mathbb R}$ is a Borel map. Proof. We first show that $F$ is bounded, hence Lipschitz, near each point of $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and find a subgradient there by separation; then we prove (1)–(4). Let $A$ be the affine span of $\operatorname {dom}F$, of dimension $k$, and let $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Choose affine coordinates on $A$ centered at $x$, with the associated Euclidean norm $|\cdot |$; since all norms on $A$ are equivalent, local Lipschitz continuity does not depend on this choice. For small $\delta >0$ the cube $Q$ of points of $A$ whose coordinates are at most $2\delta $ in absolute value lies in $\operatorname {dom}F$. Every point of $Q$ is a convex combination of the $2^ k$ vertices of $Q$; this follows by induction on $k$, since writing the last coordinate of a point as a convex combination of $\pm 2\delta $ exhibits the point as a convex combination of two points of the opposite faces of $Q$, which are cubes of dimension $k-1$. By the finite form of Jensen's inequality, $F\leq C$ on $Q$, where $C$ is the largest value of $F$ at a vertex. If $y\in Q$, then also $2x-y\in Q$, and $F(x)\leq  rac12(F(y)+F(2x-y))$ gives $F(y)\geq 2F(x)-C$. Thus $F$ is bounded on $Q$, and by ( 21.2.2 ) it is Lipschitz on the cube of half-side $\delta $ centered at $x$. Next we construct a subgradient at $x$. Since $\operatorname {dom}F\subset A$, the epigraph of $F$ lies in $A	imes \mathbb R$; let $E$ be its closure, a closed convex subset of $A	imes \mathbb R$. Because $F$ is continuous at $x$ as a function on $A$, the points $(x,F(x)-\varepsilon )$, $\varepsilon >0$, do not belong to $E$, so $(x,F(x))$ is a boundary point of $E$ in $A	imes \mathbb R$. By lemma 21.2.3 (2), applied in $A	imes \mathbb R$ with origin $(x,F(x))$, there are a linear functional $a$ on the linear subspace $A_0=\{ y-y':y,y'\in A\} $ parallel to $A$ and a real number $c$, not both zero, such that \[  \langle a,y-xangle +c\, (s-F(x))\geq 0\qquad 	ext{for all }(y,s)\in E.  \] Letting $s	o +\infty $ shows that $c\geq 0$. If $c=0$, then $a
eq 0$ and $\langle a,y-xangle \geq 0$ for all $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$; but $\operatorname {dom}F$ contains a ball of $A$ about $x$, and this ball contains points $y$ with $\langle a,y-xangle <0$. Hence $c>0$, and taking $s=F(y)$ we obtain $F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p_ A,y-xangle $ for $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$, where $p_ A=-a/c$. Extend $p_ A$ to a linear functional $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$. The inequality $F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p,y-xangle $ holds for $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$, because then $y-x\in A_0$, and also for $y
otin \operatorname {dom}F$, where $F(y)=+\infty $. Thus $p\in \partial F(x)$. From now on let $F$ be a finite convex function on the open convex set $\Omega $, so that $A=N_{\mathbb R}$ and $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)=\Omega $. Fix a basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ of $N_{\mathbb R}$, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the set $K_ r=\{ y+\sum _ is_ ie_ i:y\in K,\  |s_ i|\leq r\} $ lies in $\Omega $. If $x\in K$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at the points $x\pm re_ i$, gives $\pm r\langle p,e_ iangle \leq F(x\pm re_ i)-F(x)$, hence $|\langle p,e_ iangle |\leq 2r^{-1}\max _{K_ r}|F|$, where $F$ is bounded on the compact set $K_ r$ because it is continuous. This is the uniform bound in (1). If $x_ k	o x$ in $\Omega $, $p_ k\in \partial F(x_ k)$ and $p_ k	o p$, then letting $k	o \infty $ in $F(y)\geq F(x_ k)+\langle p_ k,y-x_ kangle $ and using that $F$ is continuous at $x$, we get $p\in \partial F(x)$. Thus the graph is closed, and each $\partial F(x)$ is closed and bounded, hence compact. For (2) and (4) we use the following slope inequalities for a convex function $\phi $ on an interval: if $s_1<s_2<s_3$, then 7BAA42793D50 21.2.5  egin{equation}   rac{\phi (s_2)-\phi (s_1)}{s_2-s_1}\leq  rac{\phi (s_3)-\phi (s_1)}{s_3-s_1}\leq  rac{\phi (s_3)-\phi (s_2)}{s_3-s_2}. \end{equation} Indeed, $s_2=\lambda s_1+(1-\lambda )s_3$ with $\lambda =(s_3-s_2)/(s_3-s_1)\in (0,1)$, and the convexity inequality $\phi (s_2)\leq \lambda \phi (s_1)+(1-\lambda )\phi (s_3)$ is equivalent to each of the two inequalities. Now fix $x$ and $v$, and apply ( 21.2.5 ) to $\phi (t)=F(x+tv)$, which is convex on the open interval of those $t$ with $x+tv\in \Omega $: with $s_1=0$ it shows that the difference quotient in (2) is nondecreasing in $t>0$, so its limit as $t\downarrow 0$ exists in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$. Each $p\in \partial F(x)$ gives $F(x+tv)-F(x)\geq t\langle p,vangle $; hence $F'(x;v)\geq \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle $, the maximum being attained by compactness. Conversely, choose $p_ t\in \partial F(x+tv)$. The subgradient inequality at $x+tv$, evaluated at $x$, gives $F(x+tv)-F(x)\leq t\langle p_ t,vangle $. By (1) the vectors $p_ t$ stay bounded as $t\downarrow 0$, and each of their cluster points lies in $\partial F(x)$. Therefore $F'(x;v)\leq \varlimsup _{t\downarrow 0}\langle p_ t,vangle \leq \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle $. For (3), suppose that $\partial F(x)=\{ p\} $, and choose $p_ h\in \partial F(x+h)$. By (1), every cluster point of $p_ h$ as $h	o 0$ lies in $\partial F(x)$, so $p_ h	o p$. The subgradient inequalities at $x$ and at $x+h$ give \[  0\leq F(x+h)-F(x)-\langle p,hangle \leq \langle p_ h-p,hangle =o(|h|),  \] so $F$ is differentiable at $x$, with $
abla F(x)=p$. Conversely, if $F$ is differentiable at $x$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, dividing $F(x+tv)-F(x)\geq t\langle p,vangle $ by $t$ and letting $t\downarrow 0$ gives $\langle

abla F(x)\} $. For (4), fix $i$, and write $D_ i^+F(x)=F'(x;e_ i)$ and $D_ i^-F(x)=-F'(x;-e_ i)$ for the one-sided partial derivatives; they are finite by (2). Let $\phi $ be the restriction of $F$ to the intersection of $\Omega $ with a line parallel to $e_ i$, parametrized as $\phi (s)=F(y+se_ i)$ on an open interval. By ( 21.2.5 ), $\phi $ has one-sided derivatives $\phi '_\pm $ at every point, $\phi '_-(s)\leq \phi '_+(s)$, and $\phi '_+(s)\leq \phi '_-(s')$ whenever $s<s'$, because both are bounded by the slope of the chord from $s$ to $s'$. Hence the open intervals $(\phi '_-(s),\phi '_+(s))$ are pairwise disjoint; each nonempty one contains a rational number, so only countably many of them are nonempty, and $\phi '_-=\phi '_+$ outside a countable set. Next, $D_ i^+F$ is the pointwise limit on $\Omega $ of the Borel functions equal to $k(F(x+e_ i/k)-F(x))$ where $x+e_ i/k\in \Omega $ and to $0$ elsewhere, so it is a Borel function, and similarly for $D_ i^-F$. Thus the set $Z_ i\subset \Omega $ where $D_ i^+F
eq D_ i^-F$ is a Borel set that meets each line parallel to $e_ i$ in a countable set, and Fubini's theorem, in the coordinates of the basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$, shows that $Z_ i$ is a null set. At a point $x
otin Z_1\cup \cdots \cup Z_ n$, (2) gives \[  \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,e_ iangle =D_ i^+F(x)=D_ i^-F(x)=\min _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,e_ iangle  \] for every $i$, so all subgradients at $x$ coincide, and $F$ is differentiable at $x$ by (3). Conversely, if $F$ is differentiable at $x$, then $D_ i^+F(x)=D_ i^-F(x)=\langle 
abla F(x),e_ iangle $ for every $i$. Therefore $\Omega _ F=\Omega \setminus (Z_1\cup \cdots \cup Z_ n)$ is a Borel set with null complement, and the coordinates $\langle 
abla F,e_ iangle =D_ i^+F$ of $
abla F$ are Borel functions on $\Omega _ F$. $\square$ Proposition 21.2.6 . EAC7AAEC7279 Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\overline F$ be its lower semicontinuous regularization, that is, the largest lower semicontinuous function on $N_{\mathbb R}$ that is at most $F$. Then $\overline F$ is a closed proper convex function, and $\overline F=F$ on $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. A closed proper convex function is determined by its values on the relative interior of its effective domain. Finally, if a sequence of finite convex functions on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$ converges to a finite limit at each point of a dense subset of $\Omega $, then it converges locally uniformly on $\Omega $ to a finite convex function. Proof. By proposition 21.2.4 , $F$ has a subgradient $p$ at some point $x_1\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, so $F$ lies above the affine function $\ell (y)=F(x_1)+\langle p,y-x_1angle $. The closure $E$ of $\operatorname {epi}F$ is convex, and it lies above the graph of $\ell $ because $\ell $ is continuous. Hence, for each $x$, the set $\{ r:(x,r)\in E\} $ is closed and bounded below by $\ell (x)$, and with each of its points $r$ it contains $[r,+\infty )$, because $\operatorname {epi}F$ has this property. So this set is either empty or a closed half-line $[\widetilde F(x),+\infty )$ with $\widetilde F(x)\geq \ell (x)>-\infty $. Setting $\widetilde F(x)=+\infty $ in the first case, we see that $E$ is the epigraph of a convex function $\widetilde F$. It is lower semicontinuous because its epigraph is closed, and $\widetilde F\leq F$, so $\operatorname {dom}\widetilde F\supset \operatorname {dom}F
eq \varnothing $. If $G\leq F$ is lower semicontinuous, then $\operatorname {epi}G$ is closed and contains $\operatorname {epi}F$, hence also $E$, and so $G\leq \widetilde F$. Thus $\widetilde F=\overline F$, which is therefore closed, proper and convex. Let $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. If $(y_ k,r_ k)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ converge to $(x,r)$, then $y_ k$ lies in the affine span of $\operatorname {dom}F$, on which $F$ is continuous at $x$; hence $r\geq \lim _ kF(y_ k)=F(x)$. This shows $\overline F(x)\geq F(x)$, and so $\overline F(x)=F(x)$. Now let $F$ be closed, fix $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and let $x\in \overline{\operatorname {dom}F}$. By lemma 21.2.3 (4), the points $(1-t)x_0+tx$ with $0\leq t<1$ lie in $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, so the convex function $\phi (t)=F((1-t)x_0+tx)$ is finite on $[0,1)$. Convexity gives $\phi (t)\leq (1-t)\phi (0)+t\phi (1)$, hence $\varlimsup _{t\uparrow 1}\phi (t)\leq \phi (1)$, while lower semicontinuity gives $\varliminf _{t\uparrow 1}\phi (t)\geq \phi (1)$. Therefore \[  F(x)=\lim _{t\uparrow 1}F((1-t)x_0+tx) \qquad (x\in \overline{\operatorname {dom}F}),  \] also when $F(x)=+\infty $. Since $F=+\infty $ outside $\overline{\operatorname {dom}F}$, which is the closure of $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, the function $F$ is determined by its restriction to $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Finally, let $(F_ j)$ be a sequence of finite convex functions on $\Omega $ converging to a finite limit at every point of a dense set $S\subset \Omega $. We show that near each point of $\Omega $ the functions $F_ j$ are uniformly bounded, hence uniformly Lipschitz, so that convergence on $S$ propagates to uniform convergence. Fix a basis of $N_{\mathbb R}$, write $Q(y,ho )$ for the closed cube of half-side $ho $ centered at $y$ in the corresponding coordinates, and let $x\in \Omega $ and $ho >0$ with $Q(x,2ho )\subset \Omega $. For each vertex $y$ of $Q(x,ho )$ choose a point of $S$ whose coordinates differ from those of $y$ by less than $ho /2$, and let $S_0\subset S\cap Q(x,2ho )$ be the finite set of these points. Its convex hull $H$ is compact as the image of a simplex under a linear map, and it contains $Q(x,ho /2)$. Indeed, let $\ell $ be a nonzero linear functional, $\ell (z)=\sum _ ia_ iz_ i$ in the chosen coordinates, and put $\| a\| =\sum _ i|a_ i|$. At a vertex $y^*$ of $Q(x,ho )$ where $\ell $ is maximal, $\ell (y^*)=\ell (x)+ho \| a\| $, and the point $s\in S_0$ chosen for $y^*$ satisfies $\ell (s)>\ell (y^*)- racho 2\| a\| =\max _{Q(x,ho /2)}\ell $. Hence no point of $Q(x,ho /2)$ can be separated from $H$ as in lemma 21.2.3 (1). The sequences $(F_ j(s))_ j$, $s\in S_0$, converge, so they are bounded above by some $C$, and the finite form of Jensen's inequality gives $F_ j\leq C$ on $H$ for all $j$. Choose $s_0\in S\cap Q(x,ho /8)$. Then $Q(s_0,3ho /8)\subset Q(x,ho /2)$, and for $y\in Q(s_0,3ho /8)$ the reflected point $2s_0-y$ lies in the same cube, so that $F_ j(y)\geq 2F_ j(s_0)-C\geq 2\inf _ kF_ k(s_0)-C$. Hence $|F_ j|\leq B$ on $Q(x,ho /4)\subset Q(s_0,3ho /8)$ for all $j$, with a constant $B$. By ( 21.2.2 ), applied with $\delta =ho /8$ and $\omega \leq 2B$, the $F_ j$ are Lipschitz on $Q(x,ho /8)$ with the common constant $L=16B/ho $, for the Euclidean norm $|\cdot |$ of the chosen coordinates. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose a finite set $S_\varepsilon \subset S\cap Q(x,ho /8)$ such that every point of $Q(x,ho /8)$ lies within distance $\varepsilon /L$ of $S_\varepsilon $. To this end, cover the compact cube $Q(x,ho /8)$ by finitely many balls of radius $\varepsilon /(2L)$ centered in the cube, and pick a point of the dense set $S$ in the intersection of each ball with the interior of the cube, a nonempty open set. For all sufficiently large $j,k$ we have $|F_ j-F_ k|<\varepsilon $ on $S_\varepsilon $, hence $|F_ j-F_ k|<3\varepsilon $ on $Q(x,ho /8)$. Thus $(F_ j)$ is uniformly Cauchy on $Q(x,ho /8)$. Finitely many such cubes cover any given compact subset of $\Omega $, so $(F_ j)$ converges locally uniformly to a finite continuous function, which is convex because the convexity inequalities pass to pointwise limits. $\square$

title: Definition 21.2.1
section: 21.2 Closed convex functions and supporting slopes
text: Definition 21.2.1 . 4A9F1082E9C2 A function $F\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is convex if its epigraph \[  \operatorname {epi}F=\{ (x,r)\in N_{\mathbb R}\times \mathbb R:r\geq F(x)\}   \] is convex. A convex function is proper if it does not take the value $-\infty $ and its effective domain $\operatorname {dom}F=\{ x:F(x)<+\infty \} $ is nonempty; a proper convex function is closed if it is lower semicontinuous. The relative interior $\operatorname {ri}C$ of a convex set $C$ is its interior in its affine span, and $\overline C\setminus \operatorname {ri}C$ is its relative boundary . For a proper convex function $F$ and $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$, the subgradient set of $F$ at $x$ is \[  \partial F(x)=\{ p\in M_{\mathbb R}:F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle \text{ for every }y\in N_{\mathbb R}\} .  \] Its elements are the subgradients , or supporting slopes , of $F$ at $x$: they are the slopes of the affine functions that lie below $F$ and agree with $F$ at $x$. We set $\partial F(x)=\varnothing $ for $x\notin \operatorname {dom}F$ and $\partial F(E)=\bigcup _{x\in E}\partial F(x)$ for $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$.

Lemma 21.2.3 . 34526AA883B2 Let $W$ be a real vector space of finite dimension $n$, and let $C\subset W$ be convex. If $C$ is closed and nonempty and $z\in W\setminus C$, there is a linear functional $\ell $ on $W$ with $\sup _ C\ell <\ell (z)$. If $C$ is closed and $z$ is a boundary point of $C$ in $W$, there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell $ on $W$ with $\sup _ C\ell =\ell (z)$; that is, $C$ has a supporting hyperplane at $z$. Every point of the convex hull of a set $S\subset W$ is a convex combination of affinely independent points of $S$, hence of at most $n+1$ points of $S$. If $C
eq \varnothing $, then $\operatorname {ri}C
eq \varnothing $, and $(1-t)x_0+ty\in \operatorname {ri}C$ whenever $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}C$, $y\in \overline C$ and $0\leq t<1$. Moreover, \[  \overline{\operatorname {ri}C}=\overline C,\qquad \operatorname {ri}C=\operatorname {ri}\overline C,  \] and the relative boundary of $C$ has Lebesgue measure zero in the affine span of $C$. The sequence $(y_ k)$ is bounded, so a subsequence converges to a point $y$, which lies in $C$ because $C$ is closed. Thus $y$ minimizes the distance to $z$ on $C$, and $y

For $w\in C$ and $0\leq t\leq 1$ the point $y+t(w-y)$ lies in $C$, so the function $t\mapsto |z-y-t(w-y)|^2$ on $[0,1]$ is minimal at $t=0$, and its derivative there, $-2(z-y)\cdot (w-y)$, is nonnegative. Hence $\ell (w)=(z-y)\cdot w$ satisfies $\ell (w)\leq \ell (y)=\ell (z)-|z-y|^2<\ell (z)$ for every $w\in C$. (2) Since $z$ is a boundary point of $C$, there are points $z_ k
otin C$ with $z_ k	o z$. By (1) there are unit vectors $a_ k$ with $a_ k\cdot w<a_ k\cdot z_ k$ for all $w\in C$. A subsequence of $(a_ k)$ converges to a unit vector $a$, and in the limit $a\cdot w\leq a\cdot z$ for all $w\in C$. As $z\in C$, the functional $\ell (w)=a\cdot w$ has the required property. (3) Let $x=\sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ ix_ i$ with $x_ i\in S$, $\lambda _ i>0$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ i=1$. If the points $x_ i$ are affinely dependent, the vectors $(x_ i,1)\in W	imes \mathbb R$ are linearly dependent, say $\sum _ i\mu _ i(x_ i,1)=0$ with not all $\mu _ i$ zero. Since $\sum _ i\mu _ i=0$, some $\mu _ i$ is positive. Replacing each $\lambda _ i$ by $\lambda _ i-s\mu _ i$, where $s=\min \{ \lambda _ i/\mu _ i:\mu _ i>0\} $, preserves $\sum _ i\lambda _ i$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ ix_ i$, keeps all coefficients nonnegative and makes at least one of them zero. We discard the points with zero coefficient and repeat. Eventually the remaining points are affinely independent, and an affinely independent subset of $W$ has at most $n+1$ elements. (4) Let $A$ be the affine span of $C$, of dimension $k$, and write $B_ A(x,r)$ for the open ball of $A$ with center $x$ and radius $r$. If $k=0$, then $C$ is a point, equal to its relative interior and to its closure, and its relative boundary is empty; so assume $k\geq 1$. A maximal affinely independent subset of $C$ spans an affine subspace containing $C$, hence equal to $A$, so it consists of $k+1$ points $x_0',\ldots ,x_ k'$. Every point $y\in A$ has unique barycentric coordinates $\lambda _ i(y)$, which are affine functions of $y$ with $\sum _ i\lambda _ i(y)=1$ and $y=\sum _ i\lambda _ i(y)x_ i'$. At the barycenter $c$ of the simplex with vertices $x_ i'$ all of them equal $1/(k+1)$, so they are positive on a ball $B_ A(c,r)$; every point of this ball is then a convex combination of the $x_ i'$ and lies in $C$. If $y\in C$, convexity gives $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty,(1-t)r)=(1-t)B_ A(x_0,r)+ty\subset C$. Letting $t\uparrow 1$, we see that every point of $\overline C$ is a limit of points of $\operatorname {ri}C$, so $\overline{\operatorname {ri}C}=\overline C$. Next, $\operatorname {ri}C\subset \operatorname {ri}\overline C$, since both are interiors in the same affine space $A$. Conversely, if $x\in \operatorname {ri}\overline C$, then $y=x+\varepsilon (x-c)$ lies in $\overline C$ for small $\varepsilon >0$, and $x=(1-t)c+ty$ with $t=1/(1+\varepsilon )<1$; hence $x\in \operatorname {ri}C$. Let $Z=\overline C\setminus \operatorname {ri}C$ be the relative boundary; it is closed in $A$, because $\operatorname {ri}C$ is open in $A$, hence Borel, and $0
otin Z$. We claim that the dilates $sZ$, $s>0$, are pairwise disjoint. Indeed, suppose that $sz=s'z'$ with $z,z'\in Z$ and $0<s<s'$. Then $z'=(s/s')z$ is of the form $(1-t)\cdot 0+tz$ with $z\in \overline C$ and $0<t<1$, so $z'\in \operatorname {ri}C$ by what we have just shown, which is impossible. Now fix $R>0$ and put $Z_ R=Z\cap B(0,R)$. The sets $sZ_ R$ with $s$ rational in $[ rac12,1]$ are pairwise disjoint subsets of $B(0,R)$, and each has measure $s^ k|Z_ R|\geq 2^{-k}|Z_ R|$. Since infinitely many of them fit into a set of finite measure, $|Z_ R|=0$. Letting $R	o \infty $, we obtain $|Z|=0$. $\square$

section: 21.2 Closed convex functions and supporting slopes
text:
Proposition 21.2.4 . 72D7B299EAB8 Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Then $F$ is locally Lipschitz on $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and $\partial F(x)
eq \varnothing $ for every $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Now let $F$ be a finite convex function on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$. Then the following hold. The sets $\partial F(x)$, $x\in \Omega $, are compact and bounded uniformly for $x$ in each compact subset of $\Omega $, and the graph $\{ (x,p):x\in \Omega ,\  p\in \partial F(x)\} $ is closed in $\Omega 	imes M_{\mathbb R}$. For $x\in \Omega $ and $v\in N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  F'(x;v)=\lim _{t\downarrow 0} rac{F(x+tv)-F(x)}t =\max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle .  \] $F$ is differentiable at $x\in \Omega $ if and only if $\partial F(x)$ is a singleton; in that case $\partial F(x)=\{ 
abla F(x)\} $, where $
abla F(x)\in M_{\mathbb R}$ denotes the differential of $F$ at $x$. $F$ is differentiable almost everywhere on $\Omega $. More precisely, the set $\Omega _ F$ of points of $\Omega $ at which $F$ is differentiable is a Borel set whose complement in $\Omega $ is a null set, and $
abla F\colon \Omega _ F	o M_{\mathbb R}$ is a Borel map. Proof. We first show that $F$ is bounded, hence Lipschitz, near each point of $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and find a subgradient there by separation; then we prove (1)–(4). Let $A$ be the affine span of $\operatorname {dom}F$, of dimension $k$, and let $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Choose affine coordinates on $A$ centered at $x$, with the associated Euclidean norm $|\cdot |$; since all norms on $A$ are equivalent, local Lipschitz continuity does not depend on this choice. For small $\delta >0$ the cube $Q$ of points of $A$ whose coordinates are at most $2\delta $ in absolute value lies in $\operatorname {dom}F$. Every point of $Q$ is a convex combination of the $2^ k$ vertices of $Q$; this follows by induction on $k$, since writing the last coordinate of a point as a convex combination of $\pm 2\delta $ exhibits the point as a convex combination of two points of the opposite faces of $Q$, which are cubes of dimension $k-1$. By the finite form of Jensen's inequality, $F\leq C$ on $Q$, where $C$ is the largest value of $F$ at a vertex. If $y\in Q$, then also $2x-y\in Q$, and $F(x)\leq  rac12(F(y)+F(2x-y))$ gives $F(y)\geq 2F(x)-C$. Thus $F$ is bounded on $Q$, and by ( 21.2.2 ) it is Lipschitz on the cube of half-side $\delta $ centered at $x$. Next we construct a subgradient at $x$. Since $\operatorname {dom}F\subset A$, the epigraph of $F$ lies in $A	imes \mathbb R$; let $E$ be its closure, a closed convex subset of $A	imes \mathbb R$. Because $F$ is continuous at $x$ as a function on $A$, the points $(x,F(x)-\varepsilon )$, $\varepsilon >0$, do not belong to $E$, so $(x,F(x))$ is a boundary point of $E$ in $A	imes \mathbb R$. By lemma 21.2.3 (2), applied in $A	imes \mathbb R$ with origin $(x,F(x))$, there are a linear functional $a$ on the linear subspace $A_0=\{ y-y':y,y'\in A\} $ parallel to $A$ and a real number $c$, not both zero, such that \[  \langle a,y-xangle +c\, (s-F(x))\geq 0\qquad 	ext{for all }(y,s)\in E.  \] Letting $s	o +\infty $ shows that $c\geq 0$. If $c=0$, then $a
eq 0$ and $\langle a,y-xangle \geq 0$ for all $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$; but $\operatorname {dom}F$ contains a ball of $A$ about $x$, and this ball contains points $y$ with $\langle a,y-xangle <0$. Hence $c>0$, and taking $s=F(y)$ we obtain $F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p_ A,y-xangle $ for $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$, where $p_ A=-a/c$. Extend $p_ A$ to a linear functional $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$. The inequality $F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p,y-xangle $ holds for $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$, because then $y-x\in A_0$, and also for $y
otin \operatorname {dom}F$, where $F(y)=+\infty $. Thus $p\in \partial F(x)$. From now on let $F$ be a finite convex function on the open convex set $\Omega $, so that $A=N_{\mathbb R}$ and $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)=\Omega $. Fix a basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ of $N_{\mathbb R}$, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the set $K_ r=\{ y+\sum _ is_ ie_ i:y\in K,\  |s_ i|\leq r\} $ lies in $\Omega $. If $x\in K$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at the points $x\pm re_ i$, gives $\pm r\langle p,e_ iangle \leq F(x\pm re_ i)-F(x)$, hence $|\langle p,e_ iangle |\leq 2r^{-1}\max _{K_ r}|F|$, where $F$ is bounded on the compact set $K_ r$ because it is continuous. This is the uniform bound in (1). If $x_ k	o x$ in $\Omega $, $p_ k\in \partial F(x_ k)$ and $p_ k	o p$, then letting $k	o \infty $ in $F(y)\geq F(x_ k)+\langle p_ k,y-x_ kangle $ and using that $F$ is continuous at $x$, we get $p\in \partial F(x)$. Thus the graph is closed, and each $\partial F(x)$ is closed and bounded, hence compact. For (2) and (4) we use the following slope inequalities for a convex function $\phi $ on an interval: if $s_1<s_2<s_3$, then 7BAA42793D50 21.2.5  egin{equation}   rac{\phi (s_2)-\phi (s_1)}{s_2-s_1}\leq  rac{\phi (s_3)-\phi (s_1)}{s_3-s_1}\leq  rac{\phi (s_3)-\phi (s_2)}{s_3-s_2}. \end{equation} Indeed, $s_2=\lambda s_1+(1-\lambda )s_3$ with $\lambda =(s_3-s_2)/(s_3-s_1)\in (0,1)$, and the convexity inequality $\phi (s_2)\leq \lambda \phi (s_1)+(1-\lambda )\phi (s_3)$ is equivalent to each of the two inequalities. Now fix $x$ and $v$, and apply ( 21.2.5 ) to $\phi (t)=F(x+tv)$, which is convex on the open interval of those $t$ with $x+tv\in \Omega $: with $s_1=0$ it shows that the difference quotient in (2) is nondecreasing in $t>0$, so its limit as $t\downarrow 0$ exists in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$. Each $p\in \partial F(x)$ gives $F(x+tv)-F(x)\geq t\langle p,vangle $; hence $F'(x;v)\geq \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle $, the maximum being attained by compactness. Conversely, choose $p_ t\in \partial F(x+tv)$. The subgradient inequality at $x+tv$, evaluated at $x$, gives $F(x+tv)-F(x)\leq t\langle p_ t,vangle $. By (1) the vectors $p_ t$ stay bounded as $t\downarrow 0$, and each of their cluster points lies in $\partial F(x)$. Therefore $F'(x;v)\leq \varlimsup _{t\downarrow 0}\langle p_ t,vangle \leq \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle $. For (3), suppose that $\partial F(x)=\{ p\} $, and choose $p_ h\in \partial F(x+h)$. By (1), every cluster point of $p_ h$ as $h	o 0$ lies in $\partial F(x)$, so $p_ h	o p$. The subgradient inequalities at $x$ and at $x+h$ give \[  0\leq F(x+h)-F(x)-\langle p,hangle \leq \langle p_ h-p,hangle =o(|h|),  \] so $F$ is differentiable at $x$, with $
abla F(x)=p$. Conversely, if $F$ is differentiable at $x$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, dividing $F(x+tv)-F(x)\geq t\langle p,vangle $ by $t$ and letting $t\downarrow 0$ gives $\langle 
abla F(x),vangle \geq \langle p,vangle $ for every $v$, hence $p=
abla F(x)$. As $\partial F(x)
eq \varnothing $, it equals $\{ 
abla F(x)\} $. For (4), fix $i$, and write $D_ i^+F(x)=F'(x;e_ i)$ and $D_ i^-F(x)=-F'(x;-e_ i)$ for the one-sided partial derivatives; they are finite by (2). Let $\phi $ be the restriction of $F$ to the intersection of $\Omega $ with a line parallel to $e_ i$, parametrized as $\phi (s)=F(y+se_ i)$ on an open interval. By ( 21.2.5 ), $\phi $ has one-sided derivatives $\phi '_\pm $ at every point, $\phi '_-(s)\leq \phi '_+(s)$, and $\phi '_+(s)\leq \phi '_-(s')$ whenever $s<s'$, because both are bounded by the slope of the chord from $s$ to $s'$. Hence the open intervals $(\phi '_-(s),\phi '_+(s))$ are pairwise disjoint; each nonempty one contains a rational number, so only countably many of them are nonempty, and $\phi '_-=\phi '_+$ outside a countable set. Next, $D_ i^+F$ is the pointwise limit on $\Omega $ of the Borel functions equal to $k(F(x+e_ i/k)-F(x))$ where $x+e_ i/k\in \Omega $ and to $0$ elsewhere, so it is a Borel function, and similarly for $D_ i^-F$. Thus the set $Z_ i\subset \Omega $ where $D_ i^+F
eq D_ i^-F$ is a Borel set that meets each line parallel to $e_ i$ in a countable set, and Fubini's theorem, in the coordinates of the basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$, shows that $Z_ i$ is a null set. At a point $x
otin Z_1\cup \cdots \cup Z_ n$, (2) gives \[  \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,e_ iangle =D_ i^+F(x)=D_ i^-F(x)=\min _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,e_ iangle  \] for every $i$, so all subgradients at $x$ coincide, and $F$ is differentiable at $x$ by (3). Conversely, if $F$ is differentiable at $x$, then $D_ i^+F(x)=D_ i^-F(x)=\langle 
abla F(x),e_ iangle $ for every $i$. Therefore $\Omega _ F=\Omega \setminus (Z_1\cup \cdots \cup Z_ n)$ is a Borel set with null complement, and the coordinates $\langle 
abla F,e_ iangle =D_ i^+F$ of $
abla F$ are Borel functions on $\Omega _ F$. $\square$
