title: Proposition 21.2.6
section: 21.2 Closed convex functions and supporting slopes
text: Proposition 21.2.6 . EAC7AAEC7279 Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\overline F$ be its lower semicontinuous regularization, that is, the largest lower semicontinuous function on $N_{\mathbb R}$ that is at most $F$. Then $\overline F$ is a closed proper convex function, and $\overline F=F$ on $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. A closed proper convex function is determined by its values on the relative interior of its effective domain. Finally, if a sequence of finite convex functions on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$ converges to a finite limit at each point of a dense subset of $\Omega $, then it converges locally uniformly on $\Omega $ to a finite convex function. Proof. By proposition 21.2.4 , $F$ has a subgradient $p$ at some point $x_1\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, so $F$ lies above the affine function $\ell (y)=F(x_1)+\langle p,y-x_1\rangle $. The closure $E$ of $\operatorname {epi}F$ is convex, and it lies above the graph of $\ell $ because $\ell $ is continuous. Hence, for each $x$, the set $\{ r:(x,r)\in E\} $ is closed and bounded below by $\ell (x)$, and with each of its points $r$ it contains $[r,+\infty )$, because $\operatorname {epi}F$ has this property. So this set is either empty or a closed half-line $[\widetilde F(x),+\infty )$ with $\widetilde F(x)\geq \ell (x)>-\infty $. Setting $\widetilde F(x)=+\infty $ in the first case, we see that $E$ is the epigraph of a convex function $\widetilde F$. It is lower semicontinuous because its epigraph is closed, and $\widetilde F\leq F$, so $\operatorname {dom}\widetilde F\supset \operatorname {dom}F\neq \varnothing $. If $G\leq F$ is lower semicontinuous, then $\operatorname {epi}G$ is closed and contains $\operatorname {epi}F$, hence also $E$, and so $G\leq \widetilde F$. Thus $\widetilde F=\overline F$, which is therefore closed, proper and convex. Let $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. If $(y_ k,r_ k)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ converge to $(x,r)$, then $y_ k$ lies in the affine span of $\operatorname {dom}F$, on which $F$ is continuous at $x$; hence $r\geq \lim _ kF(y_ k)=F(x)$. This shows $\overline F(x)\geq F(x)$, and so $\overline F(x)=F(x)$. Now let $F$ be closed, fix $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and let $x\in \overline{\operatorname {dom}F}$. By lemma 21.2.3 (4), the points $(1-t)x_0+tx$ with $0\leq t<1$ lie in $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, so the convex function $\phi (t)=F((1-t)x_0+tx)$ is finite on $[0,1)$. Convexity gives $\phi (t)\leq (1-t)\phi (0)+t\phi (1)$, hence $\varlimsup _{t\uparrow 1}\phi (t)\leq \phi (1)$, while lower semicontinuity gives $\varliminf _{t\uparrow 1}\phi (t)\geq \phi (1)$. Therefore \[  F(x)=\lim _{t\uparrow 1}F((1-t)x_0+tx) \qquad (x\in \overline{\operatorname {dom}F}),  \] also when $F(x)=+\infty $. Since $F=+\infty $ outside $\overline{\operatorname {dom}F}$, which is the closure of $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, the function $F$ is determined by its restriction to $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Finally, let $(F_ j)$ be a sequence of finite convex functions on $\Omega $ converging to a finite limit at every point of a dense set $S\subset \Omega $. We show that near each point of $\Omega $ the functions $F_ j$ are uniformly bounded, hence uniformly Lipschitz, so that convergence on $S$ propagates to uniform convergence. Fix a basis of $N_{\mathbb R}$, write $Q(y,\rho )$ for the closed cube of half-side $\rho $ centered at $y$ in the corresponding coordinates, and let $x\in \Omega $ and $\rho >0$ with $Q(x,2\rho )\subset \Omega $. For each vertex $y$ of $Q(x,\rho )$ choose a point of $S$ whose coordinates differ from those of $y$ by less than $\rho /2$, and let $S_0\subset S\cap Q(x,2\rho )$ be the finite set of these points. Its convex hull $H$ is compact as the image of a simplex under a linear map, and it contains $Q(x,\rho /2)$. Indeed, let $\ell $ be a nonzero linear functional, $\ell (z)=\sum _ ia_ iz_ i$ in the chosen coordinates, and put $\| a\| =\sum _ i|a_ i|$. At a vertex $y^*$ of $Q(x,\rho )$ where $\ell $ is maximal, $\ell (y^*)=\ell (x)+\rho \| a\| $, and the point $s\in S_0$ chosen for $y^*$ satisfies $\ell (s)>\ell (y^*)-\frac\rho 2\| a\| =\max _{Q(x,\rho /2)}\ell $. Hence no point of $Q(x,\rho /2)$ can be separated from $H$ as in lemma 21.2.3 (1). The sequences $(F_ j(s))_ j$, $s\in S_0$, converge, so they are bounded above by some $C$, and the finite form of Jensen's inequality gives $F_ j\leq C$ on $H$ for all $j$. Choose $s_0\in S\cap Q(x,\rho /8)$. Then $Q(s_0,3\rho /8)\subset Q(x,\rho /2)$, and for $y\in Q(s_0,3\rho /8)$ the reflected point $2s_0-y$ lies in the same cube, so that $F_ j(y)\geq 2F_ j(s_0)-C\geq 2\inf _ kF_ k(s_0)-C$. Hence $|F_ j|\leq B$ on $Q(x,\rho /4)\subset Q(s_0,3\rho /8)$ for all $j$, with a constant $B$. By ( 21.2.2 ), applied with $\delta =\rho /8$ and $\omega \leq 2B$, the $F_ j$ are Lipschitz on $Q(x,\rho /8)$ with the common constant $L=16B/\rho $, for the Euclidean norm $|\cdot |$ of the chosen coordinates. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose a finite set $S_\varepsilon \subset S\cap Q(x,\rho /8)$ such that every point of $Q(x,\rho /8)$ lies within distance $\varepsilon /L$ of $S_\varepsilon $. To this end, cover the compact cube $Q(x,\rho /8)$ by finitely many balls of radius $\varepsilon /(2L)$ centered in the cube, and pick a point of the dense set $S$ in the intersection of each ball with the interior of the cube, a nonempty open set. For all sufficiently large $j,k$ we have $|F_ j-F_ k|<\varepsilon $ on $S_\varepsilon $, hence $|F_ j-F_ k|<3\varepsilon $ on $Q(x,\rho /8)$. Thus $(F_ j)$ is uniformly Cauchy on $Q(x,\rho /8)$. Finitely many such cubes cover any given compact subset of $\Omega $, so $(F_ j)$ converges locally uniformly to a finite continuous function, which is convex because the convexity inequalities pass to pointwise limits. $\square$

title: 21.2.7 Invariant functions on tubes and complex tori
search_title: Invariant functions on tubes and complex tori
section: 21.2 Closed convex functions and supporting slopes
text: We now prove the correspondence between invariant plurisubharmonic functions and convex functions described at the beginning of the chapter. For a nonempty open convex set $V\subset \mathbb R^ n$, $n\geq 1$, consider the tube \[  V+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n=\{ t+\mathrm is:t\in V,\  s\in \mathbb R^ n\} \subset \mathbb C^ n,  \] with coordinates $w=t+\mathrm is$. Recall from section 5.12 , here without the variables $z$, that a function $U$ on the tube is invariant under imaginary translations if $U(w+\mathrm is')=U(w)$ for all $s'\in \mathbb R^ n$, that is, if $U(t+\mathrm is)$ depends only on $t$. As observed there, the complex Hessian of a smooth function of this kind is a quarter of its real Hessian in $t$, so plurisubharmonicity becomes convexity; the general case follows by smoothing. In addition, local integrability of $U$ excludes the value $-\infty $. Proposition 21.2.8 . 909102168A21 Let $n\geq 1$, let $V\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be a nonempty open convex set, and let $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(V+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n)$ be invariant under imaginary translations. Then there is a finite convex function $f\colon V\to \mathbb R$ such that $U(t+\mathrm is)=f(t)$ for all $t\in V$ and $s\in \mathbb R^ n$. Conversely, for every finite convex function $f$ on $V$, the function $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic on $V+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$ and invariant under imaginary translations. Proof. Define $f(t)=U(t)$, identifying $t\in V$ with $t+\mathrm i0$; by invariance, $U(t+\mathrm is)=f(t)$. By theorem 5.9.1 , $U$ is locally integrable, so the set $\{ U=-\infty \} =\{ f=-\infty \} +\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$ is a Lebesgue null set in $\mathbb C^ n$. Applying Fubini's theorem on products of compact boxes in $t$ and in $s$, we see that $\{ f=-\infty \} $ is a null set in $V$. For $\varepsilon >0$ let $V_\varepsilon =\{ t\in V:\operatorname {dist}(t,\mathbb R^ n\setminus V)>\varepsilon \} $. A point $t$ lies in $V_\varepsilon $ if and only if the closed ball $\overline{B(t,\varepsilon )}$ lies in $V$, so $V_\varepsilon $ is the intersection of the convex sets $V-y$, $|y|\leq \varepsilon $, and is convex. The points of the tube at distance more than $\varepsilon $ from its complement form the tube $V_\varepsilon +\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$. On this set let $U_\varepsilon =U*\rho _\varepsilon $, where $\rho _\varepsilon $ is the radial mollifier of section 2.5 on $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$. The function $U_\varepsilon $ is smooth, and its complex Hessian matrix $(\partial ^2U_\varepsilon /\partial w_ j\partial \bar w_ k)$ is positive semidefinite. Indeed, for $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$, the function $\sum _{j,k}(\partial ^2U_\varepsilon /\partial w_ j\partial \bar w_ k)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ is, by proposition 2.5.3 (1), the mollification of the distribution $\sum _{j,k}(\partial ^2U/\partial w_ j\partial \bar w_ k)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$, which is positive by theorem 5.9.1 and the matrix criterion of section 5.4 , so it is nonnegative by proposition 2.5.3 (3). Moreover, $U_\varepsilon \downarrow U$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ by ( 3.4.13 ), because $U$ is subharmonic and locally integrable (theorem 5.9.1 ). Since imaginary translations commute with convolution, $U_\varepsilon $ is invariant under them; write $U_\varepsilon (t+\mathrm is)=f_\varepsilon (t)$. For a function of $t=\operatorname{Re}w$ alone we have $\partial /\partial w_ j=\frac12\partial /\partial t_ j=\partial /\partial \bar w_ j$, hence \[  \frac{\partial ^2U_\varepsilon }{\partial w_ j\partial \bar w_ k} =\frac14\frac{\partial ^2f_\varepsilon }{\partial t_ j\partial t_ k}.  \] The left side is a positive semidefinite matrix, so $f_\varepsilon $ has positive semidefinite real Hessian. Hence the restriction of $f_\varepsilon $ to every segment in the convex set $V_\varepsilon $ has nonnegative second derivative, and $f_\varepsilon $ is convex on $V_\varepsilon $. Suppose that $f(t_0)=-\infty $ for some $t_0\in V$, and choose $r\in (0,1)$ with $\overline{B(t_0,3r)}\subset V$. The upper semicontinuous function $U$ is bounded above, say by $C$, on the compact set $\overline{B(t_0,3r)}+\mathrm i[-1,1]^ n$. Since $U_\varepsilon (w)$ is an average of $U$ over the ball $\overline{B(w,\varepsilon )}$, we get $U_\varepsilon \leq C$ on $B(t_0,2r)$ for $\varepsilon <r$; moreover $B(t_0,2r)\subset V_\varepsilon $ for such $\varepsilon $. For $t\in B(t_0,r)$, the point $2t-t_0$ lies in $B(t_0,2r)$, and $t$ is the midpoint of $t_0$ and $2t-t_0$. Convexity of $f_\varepsilon $ therefore gives \[  f_\varepsilon (t) \leq \tfrac 12f_\varepsilon (t_0) +\tfrac 12f_\varepsilon (2t-t_0) \leq \tfrac 12f_\varepsilon (t_0)+\tfrac 12C.  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, $f_\varepsilon (t_0)\downarrow f(t_0)=-\infty $ and $f_\varepsilon (t)\downarrow f(t)$, so $f=-\infty $ on $B(t_0,r)$. This contradicts the fact that $\{ f=-\infty \} $ is a null set. Hence $f$ is finite. Finally, every segment $[a,b]\subset V$ is compact and therefore lies in $V_\varepsilon $ for small $\varepsilon $; the convexity inequalities for $f_\varepsilon $ on $[a,b]$ pass to the pointwise limit, so $f$ is convex. Conversely, let $f$ be a finite convex function on $V$. By proposition 21.2.4 , $f$ is continuous and has a subgradient $p\in \mathbb R^ n$ at every point. Let $w_0=t_0+\mathrm is_0$ be a point of the tube, $a\in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, and $r>0$ such that the circle $\{ w_0+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a:\theta \in [0,2\pi ]\} $ lies in the tube. If $p$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $t_0$, then \[  f\bigl (\operatorname{Re}(w_0+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a)\bigr ) \geq f(t_0)+r\left\langle p, \operatorname{Re}(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a)\right\rangle =f(t_0)+r\operatorname{Re}\Bigl (\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\sum _ jp_ ja_ j\Bigr ).  \] The last term has mean zero over $\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$, so the mean of the left side over the circle is at least $f(t_0)=f(\operatorname{Re}w_0)$. Since $w_0$, $a$ and $r$ are arbitrary, the restriction of the continuous function $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ to every affine complex line satisfies the submean inequality of definition 3.4.2 at every point, and it is therefore subharmonic. As $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is finite and continuous and the tube is a domain, definition 5.8.1 shows that $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic. It is invariant under imaginary translations by construction. $\square$ Corollary 21.2.9 . 0C12F36D1EDD Let $n\geq 1$, let $V\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be a nonempty open convex set, and put \[  \Omega _ V=\{ z\in (\mathbb C^*)^ n: (\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)\in V\} .  \] Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega _ V)$ be invariant under the action of the compact torus $(S^1)^ n$ by separate rotations of the coordinates, $(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)\mapsto (\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta _1}z_1,\ldots ,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta _ n}z_ n)$. Then there is a finite convex function $f$ on $V$ such that \[  \varphi (z)=f(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)\qquad (z\in \Omega _ V).  \] Conversely, for every finite convex function $f$ on $V$ this formula defines an $(S^1)^ n$-invariant plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega _ V$. In particular, an $(S^1)^ n$-invariant plurisubharmonic function on $(\Delta ^*)^ n$ or on $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ is finite everywhere, where $\Delta ^*=\{ \zeta \in \mathbb C:0<|\zeta |<1\} $. Proof. Consider the holomorphic map \[  E\colon \mathbb C^ n\to (\mathbb C^*)^ n,\qquad E(w)=(\exp (w_1/2),\ldots ,\exp (w_ n/2)).  \] Since $\log |E_ j(w)|^2=\operatorname{Re}w_ j$, it maps the tube $V+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$ onto $\Omega _ V$; in particular, $\Omega _ V$ is connected. By proposition 5.9.3 , $\varphi \circ E$ is either plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on the tube, and the second alternative is impossible because $E$ is surjective and $\varphi $ is nontrivial. Since $E(w+\mathrm is')=(\mathrm e^{\mathrm is_1'/2}E_1(w),\ldots ,\mathrm e^{\mathrm is_ n'/2}E_ n(w))$, the rotation invariance of $\varphi $ makes $\varphi \circ E$ invariant under imaginary translations. Proposition 21.2.8 now gives a finite convex function $f$ with $\varphi (E(w))=f(\operatorname{Re}w)$, which is the asserted formula. Conversely, let $f$ be finite and convex. Then $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic on the tube by proposition 21.2.8 . Near each point of $\Omega _ V$, the map $E$ has the holomorphic local inverse $z\mapsto (2\log z_1,\ldots ,2\log z_ n)$, defined with local branches of the logarithm, and $f(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)$ is the composition of $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ with this inverse. By proposition 5.9.3 it is plurisubharmonic near that point, since it is finite. Plurisubharmonicity is a local property, so the function is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _ V$, and it is $(S^1)^ n$-invariant because it depends only on $|z_1|,\ldots ,|z_ n|$. The domains $(\Delta ^*)^ n$ and $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ are $\Omega _ V$ for $V=(-\infty ,0)^ n$ and $V=\mathbb R^ n$. $\square$

title: 21.3 Legendre duality and convex envelopes
text: The Legendre transform exchanges convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and on $M_{\mathbb R}$, and points with slopes: up to closure, the slopes of $F$ are the points where $F^*$ is finite. We prove the duality theorem and compute the conjugates of envelopes and sums. Definition 21.3.1 . 103D0D196EAF The Legendre transform , or convex conjugate , of a function $F\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is the function on $M_{\mathbb R}$ given by \[  F^*(p)=\sup _{x\in N_{\mathbb R}}(\langle p,x\rangle -F(x)).  \] The conjugate of a function on $M_{\mathbb R}$ is defined in the same way and is a function on $N_{\mathbb R}$; we write $F^{**}=(F^*)^*$. The convex indicator function $\chi _ C$ of a nonempty set $C$, in either space, is $0$ on $C$ and $+\infty $ elsewhere. The support function of a nonempty set $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is \[  h_ P(x)=\sup _{p\in P}\langle p,x\rangle \qquad (x\in N_{\mathbb R});  \] it is convex with values in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$, and it is finite when $P$ is bounded. Theorem 21.3.2 . 011FA81B0000 Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Then $F^*$ is a closed proper convex function on $M_{\mathbb R}$, and \[  F^{**}=\overline F,\qquad (\overline F)^*=F^*.  \] If $F$ is closed, then for $x\in N_{\mathbb R}$ and $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$ the following conditions are equivalent: \[  p\in \partial F(x),\qquad x\in \partial F^*(p),\qquad F(x)+F^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle ;  \] moreover, \[  \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F^*)\subset \partial F(N_{\mathbb R}) \subset \operatorname {dom}F^*,\qquad \overline{\partial F(N_{\mathbb R})} =\overline{\operatorname {dom}F^*}.  \] Finally, for every nonempty closed convex set $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$, the support function and the convex indicator function are conjugate: $h_ P=\chi _ P^*$ and $\chi _ P=h_ P^*$. Proof. The conjugate is the supremum of the continuous affine functions $p\mapsto \langle p,x\rangle -F(x)$, $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$, so it is convex and lower semicontinuous. Since $\operatorname {dom}F\neq \varnothing $, we have $F^*(p)\geq \langle p,x_0\rangle -F(x_0)>-\infty $ for any $x_0\in \operatorname {dom}F$. By proposition 21.2.4 , $F$ has a subgradient $p_0$ at some point $x_1\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and then $F^*(p_0)=\langle p_0,x_1\rangle -F(x_1)<+\infty $. Thus $F^*$ is closed and proper. The definition of $F^*$ gives $F(x)\geq \langle p,x\rangle -F^*(p)$ for all $p$, that is, $F^{**}\leq F$. We next show that $F^{**}=F$ when $F$ is closed. An affine function $\langle p,\cdot \rangle -c$ lies below $F$ if and only if $c\geq F^*(p)$. Hence $F^{**}$ is the supremum of all affine minorants of $F$, and it suffices to find, for every $x$ and every real $r<F(x)$, an affine minorant of $F$ whose value at $x$ exceeds $r$. The point $(x,r)$ does not belong to the closed convex set $\operatorname {epi}F$, so by lemma 21.2.3 (1), applied in $N_{\mathbb R}\times \mathbb R$, there are $a\in M_{\mathbb R}$, $c\in \mathbb R$ and $\delta >0$ with \[  \langle a,y\rangle +cs\geq \langle a,x\rangle +cr+\delta \qquad \text{for all }(y,s)\in \operatorname {epi}F.  \] Letting $s\to +\infty $ shows that $c\geq 0$. If $c>0$, taking $s=F(y)$ gives the affine minorant $y\mapsto r+(\delta -\langle a,y-x\rangle )/c$, whose value at $x$ is $r+\delta /c>r$. If $c=0$, then $\langle a,y\rangle \geq \langle a,x\rangle +\delta $ for all $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$. Let $L_0$ be an affine minorant of $F$, which exists by the first paragraph. For $k>0$ the affine functions \[  L_0(y)+k\bigl (\langle a,x\rangle +\delta /2-\langle a,y\rangle \bigr )  \] are again minorants of $F$, since the added term is at most $-k\delta /2$ on $\operatorname {dom}F$, and their values at $x$ tend to $+\infty $ as $k\to \infty $. In both cases the required minorant exists, so $F^{**}=F$. For a general proper convex $F$, a continuous affine function lies below $F$ if and only if it lies below the largest lower semicontinuous minorant $\overline F$. Therefore $F^*=(\overline F)^*$, and since $\overline F$ is closed and proper by proposition 21.2.6 , $F^{**}=(\overline F)^{**}=\overline F$. Let $F$ be closed. By definition, $p\in \partial F(x)$ means that $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$ and $\langle p,y\rangle -F(y)\leq \langle p,x\rangle -F(x)$ for all $y$, that is, the supremum defining $F^*(p)$ is attained at $x$; equivalently, $F(x)+F^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle $. (If $x\notin \operatorname {dom}F$, both conditions fail, since then $F(x)+F^*(p)=+\infty $.) Applying this to the closed proper function $F^*$ and using $F^{**}=F$, we find that $x\in \partial F^*(p)$ if and only if $F^*(p)+F(x)=\langle p,x\rangle $. This proves the equivalences. If $p\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F^*)$, then $F^*$ has a subgradient $x$ at $p$ by proposition 21.2.4 , and $p\in \partial F(x)$ by the equivalences; this is the first inclusion. If $p\in \partial F(x)$, then $F^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle -F(x)<+\infty $, which gives the second. The closures coincide because $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F^*)$ is dense in $\operatorname {dom}F^*$ by lemma 21.2.3 (4). Finally, $\chi _ P^*=h_ P$ by the definitions, and $\chi _ P$ is a closed proper convex function, so $h_ P^*=\chi _ P^{**}=\chi _ P$. $\square$ Proposition 21.3.3 . 53A9D470F1AC The pointwise supremum of a family of convex functions is convex. The pointwise limit of a decreasing net of convex functions is convex; it may take the value $-\infty $. Let $(F_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a nonempty family of proper convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and put \[  H(x)=\inf \sum _{j=1}^ q\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j),  \] where the infimum is taken over the values $\sum _ j\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j)$ of all admissible combinations for $x$, that is, over all $q\geq 1$, $i_ j\in I$, $x_ j\in \operatorname {dom}F_{i_ j}$ and $\lambda _ j>0$ with $\sum _ j\lambda _ j=1$ and $\sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j=x$; we set $H(x)=+\infty $ if no such combination exists. Then $H$, the convex envelope of the family, is the largest convex function below $\inf _ iF_ i$, and $H^*=\sup _ iF_ i^*$. If $H$ has an affine minorant, then its lower semicontinuous regularization $\overline H$ is the largest lower semicontinuous convex function below $\inf _ iF_ i$, and $\overline H=(\sup _ iF_ i^*)^*$. For proper convex functions $F,G$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$, the infimal convolution \[  (F\mathbin \square G)(x)=\inf _{y+z=x}(F(y)+G(z))  \] is convex, and $(F\mathbin \square G)^*=F^*+G^*$. Let $F,G$ be finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$. Then \[  (F+G)^*(p)=\min _{q+r=p}(F^*(q)+G^*(r))  \] whenever the right-hand side is finite, the minimum being attained; and $(F+G)^*(p)=+\infty $ if $F^*(q)+G^*(r)=+\infty $ for every decomposition $p=q+r$. Proof. (1) The epigraph of a supremum is the intersection of the epigraphs. Let $(F_ i)$ be a decreasing net of convex functions with limit $F=\inf _ iF_ i$, let $x,y\in N_{\mathbb R}$ and $0<\lambda <1$, and let $a>F(x)$ and $b>F(y)$ be real numbers. Choose indices $i_1,i_2$ with $F_{i_1}(x)<a$ and $F_{i_2}(y)<b$, and an index $i$ following both. Then $F_ i(x)<a$ and $F_ i(y)<b$, and convexity of $\operatorname {epi}F_ i$ gives \[  F((1-\lambda )x+\lambda y)\leq F_ i((1-\lambda )x+\lambda y)\leq (1-\lambda )a+\lambda b.  \] Since $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary, this shows that $\operatorname {epi}F$ is convex; this also covers the case where $F(x)$ or $F(y)$ equals $-\infty $. (2) If $H(x)<a$ and $H(x')<a'$, we can choose admissible combinations for $x$ and $x'$ with values below $a$ and $a'$; mixing them with weights $1-\lambda $ and $\lambda $ gives an admissible combination for $(1-\lambda )x+\lambda x'$ with value below $(1-\lambda )a+\lambda a'$. Hence $H$ is convex. Combinations with $q=1$ show $H\leq F_ i$ for each $i$. If $G$ is convex and $G\leq F_ i$ for all $i$, then for every admissible combination the points $(x_ j,F_{i_ j}(x_ j))$ lie in $\operatorname {epi}G$, and so does their convex combination with the weights $\lambda _ j$, since a convex set contains the convex combinations of its points; that is, \[  G\Bigl (\sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j\Bigr )\leq \sum _ j\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j).  \] Hence $G\leq H$. For the conjugate, the supremum defining $H^*(p)$ is the supremum over all admissible combinations of \[  \Bigl \langle p,\sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j\Bigr \rangle -\sum _ j\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j)=\sum _ j\lambda _ j\bigl (\langle p,x_ j\rangle -F_{i_ j}(x_ j)\bigr )\leq \sup _ iF_ i^*(p),  \] and combinations with $q=1$ give equality. Since affine functions are convex, an affine function lies below $H$ if and only if it lies below $\inf _ iF_ i$. Suppose that $H$ has an affine minorant. Then $H$ is proper, so $\overline H$ is a closed proper convex function by proposition 21.2.6 , and $\overline H=H^{**}=(\sup _ iF_ i^*)^*$ by theorem 21.3.2 . A lower semicontinuous convex function below $\inf _ iF_ i$ lies below $H$, and therefore below $\overline H$. (3) Convexity of $F\mathbin \square G$ follows as in (2), by mixing decompositions $x=y+z$ and $x'=y'+z'$ whose values $F(y)+G(z)$ are close to the infima. The two suprema over $y$ and $z$ in \[  (F\mathbin \square G)^*(p)=\sup _{y,z}\bigl (\langle p,y\rangle -F(y)+\langle p,z\rangle -G(z)\bigr )=F^*(p)+G^*(p)  \] are independent, which gives the conjugate formula. (4) If $n=0$, then $F$ and $G$ are constants and both sides equal $-F(0)-G(0)$; so let $n\geq 1$. Let $J(p)=\inf _{q+r=p}(F^*(q)+G^*(r))$. Each conjugate is bounded below by minus its value at the origin: $F^*\geq -F(0)$ and $G^*\geq -G(0)$. Moreover, for every $R>0$, choosing $x$ with $|x|=R$ and $\langle q,x\rangle =R|q|$ gives \[  F^*(q)\geq R|q|-\max _{|x|\leq R}F(x),  \] and the analogous bound holds for $G^*$. Consequently, if $p$ stays bounded and $F^*(q)+G^*(r)$ stays bounded above, then $q$ and $r=p-q$ stay bounded: for instance $F^*(q)\leq F^*(q)+G^*(r)+G(0)$, and the last bound with $R=1$ controls $|q|$. Lower semicontinuity of $F^*$ and $G^*$ therefore implies that the infimum defining $J(p)$ is attained whenever it is finite: a minimizing sequence of decompositions has a convergent subsequence. The same argument, applied to $p_ k\to p$ and decompositions attaining $J(p_ k)$, shows that $J$ is lower semicontinuous. By (3), $J=F^*\mathbin \square G^*$ is convex; it is bounded below by $-F(0)-G(0)$, and it is proper, since $J(q_0+r_0)\leq F^*(q_0)+G^*(r_0)<+\infty $ for subgradients $q_0\in \partial F(0)$ and $r_0\in \partial G(0)$. Finite convex functions are continuous, so $F$ and $G$ are closed and $F^{**}=F$, $G^{**}=G$. By (3), $J^*=F^{**}+G^{**}=F+G$, and theorem 21.3.2 gives $J=J^{**}=(F+G)^*$. $\square$

title: Definition 21.3.1
text: Definition 21.3.1 . 103D0D196EAF The Legendre transform , or convex conjugate , of a function $F\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is the function on $M_{\mathbb R}$ given by \[  F^*(p)=\sup _{x\in N_{\mathbb R}}(\langle p,x\rangle -F(x)).  \] The conjugate of a function on $M_{\mathbb R}$ is defined in the same way and is a function on $N_{\mathbb R}$; we write $F^{**}=(F^*)^*$. The convex indicator function $\chi _ C$ of a nonempty set $C$, in either space, is $0$ on $C$ and $+\infty $ elsewhere. The support function of a nonempty set $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is \[  h_ P(x)=\sup _{p\in P}\langle p,x\rangle \qquad (x\in N_{\mathbb R});  \] it is convex with values in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$, and it is finite when $P$ is bounded.

title: Theorem 21.3.2
text: Theorem 21.3.2 . 011FA81B0000 Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Then $F^*$ is a closed proper convex function on $M_{\mathbb R}$, and \[  F^{**}=\overline F,\qquad (\overline F)^*=F^*.  \] If $F$ is closed, then for $x\in N_{\mathbb R}$ and $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$ the following conditions are equivalent: \[  p\in \partial F(x),\qquad x\in \partial F^*(p),\qquad F(x)+F^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle ;  \] moreover, \[  \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F^*)\subset \partial F(N_{\mathbb R}) \subset \operatorname {dom}F^*,\qquad \overline{\partial F(N_{\mathbb R})} =\overline{\operatorname {dom}F^*}.  \] Finally, for every nonempty closed convex set $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$, the support function and the convex indicator function are conjugate: $h_ P=\chi _ P^*$ and $\chi _ P=h_ P^*$. Proof. The conjugate is the supremum of the continuous affine functions $p\mapsto \langle p,x\rangle -F(x)$, $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$, so it is convex and lower semicontinuous. Since $\operatorname {dom}F\neq \varnothing $, we have $F^*(p)\geq \langle p,x_0\rangle -F(x_0)>-\infty $ for any $x_0\in \operatorname {dom}F$. By proposition 21.2.4 , $F$ has a subgradient $p_0$ at some point $x_1\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and then $F^*(p_0)=\langle p_0,x_1\rangle -F(x_1)<+\infty $. Thus $F^*$ is closed and proper. The definition of $F^*$ gives $F(x)\geq \langle p,x\rangle -F^*(p)$ for all $p$, that is, $F^{**}\leq F$. We next show that $F^{**}=F$ when $F$ is closed. An affine function $\langle p,\cdot \rangle -c$ lies below $F$ if and only if $c\geq F^*(p)$. Hence $F^{**}$ is the supremum of all affine minorants of $F$, and it suffices to find, for every $x$ and every real $r<F(x)$, an affine minorant of $F$ whose value at $x$ exceeds $r$. The point $(x,r)$ does not belong to the closed convex set $\operatorname {epi}F$, so by lemma 21.2.3 (1), applied in $N_{\mathbb R}\times \mathbb R$, there are $a\in M_{\mathbb R}$, $c\in \mathbb R$ and $\delta >0$ with \[  \langle a,y\rangle +cs\geq \langle a,x\rangle +cr+\delta \qquad \text{for all }(y,s)\in \operatorname {epi}F.  \] Letting $s\to +\infty $ shows that $c\geq 0$. If $c>0$, taking $s=F(y)$ gives the affine minorant $y\mapsto r+(\delta -\langle a,y-x\rangle )/c$, whose value at $x$ is $r+\delta /c>r$. If $c=0$, then $\langle a,y\rangle \geq \langle a,x\rangle +\delta $ for all $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$. Let $L_0$ be an affine minorant of $F$, which exists by the first paragraph. For $k>0$ the affine functions \[  L_0(y)+k\bigl (\langle a,x\rangle +\delta /2-\langle a,y\rangle \bigr )  \] are again minorants of $F$, since the added term is at most $-k\delta /2$ on $\operatorname {dom}F$, and their values at $x$ tend to $+\infty $ as $k\to \infty $. In both cases the required minorant exists, so $F^{**}=F$. For a general proper convex $F$, a continuous affine function lies below $F$ if and only if it lies below the largest lower semicontinuous minorant $\overline F$. Therefore $F^*=(\overline F)^*$, and since $\overline F$ is closed and proper by proposition 21.2.6 , $F^{**}=(\overline F)^{**}=\overline F$. Let $F$ be closed. By definition, $p\in \partial F(x)$ means that $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$ and $\langle p,y\rangle -F(y)\leq \langle p,x\rangle -F(x)$ for all $y$, that is, the supremum defining $F^*(p)$ is attained at $x$; equivalently, $F(x)+F^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle $. (If $x\notin \operatorname {dom}F$, both conditions fail, since then $F(x)+F^*(p)=+\infty $.) Applying this to the closed proper function $F^*$ and using $F^{**}=F$, we find that $x\in \partial F^*(p)$ if and only if $F^*(p)+F(x)=\langle p,x\rangle $. This proves the equivalences. If $p\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F^*)$, then $F^*$ has a subgradient $x$ at $p$ by proposition 21.2.4 , and $p\in \partial F(x)$ by the equivalences; this is the first inclusion. If $p\in \partial F(x)$, then $F^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle -F(x)<+\infty $, which gives the second. The closures coincide because $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F^*)$ is dense in $\operatorname {dom}F^*$ by lemma 21.2.3 (4). Finally, $\chi _ P^*=h_ P$ by the definitions, and $\chi _ P$ is a closed proper convex function, so $h_ P^*=\chi _ P^{**}=\chi _ P$. $\square$

title: Proposition 21.3.3
text: Proposition 21.3.3 . 53A9D470F1AC The pointwise supremum of a family of convex functions is convex. The pointwise limit of a decreasing net of convex functions is convex; it may take the value $-\infty $. Let $(F_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a nonempty family of proper convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and put \[  H(x)=\inf \sum _{j=1}^ q\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j),  \] where the infimum is taken over the values $\sum _ j\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j)$ of all admissible combinations for $x$, that is, over all $q\geq 1$, $i_ j\in I$, $x_ j\in \operatorname {dom}F_{i_ j}$ and $\lambda _ j>0$ with $\sum _ j\lambda _ j=1$ and $\sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j=x$; we set $H(x)=+\infty $ if no such combination exists. Then $H$, the convex envelope of the family, is the largest convex function below $\inf _ iF_ i$, and $H^*=\sup _ iF_ i^*$. If $H$ has an affine minorant, then its lower semicontinuous regularization $\overline H$ is the largest lower semicontinuous convex function below $\inf _ iF_ i$, and $\overline H=(\sup _ iF_ i^*)^*$. For proper convex functions $F,G$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$, the infimal convolution \[  (F\mathbin \square G)(x)=\inf _{y+z=x}(F(y)+G(z))  \] is convex, and $(F\mathbin \square G)^*=F^*+G^*$. Then \[  (F+G)^*(p)=\min _{q+r=p}(F^*(q)+G^*(r))  \] whenever the right-hand side is finite, the minimum being attained; and $(F+G)^*(p)=+\infty $ if $F^*(q)+G^*(r)=+\infty $ for every decomposition $p=q+r$. If $G$ is convex and $G\leq F_ i$ for all $i$, then for every admissible combination the points $(x_ j,F_{i_ j}(x_ j))$ lie in $\operatorname {epi}G$, and so does their convex combination with the weights $\lambda _ j$, since a convex set contains the convex combinations of its points; that is, \[  G\Bigl (\sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j\Bigr )\leq \sum _ j\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j).  \] Hence $G\leq H$. For the conjugate, the supremum defining $H^*(p)$ is the supremum over all admissible combinations of \[  \Bigl \langle p,\sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j\Bigr \rangle -\sum _ j\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j)=\sum _ j\lambda _ j\bigl (\langle p,x_ j\rangle -F_{i_ j}(x_ j)\bigr )\leq \sup _ iF_ i^*(p),  \] and combinations with $q=1$ give equality. Since affine functions are convex, an affine function lies below $H$ if and only if it lies below $\inf _ iF_ i$. Suppose that $H$ has an affine minorant. Then $H$ is proper, so $\overline H$ is a closed proper convex function by proposition 21.2.6 , and $\overline H=H^{**}=(\sup _ iF_ i^*)^*$ by theorem 21.3.2 . A lower semicontinuous convex function below $\inf _ iF_ i$ lies below $H$, and therefore below $\overline H$. The two suprema over $y$ and $z$ in \[  (F\mathbin \square G)^*(p)=\sup _{y,z}\bigl (\langle p,y\rangle -F(y)+\langle p,z\rangle -G(z)\bigr )=F^*(p)+G^*(p)  \] are independent, which gives the conjugate formula. (4) If $n=0$, then $F$ and $G$ are constants and both sides equal $-F(0)-G(0)$; so let $n\geq 1$. Let $J(p)=\inf _{q+r=p}(F^*(q)+G^*(r))$. Each conjugate is bounded below by minus its value at the origin: $F^*\geq -F(0)$ and $G^*\geq -G(0)$. title: 21.4 Slope bodies and bounded growth
text: We now study the finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ whose growth at infinity is controlled by the support function $h_ P$ of a convex body $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$. By duality, such control is a condition on the set where the conjugate is finite, that is, on the slopes of the function. Definition 21.4.1 . E8746DA689A7 Let $F,G$ be finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$. As for functions on a compact manifold (section 6.18 ), we write $F\preceq G$ if $F\leq G+C$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ for some constant $C$, and $F\sim G$ if $F\preceq G$ and $G\preceq F$. The closed convex set \[  K_ F=\overline{\operatorname {dom}F^*}\subset M_{\mathbb R}  \] is nonempty, and by theorem 21.3.2 it is the closure of the set $\partial F(N_{\mathbb R})$ of all supporting slopes of $F$; when it is compact we call it the slope body of $F$. For a convex body $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$, let $\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ be the set of finite convex functions $F$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with $F\preceq h_ P$, and let the bounded class $\mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$ be the set of those with $F\sim h_ P$. If $P$ has nonempty interior, the full-mass class $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the set of $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ with $K_ F=P$; if $P$ has empty interior, we set $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)=\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$. Finally, the finite-energy class $\mathcal E^1(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the set of $F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ with $\int _ PF^*\, \mathrm dp<+\infty $. Since $F^*\geq -F(0)$ by the definition of $F^*$, this integral is well defined in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$. The notation is chosen by analogy with the classes $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )\subset \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )\subset \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ of definition 13.9.3 , definition 17.3.1 , with the support function $h_ P$ in the role of the model potential $\phi $. Proposition 21.4.2 . D6E7C0B06FAD Let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body and $F$ a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. The following conditions are equivalent: \[  F\preceq h_ P,\qquad \operatorname {dom}F^*\subset P, \qquad \partial F(N_{\mathbb R})\subset P.  \] If they hold, then $\max _ x(F(x)-h_ P(x))=F(0)$, and $F$ is Lipschitz on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with constant $\max _{p\in P}|p|$. Moreover, $F\sim h_ P$ if and only if $F^*$ is bounded on $P$ and equal to $+\infty $ outside $P$, and \[  \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)\subset \mathcal E^1(N_{\mathbb R},P)\subset \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)\subset \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P).  \] If $F,G$ are finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and $K_ F$ is compact, then \[  K_{F+G}=K_ F+K_ G.  \] In particular, if $P'\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is another convex body, $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$, then $F+G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$. Proof. If $F\leq h_ P+C$, conjugation reverses the inequality and gives $F^*\geq h_ P^*-C=\chi _ P-C$ by theorem 21.3.2 , so $\operatorname {dom}F^*\subset P$. Every subgradient of $F$ lies in $\operatorname {dom}F^*$ by the same theorem, so the second condition implies the third. If all slopes of $F$ lie in $P$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at $0$, gives \[  F(x)-F(0)\leq \langle p,x\rangle \leq h_ P(x).  \] Thus $F\leq h_ P+F(0)$, which proves the first condition and, since $h_ P(0)=0$, the identity $\max _ x(F(x)-h_ P(x))=F(0)$. If $p_ x\in \partial F(x)$ and $p_ y\in \partial F(y)$, the subgradient inequalities give $\langle p_ y,y-x\rangle \geq F(y)-F(x)\geq \langle p_ x,y-x\rangle $, so $|F(y)-F(x)|\leq \max _{p\in P}|p|\, |y-x|$. Conjugation reverses inequalities, and $F^{**}=F$ because the finite convex function $F$ is continuous. Hence $h_ P-C\leq F\leq h_ P+C$ holds if and only if $\chi _ P-C\leq F^*\leq \chi _ P+C$, that is, if and only if $F^*=+\infty $ outside $P$ and $|F^*|\leq C$ on $P$. In that case $K_ F=P$, so $F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ (by the convention if $P$ has empty interior), and $\int _ PF^*\, \mathrm dp\leq C\operatorname {vol}(P)<\infty $; thus $\mathcal E^\infty \subset \mathcal E^1$. The inclusions $\mathcal E^1\subset \mathcal E\subset \mathcal P$ hold by definition. If $P$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $P$ lies in a proper affine subspace, because its relative interior is nonempty and open in its affine span (lemma 21.2.3 (4)); hence $\operatorname {vol}(P)=0$, every integral over $P$ vanishes, and $\mathcal E^1=\mathcal E=\mathcal P$. Now let $F,G$ be finite convex functions with $K_ F$ compact. By proposition 21.3.3 (4), $(F+G)^*(p)$ is finite exactly when $p=q+r$ with $q\in \operatorname {dom}F^*$ and $r\in \operatorname {dom}G^*$, so \[  \operatorname {dom}(F+G)^*=\operatorname {dom}F^*+\operatorname {dom}G^*.  \] It remains to pass to closures. Since addition $M_{\mathbb R}\times M_{\mathbb R}\to M_{\mathbb R}$ is continuous, $K_ F+K_ G$ lies in the closure of $\operatorname {dom}F^*+\operatorname {dom}G^*$. Conversely, if $q_ k+r_ k\to s$ with $q_ k\in \operatorname {dom}F^*$ and $r_ k\in \operatorname {dom}G^*$, then a subsequence of $(q_ k)$ converges to some $q\in K_ F$, because $K_ F$ is compact, and along it $r_ k\to s-q\in K_ G$; hence $s\in K_ F+K_ G$. This proves $K_{F+G}=K_ F+K_ G$. Finally, if $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$, then $F\preceq h_ P$ and $G\preceq h_{P'}$ by the first part, and $h_ P+h_{P'}=h_{P+P'}$; hence $F+G\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$ and $K_{F+G}=P+P'$, so that $F+G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$. $\square$ For smooth approximation we use mollification, which preserves convexity and, on convex functions, is monotone in the radius. Lemma 21.4.3 . 9AEE54E3B1E1 Let $A$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\rho _\varepsilon (y)=\varepsilon ^{-n}\rho (y/\varepsilon )$ be the mollifiers of section 2.5 , in the coordinates of a basis of $N$. Then the functions $A*\rho _\varepsilon $, $\varepsilon >0$, are smooth and convex, $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ is a nondecreasing function of $\varepsilon >0$ with $A*\rho _\varepsilon \geq A$ for every $x$, and $A*\rho _\varepsilon \to A$ locally uniformly as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Proof. If $n=0$, then $A*\rho _\varepsilon =A$ and there is nothing to prove; let $n\geq 1$. Recall that $\rho $ is smooth, nonnegative, even, supported in the unit ball, and has integral one. Since $A$ is continuous, being locally Lipschitz by proposition 21.2.4 , the functions $A*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth by section 2.5 , and they converge to $A$ locally uniformly by lemma 2.5.1 (1). They are convex, because $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)=\int A(x-y)\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy$ and the convexity inequalities of the functions $x\mapsto A(x-y)$ can be integrated against $\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy\geq 0$. For fixed $x$, consider the function \[  g(\varepsilon )=\int A(x-\varepsilon y)\rho (y)\, \mathrm dy\qquad (\varepsilon \in \mathbb R),  \] which is finite because $A$ is continuous and $\rho $ has compact support. The substitution $y\mapsto \varepsilon y$ shows that $g(\varepsilon )=A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ for $\varepsilon >0$, and $g(0)=A(x)$. For each $y$, the function $\varepsilon \mapsto A(x-\varepsilon y)$ is convex, so $g$ is convex; and $g$ is even, because $\rho $ is even. A convex even function on $\mathbb R$ is nondecreasing on $[0,+\infty )$: if $0\leq a<b$, then $a=\lambda b+(1-\lambda )(-b)$ with $\lambda =(a+b)/(2b)\in (0,1]$, so that $g(a)\leq \lambda g(b)+(1-\lambda )g(-b)=g(b)$. Hence $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ is nondecreasing in $\varepsilon >0$ and bounded below by $g(0)=A(x)$. $\square$ Proposition 21.4.4 . 374D75E96CF6 Let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body. Every $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the pointwise limit of a decreasing sequence of smooth functions $F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$, and the convergence is locally uniform. If functions $F_ j\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to (-\infty ,+\infty ]$ decrease pointwise to a function $F$, then the conjugates $F_ j^*$ increase pointwise to $F^*$. A sequence of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ converges pointwise to a finite function if and only if it converges locally uniformly. Proof. Let $A_ j=\max \{ F,h_ P-j\} $. These are convex functions, decreasing in $j$, with $A_ j\sim h_ P$, and $A_ j=F$ on every compact set on which $h_ P-F\leq j$; hence $A_ j\to F$ locally uniformly. With the mollifiers $\rho _\varepsilon $ of lemma 21.4.3 , choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ and set $F_ j=A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}$. By that lemma, these functions are smooth and convex, and the monotonicity in $\varepsilon $ together with $A_{j+1}\leq A_ j$ gives $F_{j+1}=A_{j+1}*\rho _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}=F_ j$, and $F_ j\geq A_ j\geq F$. By proposition 21.4.2 , $F$ and $h_ P$ are Lipschitz with constant $\max _{p\in P}|p|$, hence so is $A_ j$, and therefore $|F_ j-A_ j|\leq C\varepsilon _ j$ with $C=\max _{p\in P}|p|\int |y|\rho (y)\, \mathrm dy$. Consequently $F_ j\sim A_ j\sim h_ P$, so $F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$, and $F_ j\to F$ locally uniformly. If $F_ j\downarrow F$ pointwise, then \[  \sup _ jF_ j^*(p)=\sup _ j\sup _ x\bigl (\langle p,x\rangle -F_ j(x)\bigr )=\sup _ x\sup _ j\bigl (\langle p,x\rangle -F_ j(x)\bigr )=F^*(p),  \] and the conjugates $F_ j^*$ increase, because conjugation reverses inequalities. Finally, if a sequence of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ converges pointwise to a finite function, it converges locally uniformly by proposition 21.2.6 , applied with $\Omega $ and the dense subset both equal to $N_{\mathbb R}$, and conversely local uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence. $\square$ Example 21.4.5 . 56EB803309C2 The hypotheses $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$ in the last assertion of proposition 21.4.2 cannot be replaced by $F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and $G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P')$: when $P$ has empty interior, membership in $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ does not force a function to use every slope in $P$. Let $N_{\mathbb R}=M_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^2$ with the standard pairing, $P=[0,1]\times \{ 0\} $ and $P'=\{ 0\} \times [0,1]$. Both bodies have empty interior, and the zero function belongs to $\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)=\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and to $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P')$, since $0\leq h_ P$ and $0\leq h_{P'}$. The sum of the zero function with itself is zero, whose slope body is $\{ 0\} $, whereas $P+P'=[0,1]^2$ has nonempty interior. Hence the zero function does not belong to $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$. Finally, we compare logarithms of sums of exponentials with linear functions. Lemma 21.4.6 . F7AECD623994 Let $m\geq 1$ and $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m,\alpha \in M_{\mathbb R}$. The function \[  x\longmapsto \log \sum _{i=1}^ m\mathrm e^{\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle } -\langle \alpha ,x\rangle  \] is bounded below on $N_{\mathbb R}$ if and only if $\alpha $ belongs to the convex hull of $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m$. Suppose that all $\beta _ i$ and $\alpha $ lie in $M$, identify $M$ with $\mathbb Z^ n$ by a basis and $N_{\mathbb R}$ with $\mathbb R^ n$ by the dual basis, and write $z^\alpha =z_1^{\alpha _1}\cdots z_ n^{\alpha _ n}$. Then this condition is also equivalent to the boundedness on $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ of \[  \frac{|z^\alpha |^2}{\sum _ i|z^{\beta _ i}|^2}.  \] Proof. If $\alpha =\sum _ i\lambda _ i\beta _ i$ is a convex combination, then $\langle \alpha ,x\rangle \leq \max _ i\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle \leq \log \sum _ i\mathrm e^{\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle }$, so the function is nonnegative. Conversely, suppose that $\alpha $ is not in the convex hull. The hull is compact, being the image of the standard simplex under the linear map $(\lambda _ i)\mapsto \sum _ i\lambda _ i\beta _ i$, and convex, so lemma 21.2.3 (1), applied in $M_{\mathbb R}$, gives $v\in N_{\mathbb R}$ with $\langle \alpha ,v\rangle >\max _ i\langle \beta _ i,v\rangle $. Since the logarithmic sum differs from $\max _ i\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle $ by a number in $[0,\log m]$, the value of the function at $x=tv$ is at most $t(\max _ i\langle \beta _ i,v\rangle -\langle \alpha ,v\rangle )+\log m$, which tends to $-\infty $ as $t\to +\infty $. For the last assertion, put $x_ j=\log |z_ j|^2$. Then $|z^\gamma |^2=\mathrm e^{\langle \gamma ,x\rangle }$ for every $\gamma \in \mathbb Z^ n$, including exponents with negative entries, so the displayed quotient equals the exponential of minus the function above; and $z\mapsto x$ maps $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ onto $\mathbb R^ n$. $\square$

title: Definition 21.4.1
text: Definition 21.4.1 . E8746DA689A7 Let $F,G$ be finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$. As for functions on a compact manifold (section 6.18 ), we write $F\preceq G$ if $F\leq G+C$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ for some constant $C$, and $F\sim G$ if $F\preceq G$ and $G\preceq F$. The closed convex set \[  K_ F=\overline{\operatorname {dom}F^*}\subset M_{\mathbb R}  \] is nonempty, and by theorem 21.3.2 it is the closure of the set $\partial F(N_{\mathbb R})$ of all supporting slopes of $F$; when it is compact we call it the slope body of $F$. For a convex body $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$, let $\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ be the set of finite convex functions $F$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with $F\preceq h_ P$, and let the bounded class $\mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$ be the set of those with $F\sim h_ P$. If $P$ has nonempty interior, the full-mass class $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the set of $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ with $K_ F=P$; if $P$ has empty interior, we set $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)=\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$. Finally, the finite-energy class $\mathcal E^1(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the set of $F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ with $\int _ PF^*\, \mathrm dp<+\infty $. Since $F^*\geq -F(0)$ by the definition of $F^*$, this integral is well defined in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$.

title: Proposition 21.4.2
text: Proposition 21.4.2 . D6E7C0B06FAD Let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body and $F$ a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. The following conditions are equivalent: \[  F\preceq h_ P,\qquad \operatorname {dom}F^*\subset P, \qquad \partial F(N_{\mathbb R})\subset P.  \] If they hold, then $\max _ x(F(x)-h_ P(x))=F(0)$, and $F$ is Lipschitz on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with constant $\max _{p\in P}|p|$. Moreover, $F\sim h_ P$ if and only if $F^*$ is bounded on $P$ and equal to $+\infty $ outside $P$, and \[  \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)\subset \mathcal E^1(N_{\mathbb R},P)\subset \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)\subset \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P).  \] If $F,G$ are finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and $K_ F$ is compact, then \[  K_{F+G}=K_ F+K_ G.  \] In particular, if $P'\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is another convex body, $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$, then $F+G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$. Proof. If $F\leq h_ P+C$, conjugation reverses the inequality and gives $F^*\geq h_ P^*-C=\chi _ P-C$ by theorem 21.3.2 , so $\operatorname {dom}F^*\subset P$. Every subgradient of $F$ lies in $\operatorname {dom}F^*$ by the same theorem, so the second condition implies the third. If all slopes of $F$ lie in $P$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at $0$, gives \[  F(x)-F(0)\leq \langle p,x\rangle \leq h_ P(x).  \] Thus $F\leq h_ P+F(0)$, which proves the first condition and, since $h_ P(0)=0$, the identity $\max _ x(F(x)-h_ P(x))=F(0)$. If $p_ x\in \partial F(x)$ and $p_ y\in \partial F(y)$, the subgradient inequalities give $\langle p_ y,y-x\rangle \geq F(y)-F(x)\geq \langle p_ x,y-x\rangle $, so $|F(y)-F(x)|\leq \max _{p\in P}|p|\, |y-x|$. Conjugation reverses inequalities, and $F^{**}=F$ because the finite convex function $F$ is continuous. Hence $h_ P-C\leq F\leq h_ P+C$ holds if and only if $\chi _ P-C\leq F^*\leq \chi _ P+C$, that is, if and only if $F^*=+\infty $ outside $P$ and $|F^*|\leq C$ on $P$. In that case $K_ F=P$, so $F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ (by the convention if $P$ has empty interior), and $\int _ PF^*\, \mathrm dp\leq C\operatorname {vol}(P)<\infty $; thus $\mathcal E^\infty \subset \mathcal E^1$. The inclusions $\mathcal E^1\subset \mathcal E\subset \mathcal P$ hold by definition. If $P$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $P$ lies in a proper affine subspace, because its relative interior is nonempty and open in its affine span (lemma 21.2.3 (4)); hence $\operatorname {vol}(P)=0$, every integral over $P$ vanishes, and $\mathcal E^1=\mathcal E=\mathcal P$. Now let $F,G$ be finite convex functions with $K_ F$ compact. By proposition 21.3.3 (4), $(F+G)^*(p)$ is finite exactly when $p=q+r$ with $q\in \operatorname {dom}F^*$ and $r\in \operatorname {dom}G^*$, so \[  \operatorname {dom}(F+G)^*=\operatorname {dom}F^*+\operatorname {dom}G^*.  \] It remains to pass to closures. Since addition $M_{\mathbb R}\times M_{\mathbb R}\to M_{\mathbb R}$ is continuous, $K_ F+K_ G$ lies in the closure of $\operatorname {dom}F^*+\operatorname {dom}G^*$. Conversely, if $q_ k+r_ k\to s$ with $q_ k\in \operatorname {dom}F^*$ and $r_ k\in \operatorname {dom}G^*$, then a subsequence of $(q_ k)$ converges to some $q\in K_ F$, because $K_ F$ is compact, and along it $r_ k\to s-q\in K_ G$; hence $s\in K_ F+K_ G$. This proves $K_{F+G}=K_ F+K_ G$. Finally, if $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$, then $F\preceq h_ P$ and $G\preceq h_{P'}$ by the first part, and $h_ P+h_{P'}=h_{P+P'}$; hence $F+G\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$ and $K_{F+G}=P+P'$, so that $F+G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$. $\square$

title: Lemma 21.4.3
text: Lemma 21.4.3 . 9AEE54E3B1E1 Let $A$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\rho _\varepsilon (y)=\varepsilon ^{-n}\rho (y/\varepsilon )$ be the mollifiers of section 2.5 , in the coordinates of a basis of $N$. Then the functions $A*\rho _\varepsilon $, $\varepsilon >0$, are smooth and convex, $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ is a nondecreasing function of $\varepsilon >0$ with $A*\rho _\varepsilon \geq A$ for every $x$, and $A*\rho _\varepsilon \to A$ locally uniformly as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Proof. If $n=0$, then $A*\rho _\varepsilon =A$ and there is nothing to prove; let $n\geq 1$. Recall that $\rho $ is smooth, nonnegative, even, supported in the unit ball, and has integral one. Since $A$ is continuous, being locally Lipschitz by proposition 21.2.4 , the functions $A*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth by section 2.5 , and they converge to $A$ locally uniformly by lemma 2.5.1 (1). They are convex, because $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)=\int A(x-y)\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy$ and the convexity inequalities of the functions $x\mapsto A(x-y)$ can be integrated against $\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy\geq 0$. For fixed $x$, consider the function \[  g(\varepsilon )=\int A(x-\varepsilon y)\rho (y)\, \mathrm dy\qquad (\varepsilon \in \mathbb R),  \] which is finite because $A$ is continuous and $\rho $ has compact support. The substitution $y\mapsto \varepsilon y$ shows that $g(\varepsilon )=A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ for $\varepsilon >0$, and $g(0)=A(x)$. For each $y$, the function $\varepsilon \mapsto A(x-\varepsilon y)$ is convex, so $g$ is convex; and $g$ is even, because $\rho $ is even. A convex even function on $\mathbb R$ is nondecreasing on $[0,+\infty )$: if $0\leq a<b$, then $a=\lambda b+(1-\lambda )(-b)$ with $\lambda =(a+b)/(2b)\in (0,1]$, so that $g(a)\leq \lambda g(b)+(1-\lambda )g(-b)=g(b)$. Hence $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ is nondecreasing in $\varepsilon >0$ and bounded below by $g(0)=A(x)$. $\square$

title: Proposition 21.4.4
text: Proposition 21.4.4 . 374D75E96CF6 Let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body. Every $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the pointwise limit of a decreasing sequence of smooth functions $F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$, and the convergence is locally uniform. If functions $F_ j\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to (-\infty ,+\infty ]$ decrease pointwise to a function $F$, then the conjugates $F_ j^*$ increase pointwise to $F^*$. A sequence of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ converges pointwise to a finite function if and only if it converges locally uniformly. Proof. Let $A_ j=\max \{ F,h_ P-j\} $. These are convex functions, decreasing in $j$, with $A_ j\sim h_ P$, and $A_ j=F$ on every compact set on which $h_ P-F\leq j$; hence $A_ j\to F$ locally uniformly. With the mollifiers $\rho _\varepsilon $ of lemma 21.4.3 , choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ and set $F_ j=A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}$. By that lemma, these functions are smooth and convex, and the monotonicity in $\varepsilon $ together with $A_{j+1}\leq A_ j$ gives $F_{j+1}=A_{j+1}*\rho _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}=F_ j$, and $F_ j\geq A_ j\geq F$. By proposition 21.4.2 , $F$ and $h_ P$ are Lipschitz with constant $\max _{p\in P}|p|$, hence so is $A_ j$, and therefore $|F_ j-A_ j|\leq C\varepsilon _ j$ with $C=\max _{p\in P}|p|\int |y|\rho (y)\, \mathrm dy$. Consequently $F_ j\sim A_ j\sim h_ P$, so $F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$, and $F_ j\to F$ locally uniformly. If $F_ j\downarrow F$ pointwise, then \[  \sup _ jF_ j^*(p)=\sup _ j\sup _ x\bigl (\langle p,x\rangle -F_ j(x)\bigr )=\sup _ x\sup _ j\bigl (\langle p,x\rangle -F_ j(x)\bigr )=F^*(p),  \] and the conjugates $F_ j^*$ increase, because conjugation reverses inequalities. Finally, if a sequence of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ converges pointwise to a finite function, it converges locally uniformly by proposition 21.2.6 , applied with $\Omega $ and the dense subset both equal to $N_{\mathbb R}$, and conversely local uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence. $\square$

title: 21.5 The real Monge–Ampère measure
text:
Let $F$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Following Alexandrov, we measure a set $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$ by the volume of the set $\partial F(E)$ of supporting slopes of $F$ at points of $E$. For a smooth $F$ with positive definite Hessian, $\partial F(E)=
abla F(E)$, and the change of variables formula gives $\operatorname {vol}(
abla F(E))=\int _ E\det (D^2F)\, \mathrm dx$, so this is a weak form of the real Monge–Ampère operator (see proposition 21.5.4 ). Two difficulties arise in general: the subgradient map is multivalued, and it is not clear a priori that $\partial F(E)$ is measurable. Both are resolved by looking at the inverse map. By duality, a slope $p$ belongs to $\partial F(E)$ if and only if $E$ meets $\partial F^*(p)$, and $\partial F^*(p)$ is a single point for almost every $p$ in the domain of $F^*$. Theorem 21.5.1 . 409656CC47D4 Let $F$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, let $G=F^*$, and let $D$ be the set of points of the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$ at which $G$ is differentiable. For every Borel set $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$, the set $\partial F(E)$ is measurable for the completed Lebesgue measure, and \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(E)=n!\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))  \] defines a positive Radon measure on $N_{\mathbb R}$, the real Monge–Ampère measure of $F$. It is given by \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F) =(
abla G)_*(n!\mathbf1_ D\, \mathrm dp).  \] If $\operatorname {dom}G$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)=0$. In every case \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(N_{\mathbb R}) =n!\operatorname {vol}(K_ F).  \] Proof. The set $\operatorname {dom}G$ is convex, and its difference from its interior is a null set: if the interior is nonempty, this difference lies in the relative boundary, which is null by lemma 21.2.3 (4); otherwise $\operatorname {dom}G$ lies in a proper affine subspace. By proposition 21.2.4 (4), applied to the finite convex function $G$ on the interior of its domain, $D$ is a Borel set, the gradient $
abla G\colon D	o N_{\mathbb R}$ is a Borel map, and the complement of $D$ in the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$ is a null set. Therefore the complement of $D$ in $\operatorname {dom}G$ is a null set; it is a Borel set, because $\operatorname {dom}G= igcup _ k\{ G\leq k\} $ is a countable union of closed sets, $G$ being lower semicontinuous. Let $p\in D$. Then $\partial G(p)=\{ 
abla G(p)\} $. Indeed, $\partial G(p)$ is nonempty by proposition 21.2.4 , and every subgradient of $G$ at $p$ is also a subgradient at $p$ of the restriction of $G$ to the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$, whose only subgradient at $p$ is $
abla G(p)$ by proposition 21.2.4 (3). Hence theorem 21.3.2 gives, for every $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  p\in \partial F(E)\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad 
abla G(p)\in E.  \] Every subgradient of $F$ lies in $\operatorname {dom}G$, so $\partial F(E)$ differs from the Borel set $(
abla G)^{-1}(E)\cap D$ by a subset of the fixed null set $\operatorname {dom}G\setminus D$. Hence $\partial F(E)$ is measurable for the completed measure, and $\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))=\operatorname {vol}((
abla G)^{-1}(E)\cap D)$. This proves the pushforward formula, which in turn shows that $E\mapsto n!\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))$ is countably additive on Borel sets. If $K$ is compact, $\partial F(K)$ is bounded by proposition 21.2.4 (1), and it is closed, since the graph of $\partial F$ is closed and $K$ is compact; so $\partial F(K)$ is compact and has finite volume. Thus the measure is finite on compact sets, and it is a Radon measure by proposition 2.2.2 . If $\operatorname {dom}G$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $D=\varnothing $ and the measure vanishes. In general, the total mass is $n!\operatorname {vol}(D)=n!\operatorname {vol}(\operatorname {dom}G)$, and $\operatorname {vol}(\operatorname {dom}G)=\operatorname {vol}(K_ F)$ because $K_ F\setminus \operatorname {dom}G$ lies in the relative boundary of $\operatorname {dom}G$, or in a proper affine subspace. In dimension zero, $F$ is a constant, $D$ is the single point of $M_{\mathbb R}$, and the formula gives unit mass, with $0!=1$. $\square$ Theorem 21.5.2 . F4072D9ED060 Let $F_ j$ and $F$ be finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ such that $F_ j	o F$ locally uniformly. Then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)	o \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ vaguely. Moreover, let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body. A function $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ belongs to $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ if and only if \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(N_{\mathbb R})=n!\operatorname {vol}(P).  \] If $F$ and $H$ are finite convex functions with $F\preceq H$, then $K_ F\subset K_ H$, and the total mass of $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ is at most that of $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(H)$. Proof. Write $\mu _ j=\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)$ and $\mu =\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$. Steps 1 and 2 compare the masses of compact and of open sets, and Step 3 deduces vague convergence. Step 1: compact sets. Let $K$ be compact. If $x\in K$ and $0
eq p\in \partial F_ j(x)$ (in particular $n\geq 1$), choose $e\in N_{\mathbb R}$ with $|e|=1$ and $\langle p,eangle =|p|$; the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at $x+e$, gives $|p|\leq F_ j(x+e)-F_ j(x)\leq 2\sup \{ |F_ j(y)|:\operatorname {dist}(y,K)\leq 1\} $. By local uniform convergence, the sets $\partial F_ j(K)$ are therefore contained in a fixed ball for all large $j$. If $x_ j\in K$, $p_ j\in \partial F_ j(x_ j)$, $x_ j	o x$ and $p_ j	o p$, then letting $j	o \infty $ in the subgradient inequalities gives $p\in \partial F(x)$. The set $\partial F(K)$ is compact, being bounded and closed by proposition 21.2.4 (1), since $K$ is compact. Consequently, for every $\varepsilon >0$, the set $\partial F_ j(K)$ lies in the closed $\varepsilon $-neighborhood $(\partial F(K))^\varepsilon $ of $\partial F(K)$ for all large $j$. Otherwise, for infinitely many $j$ there would be points $x_ j\in K$ and $p_ j\in \partial F_ j(x_ j)$ at distance at least $\varepsilon $ from $\partial F(K)$; as $K$ is compact and the $p_ j$ are bounded, a subsequence of $(x_ j,p_ j)$ would converge to some $(x,p)$ with $p\in \partial F(x)$, which is impossible. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, these neighborhoods decrease to $\partial F(K)$, and continuity from above of Lebesgue measure on sets of finite measure gives \[  \varlimsup _ j\mu _ j(K)\leq \mu (K).  \] Step 2: open sets. Let $U$ be open and let $G=F^*$, with $D$ as in theorem 21.5.1 . For $p\in \partial F(U)\cap D$, the point $x=
abla G(p)$ lies in $U$ and is the only point with $p\in \partial F(x)$, so $x$ is the unique minimum point of $F-\langle p,\cdot angle $. Choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset U$. Since the sphere $\{ y:|y-x|=r\} $ is compact, $F-\langle p,\cdot angle $ exceeds its minimum by some $\delta >0$ on it. For large $j$ we have $|F_ j-F|<\delta /3$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$, so the minimum of $F_ j-\langle p,\cdot angle $ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$ is attained at a point $x_ j\in B(x,r)$. A local minimum of a convex function is a global minimum, because the function is convex along each segment starting at that point; hence $p\in \partial F_ j(x_ j)\subset \partial F_ j(U)$ for all large $j$. Since $\partial F(U)\setminus D$ is a null set, Fatou's lemma, applied to the indicator functions of the sets $\partial F_ j(U)$, gives \[  \mu (U)\leq \varliminf _ j\mu _ j(U).  \] Step 3: vague convergence. Let $f\geq 0$ be continuous with compact support $S$. By Step 1 there is $C$ with $\mu _ j(S)\leq C$ for all large $j$. For $t>0$, the set $\{ f\geq t\} $ is compact and $\{ f>t\} $ is open. By Tonelli's theorem, $\int f\, \mathrm d
u =\int _0^\infty 
u (\{ f>t\} )\, \mathrm dt=\int _0^\infty 
u (\{ f\geq t\} )\, \mathrm dt$ for every positive measure $
u $. abla G)_*(n!\mathbf1_ D\, \mathrm dp).  \] If $\operatorname {dom}G$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)=0$. abla G\colon D	o N_{\mathbb R}$ is a Borel map, and the complement of $D$ in the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$ is a null set. Therefore the complement of $D$ in $\operatorname {dom}G$ is a null set; it is a Borel set, because $\operatorname {dom}G= igcup _ k\{ G\leq k\} $ is a countable union of closed sets, $G$ being lower semicontinuous. Let $p\in D$. Then $\partial G(p)=\{ 
abla G(p)\} $. Indeed, $\partial G(p)$ is nonempty by proposition 21.2.4 , and every subgradient of $G$ at $p$ is also a subgradient at $p$ of the restriction of $G$ to the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$, whose only subgradient at $p$ is $
abla G(p)$ by proposition 21.2.4 (3). Hence theorem 21.3.2 gives, for every $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  p\in \partial F(E)\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad 
abla G(p)\in E.  \] Every subgradient of $F$ lies in $\operatorname {dom}G$, so $\partial F(E)$ differs from the Borel set $(
abla G)^{-1}(E)\cap D$ by a subset of the fixed null set $\operatorname {dom}G\setminus D$. Hence $\partial F(E)$ is measurable for the completed measure, and $\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))=\operatorname {vol}((
abla G)^{-1}(E)\cap D)$. This proves the pushforward formula, which in turn shows that $E\mapsto n!\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))$ is countably additive on Borel sets. With the mollifiers $ho _\varepsilon $ of lemma 21.4.3 , in the same coordinates, the functions $F_\varepsilon =F*ho _\varepsilon $ are smooth and convex, and they converge to $F$ locally uniformly, by that lemma. Hence, for $\varepsilon \leq 1$, the Hessians $D^2F_\varepsilon $ are bounded on each compact set $K$ by the bound of $D^2F$ on the set of points at distance at most $1$ from $K$, and by theorem 2.8.3 they converge to $D^2F(x)$ at every point $x$ that is a Lebesgue point of all the entries $H_{kl}$, that is, almost everywhere. Indeed, after the expansion, a term $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_{\sigma (1)},\ldots ,F_{\sigma (n)})$ with $\sigma \colon \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} 	o \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $ appears with total coefficient $\sum _{J\supset \sigma (\{ 1,\ldots ,n\} )}(-1)^{n-|J|}$, which vanishes unless $\sigma $ is a bijection, and the $n!$ bijections all give $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$ by symmetry. For every $J$, $\sum _{j\in J}F_{j,\varepsilon }	o \sum _{j\in J}F_ j$ locally uniformly as $\varepsilon 	o 0$ (lemma 2.5.1 (1)). Let $\varepsilon $ run through a sequence tending to zero. We add two complements. First, the convex envelope of finitely many closed convex functions whose effective domains lie in a common compact set, such as the conjugates of finitely many functions in $\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$, is closed, and the infimum defining it is attained. Second, vague convergence of real Monge–Ampère measures improves to narrow convergence when the total masses converge, as they do for functions of full mass. Lemma 21.6.1 . FCDAD9CEC8CE Let $G_1,\ldots ,G_ r$, with $r\geq 1$, be closed proper convex functions on a finite-dimensional real vector space, whose effective domains lie in a common compact set $K$, and let $H$ be the largest convex function below $\min _ iG_ i$, given by the formula of proposition 21.3.3 (2). Then $H$ is closed and proper, and at every point $x$ with $H(x)<+\infty $ the infimum defining $H(x)$ is attained. Consequently $H=(\max _ iG_ i^*)^*$. In particular, if $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is a convex body and $F_1,\ldots ,F_ r\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$, then the convex envelope of $F_1^*,\ldots ,F_ r^*$ is closed and equals $(\max _ iF_ i)^*$. Proof. Each $G_ i$ is bounded below: the increasing open sets $\{ G_ i>-k\} $, $k\in \mathbb N$, cover the compact set $K$, because $G_ i$ is lower semicontinuous and does not take the value $-\infty $, so one of them contains $K$; and $G_ i=+\infty $ outside $K$. Let $B$ be a common lower bound. In a combination $\sum _ j\lambda _ jG_{i_ j}(x_ j)$ as in proposition 21.3.3 (2), the terms with the same function $G_ i$ can be merged: if $\Lambda _ i$ is the sum of their weights, the convexity of $G_ i$ gives $\sum _{j:i_ j=i}\lambda _ jG_ i(x_ j)\geq \Lambda _ iG_ i(y_ i)$ with $y_ i=\Lambda _ i^{-1}\sum _{j:i_ j=i}\lambda _ jx_ j$, and the barycenter is unchanged. Hence it suffices to consider combinations $\sum _{\lambda _ i>0}\lambda _ iG_ i(x_ i)$ with one point $x_ i\in \operatorname {dom}G_ i$ for each $i$ and weights $\lambda _ i\geq 0$ summing to one; for an index $i$ with $\lambda _ i=0$ we let $x_ i$ be a fixed point of $\operatorname {dom}G_ i$, and the corresponding term is omitted. F2FABB0A312F Let $\mu _ j$ and $\mu $ be finite positive Radon measures on a finite-dimensional real vector space $W$ such that $\mu _ j	o \mu $ vaguely and $\mu _ j(W)	o \mu (W)$. Then $\int h\, \mathrm d\mu _ j	o \int h\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every bounded continuous function $h$ on $W$, that is, $\mu _ j	o \mu $ narrowly (section 2.6 ). In particular, if $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is a convex body, $F_ j,F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and $F_ j	o F$ locally uniformly, then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)	o \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ narrowly. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$. By inner regularity there is a compact set $S$ with $\mu (W\setminus S)<\varepsilon $; let $\eta $ be a continuous function with compact support, $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ and $\eta =1$ on $S$. Since $\int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu _ j	o \int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu $ and the total masses converge, we have \[  \lim _ j\int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ j =\int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu <\varepsilon ,  \] so that $\mu _ j(W\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\eta )\leq \int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ j<\varepsilon $ for all large $j$. Thus the sequence $(\mu _ j)$ is eventually uniformly tight, and proposition 2.6.3 gives narrow convergence. (If $W$ is a point, every function on $W$ has compact support, and vague and narrow convergence coincide.) For the real Monge–Ampère measures, theorem 21.5.2 gives vague convergence and the common total mass $n!\operatorname {vol}(P)$. $\square$

F2FABB0A312F Let $\mu _ j$ and $\mu $ be finite positive Radon measures on a finite-dimensional real vector space $W$ such that $\mu _ j\to \mu $ vaguely and $\mu _ j(W)\to \mu (W)$. Then $\int h\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\to \int h\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every bounded continuous function $h$ on $W$, that is, $\mu _ j\to \mu $ narrowly (section 2.6 ). In particular, if $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is a convex body, $F_ j,F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and $F_ j\to F$ locally uniformly, then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)\to \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ narrowly. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$. By inner regularity there is a compact set $S$ with $\mu (W\setminus S)<\varepsilon $; let $\eta $ be a continuous function with compact support, $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ and $\eta =1$ on $S$. Since $\int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu _ j\to \int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu $ and the total masses converge, we have \[  \lim _ j\int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ j =\int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu <\varepsilon ,  \] so that $\mu _ j(W\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\eta )\leq \int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ j<\varepsilon $ for all large $j$.
