Proposition 21.9.2 . 7B4A7CC50CDC The $T$-orbits in $X_ P$ are indexed by the faces $Q$ of $P$, and the orbit indexed by $Q$ has dimension $\dim Q$. The closure of the orbit indexed by $Q$ is the union of the orbits indexed by the faces of $P$ contained in $Q$. The complement of $\iota (T)$ is the union of the $T$-invariant prime divisors $D_ho $, the closures of the orbits indexed by the facets $ho $. For every $m\in M$ and every facet $ho $, the character $\chi ^ m$ extends to a meromorphic function on $X_ P$, with order \[  \operatorname {ord}_{D_ho }\chi ^ m=\langle m,u_ho angle  \] along $D_ho $. Finally, for every vertex $v$ of $P$ and every $m\in M$, the character $\chi ^ m$ is holomorphic on the chart $U_ v$ if and only if $\langle m,xangle \geq 0$ for all $x$ in the cone $\sigma _{\{ v\} }$ of proposition 21.9.1 . Proof. Fix a vertex $v$ and use the chart $U_ v\cong \mathbb C^ n$ of theorem 21.8.3 . For $	au \in T$ we have $w_ i(	au \cdot z)=\chi ^{e_ i}(	au )w_ i(z)$, and $	au \mapsto (\chi ^{e_ i}(	au ))_ i$ maps $T$ onto $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$; so $T$ acts on $U_ v$ by independent scalings of the coordinates. The orbits in $U_ v$ are therefore the sets \[  O_{v,I}=\{ w:w_ i=0	ext{ for }i\in I,\  w_ j
eq 0	ext{ for }j
otin I\} ,\qquad I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} ,  \] and $O_{v,I}$ has dimension $n-|I|$. Let $Q_{v,I}=\{ m\in P:\ell _ i(m)=0	ext{ for }i\in I\} $. It is a face, namely the set where $\sum _{i\in I}\langle \cdot ,u_ iangle $ is minimal on $P$. It contains $v$ and the points $v+se_ j$ for $j
otin I$ and small $s>0$, and it lies in $v+\operatorname {span}\{ e_ j:j
otin I\} $, because $m-v=\sum _ i\ell _ i(m)e_ i$; so $\dim Q_{v,I}=n-|I|$. Since $Z_ m/Z_ v=\prod _ iw_ i^{\ell _ i(m)}$, a homogeneous coordinate $Z_ m$, $m\in A$, is nonzero on $O_{v,I}$ if and only if $\ell _ i(m)=0$ for all $i\in I$, that is, if and only if $m\in Q_{v,I}$. The charts $U_ v$ are $T$-invariant, because the action of $T$ multiplies $Z_ v$ by $\chi ^ v(	au )
eq 0$. Hence every orbit $O$ in $X_ P$ meets, and therefore lies in, some chart $U_ v$, so it is one of the sets $O_{v,I}$. The set of $m\in A$ with $Z_ m
eq 0$ on $O$ does not depend on the chart, and it equals $Q_{v,I}\cap A$; since a face is the convex hull of its vertices, which are lattice points, $Q_{v,I}$ is the convex hull of this set. Thus each orbit $O$ determines a face $Q(O)$, with $\dim Q(O)=\dim O$. Distinct orbits determine distinct faces: if $Q(O)=Q(O')=Q$ and $v$ is a vertex of $Q$, then $Z_ v
eq 0$ on both orbits, so both lie in $U_ v$, where an orbit is determined by the set of indices $i$ with $v+e_ i
otin Q$. Every face $Q$ arises: choose a vertex $v\in Q$ and let $I$ be the set of indices of the facets at $v$ that contain $Q$; then $Q_{v,I}=Q$, because $Q$ is the intersection of $P$ with the facets containing it (proposition 21.9.1 ), and these facets all pass through $v$. We write $O_ Q$ for the orbit of the face $Q$; in particular $O_ P=\iota (T)$. The closure $\overline{O_ Q}$ is $T$-invariant, hence a union of orbits, and it lies in the closed set $\{ Z_ m=0	ext{ for }m\in A\setminus Q\} $. If $O_{Q'}\subset \overline{O_ Q}$, then $Q'\cap A\subset Q$, and so $Q'\subset Q$. Conversely, let $Q'\subset Q$ be faces, let $v$ be a vertex of $Q'$, and let $I\subset I'$ be the index sets of $Q$ and $Q'$ at $v$. A point $w\in O_{Q'}=O_{v,I'}$ is the limit as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ of the points obtained from $w$ by replacing the coordinates $w_ i=0$, $i\in I'\setminus I$, by $\varepsilon $, and these points lie in $O_{v,I}=O_ Q$. Hence $O_{Q'}\subset \overline{O_ Q}$. Let $ho $ be a facet and $D_ho =\overline{O_ho }$. If $v\in ho $ and $ho $ is the $i$th facet at $v$, the orbits in $U_ v$ indexed by faces contained in $ho $ are the sets $O_{v,I}$ with $i\in I$, so $D_ho \cap U_ v=\{ w_ i=0\} $; if $v
otin ho $, then $D_ho \cap U_ v=\varnothing $, because $Z_ v=0$ on $D_ho $. Hence $D_ho $ is a $T$-invariant closed submanifold of codimension one. Every proper face is contained in a facet, being the intersection of the facets containing it; hence $X_ P\setminus \iota (T)$, the union of the orbits of the proper faces, is the union of the divisors $D_ho $. Each $D_ho $ is irreducible, that is, not the union of two analytic subsets different from $D_ho $. First, $D_ho $ is connected, being the closure of the orbit $O_ho $: in a chart $U_ v$ in which $ho $ is the $i$th facet at $v$, the coordinates $w_ j$, $j
eq i$, identify $O_ho =O_{v,\{ i\} }$ with the connected set $(\mathbb C^*)^{n-1}$. Next, let $Z\subsetneq D_ho $ be an analytic subset. The set of interior points of $Z$ in $D_ho $ is open, and it is closed in $D_ho $. Indeed, if $p$ lies in its closure, then $p\in Z$, and on a connected coordinate neighborhood of $p$ in $D_ho $ the local holomorphic functions defining $Z$ vanish on a nonempty open set, hence identically by the identity theorem, so that $p$ is an interior point. As $D_ho $ is connected and $Z
eq D_ho $, the set $Z$ has empty interior in $D_ho $. If $D_ho =Z_1\cup Z_2$ with analytic subsets $Z_1,Z_2
eq D_ho $, then the nonempty open set $D_ho \setminus Z_1$ would be contained in $Z_2$, which has empty interior. Let $m\in M$. Since $m=\sum _ j\langle m,u_ jangle e_ j$, the character $\chi ^ m$ is the Laurent monomial $\prod _ jw_ j^{\langle m,u_ jangle }$ in the coordinates of $U_ v$. Hence it extends to a meromorphic function on each $U_ v$, and these extensions agree on the dense set $\iota (T)$, hence on overlaps. Near each point of the dense orbit $O_ho \cap U_ v$ of $D_ho \cap U_ v=\{ w_ i=0\} $, it is $w_ i^{\langle m,u_ iangle }$ times a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function; so its order along $D_ho $, the difference of the orders of numerator and denominator in the sense of definition 6.12.3 , is $\langle m,u_ iangle =\langle m,u_ho angle $. In particular, $\chi ^ m$ is holomorphic on $U_ v\cong \mathbb C^ n$ if and only if all the exponents $\langle m,u_ jangle $ are nonnegative, that is, if and only if $\langle m,xangle \geq 0$ for every $x$ in $\sigma _{\{ v\} }=\operatorname {cone}(u_1,\ldots ,u_ n)$. $\square$

title: Proposition 21.9.3
text: Proposition 21.9.3 . C62B8871AA1C Let $v$ and $v'$ be vertices of $P$, with primitive edge bases $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ and $e_1',\ldots ,e_ n'$ and vertex charts $w$ and $w'$, and let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be the inward normals of the facets through $v$, as in lemma 21.8.2 (4). A lattice point $m\in M$ satisfies $\langle m,x\rangle \geq 0$ for all $x\in \sigma _{\{ v\} }$ if and only if $m=\sum _ jc_ je_ j$ with integers $c_ j\geq 0$. Consequently, the characters that are holomorphic on $U_ v$ are exactly the monomials $w^ c=\prod _ jw_ j^{c_ j}$, $c\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 0}^ n$. The character $\chi ^{v'-v}$ is holomorphic on $U_ v$, and $U_ v\cap U_{v'}$ is the set of points of $U_ v$ at which it does not vanish. On this set \[  w'_ i=\prod _ jw_ j^{\langle e'_ i,u_ j\rangle }\qquad (1\leq i\leq n),  \] where the factors with negative exponents do not vanish. Let $Q$ be the intersection of $P$ with the facets containing both $v$ and $v'$, the smallest face of $P$ containing $v$ and $v'$. Then \[  \sigma _{\{ v\} }\cap \sigma _{\{ v'\} }=\sigma _ Q=\{ x\in \sigma _{\{ v\} }:\langle v'-v,x\rangle =0\} .  \] Proof. (1) Since $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ is the basis of $N$ dual to $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$, every $m\in M$ is $m=\sum _ j\langle m,u_ j\rangle e_ j$ with integer coefficients, and $\sigma _{\{ v\} }=\operatorname {cone}(u_1,\ldots ,u_ n)$. Hence $\langle m,\cdot \rangle \geq 0$ on $\sigma _{\{ v\} }$ if and only if all coefficients $\langle m,u_ j\rangle $ are nonnegative. The second assertion follows from the last assertion of proposition 21.9.2 , since $\chi ^ m=\prod _ jw_ j^{\langle m,u_ j\rangle }$ on $U_ v$. (2) By theorem 21.8.3 , $Z_{v'}/Z_ v=\prod _ jw_ j^{b_ j(v')}$ on $U_ v$, with $b_ j(v')=\ell _ j(v')=\langle v'-v,u_ j\rangle \geq 0$; this holomorphic function is the extension of $\chi ^{v'-v}$ to $U_ v$. Since $U_ v\cap U_{v'}=U_ v\cap \{ Z_{v'}\neq 0\} $, the first assertion follows. On $U_ v\cap U_{v'}$ we have $w'_ i=Z_{v'+e_ i'}/Z_{v'}=w^{b(v'+e_ i')}/w^{b(v')}$, a quotient of monomials whose denominator does not vanish there, and $b_ j(v'+e'_ i)-b_ j(v')=\langle e'_ i,u_ j\rangle $. A negative exponent $\langle e'_ i,u_ j\rangle $ forces $b_ j(v')>0$, so the corresponding factor $w_ j$ divides the denominator and does not vanish on $U_ v\cap U_{v'}$. (3) By proposition 21.9.1 , applied to the faces $\{ v\} $ and $\{ v'\} $, the set $Q$ is the smallest face containing $v$ and $v'$, and $\sigma _{\{ v\} }\cap \sigma _{\{ v'\} }=\sigma _ Q$. The facets containing $Q$ are the facets $\rho _ j$ through $v$ with $\ell _ j(v')=0$. If $x=\sum _ j\alpha _ ju_ j\in \sigma _{\{ v\} }$ with $\alpha _ j\geq 0$, then $\langle v'-v,x\rangle =\sum _ j\alpha _ j\ell _ j(v')$ is a sum of nonnegative terms, so it vanishes if and only if $\alpha _ j=0$ whenever $\ell _ j(v')>0$, that is, if and only if $x\in \operatorname {cone}\{ u_ j:\ell _ j(v')=0\} =\sigma _ Q$. $\square$

title: Lemma 21.9.4
text: Lemma 21.9.4 . 00432B20A966 Let $n\geq 1$, and let $f$ be a holomorphic function on $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$. For $m\in \mathbb Z^ n$ and $r\in (0,\infty )^ n$ put \[  c_ m(r)=\frac1{(2\pi )^ n}\int _{[0,2\pi ]^ n}f(r_1\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta _1},\ldots ,r_ n\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta _ n})\, r^{-m}\mathrm e^{-\mathrm i\langle m,\theta \rangle }\, \mathrm d\theta ,  \] where $r^{-m}=\prod _ jr_ j^{-m_ j}$ and $\langle m,\theta \rangle =\sum _ jm_ j\theta _ j$. Then $c_ m=c_ m(r)$ does not depend on $r$, and the Laurent series $\sum _{m\in \mathbb Z^ n}c_ mz^ m$, where $z^ m=\prod _ jz_ j^{m_ j}$, converges normally on every compact subset of $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$, with sum $f$. If a series $\sum _ mc'_ mz^ m$ converges normally to $f$ on one torus $\{ z:|z_ j|=r_ j\text{ for all }j\} $, then $c'_ m=c_ m$ for every $m$. If $f$ extends holomorphically to $\mathbb C^ n$, then $c_ m=0$ unless $m_ j\geq 0$ for every $j$. Proof. Fix $j$ and the variables other than $z_ j$. The resulting function $g(\zeta )$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C^*$, and for $k\in \mathbb Z$ the integral $\frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }g(\varrho \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta })\varrho ^{-k}\mathrm e^{-\mathrm ik\theta }\, \mathrm d\theta =\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=\varrho }g(\zeta )\zeta ^{-k-1}\, \mathrm d\zeta $ does not depend on $\varrho >0$, by Cauchy's theorem on the annulus between two such circles. Integrating over the other angles, by Fubini's theorem, we see that $c_ m(r)$ does not depend on $r_ j$; hence it does not depend on $r$. The definition gives the Cauchy estimates $|c_ m|\leq C(r)r^{-m}$, where $C(r)$ is the maximum of $|f|$ on the torus $\{ |z_ j|=r_ j\} $. Let $K\subset (\mathbb C^*)^ n$ be compact, and choose $0<a\leq b$ with $a\leq |z_ j|\leq b$ on $K$ for all $j$. Given $m$, take $r_ j=2b$ if $m_ j\geq 0$ and $r_ j=a/2$ if $m_ j<0$. Then, for $z\in K$, \[  |c_ mz^ m|\leq C_ K\prod _ j\Bigl (\frac{|z_ j|}{r_ j}\Bigr )^{m_ j}\leq C_ K2^{-(|m_1|+\cdots +|m_ n|)},  \] where $C_ K$ is the largest of the numbers $C(r)$ for the $2^ n$ tori with $r_ j\in \{ a/2,2b\} $. Since $\sum _{m\in \mathbb Z^ n}2^{-(|m_1|+\cdots +|m_ n|)}=3^ n$, the series converges normally on $K$. We show by induction on $n$ that its sum is $f$. For $n=1$ this is the Laurent theorem of one-variable theory, with the coefficients given by the integral above. Let $n\geq 2$, and write $z=(z',z_ n)$ with $z'\in (\mathbb C^*)^{n-1}$. For fixed $z'$, the one-variable theorem gives $f(z',z_ n)=\sum _ ka_ k(z')z_ n^ k$ with $a_ k(z')=\frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }f(z',\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta })\mathrm e^{-\mathrm ik\theta }\, \mathrm d\theta $. Differentiation under the integral sign shows that $a_ k$ is smooth and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations, so it is holomorphic on $(\mathbb C^*)^{n-1}$, and by Fubini's theorem its Laurent coefficients are the numbers $c_{(m',k)}$, $m'\in \mathbb Z^{n-1}$. By the induction hypothesis, $a_ k(z')=\sum _{m'}c_{(m',k)}z'^{m'}$, so $f(z)=\sum _ k\sum _{m'}c_{(m',k)}z'^{m'}z_ n^ k$. This double series converges absolutely, by the previous paragraph, so it may be summed as $\sum _ mc_ mz^ m$. For the uniqueness, integrate the normally convergent series $\sum _{m''}c'_{m''}r^{m''}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\langle m'',\theta \rangle }=f(r_1\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta _1},\ldots )$ term by term against $(2\pi )^{-n}r^{-m}\mathrm e^{-\mathrm i\langle m,\theta \rangle }\, \mathrm d\theta $; since $\int _0^{2\pi }\mathrm e^{\mathrm il\theta }\, \mathrm d\theta =0$ for every integer $l\neq 0$, only the term $m''=m$ survives, and we obtain $c'_ m=c_ m(r)=c_ m$. Finally, if $f$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C^ n$, its Taylor series at the origin converges normally on every polydisc by ( 5.2.1 ), in particular on every torus, so by uniqueness the coefficients $c_ m$ are the Taylor coefficients for $m\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 0}^ n$ and vanish for all other $m$. $\square$

title: Theorem 21.9.5
text: Theorem 21.9.5 . 69D3D97E7701 There is a meromorphic section $s_0$ of $L$ with divisor \[  D_ P=\sum _\rho a_\rho D_\rho ,  \] so that $L$ is isomorphic to the line bundle $\mathcal O_{X_ P}(D_ P)$ of this divisor. For every integer $k\geq 0$, \[  H^0(X_ P,L^ k)=\bigoplus _{m\in kP\cap M}\mathbb C\, \chi ^ m s_0^ k,  \] where $0P=\{ 0\} $. Each summand is a line on which the natural action of $T$ is given by a character, and the dimensions $h^0(X_ P,L^ k)=\dim H^0(X_ P,L^ k)$ satisfy \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }\frac{n!}{k^ n}h^0(X_ P,L^ k)=n!\operatorname {vol}(P).  \] Proof. For vertices $v$ and $v'$, the coordinate sections satisfy $s_ v/s_{v'}=Z_ v/Z_{v'}=\chi ^{v-v'}$ on $\iota (T)$. Hence the section $s_0=\chi ^{-v}s_ v$ of $L$ over $\iota (T)$ does not depend on the vertex $v$. In the chart $U_ v$, its coefficient $\chi ^{-v}$ with respect to the frame $s_ v$ is a Laurent monomial in $w$, so $s_0$ extends to a meromorphic section on each $U_ v$; the extensions agree on overlaps, because they agree on the dense set $\iota (T)$. By proposition 21.9.2 , if $v$ is a vertex of the facet $\rho $, then $\operatorname {ord}_{D_\rho }s_0=\operatorname {ord}_{D_\rho }\chi ^{-v}=-\langle v,u_\rho \rangle =a_\rho $, since $\ell _\rho (v)=0$. As $s_0$ has no zeros or poles on $\iota (T)$, its divisor is $D_ P$. Similarly, the meromorphic function $f_ v=\chi ^{-v}$ on $U_ v$ has divisor $\sum _{\rho \ni v}a_\rho (D_\rho \cap U_ v)$, which is the restriction of $D_ P$ to $U_ v$, because $D_\rho \cap U_ v=\varnothing $ for $v\notin \rho $. The line bundle $\mathcal O_{X_ P}(D_ P)$ of the divisor therefore has over $U_ v$ the local frame $1/f_ v$, and its transition functions, in the sense of definition 6.14.9 , are $f_{v'}/f_ v=\chi ^{v-v'}$. These are the transition functions of $L$ in the frames $s_ v$, since $s_ v=\chi ^{v-v'}s_{v'}$. Hence the map sending $s_ v$ to $1/f_ v$ for every vertex $v$ is an isomorphism $L\cong \mathcal O_{X_ P}(D_ P)$. Let $s$ be a holomorphic section of $L^ k$ and write $s=fs_0^ k$ on $\iota (T)$, with $f$ holomorphic on $T\cong (\mathbb C^*)^ n$. By lemma 21.9.4 , applied in the coordinates of a basis of $M$, we have $f=\sum _{m\in M}c_ m\chi ^ m$, with normal convergence on compact subsets of $T$. The coefficients $c_ m$ do not depend on the basis: a change of basis replaces each character by the corresponding monomial in the new coordinates and preserves normal convergence on compact sets, so the uniqueness assertion of the lemma applies. Now fix a vertex $v$. The coefficient $g_ v$ of $s$ with respect to the frame $s_ v^ k$ is a holomorphic function on $U_ v\cong \mathbb C^ n$, and on $\iota (T)$ \[  g_ v=f\chi ^{-kv}=\sum _ mc_ m\prod _ iw_ i^{\langle m-kv,u_ i\rangle }.  \] Since $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ is the basis of $N$ dual to the basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ of $M$, the map $m\mapsto (\langle m-kv,u_ i\rangle )_ i$ is a bijection of $M$ onto $\mathbb Z^ n$, so this is the Laurent expansion of $g_ v$ in the coordinates $w$. By the last assertion of lemma 21.9.4 , $c_ m=0$ unless $\langle m-kv,u_ i\rangle \geq 0$ for every facet $i$ at $v$. Since $\langle v,u_\rho \rangle =-a_\rho $ for $v\in \rho $, this condition reads $\langle m,u_\rho \rangle +ka_\rho \geq 0$. Every facet contains a vertex, so for $k>0$ the conditions at all vertices say exactly that $m/k\in P$, that is, $m\in kP$. For $k=0$ they say that $\langle m,u_\rho \rangle \geq 0$ for every $\rho $; then $p+sm\in P$ for $p\in P$ and all $s\geq 0$, so $m=0$ by boundedness. Thus only the finitely many $m\in kP\cap M$ occur. Hence $s=\sum _{m\in kP\cap M}c_ m\chi ^ ms_0^ k$ on the dense set $\iota (T)$, and therefore on $X_ P$, once we know that the sections on the right are holomorphic. Indeed, for $m\in kP\cap M$ all exponents $\langle m-kv,u_ i\rangle $ are nonnegative, so $\chi ^ ms_0^ k$ extends holomorphically to every chart. Finally, the uniqueness of Laurent coefficients shows that the sections $\chi ^ ms_0^ k$ are linearly independent. The action of $T$ on $\mathbb C^ A$ by $\tau \cdot (Z_ m)=(\chi ^ m(\tau )Z_ m)$ induces actions on the tautological line bundle (example 10.6.6 ), whose fiber over $[Z]$ is the line $\mathbb CZ$, on its dual $\mathcal O(1)$, on $L^ k$, and on $H^0(X_ P,L^ k)$ by $(\tau \cdot s)(x)=\tau \cdot s(\tau ^{-1}\cdot x)$. It multiplies the linear form $Z_ v$, and hence $s_ v$, by $\chi ^{-v}(\tau )$, and it maps the function $\chi ^ v$ to $\chi ^ v(\tau ^{-1}\, \cdot \, )=\chi ^{-v}(\tau )\chi ^ v$; therefore it fixes $s_0$ and multiplies $\chi ^ ms_0^ k$ by $\chi ^{-m}(\tau )$. So each summand is a line on which $T$ acts through a character. Finally, $h^0(X_ P,L^ k)=\# (kP\cap M)$, and the limit follows from theorem 21.7.3 . In dimension zero there is one section, and the volume is one. $\square$

title: 21.10 The Guillemin reference metric
text:
The Fubini–Study metric of theorem 21.8.3 already gives a smooth metric on $L$ with positive definite curvature form. In integrability calculations, however, it is useful to have a reference metric whose potential on $N_{\mathbb R}$ is the Legendre transform of an explicit function on $P$ whose gradient has logarithmic singularities along the facets. Guillemin's metric, defined through the entropy function $G_0$ below, has this property; the content of the next theorem is that it is nevertheless smooth on all of $X_ P$, with positive definite curvature form. Theorem 21.10.1 . B471B994CE64 With the convention $0\log 0=0$, define the closed proper convex function \[  G_0(m)=\sum _ho \ell _ho (m)\log \ell _ho (m)\quad (m\in P), \qquad G_0=+\infty \quad 	ext{outside }P,  \] and put $F_0=G_0^*$. Then $F_0$ is smooth on $N_{\mathbb R}$, its Hessian is positive definite, and $F_0\sim h_ P$. The gradient $
abla G_0$ is a diffeomorphism of $\operatorname{Int}P$ onto $N_{\mathbb R}$. abla G_0$ near the boundary of $P$ in the coordinates of a vertex chart (Step 2); the logarithmic singularities in $H_ v$ then cancel. Step 1: the potentials on $N_{\mathbb R}$. abla G_0=\sum _ho (\log \ell _ho +1)u_ho , \qquad D^2G_0=\sum _ho  rac{u_ho \otimes u_ho }{\ell _ho }.  \] The normals $u_ho $ span $N_{\mathbb R}$, since a nonzero $y\in M_{\mathbb R}$ annihilated by all of them would give $P+\mathbb Ry\subset P$ by the facet presentation, which is impossible because $P$ is bounded; so $D^2G_0(y,y)=\sum _ho \langle y,u_ho angle ^2/\ell _ho >0$ for $y
eq 0$, and the Hessian is positive definite. Let $x\in N_{\mathbb R}$. The continuous function $G_0-\langle \cdot ,xangle $ attains its minimum on the compact set $P$, and not at a boundary point $m_0$. Indeed, let $p\in \operatorname{Int}P$ and move from $m_0$ towards $p$: for each facet with $\ell _ho (m_0)=0$ we have $\ell _ho (m_0+s(p-m_0))=s\ell _ho (p)$ with $\ell _ho (p)>0$, and the term $s\ell _ho (p)\log (s\ell _ho (p))$ has right derivative $-\infty $ at $s=0$, while all other terms have finite derivatives; so the function decreases initially. The minimum is therefore attained in $\operatorname{Int}P$, at a solution of $
abla G_0(m)=x$. Conversely, every solution of $
abla G_0(m)=x$ in $\operatorname{Int}P$ is a minimum point, by convexity, and the minimum point is unique because $G_0$ is strictly convex on $\operatorname{Int}P$. Hence $
abla G_0$ is a smooth bijection of $\operatorname{Int}P$ onto $N_{\mathbb R}$ with invertible derivative, and so a diffeomorphism by the inverse function theorem. Writing $m(x)=(
abla G_0)^{-1}(x)$, we have $F_0(x)=\langle m(x),xangle -G_0(m(x))$, so $F_0$ is smooth, and differentiating gives $
abla F_0(x)=m(x)$ and $D^2F_0(x)=(D^2G_0(m(x)))^{-1}$, which is positive definite. Since $G_0$ is bounded on $P$, say $|G_0|\leq C$ there, we have $\chi _ P-C\leq G_0\leq \chi _ P+C$, and conjugation gives $h_ P-C\leq F_0\leq h_ P+C$. Step 2: local inversion at a boundary point. Fix a vertex $v$, number the facets at $v$ as in lemma 21.8.2 (4), and use on $M_{\mathbb R}$ the coordinates $t_ k=\ell _ k(m)$, so that $m=v+\sum _ kt_ ke_ k$, and on $N_{\mathbb R}$ the dual coordinates $x_ k=\langle e_ k,xangle $, so that $x=\sum _ kx_ ku_ k$ and $\langle m-v,xangle =\sum _ kt_ kx_ k$. If $z\in \iota (T)$ and $x=\operatorname {Trop}(z)$, then $x_ k=\log |\chi ^{e_ k}(z)|^2=\log |w_ k(z)|^2$. Let $w^0\in U_ v$, let $I=\{ i:w^0_ i=0\} $ and $J$ its complement, and let $Q=\{ m\in P:t_ i=0	ext{ for }i\in I\} $ be the corresponding face (proposition 21.9.2 ). Put $x^0_ j=\log |w^0_ j|^2$ for $j\in J$. The facet functions other than $t_ i$, $i\in I$, are positive on the relative interior of $Q$. Indeed, if such a function vanished at a point of the relative interior of $Q$, it would vanish on $Q$ by the observation preceding lemma 21.8.2 , so its facet would contain $Q$ and $v$. It would then be one of the facets at $v$ containing $Q$, and these are the facets $i\in I$, because $v+se_ j\in Q$ for $j\in J$ and small $s>0$. Now consider the function $G_0-\sum _{j\in J}t_ jx^0_ j$ on the compact set $Q$, on which the terms of the facets $i\in I$ vanish identically. As in Step 1, applied within the affine span of $Q$, its minimum is not attained on the relative boundary of $Q$. Indeed, if all facet functions other than $t_ i$, $i\in I$, are positive at a point of $Q$, then they are positive on a neighborhood of this point in the affine span $\{ t_ I=0\} $ of $Q$, which therefore lies in $Q$. Hence at a relative boundary point $m_0$ some facet function that is positive on the relative interior vanishes, and moving from $m_0$ towards a relative interior point decreases the function initially, as in Step 1. The minimum point $q$ is unique, because on the relative interior of $Q$ the Hessian of $G_0$ in the directions $e_ j$, $j\in J$, of $Q$ dominates the positive definite matrix $\operatorname {diag}(1/t_ j)_{j\in J}$ coming from the terms $t_ j\log t_ j$. Near $q$ all facet functions except $t_ i$, $i\in I$, are positive, so on a neighborhood $W$ of $q$ in $M_{\mathbb R}$ \[  G_0(t)=\sum _{i\in I}t_ i\log t_ i+g(t)\qquad (t\in P\cap W),  \] where $g$, the sum of the remaining terms, is smooth on $W$. Write $g_ k=\partial g/\partial t_ k$ and $g_{jk}=\partial ^2g/\partial t_ j\partial t_ k$. The point $q$ is characterized by $g_ j(q)=x_ j^0$ for $j\in J$, since on $Q$ we have $G_0=g$. At points of $\operatorname{Int}P\cap W$ the equation $
abla G_0(t)=x$ reads \[  x_ i=\log t_ i+1+g_ i(t)\quad (i\in I),\qquad x_ j=g_ j(t)\quad (j\in J).  \] Exponentiating the first equations and putting $y_ i=\mathrm e^{x_ i}$, which equals $|w_ i|^2$ on $\iota (T)$, we obtain the system $\Psi (t)=(y_ I,x_ J)$ with \[  \Psi (t)=\Bigl ( igl (t_ i\exp (1+g_ i(t)) igr )_{i\in I},\   igl (g_ j(t) igr )_{j\in J}\Bigr ),  \] a smooth map on all of $W$. At $t=q$, where $t_ I=0$, the Jacobian matrix of $\Psi $ is block triangular: its $I	imes I$ block is the diagonal matrix with entries $\exp (1+g_ i(q))>0$, its $I	imes J$ block vanishes, and its $J	imes J$ block $(g_{jk}(q))$ is positive definite, because $g$ contains the terms $t_ j\log t_ j$, $j\in J$, and its other terms are convex. Since $\Psi (q)=(0,x_ J^0)$, the inverse function theorem gives a smooth local inverse $t=\Psi ^{-1}(y_ I,x_ J)$ near $(0,x_ J^0)$, with values near $q$. For $y_ I\geq 0$ the solution satisfies \[  t_ i=y_ i\exp (-1-g_ i(t))\geq 0\quad (i\in I),  \] and its other facet functions are positive, so it lies in $P$. If $y_ I>0$, it lies in $\operatorname{Int}P$ and solves $
abla G_0(t)=x$ with $x_ i=\log y_ i$; since $
abla G_0$ is injective on $\operatorname{Int}P$, $t=
abla F_0(x)$. Step 3: smooth extension. Let $z\in \iota (T)$ be close to $w^0$, put $x=\operatorname {Trop}(z)$, and let $t$ be the coordinates of $
abla F_0(x)$. Since $F_0(x)=\langle 
abla F_0(x),xangle -G_0(
abla F_0(x))$ and $\log |\chi ^ v(z)|^2=\langle v,xangle $, we obtain, using the equations for $i\in I$, \[  H_ v=\sum _ kt_ kx_ k-\sum _{i\in I}t_ i\log t_ i-g(t) =\sum _{i\in I}t_ i(1+g_ i(t))+\sum _{j\in J}t_ jx_ j-g(t).  \] The singular logarithms have canceled. By Step 2, $t=\Psi ^{-1}(|w_ I|^2,\log |w_ J|^2)$, so the right-hand side is a smooth function $h(y_ I,x_ J)$ of $(y_ I,x_ J)=(|w_ I|^2,\log |w_ J|^2)$, which in turn is a smooth function of $w$ near $w^0$, because $w^0_ j
eq 0$ for $j\in J$. Hence $H_ v$ extends smoothly to a neighborhood of $w^0$, and, $w^0\in U_ v$ being arbitrary, to $U_ v$. Step 4: positivity. On $\iota (T)$ we have $\partial F_0/\partial x_ k=\langle 
abla F_0(x),u_ kangle =\langle v,u_ kangle +t_ k$, hence $\partial H_ v/\partial x_ k=t_ k$. In the variables $(y_ I,x_ J)$ this says \[   rac{\partial h}{\partial x_ j}=t_ j\quad (j\in J),\qquad  rac{\partial h}{\partial y_ i}= rac{t_ i}{y_ i}=\exp (-1-g_ i(t))\quad (i\in I),  \] and both identities persist at $y_ I=0$, because both sides are continuous functions of $(y_ I,x_ J)$. We now compute the complex Hessian of $H_ v$ at $w^0$, where $w_ I=0$. Since $\partial y_ i/\partial  ar w_ k=\delta _{ik}w_ i$ for $i\in I$ and $\partial x_ j/\partial  ar w_ k=\delta _{jk}/ ar w_ k$ for $j\in J$, the chain rule gives at $w^0$ \[   rac{\partial ^2H_ v}{\partial w_ i\partial  ar w_ k}=\delta _{ik} rac{\partial h}{\partial y_ i}\quad (i\in I),\qquad  rac{\partial ^2H_ v}{\partial w_ j\partial  ar w_ k}= rac1{w_ j ar w_ k} rac{\partial ^2h}{\partial x_ j\partial x_ k}\quad (j,k\in J);  \] all other terms contain a factor $w_ i$ or $ ar w_ i$ with $i\in I$. On $\{ y_ I=0\} $ we have $t_ I=0$ and $x_ J=g_ J(t)$, so $\partial ^2h/\partial x_ j\partial x_ k=\partial t_ j/\partial x_ k$ is the inverse of the positive definite matrix $(g_{jk})_{j,k\in J}$. Hence the complex Hessian of $H_ v$ at $w^0$, where $t=q$, is block diagonal, with the positive numbers $\exp (-1-g_ i(q))$ on the $I$ block and, on the $J$ block, a positive definite matrix congruent to $(\partial t_ j/\partial x_ k)$ by the invertible diagonal matrix $\operatorname {diag}(1/w_ j)$. It is therefore positive definite at $w^0$. Every point of $U_ v$ arises as such a $w^0$ (with $I=\varnothing $ on $\iota (T)$), so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ v$ is positive definite on $U_ v$. Step 5: the metric. On $\iota (T)$, for vertices $v$ and $v'$, we have $H_ v-H_{v'}=\log |\chi ^{v'-v}|^2$ and $s_ v=\chi ^{v-v'}s_{v'}$. The function $\chi ^{v-v'}=s_ v/s_{v'}$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero on $U_ v\cap U_{v'}$, so both sides of the identity $\mathrm e^{-H_ v}=|\chi ^{v-v'}|^2\mathrm e^{-H_{v'}}$ are continuous on $U_ v\cap U_{v'}$; as they agree on the dense subset $\iota (T)$, the identity holds on $U_ v\cap U_{v'}$. Thus the squared norms $|s_ v|^2=\mathrm e^{-H_ v}$ satisfy the transition law of definition 6.14.9 and define a smooth quadratic metric on $L$, with curvature $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ v$ on $U_ v$, which is positive definite by Step 4. For $	au \in T_ c$ we have $|\chi ^ m(	au )|=1$, so $\operatorname {Trop}(	au z)=\operatorname {Trop}(z)$, the weights $H_ v$ are $T_ c$-invariant, and $T_ c$ multiplies the frames $s_ v$ by factors of modulus one; hence the metric is $T_ c$-invariant. On $\iota (T)$ the curvature is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ v=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(F_0\circ \operatorname {Trop})$, because $\log |\chi ^ v|^2$ is pluriharmonic; since $\iota (T)$ is dense, the curvature form is the unique smooth extension of this form and represents $c_1(L)$ (section 10.6 ). In dimension zero the facet sum and both potentials vanish, $L$ is trivial over a point, and its curvature is zero. $\square$

title: 9.1 Complex spaces and modifications
text: Analytic sets enter pluripotential theory as the pole sets of potentials with analytic singularities, as the zero sets of the ideals that describe these poles, and as the exceptional divisors of modifications. This appendix collects the facts about analytic sets, reduced complex spaces and modifications that are used from section 6.6 on: for multiplier ideals and Lelong numbers along divisors in section 6.6 , for analytic singularities and their log resolutions in section 6.13 , for currents supported on analytic sets in section 10.1 , and for the non-Kähler locus in section 16.10 . It can be consulted when these tools first appear. Besides results of the earlier chapters, such as the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 5.5.2 ), only two existence theorems are used without proof: the resolution of singularities and the principalization of coherent ideals, stated as theorem 9.6.6 , theorem 9.6.7 . The local theory rests on the Weierstrass division theorem. It shows that the ring of germs of holomorphic functions is Noetherian and, through Oka's theorem, that the sheaf of holomorphic functions is coherent, so that statements about one stalk extend to a neighborhood. The local parametrization theorem (theorem 9.3.4 ) presents an irreducible germ of an analytic set as a finite branched covering of a polydisc. From it we deduce the analytic Nullstellensatz, the basic properties of dimension, Cartan's theorem on the coherence of the ideal sheaf of an analytic set, and the decomposition of an analytic set into irreducible components. We also show that a closed real $(1,1)$-current with measure coefficients supported on a nowhere dense analytic set is a combination of currents of integration along hypersurfaces (theorem 9.3.20 ). One phenomenon requires care: an irreducible analytic set can have several local branches at one point. The normalization (theorem 9.4.6 ) separates these branches; its holomorphic functions are the weakly holomorphic functions, that is, the functions that are holomorphic on the regular locus and locally bounded near the singular locus. The cusp shows that a space with only one branch at each point need not be normal (example 9.4.10 ). For modifications, explicit charts describe blowups along submanifolds and the transformation of ideals under them (proposition 9.6.2 , proposition 9.6.3 ); together with the two existence theorems they give log resolutions of coherent ideals. Remmert's theorem, proved together with the Remmert–Stein extension theorem, shows that images of analytic sets under proper holomorphic maps, in particular the images of exceptional divisors, are analytic (theorem 9.7.2 ). We then prove a relative principalization theorem, which controls an ideal and its restriction to a submanifold simultaneously (theorem 9.7.5 ), show that proper bimeromorphic maps onto spaces with one local branch at each point have connected fibers (theorem 9.8.1 ), and prove that every prime divisor over a compact complex space appears on a model obtained by finitely many blowups with smooth centers (theorem 9.8.6 ). The last section defines plurisubharmonic functions on reduced complex spaces by local extension to an ambient space, proves that they are constant on compact connected spaces, and shows that they are locally bounded above near analytic subsets of codimension at least two. Holomorphic curves through singular points, constructed in section 9.5 , reduce these statements to the maximum principle in one variable. Historical remarks and references for this appendix are collected in subsection 25.1.21 .

title: 9.2 Division and finite analytic modules
text:
Let $n\geq 0$. We write $\mathcal O_ n$ for the ring of germs at $0\in \mathbb C^ n$ of holomorphic functions; two functions defined near $0$ have the same germ if they agree on some neighborhood of $0$, and identities between germs are understood in this sense. By the iterated Cauchy formula of section 5.2 , every germ is given near $0$ by its Taylor series ( 5.2.1 ), which converges normally on a small polydisc. Conversely, a power series $\sum _\alpha c_\alpha z^\alpha $ with $\sum _\alpha |c_\alpha |r^{|\alpha |}<\infty $ for some $r>0$ defines a holomorphic function on the polydisc $\{ |z_ j|<r\} $: since $|c_\alpha |\leq Cr^{-|\alpha |}$, the series of partial derivatives of each order converge normally on every polydisc $\{ |z_ j|\leq s\} $ with $s<r$, so the sum is smooth, may be differentiated termwise, and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations. Thus germs are the same as convergent power series, $\mathcal O_ n=\mathbb C\{ z_1,\ldots ,z_ n\} $, and $\mathcal O_0=\mathbb C$. The ring $\mathcal O_ n$ is an integral domain: if $fg=0$ near $0$ and $f
eq 0$, then $g$ vanishes on the nonempty open subset $\{ f
eq 0\} $ of a connected neighborhood of $0$, so $g=0$ by the identity theorem. A germ that does not vanish at the origin has a holomorphic reciprocal near the origin; hence $\mathcal O_ n$ is a local ring, whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ consists of the germs vanishing at the origin. The order $\operatorname {ord}_0f$ of a nonzero germ $f$ is the degree of the first nonzero homogeneous term of its Taylor expansion. The order of a product is the sum of the orders. Indeed, if $P_ s$ and $Q_ t$ are the first nonzero homogeneous terms of $f$ and $g$, then $P_ sQ_ t$ is the homogeneous term of degree $s+t$ of $fg$. It is not zero: a polynomial vanishing on a nonempty open set is zero, so the sets $\{ P_ s
eq 0\} $ and $\{ Q_ t
eq 0\} $ are open and dense, and therefore meet. Hence every element of the $k$th power $\mathfrak m^ k$ has order at least $k$. Conversely, let $f=\sum _ eta c_ eta z^ eta $ have order at least $k$. Assign to each $ eta $ with $| eta |\geq k$ the first multi-index $\alpha \leq  eta $ with $|\alpha |=k$ in the lexicographic order, and let $f_\alpha =\sum c_ eta z^{ eta -\alpha }$, the sum over the $ eta $ assigned to $\alpha $. These series converge normally wherever the series of $f$ does, so $f_\alpha \in \mathcal O_ n$, and $f=\sum _{|\alpha |=k}z^\alpha f_\alpha \in \mathfrak m^ k$. Thus $\operatorname {ord}_0f\geq k$ if and only if $f\in \mathfrak m^ k$. A holomorphic change of coordinates fixing $0$ induces a ring automorphism of $\mathcal O_ n$ that preserves $\mathfrak m$ and its powers; so the order does not depend on the coordinates. For a holomorphic function $f$ near a point $a$ of a complex manifold whose germ at $a$ is nonzero, $\operatorname {ord}_ af$ is the order of its germ in local coordinates centered at $a$. This is the order used for Lelong numbers in proposition 6.7.9 ; section 6.6 also defines the order of a coherent ideal at a point and the order along a prime divisor (definition 6.12.3 ). Write points of $\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, as $(z',w)$ with $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$. A Weierstrass polynomial of degree $m\geq 0$ in $w$ is a polynomial \[  P(z',w)=w^ m+a_1(z')w^{m-1}+\cdots +a_ m(z'),\qquad a_ j\in \mathcal O_{n-1},\quad a_ j(0)=0.  \] We shall often use the following bound for the roots $t$ of a monic polynomial with complex coefficients: 667706D7A5E8 9.2.1  egin{equation}  t^ m+d_1t^{m-1}+\cdots +d_ m=0\quad \Longrightarrow \quad |t|\le 2\max _{1\leq j\leq m}|d_ j|^{1/j}. \end{equation} Indeed, otherwise $|d_ j|<(|t|/2)^ j$ for all $j$, and dividing the equation by $t^ m$ gives $1\le \sum _{j=1}^ m|d_ j/t^ j|<\sum _{j=1}^ m2^{-j}<1$. In particular, the roots of $P(z',\cdot )$ tend to $0$ as $z'	o 0$. A germ $f\in \mathcal O_ n$ is distinguished in $w$ if $f(0,w)$ is not identically zero. If $f(0,w)$ vanishes to order $m\geq 1$ at $w=0$, the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 5.5.2 ) writes $f$ as a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $m$; if $f(0)
eq 0$, then $f$ is itself a unit, which is the case $m=0$. Every nonzero germ becomes distinguished in the last coordinate after a linear change of coordinates. Indeed, let $P_ s$ be the first nonzero homogeneous term of $f$ and choose $v$ with $P_ s(v)
eq 0$; in linear coordinates whose last basis vector is $v$, we have $f(0,w)=P_ s(v)w^ s+O(w^{s+1})$, which vanishes to order exactly $s$, the order of $f$. Since $P_ s
eq 0$, the admissible vectors $v$ form a dense open set. Hence the new coordinates can be chosen arbitrarily close to given ones, and finitely many nonzero germs become distinguished simultaneously if $v$ avoids the zero set of the product of their first homogeneous terms. Proposition 9.2.2 (Weierstrass division) . 611958EF0AB8 Let $n\geq 1$ and $m\geq 0$, and let $P$ be a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $m$ in $w$. Then every germ $f\in \mathcal O_ n$ can be written uniquely as \[  f=Pq+R,\qquad q\in \mathcal O_ n,\quad R\in \mathcal O_{n-1}[w],\quad \deg _ w R<m.  \] Moreover, let $\Delta '\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$ be a polydisc centered at $0$ and $\Delta =\{ |w|<r\} $ a disc such that the coefficients of $P$ are holomorphic near $\overline{\Delta '}$ and all roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in \Delta '$, lie in $\{ |w|\leq ho \} $ for some $ho <r$; such polydiscs $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ exist with arbitrarily small radii. Then every holomorphic function $f$ on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ can be written uniquely as $f=Pq+R$, where $q$ is holomorphic on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ and $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$ with holomorphic coefficients on $\Delta '$; for every $s\in (ho ,r)$, $z'\in \Delta '$ and $|w|<s$, A61080C94D0B 9.2.3  egin{equation}   egin{aligned}  q(z',w)& = rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s}  rac{f(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\  R(z',w)& = rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s}  rac{f(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )}\,   rac{P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w)}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta . \end{aligned} \end{equation} Division is a bounded linear operation on bounded holomorphic functions on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $: there is a constant $C$, independent of $f$, with \[  \sup _{\Delta '	imes \Delta }|q|+\sup _{\Delta '	imes \Delta }|R|\le C\sup _{\Delta '	imes \Delta }|f|.  \] Proof. Polydiscs as in the statement exist with arbitrarily small radii, because the roots of $P(z',\cdot )$ tend to $0$ as $z'	o 0$, by ( 9.2.1 ). Let $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ be such a polydisc and $f$ a holomorphic function on it. For $ho <s<r$ and $|w|<s$ define $q$ and $R$ by ( 9.2.3 ). For fixed $z'$ and $w$, both integrands are holomorphic in $\zeta $ on the annulus $\{ ho <|\zeta |<r\} $, except for the pole of the first one at $\zeta =w$; by Cauchy's theorem the integrals do not depend on $s$ as long as $|w|<s$, and the second one does not depend on $s\in (ho ,r)$ at all. Hence $q$ and $R$ are defined on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $, and they are holomorphic by differentiation under the integral sign. The difference quotient $(P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w))/(\zeta -w)$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree $m-1$ whose coefficients are polynomials in $\zeta $ and in the $a_ j(z')$; hence $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$ with holomorphic coefficients on $\Delta '$. Adding the two integrals, we obtain $Pq+R=(2\pi \mathrm i)^{-1}\int _{|\zeta |=s}f(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)^{-1}\, \mathrm d\zeta =f$ by Cauchy's formula. For the estimate, let $f$ be bounded, and fix $s_0=(ho +r)/2$. For $|\zeta |\geq s_0$ we have $|P(z',\zeta )|=\prod _ l|\zeta -\lambda _ l(z')|\geq (s_0-ho )^ m$, where $\lambda _ l(z')$ are the roots, and the coefficients of the difference quotient are bounded for $z'\in \Delta '$, $|\zeta |=s_0$ and $|w|<r$, since the $a_ j$ are bounded on $\Delta '$. The integral over $|\zeta |=s_0$ therefore gives $|R|\leq C_1\sup |f|$ on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $. For $s_0\leq |w|<r$ we have $|q|=|f-R|/|P|\leq (1+C_1)(s_0-ho )^{-m}\sup |f|$, and the maximum principle for the holomorphic functions $q(z',\cdot )$ on the discs $\{ |w|\leq s\} $, $s_0\leq s<r$, extends this bound to all of $\Delta '	imes \Delta $. For uniqueness, suppose that $Pq+R=0$ on a polydisc as above, with $R$ a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$. For each $z'$, the polynomial $R(z',\cdot )=-P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes at the $m$ roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, counted with multiplicity, all of which lie in $\Delta $. Its degree is less than $m$, so $R(z',\cdot )=0$. Then $P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )=0$, and since $P(z',\cdot )$ has only finitely many zeros, the continuous function $q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes on a dense set, hence everywhere. Finally, every germ is represented by a bounded holomorphic function on some polydisc as above, and an identity between germs holds on some such polydisc; so the assertions for germs follow. $\square$ The first consequence of division is the Noetherian property of $\mathcal O_ n$. Proposition 9.2.4 . 4B4DFDFC5DBA Every ideal of $\mathcal O_ n$ is finitely generated, and every submodule of $\mathcal O_ n^ r$, $r\geq 1$, is finitely generated. Consequently, every increasing sequence of ideals of $\mathcal O_ n$, or of submodules of a finitely generated $\mathcal O_ n$-module, is eventually constant. Proof. We first recall three algebraic facts about a commutative ring $\Lambda $ all of whose ideals are finitely generated. Every submodule $N$ of $\Lambda ^ r$ is finitely generated, by induction on $r$: the projection of $N$ to the last coordinate is an ideal; choose elements of $N$ whose last coordinates generate it, and add generators of $N\cap (\Lambda ^{r-1}	imes \{ 0\} )$, which exist by the induction hypothesis. A finitely generated module is a quotient of some $\Lambda ^ r$, and the inverse image of a submodule is a submodule of $\Lambda ^ r$; hence submodules of finitely generated modules are finitely generated. Finally, the union of an increasing sequence of submodules is a submodule; its finitely many generators already lie in one member of the sequence, which is therefore stationary from then on. It remains to prove that the ideals of $\mathcal O_ n$ are finitely generated, which we do by induction on $n$. The ring $\mathcal O_0=\mathbb C$ is a field. Let $n\geq 1$ and let $I\subset \mathcal O_ n$ be an ideal. If $I=0$ or $I$ contains a unit, it is generated by one element. Otherwise choose a nonzero germ in $I$, and coordinates in which it is distinguished in $w$. By the preparation theorem it is a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial $P$ of some degree $m\geq 1$, and $P\in I$. Divide every $f\in I$ by $P$ using proposition 9.2.2 ; the remainder $R_ f=f-Pq$ again belongs to $I$. The remainders of degree less than $m$ that lie in $I$ form an $\mathcal O_{n-1}$-submodule of $\mathcal O_{n-1}[w]$, which we identify, through their coefficients, with a submodule of $\mathcal O_{n-1}^ m$. By the induction hypothesis and the first paragraph, it is generated by finitely many remainders $R_1,\ldots ,R_ k$. Then $P,R_1,\ldots ,R_ k$ generate $I$. $\square$ Division also factors a monic polynomial near each of its roots. Lemma 9.2.5 . C47992939550 Let $n\geq 1$, let $P(z',w)=w^\mu +a_1(z')w^{\mu -1}+\cdots +a_\mu (z')$ be a monic polynomial in $w$ whose coefficients are holomorphic near a point $x'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and let $w_0$ be a root of multiplicity $\mu '\geq 1$ of $P(x',\cdot )$. Then, near $x=(x',w_0)$, \[  P=P_ xQ_ x,  \] where $P_ x$ is a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$ with respect to the coordinates $(z'-x',w-w_0)$, and $Q_ x$ is a monic polynomial of degree $\mu -\mu '$ in $w$ with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$ and $Q_ x(x)
eq 0$. Proof. In the coordinates $(z'-x',w-w_0)$ centered at $x$, the function $w\mapsto P(x',w)$ has a zero of order $\mu '$ at $w_0$. By the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 5.5.2 ), $P$ is, near $x$, a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function $U$ times a Weierstrass polynomial $P_ x$ of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$. Since $P_ x$ is monic in $w$, Euclidean division of the polynomial $P$ by $P_ x$, with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$, gives $P=P_ xQ+R$, where $Q$ is a monic polynomial of degree $\mu -\mu '$ in $w$ and $R$ is a polynomial in $w$, equivalently in $w-w_0$, of degree less than $\mu '$. The identities $P=P_ xQ+R$ and $P=P_ xU+0$ are two divisions of the germ of $P$ at $x$ by $P_ x$; by the uniqueness in proposition 9.2.2 , applied in the coordinates centered at $x$, we get $Q=U$ near $x$ and $R=0$. Hence $Q_ x=Q$ has the required properties, with $Q_ x(x)=U(x)
eq 0$. $\square$ We use sheaves in the following elementary form. A sheaf $\mathcal F$ of modules on a topological space assigns to each open set $U$ a module $\mathcal F(U)$ of sections, with restriction maps, such that sections that agree locally are equal and compatible local sections glue. The stalk $\mathcal F_ x$ consists of the germs at $x$ of sections defined near $x$. Kernels and images of morphisms of sheaves are defined stalkwise, and a sequence of morphisms is exact if it is exact on every stalk; in particular, a section of the image of a morphism is, near each point, the image of a section of the source. Similarly, the quotient $\mathcal S/\mathcal F$ of a sheaf of modules by a subsheaf has the stalks $\mathcal S_ x/\mathcal F_ x$, and its sections are the families of classes that are, near each point, the classes of a section of $\mathcal S$; so sections of $\mathcal S/\mathcal F$ can be lifted locally to sections of $\mathcal S$. The cokernel of a morphism is the quotient of its target by its image. Let $\mathcal A$ be a sheaf of rings and $\mathcal F$ a sheaf of $\mathcal A$-modules. We say that $\mathcal F$ is locally finitely generated if every point has a neighborhood $U$ and finitely many sections $s_1,\ldots ,s_ p\in \mathcal F(U)$ whose germs generate $\mathcal F_ y$ over $\mathcal A_ y$ for every $y\in U$. This requires one family of generators on a whole neighborhood, not merely finite generation of each stalk. The sheaf of relations of sections $s_1,\ldots ,s_ p\in \mathcal F(U)$ is the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal A^ p|_ U	o \mathcal F|_ U$, $(a_ i)\mapsto \sum _ ia_ is_ i$. The sheaf $\mathcal F$ is coherent if it is locally finitely generated and the sheaf of relations of every finite family of sections over every open set is locally finitely generated. Lemma 9.2.6 . 4AA3D030C896 Let $\mathcal A$ be a sheaf of rings. Kernels, images and cokernels of morphisms between coherent $\mathcal A$-modules are coherent. If two of the three sheaves in an exact sequence $0	o \mathcal F	o \mathcal S	o \mathcal G	o 0$ of $\mathcal A$-modules are coherent, so is the third. Finite direct sums of coherent sheaves are coherent. If $\mathcal A$ is coherent as a module over itself, every locally finitely generated $\mathcal A$-submodule of $\mathcal A^ r$ is coherent. Proof. A locally finitely generated submodule of a coherent sheaf is coherent, because its sections have the same relations when they are regarded as sections of the larger sheaf. The image of a morphism from a coherent sheaf is locally generated by the images of local generators of the source, so the image of a morphism between coherent sheaves is coherent. For the kernel of a morphism $\phi \colon \mathcal F	o \mathcal G$ between coherent sheaves, choose local generators $F_1,\ldots ,F_ p$ of $\mathcal F$ and local generators $R_ j=(R_{j1},\ldots ,R_{jp})$ of the relations of $\phi (F_1),\ldots ,\phi (F_ p)$. If $\sum _ ia_ iF_ i$ lies in the kernel, then $(a_ i)$ is a relation of the $\phi (F_ i)$, hence a combination of the $R_ j$; so the sections $\sum _ iR_{ji}F_ i$ generate the kernel, which is therefore coherent. Let $\mathcal F\subset \mathcal S$ be coherent sheaves and consider $\mathcal G=\mathcal S/\mathcal F$; this covers cokernels, because images are coherent. Local generators of $\mathcal S$ map to local generators of $\mathcal G$. Given sections $G_1,\ldots ,G_ p$ of $\mathcal G$, lift them locally to sections $S_1,\ldots ,S_ p$ of $\mathcal S$, and choose local generators $F_1,\ldots ,F_ k$ of $\mathcal F$. A tuple $(a_ i)$ is a relation of the $G_ i$ exactly when $\sum _ ia_ iS_ i\in \mathcal F$, that is, when $(a,b)$ is a relation of $(S_1,\ldots ,S_ p,F_1,\ldots ,F_ k)$ in $\mathcal S$ for some $b$. Hence the projections to the first $p$ coordinates of local generators of the latter relations generate the relations of the $G_ i$, and $\mathcal G$ is coherent. Now let $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal G$ be coherent. Local lifts of generators of $\mathcal G$, together with local generators of $\mathcal F$, generate $\mathcal S$. Given sections $S_1,\ldots ,S_ p$ of $\mathcal S$, let $R_1,\ldots ,R_ l$ generate the relations of their images in $\mathcal G$. The combinations $H_ j=\sum _ iR_{ji}S_ i$ lie in $\mathcal F$; let $Q_1,\ldots ,Q_ k$ generate their relations. Every relation $(a_ i)$ of the $S_ i$ is first a relation of their images, so $a=\sum _ jc_ jR_ j$, and then $\sum _ jc_ jH_ j=\sum _ ia_ iS_ i=0$, so $c$ is a combination of $Q_1,\ldots ,Q_ k$. Hence the tuples $\sum _ jQ_{
u j}R_ j$, $1\leq 
u \leq k$, which are relations of the $S_ i$, generate all of them, and $\mathcal S$ is coherent. The remaining case of the exact sequence, with $\mathcal S$ and $\mathcal G$ coherent, is the kernel case. A finite direct sum is an extension $0	o \mathcal F	o \mathcal F\oplus \mathcal G	o \mathcal G	o 0$. Finally, if $\mathcal A$ is coherent, so is $\mathcal A^ r$, and the last assertion follows from the first sentence of the proof. $\square$ Theorem 9.2.7 (Oka's coherence theorem) . F28642698B29 The sheaf $\mathcal O_ M$ of holomorphic functions on a complex manifold $M$ is coherent. In particular, the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal O_ U^ q	o \mathcal O_ U^ p$ defined by a $p	imes q$ matrix of holomorphic functions on an open set $U\subset M$ is locally finitely generated. Proof. The sheaf $\mathcal O_ M$ is generated by the constant $1$, and the statement is local, so we must show that the relations of finitely many holomorphic functions $F_1,\ldots ,F_ q$ near a point of $\mathbb C^ n$, which we take to be the origin, are locally finitely generated. We argue by induction on $n$: we reduce to relations that are polynomials in one variable of bounded degree, and apply the induction hypothesis to their coefficients. For $n=0$ the assertion is finite-dimensional linear algebra. Let $n\geq 1$. If the germ of some $F_ j$ at $0$ is zero, then $F_ j$ vanishes on a connected neighborhood, and the relations of the $F_ i$ are those of the remaining functions, with an arbitrary $j$th coordinate; so we may assume that no germ $F_ j$ is zero (if all are zero, every tuple is a relation). Choose coordinates $(z',w)$ in which all $F_ j$ are distinguished in $w$. By the preparation theorem, on a small polydisc each $F_ j$ is a holomorphic unit $u_ j$ times a Weierstrass polynomial; since $(g_ j)$ is a relation of the $F_ j$ exactly when $(u_ jg_ j)$ is a relation of the Weierstrass polynomials, we may assume that each $F_ j$ is a Weierstrass polynomial in $w$ whose coefficients are holomorphic on a polydisc $\Delta '\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$. Renumbering, let $F_ q$ have the maximal degree $\mu $. We claim that at every point $x=(x',w_0)$ of the polydisc, the stalk of relations is generated by relations whose coordinates are polynomials in $w$ of degree at most $\mu $ with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$. If $F_ q(x)
eq 0$, then for a relation $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ q)$ we have $g_ q=-\sum _{j<q}g_ jF_ j/F_ q$, so $g=\sum _{j<q}(g_ j/F_ q)(F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q)$ is a combination of the elementary relations $F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q$, which are polynomial of degree at most $\mu $. Suppose that $F_ q(x)=0$, and let $\mu '\geq 1$ be the order of the root $w_0$ of $F_ q(x',\cdot )$. By lemma 9.2.5 , near $x$ the monic polynomial $F_ q$ is the product of a Weierstrass polynomial $P_ x$ of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$ and a monic polynomial $Q_ x$ in $w$ of degree $\mu -\mu '$: \[  F_ q=P_ xQ_ x,\qquad Q_ x(x)
eq 0.  \] Let $g$ be a relation at $x$. Dividing each $g_ j$, $j<q$, by $P_ x$ (proposition 9.2.2 ) and writing $P_ x=F_ qQ_ x^{-1}$, we obtain $g_ j=F_ qt_ j+r_ j$ with $\deg _ wr_ j<\mu '$. Subtracting $\sum _{j<q}t_ j(F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q)$ from $g$, we obtain a relation whose first $q-1$ coordinates are $r_1,\ldots ,r_{q-1}$; we call its last coordinate $r_ q$. Then \[  P_ xQ_ xr_ q=-\sum _{j<q}F_ jr_ j.  \] The right-hand side is a polynomial in $w$; dividing it by $P_ x$ as a polynomial and comparing with the uniqueness of division at $x$, we find that $Q_ xr_ q$ is a polynomial of degree less than $\mu $. Each $Q_ xr_ j$, $j<q$, is also a polynomial of degree at most $(\mu -\mu ')+(\mu '-1)<\mu $. Thus $(Q_ xr_1,\ldots ,Q_ xr_ q)$ is a polynomial relation of degree less than $\mu $, and $(r_ j)$ is its product with the unit $Q_ x^{-1}$. This proves the claim. A tuple of polynomials $g_ j=\sum _{k=0}^{\mu }c_{jk}(z')w^ k$ is a relation exactly when the $2\mu +1$ coefficients of the polynomial $\sum _ jF_ jg_ j$ vanish. These coefficients are given by a holomorphic matrix acting on the coefficient vectors $(c_{jk})$, with entries formed from the coefficients of the $F_ j$. By the induction hypothesis and lemma 9.2.6 , the kernel of this matrix is coherent, so it has finitely many generators on a smaller polydisc $\Delta '_1$, generating its stalk at every point of $\Delta '_1$. The corresponding polynomial tuples are relations of the $F_ j$, and they generate, over the rings of germs on the base, all polynomial relations of degree at most $\mu $ at every point over $\Delta '_1$. By the claim, they generate all relations at every point of the polydisc over $\Delta '_1$. This proves that $\mathcal O_ M$ is coherent. The last assertion follows from lemma 9.2.6 , since the kernel of a morphism between the coherent sheaves $\mathcal O_ U^ q$ and $\mathcal O_ U^ p$ is coherent. $\square$ We now turn to the zero sets of holomorphic functions. An analytic subset of a complex manifold $M$ (definition 5.2.3 ) is a closed subset $A\subset M$ such that every point of $M$ has a neighborhood $U$ and finitely many holomorphic functions $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ on $U$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $. It is proper if $A
eq M$. Lemma 9.2.8 . 4D71178D595A Let $A$ be a proper analytic subset of a connected complex manifold $M$. Then $A$ is nowhere dense in $M$. Moreover, if $U\subset M$ is a nonempty connected open set and $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ are holomorphic functions on $U$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $, then some $g_ i$ is not identically zero on $U$. In particular, every point of $A$ has a connected open neighborhood $U$ with a holomorphic function $g
ot\equiv 0$ on $U$ such that $A\cap U\subset \{ g=0\} $. Proof. The interior of $A$ is open, and we show that it is closed in $M$. Let $a\in M$ be a limit of interior points of $A$, and choose a connected coordinate neighborhood $U$ of $a$ and functions $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $. Each $g_ i$ vanishes on a nonempty open subset of $U$, hence on $U$ by the identity theorem; so $U\subset A$, and $a$ is an interior point. Since $M$ is connected and $A
eq M$, the interior of $A$ is empty. In the second assertion, if all $g_ i$ vanished identically on $U$, the nonempty open set $U$ would lie in $A$, contradicting the first. For the third, take for $U$ a connected coordinate ball on which $A$ is the common zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions, and for $g$ one of them that is not identically zero, which exists by the second assertion. $\square$ We recall some algebraic terminology. The field of fractions $\operatorname {Frac}(R)$ of an integral domain $R$ consists of the formal quotients $b/c$ with $b,c\in R$ and $c
eq 0$, where $b/c=b'/c'$ if $bc'=b'c$, with the usual addition and multiplication; it contains $R$ through $b\mapsto b/1$. More generally, the total ring of fractions of a commutative ring $R$ is defined in the same way, with denominators restricted to the nonzerodivisors of $R$. An element of a commutative ring containing $R$ is integral over $R$ if it is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $R$, and $R$ is integrally closed if every element of $\operatorname {Frac}(R)$ that is integral over $R$ belongs to $R$. Lemma 9.2.9 . AA4164301998 Let $A$ be a proper analytic subset of a connected complex manifold $M$. Every holomorphic function on $M\setminus A$ which is locally bounded near $A$ extends uniquely to a holomorphic function on $M$, and $M\setminus A$ is connected. Moreover, let $b,c\in \mathcal O_ n$ with $c
eq 0$, and suppose that representatives satisfy $|b|\leq C|c|$ on a neighborhood of $0$ for a constant $C$. Then $b\in c\, \mathcal O_ n$. In particular, the ring $\mathcal O_ n$ is integrally closed. Proof. Let $f$ be holomorphic on $M\setminus A$ and locally bounded near $A$. If $\dim M=0$, then $A=\varnothing $ and there is nothing to prove. Fix $a\in A$. By lemma 9.2.8 there is a holomorphic function $g
ot\equiv 0$ on a connected neighborhood of $a$ vanishing on $A$; choose linear coordinates $(z',w)$ centered at $a$ in which $g$ is distinguished in $w$. By the Weierstrass preparation theorem and ( 9.2.1 ), there is a polydisc $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ centered at $a$, with $\Delta =\{ |w|<r\} $, on which $g$ is a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial $W$ and $f$ is bounded off $A$, such that all roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in \Delta '$, have modulus at most some $ho <r$. For fixed $z'\in \Delta '$, the function $f(z',\cdot )$ is holomorphic on $\Delta $ outside the finitely many points of $A$ in the fiber, which are roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, and it is bounded near them; by the removable singularity theorem in one variable it extends holomorphically to $\Delta $. For $ho <s<r$ the function \[  F(z',w)= rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s} rac{f(z',\zeta )}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\qquad z'\in \Delta ',\  |w|<s,  \] is holomorphic, by differentiation under the integral sign, since $f$ is holomorphic near $\Delta '	imes \{ |\zeta |=s\} $, a set disjoint from $A$. By Cauchy's formula for the extended functions $f(z',\cdot )$, it agrees with $f$ outside $A$. Letting $s\uparrow r$, we obtain a holomorphic extension of $f$ to $\Delta '	imes \Delta $. Since $A$ is nowhere dense, two holomorphic extensions on overlapping open sets agree, being continuous functions that coincide on a dense subset; so the local extensions glue to a holomorphic function on $M$, and this extension is unique. If $M\setminus A$ were disconnected, the function equal to $0$ on one nonempty union of its connected components and to $1$ on the others would be bounded and holomorphic on $M\setminus A$. Its holomorphic extension is continuous and takes values in $\{ 0,1\} $ on the dense set $M\setminus A$, hence everywhere; since $M$ is connected, it is constant, a contradiction. Now let $b,c\in \mathcal O_ n$, $c
eq 0$, with $|b|\leq C|c|$ on a connected neighborhood $U$ of the origin on which both are defined. The set $\{ c=0\} $ is a proper analytic subset of $U$, and the holomorphic function $b/c$ on $U\setminus \{ c=0\} $ is bounded by $C$. By the first part it extends to a holomorphic function $h$ on $U$, and $ch=b$ on the dense set $U\setminus \{ c=0\} $, hence on $U$; so $b\in c\, \mathcal O_ n$. eq 0$, satisfy a monic equation $(b/c)^ m+a_1(b/c)^{m-1}+\cdots +a_ m=0$ with $a_ j\in \mathcal O_ n$. Multiplying by $c^ m$, we obtain the identity $b^ m+a_1b^{m-1}c+\cdots +a_ mc^ m=0$ between germs, which holds on a connected neighborhood of $0$ on which the $a_ j$ are bounded. At the points of this neighborhood where $c

title: Proposition 9.2.2 (Weierstrass division)
text: Proposition 9.2.2 (Weierstrass division) . 611958EF0AB8 Let $n\geq 1$ and $m\geq 0$, and let $P$ be a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $m$ in $w$. Then every germ $f\in \mathcal O_ n$ can be written uniquely as \[  f=Pq+R,\qquad q\in \mathcal O_ n,\quad R\in \mathcal O_{n-1}[w],\quad \deg _ w R<m.  \] Moreover, let $\Delta '\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$ be a polydisc centered at $0$ and $\Delta =\{ |w|<r\} $ a disc such that the coefficients of $P$ are holomorphic near $\overline{\Delta '}$ and all roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in \Delta '$, lie in $\{ |w|\leq \rho \} $ for some $\rho <r$; such polydiscs $\Delta '\times \Delta $ exist with arbitrarily small radii. Then every holomorphic function $f$ on $\Delta '\times \Delta $ can be written uniquely as $f=Pq+R$, where $q$ is holomorphic on $\Delta '\times \Delta $ and $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$ with holomorphic coefficients on $\Delta '$; for every $s\in (\rho ,r)$, $z'\in \Delta '$ and $|w|<s$, A61080C94D0B 9.2.3 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  q(z',w)& =\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s} \frac{f(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\\  R(z',w)& =\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s} \frac{f(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )}\,  \frac{P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w)}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta . \end{aligned} \end{equation} Division is a bounded linear operation on bounded holomorphic functions on $\Delta '\times \Delta $: there is a constant $C$, independent of $f$, with \[  \sup _{\Delta '\times \Delta }|q|+\sup _{\Delta '\times \Delta }|R|\le C\sup _{\Delta '\times \Delta }|f|.  \] Proof. Polydiscs as in the statement exist with arbitrarily small radii, because the roots of $P(z',\cdot )$ tend to $0$ as $z'\to 0$, by ( 9.2.1 ). Let $\Delta '\times \Delta $ be such a polydisc and $f$ a holomorphic function on it. For $\rho <s<r$ and $|w|<s$ define $q$ and $R$ by ( 9.2.3 ). For fixed $z'$ and $w$, both integrands are holomorphic in $\zeta $ on the annulus $\{ \rho <|\zeta |<r\} $, except for the pole of the first one at $\zeta =w$; by Cauchy's theorem the integrals do not depend on $s$ as long as $|w|<s$, and the second one does not depend on $s\in (\rho ,r)$ at all. Hence $q$ and $R$ are defined on $\Delta '\times \Delta $, and they are holomorphic by differentiation under the integral sign. The difference quotient $(P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w))/(\zeta -w)$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree $m-1$ whose coefficients are polynomials in $\zeta $ and in the $a_ j(z')$; hence $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$ with holomorphic coefficients on $\Delta '$. Adding the two integrals, we obtain $Pq+R=(2\pi \mathrm i)^{-1}\int _{|\zeta |=s}f(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)^{-1}\, \mathrm d\zeta =f$ by Cauchy's formula. For the estimate, let $f$ be bounded, and fix $s_0=(\rho +r)/2$. For $|\zeta |\geq s_0$ we have $|P(z',\zeta )|=\prod _ l|\zeta -\lambda _ l(z')|\geq (s_0-\rho )^ m$, where $\lambda _ l(z')$ are the roots, and the coefficients of the difference quotient are bounded for $z'\in \Delta '$, $|\zeta |=s_0$ and $|w|<r$, since the $a_ j$ are bounded on $\Delta '$. The integral over $|\zeta |=s_0$ therefore gives $|R|\leq C_1\sup |f|$ on $\Delta '\times \Delta $. For $s_0\leq |w|<r$ we have $|q|=|f-R|/|P|\leq (1+C_1)(s_0-\rho )^{-m}\sup |f|$, and the maximum principle for the holomorphic functions $q(z',\cdot )$ on the discs $\{ |w|\leq s\} $, $s_0\leq s<r$, extends this bound to all of $\Delta '\times \Delta $. For uniqueness, suppose that $Pq+R=0$ on a polydisc as above, with $R$ a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$. For each $z'$, the polynomial $R(z',\cdot )=-P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes at the $m$ roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, counted with multiplicity, all of which lie in $\Delta $. Its degree is less than $m$, so $R(z',\cdot )=0$. Then $P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )=0$, and since $P(z',\cdot )$ has only finitely many zeros, the continuous function $q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes on a dense set, hence everywhere. Finally, every germ is represented by a bounded holomorphic function on some polydisc as above, and an identity between germs holds on some such polydisc; so the assertions for germs follow. $\square$
